THE COLLECTED LETTERS OF
THOMAS AND JANE WELSH CARLYLE

div1.p: The editors are very grateful to the National Endowment for the Humanities, which has generously awarded the project a three-year grant (2018–21) under the auspices of its Scholarly Editions program, and to the Research Libraries Program of the Gladys Krieble Delmas Foundation, which has provided invaluable grant support for the Carlyle Letters Online. We are also grateful to the Binks Trust for its continuing financial contributions to the funding of the Edinburgh editorial team and office. The editors again express their gratitude to the British Academy, which made the Carlyle Letters a British Academy Research Project and continues to support us with an annual grant, and to the members of its Committee on Academy Research Projects and its assistant secretary, Ken Emond. The editors also express their gratitude to those private individuals who have made donations for the support of the Edinburgh Carlyle Letters office, to the University of Edinburgh Development Trust, to Joyce Caplan and the Friends of Edinburgh University Library, and to Maureen Reilly, nee Gilhooly.

We remain extremely grateful for the advice of Paolo Mangiafico, Scholarly Communications Strategist and Co-Director, ScholarWorks Center for Scholarly Publishing, Duke University Library; and we continue to extend our appreciation for early critiques of the electronic edition to the late David Chesnutt, formerly of the Model Editions Partnership at the University of South Carolina, and to Natalia Smith of the DocSouth project at the University of North Carolina. Brent E. Kinser serves as coordinating editor of The Carlyle Letters Online in addition to his editorial service to the print edition. DNC Data Systems of Mumbai, India, has electronically encoded volumes 1 through 47 of the Carlyle Letters. Colin Wilder and staff at University of South Carolina host the online edition at the Center for Digital Humanities.

We recognize a continued indebtedness and gratitude for help and permissions to the following institutions and their staffs: Rita Patteson, Melinda Creech, Melvin Schuetz and Jennifer Borderund of the Armstrong Browning Library, Baylor University; Bodleian Libraries, Oxford University; the British Library and its Special Collections; the National Trust and Lin and Geff Skippings, former curators of Carlyle's House, Chelsea, and Linda Chinnery; National Trust for Scotland and Carlyle's Birthplace, Ecclefechan; Sean M. Quimby, director, Tara C. Craig, Emily Holmes, Meredith A. Self, and Jane R. Siegel, Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Columbia University in the City of New York, for their help with reproductions from the Thomas Carlyle
Photograph Albums; Duke University Library and librarians Andrew Armacost, Sara Seten Berghausen, Molly Bragg, Elizabeth Dunn, Andrea Loigman, and Naomi Nelson; Jeremy Upton, director of library services, Edinburgh University Library, Joseph Marshall, director of the Centre for Research Collections, and Edinburgh University Library Special Collections; Richard Kuhta of the Folger Shakespeare Library, Washington, D.C.; Alex Jordan, lecturer in the Department for English Literature and Cultural Studies at Göttingen University; the Houghton Library, Harvard University, and librarians Leslie Morris and Karen Nipps; Sara S. Hodson, curator of literary manuscripts, and Gayle Richardson at the Huntington Library, California; Margaret Burri and John Buchtel, Special Collections Department, Eisenhower Library, Johns Hopkins University; Library of Congress manuscripts division and librarian Bruce Kirby; Marilyn Palmeri and the Morgan Library and Museum; the trustees and the librarian and chief executive, John Scally, of the National Library of Scotland, the Department of Manuscripts, and the Issue Desk; Elizabeth
Denlinger, Carl H. Pforzheimer Collection, New York Public Library; University of Pittsburgh Library and curator Jeanann Croft Haas; Sir Roland Jackson, Frank A. J. L. James, and the Royal Institution, London; Christine Bunting, head of Special Collections and Archives, University Library, University of California, Santa Cruz, and Luisa Haddad; the Frederick W. Hilles Manuscript Collection, General Collection, Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, and librarian Karen Nangle.

We wish to thank Steve Cohn, former director of Duke University Press who retired on 30 June 2019, a tireless supporter of this project throughout his tenure, and the present director Dean Smith, who has given his immediate support to this long-standing DUP commitment that began with the publication of the first four volumes in 1970; and, also of the Press, Allison Belan, Jocelyn Dawson, Rob Dilworth, Cynthia Gurganus, Stacy Lavin, and Cason Lynley; the dean of arts and sciences, the provost, and the vice provost of Duke University; Dorothy Miell, head of the College of Humanities and Social Science, Jeremy Robbins, head of the School of Literatures, Languages, and Cultures, Alex Thomson, head of English Literature, Greg Walker, English Literature, Janet Black, and Julie Robertson of the School, Fiona Carmichael, and Neil Young, of LLC Computing Service, all of Edinburgh University; Neil Burns and the Edinburgh University Development Trust; Nathaniel Banfich, Anthony Burns, Kathy Chamberlain, Todd Endelman, Mark Engel, Bryan Homer, Travis Mullen, Terence Muzzell, Harrold Nuttall, Tom Raworth, Hilary Smith, Chris Stray, Greer Thomas, James Turner, Chris Vanden Bossche, and Joe Viscomi. We remain very grateful to many members of the Carlyle family. Clare Cain continues to provide valuable research support at the Edinburgh office. We owe special thanks to Stacy Lavin, managing editor of the Carlyle Letters office at Duke University Press. Finally, we
honor the memories of Aileen Christianson, researcher and co-editor of the Carlyle Letters from 1967 to 2020, and David Southern, managing editor of the Carlyle Letters office at Duke University Press from 1998 to 2021. Their contribution, knowledge, and experience over the preceding decades have informed our continuing work.

The letters in this volume cover December 1875 through February 1881, including 80 letters dictated by Thomas Carlyle, 11 letters written by Mary Aitken or Alick Carlyle at TC's request, 12 letters written by Mary Aitken to friends and family members that give useful information about TC's health and activities, and a final letter from Alick Carlyle giving details of TC's death and funeral. TC's shaky hand had by now become so bad that he had entirely given up writing anything, and toward the end he even gave up signing his letters.

Two constants run through this final volume of the Duke-Edinburgh edition of the Carlyle Letters. One is the friendship between Thomas and his brother John, which lasts almost to the end of this volume and Thomas's own death. The letters between them run right through to John's long final illness and the summer of 1879 when Thomas and Mary lodged nearby in Dumfries almost to the end of John's life, though Thomas had left for Chelsea before his brother passed away. The other constant is Mary Aitken, niece to Thomas and soon to be a closer family member still after her marriage to her cousin Alexander, when in 1879 he arrived from Canada and settled in the Chelsea ménage as part of the close and loving team who sheltered Thomas's last years. The devotion and patience of Mary, “unwearied in her attention” (TC to JAC, 14 Dec. 1878), can hardly be imagined when one contemplates the volume of dictated correspondence she produced for Thomas, letters not only to family and friends but also the multitude of business and literary affairs that were a daily feature of life in Chelsea. “If I had any fingers of my own I wd write to [sic] oftener than I do” (TC to JAC, 5 May 1878). Though occasionally Mary confessed to exhaustion or ill health, she was indefatigable, as John Carlyle wrote to Meta Wellmer, Mary's German friend and an admirer of TC: “Mary is a very dextrous amanuensis, & ready at all times” (JAC to Meta Wellmer, 12 Feb 1877; MS: NLS Acc. 9207).

This volume may depict the physical weakness that was overtaking Thomas Carlyle in these last months of his life, but the letters simultaneously reflect his continuing mental energy, his interest in the enormous circle of his acquaintances and correspondents, and the literature he devoured in these last years, when reading largely replaced the physical exercise that had been such a feature of his mature existence. He remained acutely interested in continental Europe, and in the Eastern Crisis, which he followed in the newspapers; for, in David Sorensen's words, despite the death of so many contemporaries, he was “not quite ready to retire submissively into the ‘evening’” (CL 45:xv). The
letters paint a broad picture, including the less attractive features of Carlyle's thinking on colonization and other countries, as Katherine Inglis points out in CL 47:xviii. With so many letters surviving, we have a wide range of opinion to draw on, and we can only imagine the torrent of monologue with which he enthralled many visitors to Chelsea, who on returning home could only commit their outlines to paper before their recollection faded.

Carlyle certainly lived in his mind far beyond the confines of an increasingly sedentary Chelsea existence. Although he asked Charles Eliot Norton, “what is there for me now in Scotland but a field of the dead?” (TC to CEN, 2 Dec. 1875),
he displayed mental firmness in keeping up with American correspondents, his interest in an increasingly frail Emerson “suffering from an attack of old age, which made itself felt in loss of memory, especially of names” (CEN to TC, 29 Jan. 1876), and his interest in his brother Alick in Canada, from whom he had been parted for many years—“there are few days in which you are not vividly present to my thoughts” (TC to AC, 15 Feb. 1876). However, “I many a time wonder that I have any friends left, who can be taken away from me & added to the great multitude already gone” (TC to JAC, 27 April 1878).

The letters show an omnivorous interest in politics both in the United Kingdom and overseas, as well as trenchant criticism of a political class for which he had little respect—though he did backtrack from decades of dismissive criticism of Disraeli when the latter unexpectedly proposed to honor a distinguished British literary figure, who not ungraciously declined the public honor (CL 49:175–78), as he had declined the doctorate from Edinburgh University (CL 43:138–39) on the occasion (1866) of his rectorial address. Public admiration was not to be denied even by his reticence; an 80th birthday medal with over a hundred signatories was organized by David Masson, and many congratulatory letters and telegrams arrived, including letters from Charles Alexander, Duke of Weimar, and Otto von Bismarck, with “cordial congratulations [and] the assurance of my sincere respect” (Bismarck to TC, 2 Dec. 1875). He also accepted honors from the Royal Irish Academy and the Antiquarian Society of Pennsylvania, but in his correspondence his prevailing mood was to downplay the celebrity of these closing years.

Newspapers and gifts of new publications (from Ruskin, for instance) were keenly scanned, and often passed on to family members in Scotland. To John, for instance, he complains of “multitudes of useless books & there are very few of them which seem worthy of being sent to you” (TC to JAC, 29 Sept. 1877). “I have, however no really interesting reading & have sometimes thought even of going into the Bible the significance of which is deep & wonderful almost as much as it ever used to be to me” (TC to JAC, 2 Nov 1878). Contemporary writers seemed to hold less interest for Carlyle—who, in these last years, was reading Ruskin, Plutarch, Suetonius, and Swift—while he was hurt by the loss of those contemporary writers and scholars he did admire, including David
Laing, who had disagreed with him (a most unusual thing) over the portraits of Knox but had now passed away: “A considerable light of knowledge is thus extinguished & a very harmless brother mortal is carried away into eternity before us” (TC to JAC, 26 Oct. 1878). Froude, one of his most constant companions, was “ready to talk at great length, though about nothing that I had much interest in.…I get extremely little good of any kind of company now left me in the world” (TC to JAC, 26 Oct. 1878). The loss of John Forster was a serious blow, for in addition to a close friendship, the relationship had been the means of much of Carlyle's business with publishers being taken over and conducted professionally and smartly on his behalf. Forster's death on 1 February 1876 was “the end of a chapter in my life” (TC to JAC, 5 Feb. 1876).

In these last years Carlyle became very conscious of his physical enfeeblement, though Mary “is unwearied in her attention; rose last night for example as she ever does on my summons” (TC to JAC, 14 Dec. 1878). His mind he felt, even in his last years, still to be his own: “I am grateful to heaven for one thing that the state of my head continues unaltered and perfectly clear, surely a blessing beyond expression compared with what the contrary would be” (TC to JAC, 2 Nov. 1878). One of the changes to London Carlyle thoroughly approved was the new Embankment, which had altered beyond recognition the foot of Cheyne Row and the banks of the river. It allowed him the main part of his daily exercise, “my poor cripply walk half way down the embankment. I am not now able to get to the bottom of the embankment but have to stop half way and rest a little and return” (TC to JAC, 15 Nov. 1878). With Mary or some other companion—William Allingham was a frequent walker with him, and to this we owe his copious recollections of the elderly Carlyle's conversation—Carlyle would use the omnibus to extend the range of his exercise. “On the Sundays we omit carriage driving & go usually in the Chelsea omnibus to St Paul's Cathedral which is a beautiful serene place in itself and sometimes affords us in the Anthem and doxology a peal of exquisite music from the organ and vox humana” (TC to JAC, 25 Jan. 1879). Carlyle's appreciation of Anglican music was an unexpected change of taste in his later years. He also had to submit to repeated sittings for portraits, and although he found the experience boring, he warmed to some of the artists, such as Helen Allingham (see TC to JAC, 9 Nov. 1878), and Robert Herdman (see CL 49:213–15TC to JAC, 24 April 1875), for instance; and from the experience he saw something of the art of painting and of statuary. He commented on the Millais portrait: “The picture I think does not please Mary, nor in fact myself altogether; but it is surely strikingly like in every feature & the fundamental condition was that Millais should paint what he himself was able to see there” (TC to JAC, 16 June 1877).

As he grew yet older, Carlyle's correspondence does reveal an encroaching feebleness. He told brother John that “with me the two hours of driving are as it were the work of the day” (TC to JAC, 1 March 1879). The arrival of
Alexander Carlyle from Canada in July 1879 must have given Mary some relief, though Mary's account to Janet Hanning of 1880 indicates just how far weakness had overtaken her uncle:

He generally spends his mornings till about half past two o’clock between lying on the sofa, reading in his easy chair, and smoking an occasional pipe; at half past two he goes out to drive for two or two and a half hours, sleeps on the sofa until dinner time (half past six) then after dinner sleeps again, at nine has tea, reads or smokes or talks, or lies on the sofa till bed time, which is usually about midnight. (MAI to JCHA, 18 July 1880)
To the same correspondent she later gave a low-key but vivid account of the very last days:
div1.q:
Last July, as I think I told you, Uncle had a short though rather bad turn of illness evidently brought on by the heat; he seemed to a great extent
to recover from it, but he never got up any considerable strength after it; he seemed to grow a little weaker month by month and week by week. He was out on New Year's Day for the last time, a short drive of an hour or so; he complained of the fatigue very much after he came back. He was confined to his bed exactly three weeks all but a day. Until the last few days he was, though now and then delirious, for the most part quiet and collected, and able to talk to us.…In the last few days his mind seemed to turn altogether to the old Ecclefechan days; he often took Alick for his Father (Uncle Sandy) and he would put his arms round my neck and say to me, “My dear Mother.” (MAI to JCHA, 3 March 1881; pbd: Copeland 259–60)
div1.p: Mary spent many hours sitting with the old man; the last book he read, she noted, was the library edition of The Works of Robert Burns (MAI to WSD, 6 Oct. 1877).

The news of TC's death filled the press. Westminster Abbey was offered by Dean Stanley, who visited Mary and Alexander Carlyle in Chelsea, but was declined in favor of Ecclefechan, where Thomas Carlyle had decided to join his parents in the parish kirkyard. The funeral was a family affair, attended by Alexander and Mary and Carlyle's brother James, with few others.For more, see “After the Funeral,” Carlyle Society Occasional Papers 32 (Edinburgh 2019): 33–48, an account partly based on Carlyle family papers in private hands. The controversy spurred by Froude's hasty publication of his edition of the Reminiscences and subsequently the Letters and Memorials, with all their editorial imperfections, lay ahead. But the extraordinary run of correspondence that Thomas and Jane had produced, and which Thomas had done so much to preserve, was over.

The beginnings of the Duke-Edinburgh edition owe everything to Charles Richard Sanders, who, with John Butt in Edinburgh, laid the foundation of the gathering of copy for the edition—manuscript when possible and reproduction when not. The search was enormous and continues to this day, for new Carlyle letters, both Jane's and Thomas's, continue to surface; and after the Duke-Edinburgh edition is finished with this volume, they will find their way onto the internet (Carlyle Letters Online), where the edited matter of the main edition is already secure. Sanders listed early editions and collections in the first volume of the edition (CL 1:xix–xxii), and Sanders also produced a “A Brief History of the Duke-Edinburgh Edition of the Carlyle Letters” in Studies in Scottish Literature 17 (1982): 1–12. “Without him [Sanders] the Collected Letters of Thomas and Jane Welsh Carlyle would not have begun and would not have proceeded to volumes 10–12” (CL 10:viii). Alongside and after him in the United States came Clyde Ryals, John Clubbe, Hilary Smith, and the late David Southern, whose death came just before he could complete the years of editorial service he gave at Duke University Press. At Duke Press, too, the edition would not have come to fruition without the constant encouragement and support of Steve Cohn. We are also grateful to his successor, Rob Dilworth, for ably managing the finances of the project in the midst of a pandemic. There is a tribute to both Sanders and Ryals in CL 27:ix and to K. J. Fielding in CL 33:xiii.

The appointment of K. J. Fielding to the Saintsbury chair in Edinburgh was to give the impetus to the United Kingdom end of the editorial term that sustained it through decades, since he brought to it not only a lifetime's Victorian scholarship but also energy and determination to meet the deadlines that an edition of this kind inevitably present, year after year. Alongside him, Aileen Christianson worked tirelessly to meet those same deadlines, often losing vacation after vacation, and her death so near the end of the great project is a hard one. Others have been invaluable: Sheila McIntosh, and quietly over the last decades Jane Roberts and Liz Sutherland, who have moved the edition steadily forward, volume by volume, even in the COVID-19 difficulties of recent years. Their persistent energy is what has kept the Edinburgh office functioning, while in the United States the tireless efforts of David Sorensen and Brent Kinser, juggling teaching with editorial work, can hardly be overestimated. David Sorensen's successes in fundraising took enormous energy and were crucial to keeping the project afloat, and Brent Kinser's expertise has been the main impulse behind the establishment of the Carlyle Letters Online, already an indispensable tool in Victorian research. One important factor is the possibility of restoring imperfect texts; the proportion of letters published for the first time has throughout been a strong feature of the edition. More than half in this volume appear for the first time, and many others have only appeared before in imperfect form (see CL 22:ix22:introduction).

The acknowledgments pages of each volume hardly do justice to the generosity of public bodies, trusts, and individuals who have helped the project, though it would be wrong not to acknowledge the British Academy, which has made the Carlyle Letters one of its research projects for years, and the Binks Trust, which by its extraordinary generosity has helped make the Scottish end of the edition possible. In the United States, the National Endowment of the Humanities has generously funded the project since 1997, and the editors are especially grateful to Margot Backus, Ann R. Meyer, and Lydia Medici for their expert advice, support and encouragement. We are also grateful to the Gladys Krieble Delmas Foundation for funding the technical initiatives in the Carlyle Letters Online that have enabled us to digitize an extensive collection of Carlyle Photograph Albums loaned to the project by Columbia University Library. We have also benefited from the generosity of individuals, and most of all from Aileen Christianson's own substantial financial contributions over several years. While she was alive she did not want this to be known, but now we can acknowledge her gift and thank her openly.

A special word of thanks to the members of the Carlyle family who over the decades have encouraged and supported the project and generously provided access to family papers that have been literally indispensable. An outstanding example is Jane Welsh Carlyle's “Much Ado about Nothing” in CL 24:159–71. The warm support and long friendship of the family members has been one of the greatest pleasures of the enterprise.

With each volume or set of volumes we try in the acknowledgments pages to mention all the public office, university, and library figures who have provided assistance and information. Over half a century (my own involvement began in 1964), the list has become a kind of history of the edition, and it is good to be able to look back and say, again, our thanks to them, to the university and public figures who gave support, to the Carlyle Society in Edinburgh and the National Trust houses that opened their doors and their archives, to the libraries all over the world (but the National Library of Scotland above all), that hold the documents on which the edition is built.

As the later volumes have appeared, the growing awareness of women's writing in the nineteenth century, and of life-writing in general, has made Jane Welsh Carlyle's material in the edition of the very first importance, as Aileen Christianson showed in her introduction to volume 29 (CL 29:ix–xvi). Among the wonderfully rediscovered lost papers of the Carlyle family, several of Jane Welsh Carlyle's other writings (in CL 30) give a vivid insight into her acuity and skill. Sheila McIntosh enters a useful caveat: “Constructing a narrative from their letters is not straightforward; their tone and energy is often inconsistent with the misery they say they are enduring and with their own overt narrative” (CL 33:xxiii33:introduction). Revaluation of Jane Welsh Carlyle continues in recent publications as
the largely complete run of letters can be critically read, its gaps recognized, its refraction and reshaping of events and opinions acknowledged. “Careless as she seems of her writing, Jane knew her value. Anna Montagu had said it should be her life-mission ‘to write little notes’; and already fashionable ladies had been known to cross London just to beg to see their author” (CL 19:xiii19:introduction).

The treasure trove of letters is a vivid illustration of that London, and importantly also of the Scotland from which both Carlyles came and which shaped their reading and their early lives. Carlyle's loyal writing to his family casts a vivid light on working-class life in southwest Scotland in wartime and after, in the politically troubled years of the late 1810s and early 1820s, and on the Edinburgh of the two years the Carlyles spent there as a married couple (1826–28) when the city was still an exciting place to live and write in, even though its brilliance was soon to be overtaken by the bankruptcy of Scott, the departure of Lockhart (and many others) to London, and the Carlyles’ own abrupt removal to Craigenputtoch, where they could live cheaply and Carlyle could write undisturbed, though Jane was to find the silence and loneliness oppressive. We are fortunate that the letters from their London visit of 1831–32 coincide with the political ferment of that time, and their 1832–33 visit to Edinburgh also shows a literary city in its transition to something less brilliant after the age of Sir Walter Scott.

The Duke-Edinburgh Letters give a startlingly vivid picture of these decades: the brilliance of the love letters, the slow emergence of the public literary Carlyle, Jane's electric conversation and character, her circle that flourished alongside Carlyle's, and the international writers who visited and wrote and who underline to us today the impact that Carlyle had during the decades of his productive years up to 1866, with the end of Frederick and Jane's death. Startling flashes of description, satire, affection, and hurt are everywhere. The correspondence of two writers of genius so plainly bound by love and loyalty now is permanently available for readers of nineteenth-
century cultural history to approach. We can hold alongside the letters Carlyle's incomparable Reminiscences of 1866, reliving the years spent with Jane, and we can live in Haddington again in Jane's brilliant recollection of her 1849 visit: “It looked, the old place, just as I had seen it at Chelsea in my dreams—only more dreamlike!” (CL 24:162).

With The Carlyle Letters Online available for searching via the internet, the body of the Carlyle correspondence is now ready to take its place as an indispensable Victorian asset, though the indexes to each set of early volumes, and to each volume latterly, are a fine tool for anyone seeking a deeper understanding of both Carlyles. The ongoing labor of the footnoting is a tribute to David Sorensen, Jane Roberts, and Liz Sutherland, with Liz also indefatigable in the indexing of each volume as it reaches the printer. The adventure of
finding the Carlyle papers and putting them into print has been an enriching and wonderful one, and it will continue to reveal new riches as new material comes to light. With the aid of the internet, the adventure of exploring the nineteenth century through their papers continues.
Ian Campbell
Edinburgh, February 2022

div1.p: December 1875–February 1881

row.cell: American Academy of Arts and Sciences

div1.p: December 1875. TC apologizes to Charles Eliot Norton for his long silence, blaming his weak hand and his dislike of writing to dictation (2). He tells of his summer visit to Scotland, “a field of the dead” to him. He has been reading history extensively, but the hard winter “plagues…me not a little.” He writes to tell brother John A. Carlyle of “a whirlwind of birthday gifts” and letters, including one from Bismarck (4). The weather is dark and depressing, but his sister Jean Aitken and niece Mary Aitken are looking after him well. They are to dine at the Forsters’. He writes David Masson to thank him for the 80th Birthday Medal and Address that Masson had organized (), and he writes to thank Bismarck for his letter (10). Despite snow and servant problems, TC tells his brother John that these “trifling events” have been dealt with, though they cause him “fidgetty annoyance” (15). Mary has answered a “wheelbarrowful of Letters.” An old family friend, Mary Russell of Holmhill, dies in Scotland (17). He acknowledges his election to honorary membership of the Numismatic and Antiquarian Society of Pennsylvania (21). J. A. Froude returns from South Africa, and TC welcomes his company. He continues to have problems with his teeth (22). Mary tells Maria Henshaw of the problems she has faced in Cheyne Row with servants, and the shock of Maggie Welsh's death; her mother, Jean (who had been in Chelsea since late October), will return to Scotland shortly.

January 1876. Mary writes to thank Meta Wellmer for gifts, and reports on TC's good health: “[H]e can read still for three or four hours at a sitting & his chief enjoyment is in a good book”(2). TC thanks the Duke of Weimar for his birthday letter and sends a gift of a book in thanks (10). Complaining of “dark and miserable” weather, TC apologizes for his slowness in replying to his brother John; he has had extensive reading in historical subjects and enjoys the company of Froude (“whom I generally see every alternate day”), though he misses Forster, who is “rarely visible when I call” and is “dreadfully depressed in spirits” (15). John Tyndall writes of his impending marriage to Louisa Hamilton (27). William Allingham visits, and they study German books together (29). Norton writes from Cambridge, Massachusetts, with news of mutual friends, particularly Emerson, whose “spirit is as young as ever,” though his memory is beginning to fail (29). TC congratulates Tyndall on his engagement and invites him to bring his fiancée to Chelsea (31).

February 1876. John Forster dies (1); TC attends the funeral with Mary and Froude, as one of the chief mourners (5). Winter weather is severe with frost and fog; TC's chief visitors are William Lecky and Allingham. After long delaying, TC writes his “dear and true” brother Alick in Canada with a substantial gift of money (15). Tyndall writes (25) to invite TC to his wedding in Westminster Abbey (29).

March 1876. TC regrets the loss of Forster: “I never had a kinder or more constantly helpful fellow-man in the world beside me” (1). Forster has bequeathed to TC a gold repeater watch he had received from Dickens, and TC gives it to Mary. TC hears from John that Thomas Aird, a very old friend, is unwell in Scotland. A new set of false teeth proves to be a success. TC goes to Westminster Abbey, first for Tyndall's wedding, and then for Lady Augusta Stanley's funeral (9). John Motley and TC walk together, so being “roused up & forced to talk” had “its useful effects on a torpid old mind” (17). He tells John that despite “wild and stormy” weather he has put in the time reading history and a new life of Godwin, “a dull stony man,” and other books that Allingham brings him (18). TC had promised to support Frances Cobbe in a deputation to the Home Office to oppose the practise of vivisection (20), but on learning that Cardinal Manning would be present, he refused to go (18). The Kensington Museum has accepted Forster's bequest of books and papers. Lady Ashburton writes from Egypt during her travels; TC replies, telling her how much he misses Forster; “[H]is death is a very great loss to me as to yourself” (21). Caroline Davenport Bromley is a regular visitor. TC hears he has been elected an honorary member of the Royal Irish Academy (28). He is reading widely but with little pleasure. TC's brother John writes to tell him that their brother Alick in Canada is failing (30). TC hears from John Stuart Blackie in Edinburgh about the plans for a professorship in Gaelic studies. He writes to an unidentified young man that in his opinion, “[l]iterature, as a profession, is what I would counsel no faithful man to be concerned with, except when absolutely forced into it” (30). Brother Alick dies (30).

April 1876. With warmer weather, TC resumes walking in Hyde Park or Battersea Park: “Froude is the company I like best and oftenest have” (8). He is reading Trevelyan's Life of Macaulay; Vigfusson visits twice. The weather is uncertain, but TC and Mary go out together, including visits to Forster's widow, Eliza, “when we decide to make an effort & call there” (15). Thomas Aird dies in Dumfries (25): “no more innocent man has been known to me” (29). John is planning a visit to Chelsea when the new railway timetables settle down; he sends family news regularly to TC.

May 1876. TC writes his nephew Tom in Canada to thank him for the news of Alick's death (4). The Lord Mayor of London pressingly invites TC to a formal
banquet to honor literary figures (5), but TC contrives to avoid it, instead sending a letter which is read out to the company. Meta Wellmer is visiting London; Mary writes to apologize that they cannot offer her a room in the house, since John is now in London staying at Chelsea, but she will find her a room nearby (20).
June 1876. TC is asked to authenticate signatures by Oliver Cromwell for a dealer (25). TC and Mary leave for Dumfries (29 or 30).

July–August 1876. TC has been asked to stand godfather to John Constantine Stanley's first child (2). TC and Mary arrive in Old Ballikinrain as guests of Annabella Anstruther (10), and TC enjoys being driven around the countryside; they then go to Dumfries, via Glasgow, remaining until mid-August.

September 1876. John, as well as helping TC with his investments in Scottish railway stock, is trying to help with Froude's Scottish arrangements, though bad weather is interfering (4). Froude, staying at Naworth Castle with George James Howard and Maude Stanley, eventually visits Craigenputtoch (6). Allingham reports on a visit and walk with TC, “rather better than he was” (6). He is using the Brompton and Chelsea omnibuses to lengthen his daily walks. He visits Erasmus Darwin and Peyton Blakiston; Allingham and Lecky are “diligent enough in calling” (7). A mistaken report in the press that Carlyle had cut his throat causes a short-lived sensation and a quantity of letters that Mary has to deal with. John's stepson Henry Watt visits. TC is reading Swift. Chapman is setting type for the people's edition of Early Kings of Norway and The Portraits of John Knox (23).

October 1876. TC misses visits by John Constantine Stanley and Miss Bromley, he tells Lady Ashburton (16). John in Scotland was planning a visit to Chelsea, but he reports that his health is too poor: “I could only be a burden to you & Mary under such circumstances” (21). Froude wants TC to make a winter visit to Madeira, but TC thinks “there will nothing practically come of it” (21). Froude is TC's chief visitor, along with Allingham, Lecky, and James Fitzjames Stephen, “who are of inferior value.”

November 1876. John arrives in Cheyne Row for a visit in mid-November. With “very great reluctance” TC writes George Howard (24) with his considered opinion on the political crisis in eastern Europe and the unrest there: TC feels that the Russians are a “good and even noble element in Europe” and strongly opposes the idea of a war against them in support of the Turkish empire, and he insists on the importance of Britain “securing its road to India, which depends on Egypt and the Suez Canal.”

December 1876. Tyndall relays Mme. Novikov's grateful thanks to TC for his letter on the “Eastern Question” (5). Mary sends her cousin Thomas in
Canada an inscription for Alick's tombstone that TC has composed (13). TC writes Gavan Duffy to ask him to help a correspondent in Australia who had written TC for assistance (30).
January 1877. Mary writes to Amelie Bölte with TC's thanks for her gift of Neues Frauenbrevier (14).

April 1877. John returns to Dumfries mid-April. Missing his brother, TC writes that he can “find only a mournful remembrance that the Dr is away.” He forecasts that “we have no long time to be together in this same world.” Apart from dental problems, TC is “not usually worse in health.” Walking, driving, and visits help fill his days. “On the whole I have no intimate here,” but he is keen to hear from John news of the family in Dumfries (28).

May 1877. TC writes to the Times (4) on the rumors of impending war, and he tells John about his “dead-lift effort against my burdens & incumbrances” that induced him to attack Disraeli and the government (5). TC is saddened by the death of JWC's aunts Elizabeth (4) and Ann (10) Welsh in Scotland, and he has a wearisome visit from Paterson Erskine of Linlathen (12). Mary writes to David Davidson to thank him for sending news of the aunts’ decease (17). “The earth grows very solitary,” TC writes to John, “when all our loved ones are faded away to the unseen Land” (19). Millais has been busy painting TC, “in a state of almost frenzy about finishing with the extremest perfection.” He tells his brother John he wishes to be buried in Ecclefechan beside his parents; he also wants to write something to mark his debt to Forster for many years of literary help (29).

June 1877. Millais has completed the portrait (9), though he asks for some extra sittings. TC enjoys the better weather, and though “reading fills up my time” he finds it “utterly bad and stupid” including books about himself, which he prefers to have nothing to do with. Edward Sterling dies (3), “eldest son of my Sterling” (9). TC appreciates regular letters from his brother John, “duly minute about everything” and keeping him informed about his family in Scotland. Millais’ portrait is complete: “a rational enough kind of man, with plenty of common sense, whom I did not at all dislike.” Lady Ashburton sends her carriage for TC to enjoy “brilliant summer weather, sunshine generally with, occasionally, strong east wind” (16). Friends are away traveling, so he has only “the mournful company of myself,” though he has visits from David Masson and Annabella Anstruther. “I am reading Gibbon; a repetition after above fifty years” (22 [23]). Mary writes to Meta Wellmer (25) complaining about her health; she has tried vegetarianism but without success. Princess Louise visits, escorted by the Duke of Argyll (25). Mary would benefit from a holiday, and TC admits he would too, though he shrinks from the bother and disruption (30).

July 1877. Rereading Gibbon after many years, TC finds “a great deduction from the high esteem I have had of him ever since old Kirkcaldy days,” he tells John (21). Mary, fatigued from her long care of her uncle, desperately needs a holiday; John offers to come from Scotland to provide cover, but Mary arranges for Mary Craik to come (28).
August 1877. TC stays with Caroline Bromley near Epsom (10) for a brief holiday.

September 1877. TC and Lady Ashburton and her daughter Mary visit the National Portrait Gallery (10), and TC visits Grosvenor House (11) to meet Lord Gower and view his statue of Marie Antionette. TC is now reading Suetonius, though he tells John he has “multitudes of useless books & there are very few of them which seem worthy of being sent to you.” He takes daily exercise walking to the Embankment and riding in the Brompton omnibus. He is glad Froude has returned to London. TC would be glad to see his family come to visit from Scotland, but so far all attempts have failed (29).

October 1877. TC praises Allingham, who has “a good deal of natural faculty & worth, and has met with no due recognition hitherto.” He is very glad to have a set of photographs of his Scottish relatives, and tells John he expects his sister Jean and her daughter Maggie shortly for a visit (14 [13]). TC continues reading widely, and “I see Froude about twice a week.” He pays a tribute to Thomas Erskine, having read the second volume of Hanna's biography (27).

November 1877. Reading now in magazines causes “nothing but distress to me,” but TC is initially cheered by Mary's suggestion of hiring a brougham for their excursions. With Froude he enjoys a drive and a walk in Regent's Park (3). On the other hand, building work on the Embankment has been a nuisance, “a terrible plunge of absurdity.” He is glad to hear of news from Scotland and worries about his sister Mary Austin, who has dental problems; TC offers to help pay for any help possible. He sees Lecky and Blakiston, and he just misses seeing Darwin. The brougham looks unlikely to be practicable (10). He is reading widely, particularly about John Paul Jones from a poor biography, “but I get from it for the first time some flickering authentic notion of who and what Paul Jones really was” (17). TC still hopes his sister Jean or brother John will visit in London, and he is very glad to hear from his nephew Tom in Canada. A heavy cold upsets his normal routine (24).
December 1877. John arrives for a visit in Cheyne Row. TC sends his apologies (via Mary) for missing the funeral of Thomas Wright (29).
March 1878. TC's brother-in-law Robert Hanning dies (22).

April 1878. John returns to Dumfries (18). TC sees the Blakistons and Caroline Bromley. John Constantine Stanley and Stauros Dilberoglue die (23). TC writes to John: “I many a time wonder that I have any friends left, who can be taken away from me & added to the great multitude already gone.” Of his brother John, he writes, “[o]f you I have great miss & indeed see nobody or hardly anybody that gives me the least satisfaction.” He is reading Renan (27).

May 1878. TC is glad to hear John is well enough to go out for drives, which TC also does with various companions. “We are puddling along here in the usual element of vague unpleasant rumour,” and he has seen Lecky and Darwin. “I miss you here very much.” He also misses his sister Jean, and he asks frequently for news of her (5 [4]). “I am busy reading Goethe.…[T]here is endless ingenuity, grace of execution & other fine quality.” John is reading TC's Frederick, which TC thinks “often enough…worth nothing but it did cost me a deal of trouble.” He enjoys the company of Tyndall and discusses Goethe with him (25).

June 1878. “The usual Saturday's gazette” to John brings odd snippets of news and a description of the hot weather, “considerable changing of costume in consequence & practice of sitting on the Japanese chair at the back of the house, as now with poor Mary writing on her knee” (22). TC joins Froude in Kew Gardens (21) using the underground and overground railways, greatly admiring the gardens though finding the excursion exhausting.
July–August 1878. TC and Mary go to Dumfries, staying some of the time with family and some of the time in a rented house.

September 1878. TC and Mary return to London (13). TC condoles with John on his “present sad imprisonment” by bad weather, and he compares it with London weather, where he and Mary “get out daily in a drive of two hours” (21). He sees the Blakistons but misses seeing Darwin; Froude is away, and “[t]he Town is very empty.” Sister Mary's husband, James Austin, dies (20).

October 1878. Mary writes Ellen Conway to apologize on her uncle's behalf for declining an invitation (4). TC is always glad to hear from his brother John, though he worries about his health: “Could I but once get you up here again to be beside me, what an immense improvement it would be and solacement to my feelings!” TC and Mary take a daily two-hour drive, often with friends—Catharina Lecky, Mme. Novikov, Lecky himself. News of Ruskin's health is disturbing, for he is “threatened with softening of the brain.” Froude will soon return to London, “useful twice a week in taking me intelligible roads which he alone of all my carriage friends can do.” TC has a photograph of his brother Alick's tomb in Canada. He feels sad for his sister Mary, whose husband had died: “I feel as if I should have written to her, but what could I
say” (11 [12]). The weather is colder: “[M]ost mornings I contrive to get down to the bottom of the embankment though it becomes more difficult to me.” He is reading the life of Sterling, and Swift's Gulliver, “a work of consummate talent” (18). David Laing dies (18): “[A] considerable light of knowledge is thus extinguished & a very harmless brother mortal is carried away into eternity before us.” TC is glad of news from his Scottish family; he is reading Sterne (26).

November 1878. TC is reading Voltaire, and Pushkin in translation. He meets Darwin “looking very lean and pale,” Lecky, and “a Jew named Friedmann who has wandered much over the world & has many a curious anecdote to tell.” Helen Allingham is painting TC while he sits reading, “& has made two small water colour sketches which appear to me to have a great deal of likeness.” (9). He sympathizes with his brother John's difficulty in getting out of the house in the cold weather. He is regularly visited by Froude, both Leckys, and his new much-traveled friend, Friedmann—as for other people, “their intercourse bringing to me nothing but trouble” (15). The end of the month brings frost and the first real winter weather; TC sees Darwin, and tells John of the Blakistons’ financial problems (30).

December 1878. TC writes sympathetically to his brother about his ill health, for “there is no good news to be expected from either side. God's will be done!” He praises Mary, “unwearied in her attention” (14). Blakiston dies from heart disorder (17). Elizabeth Paulet is also ill from asthma. “I go out daily to drive & manage to endure two hours of sheltered locomotion of that kind & suffer less not more than you would expect” (21).

January 1879. TC writes his brother John, glad to hear that John's health is no worse; he has seen Bessy Blakiston and Darwin, “close prisoner to the house and looks very weak” (11). He congratulates his brother on creating medical bursaries at Edinburgh University, which will “do good to fellow creatures yet unborn.” He no longer enjoys tobacco because of his weak digestion (18). Despite the hard weather, he manages some outings with Mary, particularly by omnibus to St Paul's, where he enjoys the music (25). Elizabeth Paulet dies (30).

February 1879. The weather is a little less hard: “I get along here in regard to health in all these outward respects tolerably well,” though TC also has very dark moods: “I often think with myself I am fairly too long here” (1). The cold weather recedes, and “it almost seems as if spring itself had arrived at this premature season” (8). John in Dumfries is more of a prisoner with the cold, and his eyesight is failing. TC receives Proserpina V from Ruskin, but while admiring it, he notes “I have understood that he is quite gone over to what they call Spiritualism” (15). Heavy snow falls, though TC is not affected
“except from the of course increasing weakness that acts chiefly through the stomach” (22).

March 1879. TC feels his health is “tolerably well,” he tells John, and “I still read and can get something more or less tolerable to read.” He discusses Ruskin's St. George's Guild with John, a better notion than “spiritualism so-called,” which TC despises (1). The cold abates, though John is still housebound in Dumfries. A “foolish Yankee” visits (15). The Chelsea servant Rose has been nursing her young man, but he dies (21), leaving an exhausted Rose who is looked after by Mary. A cousin in Bonerick has also died—“a year younger than myself” (22).
No further letters from TC, direct or dictated to Mary, survive. Allingham notes that in the spring of 1879 TC's health suddenly worsened.
June–July 1879. TC and Mary leave for Dumfries, to be near John A. Carlyle, who is dying. They stay at first with Jean Aitken at the Hill, then move to Cassalands House, Dumfries.
August 1879. Mary marries her cousin Alexander Carlyle (21). They go to Moffat for their honeymoon, where TC soon joins them.
September 1879. Allingham visits TC in Moffat (5–8); John A. Carlyle dies (15). TC, Mary, and Alick return to Chelsea.
October 1879. TC sends a gift of money to Henry Larkin and recommends his writings to the editor of the British Quarterly Review.
November 1879. TC gives his sister Jean £1000 to save their house from being sold.
January–May 1880. Mary's sister Margaret comes to stay in Cheyne Row for a few weeks. TC still goes for drives most days, sees visitors, and reads.
June 1880. Mary and Alick's son, Thomas, is born (2).

July 1880. Describing TC's health, Mary writes that he is “exceedingly weak, hardly able to walk fifty yards without help,” yet despite an attack of diarrhea is “what one might call for him very well.…He sees and hears quite well; but he is not good at moving about” (18).
September 1880. Mary and her baby son go to visit her mother in Dumfries, Alick staying behind to look after TC.

January 1881. TC takes his last outdoor exercise in a carriage (1). Then “he was confined to his bed exactly three weeks all but a day,” Mary reports, “for the most part quiet and collected” and occasionally imagining himself back with his family in his youth.

February 1881. Death of Thomas Carlyle “without a struggle or without any apparent pain” (5). Mary writes a number of short letters to let various friends and associates know the news (6). She tells them the funeral will be a private event in Ecclefechan, and despite offers by Dean Stanley of Westminster Abbey, there will be no public ceremony in London. The funeral in Ecclefechan (10) is attended by Mary and Alexander Carlyle, and other local family members; also there were Froude, Lecky, and Tyndall from London, and Alexander Welsh and Henry Watt from Liverpool (10).

div3.sourceNote: TC-CEN, 2 Dec. MS: Harvard. Hitherto unpbd. Charles Eliot Norton, American author, journalist, and academic. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO CHARLES ELIOT NORTON

docBody.p: In late months you have sent me many kind and friendly Notes, every one of which has been welcome and pleasant to me; and I on my side have seemed remiss and negligent to a degree;—I say seemed, not altogether been, for the truth is there has been not a little obstruction from without, while from within there is, with the inability to write at all myself, a growing reluctance to try dictation in any measure & in short a kind of horror of attempting to write on any terms. Two of your beautiful bits of post cardsNorton had recently suggested that he and TC should write weekly postcards to each other; see 49:261TC to JAC, 20 Nov. 1845. have successively arrived; but, alas, could get no corresponding response: if more of them could continue to come from you they would be right welcome. But, woe's me, with “the reciprocity all on one side,”Coterie speech; see 19:196JWC to CGD, [1845]. how can I hope such a thing!— But enough of all this, enough & too much.

We did not go to Scotland this last autumn perhaps I shall never go again, the misery I endure in all modes of travelling is one repellant cause, but not the chief one by any means—what is there for me now in Scotland but a field of the dead; and among the inane noises that prevail there as here sombre, solemnly piercing and tender voices from Eternity; a mixture of noises from which one shudders! On the kind offer of a Great Lady (Countess of Derby)Mary Catherine Stanley, Lady Derby. who takes all manner of generous pains with me, we were shoved off, my niece Mary and I, to a charming hermitage a little way from London, Keston Lodge,Keston Lodge, Kent, was loaned to TC and Mary Aitken by Lady Derby, Aug.–Sept. 1875; see 49:226TC to JF, 4 Aug. 1875. close adjoining Hollwood Park in which country, to my surprize, I learnt that you were well acquainted several years ago, & were still lovingly remembered.Holwood Park, near Keston. Norton had stayed at Keston Rectory, Aug.–Oct. 1868; he wrote to Mary Aitken, 28 Dec.: “[S]even years ago I learned to know the neighborhood of Holwood Park so familiarly that no place in England is better known to me. We lived for three months in the Rectory, close to the little old church, & within a stone's throw of a gate into the Park to which we had free access” (MS: privately owned). While there he became friendly with Charles Darwin and his family (see Norton's Letters 1:305 and 309), with whom TC also became friendly while staying at Keston; see 49:234TC to JAC, 2 Sept. 1875. In this hermitage, waited on & supplied for every reasonable want by a pair of the best servantsWilliam Porter (b. 1835) and his wife, Mary (b. 1838); see 49:229MAI to GHOG, 28 Aug. 1875. I ever saw, we had two brilliant sunshiny
months of the most perfect solitude & silence that were well possible in the world. They were very strange to me, these two months, and gave birth to many thoughts not uttered, and indeed mostly unutterable to any heart but my own, thoughts very sad, but sometimes very beautiful. I sat mostly in the woods with a book, Ruskin,TC presumably refers to Ruskin's Fors Clavigera, letter 57; see 49:235TC to JAC, 9 Sept. 1875. MicheletJules Michelet, Histoire de France, 19 vols. (Paris, 1833–67); see 49:229MAI to GHOG, 28 Aug. 1875. and singular to say Southey's Life of WesleyRobert Southey (1774–1843, ODNB), poet, The Life of Wesley; and the Rise and Progress of Methodism, 2 vols. (1820). re-read,—reading, alas, is now the only kind of even imaginary work that I can do and with good Books, were such always to be had, I could still find consolations and assuagements. Since returning hither, I have carefully gone through Thucydides's History in Dean Smith's TranslationThucydides, ancient Greek historian; TC had been reading his History of the Peloponnesian War. Translated from the Greek of Thucydides, ed. William Smith (1711–87; ODNB; classical scholar, dean of Chester 1758–87), 2 vols. (1753); TC's copy; Carlyle's House 77; see 49:258TC to JAC, 13 Nov. 1875. (for with Thucydides in Greek, I can of course do no good whatever) he seemed to me a spirit of the very first order comparable almost to Dante, but in real historical faculty decididly inferior to Herodotus.Herodotus (ca. 484–ca. 425 B.C.), Greek historian. I am at this moment deep in PlutarchPlutarch's Lives: The Translation Called Dryden's. Corrected from the Greek and Revised by A. H. Clough, 5 vols. (Boston, 1857); see 43:30TC to JAC, 7 Nov. 1865, and 49:260TC to JAC, 20 Nov. 1875. Arthur Hugh Clough (1819–61; ODNB), poet and friend of TC; see 38:15–17TC to JAF, 30 Nov. 1861. again, only interrupted by the deluge of monthly Periodicals in which I have read nothing that in the least pleased me except in a thing called the Contemporary Review, an article on Walt WhitmanPeter Bayne, “Walt Whitman's Poems,” Contemporary Review 27 (Dec. 1875): 49–69. Walt Whitman (1819–92), American poet, essayist, and journalist. superlatively good and fairly confirming my first notion about Walt, fifteen years ago: “If you could endow the parish bull with the faculty of human utterance and holding a pen between the halves of his hoof, this, I imagine is much the thing he would write.”TC had been given a copy of Whitman's Leaves of Grass (New York, 1855) and later wrote very similar comments to a friend about Whitman; see 48:58–59TC to TDI, 23 May 1872. William Allingham also noted in his diary, 3 Oct. 1872: “C was accustomed to say of W. W., ‘It is as though the town-bull had learnt to hold a pen’” (Allingham Diary 212). Norton wrote to Mary Aitken, 28 Dec., thanking TC for recommending the article, with which he entirely agreed. Read that article, if you can easily lay hold of it. The author is Peter Bayne,Peter Bayne (1830–96; ODNB), Scottish author and journalist; for TC's earlier contact with him, see 29:339TC to JCA, 25 June 1855. a friend of Ruskin's for many years back.

Enough now of this dull stuff. The winter which is very ugly here plagues and obstructs me not a little; and you plainly see I do not shine in writing at present and ought to end. I send all manner of salutations to your household
and dear relatives, to little SallySara, Norton's eldest daughter; see 48:183TC to CEN, 22 March 1873, and 49:13–14TC to CEN, 3 Nov. 1873. a kiss and a blessing. My heart is very sore for poor Maggie Welsh;Maggie Welsh, JWC's cousin, who d. 29 April 1875; see 49:216–17TC to JW, 5 May 1875. and I have much miss of her and shall have. But Mary is a most deft and ready writer, and will punctually answer any special enquiry you may make about Chelsea and its affairs. Adieu, dear Norton. Remember me kindly as long as you can in this fast-fleeting world. Say something about EmersonNorton wrote to Mary Aitken, 28 Dec.: “The last word I had from [Emerson] was on Christmas Day when he sent me the new volume of his Essays which, I doubt not, has already reached your Uncle. The cheerfulness of his perennial youth shines through the volume…. Two or three weeks since he read to a little audience gathered here in Cambridge…. That evening he looked well & vigorous” (MS: privately owned). next time you write. I ever am
docBody.closer: Affectionately Yours, / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 4 Dec. MS: NLS 528.45. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:320–21 inc. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:435; Wilson, Carlyle 6:375. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
There has been this morning a complete whirlwind of birthday gifts and congratulations about the poor arrival of my 80th & probably last 4th of Decr,—from the whole of which Mary and Jean,TC's niece Mary, and his sister Jean Aitken, who had been visiting since Oct.; see 49:252TC to JAC, 26 Oct. 1875. with the good sense of the senders have mercifully delivered me; so that I have got little harm from them which is a mercy. All this ended & here has come down a dark sleety cloud, more suitable for midnight in regard to which I have set down Mary with two candles to write a word or two to you, generally announcing the thing and copying the two most remarkable of these birthday documents, both of them from Berlin,The two documents from Berlin were a letter from Otto von Bismarck, chancellor of Germany, and a telegram signed by 10 German historians, including Leopold von Ranke (1795–1886), whose works TC had consulted while writing Frederick; see 27:76TC to JAC, 27 March 1852, and Carlyle, Works 15:472. with purpose to send you at least a selection from the others were a new day with visible or presumable sun once come. Prince Bismarck, you will observe, thinks it is my 70th birthday,Bismarck wrote, 2 Dec.: “Highly honoured Sir— The celebration of your seventieth birthday concerns Germany too, and to you I may say that in my mother tongue. As you introduced Schiller to your countrymen, so you have placed before the Germans our great Prussian King in his full figure, like a living statue. What you said long years ago of the ‘Hero as Man of Letters,’—that he is under the noble obligation to be true,—has been fulfilled in yourself; but, more fortunate than those of whom you then spoke, you may rejoice in what you have accomplished, and continue your work in full vigour, which may God long preserve to you. Accept with my cordial congratulations the assurance of my sincere respect” (trans.: A. Carlyle, NL 2:319–20). which is enough to quench
any vanity one might have on a missive from such a man: but I own to being truly pleased with the word or two he says about Frederick the Great, which seems to me a valuable memorial and certificate of the pains I took in that matter,—not unwelcome in the circumstances.

Besides German documents, more or less remarkable there is an Edinr affair,TC refers to the 80th Birthday Medal and Address, organized by David Masson, who invited and collected signatures and subscriptions, and drafted the address, and George Lillie Craik (1837–1905; see 43:269–7043:biographical notes), partner in Macmillan's publishing firm, who coordinated the production of the medal and the printing of the address. The address was pbd. in the Times, 6 Dec.; see TC to DM, 9 Dec. got up, I think, by MassonAlthough organized by Masson, the birthday address was not originally his idea; Masson wrote, 25 Dec.: “the desire for something to be done originated in the far-off Shetlands. There is an ‘Arthur Laurenson’ among the subscribers. He is the man. He lives at Lerwick, cut off from us all by seas and storms; and I have never seen him.” Arthur Laurenson (1832–90), Norse scholar, author, and antiquarian from Lerwick in Shetland. which has issued in a fine gold medal done by Boehm,The portrait for the medal was designed by the sculptor Joseph Edgar Boehm and engraved by George Morgan (1845–1925), die engraver, with TC's head on one side and “In commemoration; December 4, 1875” on the obverse; see opp. TC was given the gold medal, and subscribers could obtain silver or bronze copies. Joseph Boehm wrote to Thomas Dixon (1831–80; see 47:121–22TC to TDI, 7 Dec. 1870), cork-cutter from Sunderland, 9 Nov.: “You will perhaps be interested to hear that the friends of Carlyle intend to give him on his 80th birthday a gold medal of himself with a suitable address— I am doing the Head for the medallion & shall send you a copy when struck. Please do not tell this to any body yet as it is a surprise & to be kept quiet till beginning of Decbr 4th I think is his birthday” (MS: NLS 1778.9). with many signatures appended; of which you shall hear more specially by & by. Let this, with the two copies accompanying suffice at present on that head.TC indicated a new paragraph here.
Thomas Carlyle's 80th Birthday Medal by Joseph Boehm
Courtesy of Ian Campbell

We have horrible weather here, which I doubt you abundantly share in at Dumfries, nothing but perpetual darkness, more or less intense, with a pluster of snow, odious to human nature; which indeed in regard to its dangerous slipperiness I find myself considerably able to disdain and have at least my mid-day walk as before, hitherto without the least accident, though with much increase of disagreeableness. Mary & Jean are very busy & quite in their usual way of health nor has anything gone wrong about the house and its affairs; but during the last two or almost three weeks there has on poor me come a new affliction: that of awakening every morning between 5 & 6 & passing the two hours or more till somebody get up in the house in a most agitated tremulous & uncomfortable manner. This distresses & frightens me in some measure & I am trying since yesterday a dose of blue pill & castor,
which has brought some alleviation & determines me to try farther in that same direction. This is really all the home news I have to send you. There has come a Letter from Canada TomTheir nephew Thomas Carlyle, son of Alexander (Alick) Carlyle, living in Canada. yesterday morning; which distresses us all, announcing the great frailty & constant suffering of poor Alick, who perhaps will not survive me, as by nature he should.Alick was 20 months younger than TC; he suffered badly from asthma (see 49:236TC to JAC, 9 Sept. 1875). God help him & me & all of us!— Mary has much to do & Forster has positively by the most obstinate persistence managed to have us all to dine with him tonight;John Forster; he often invited TC to dinner on his birthday. so at present I will not add another word. God's blessing on you all.

div3.sourceNote: TC-DM [DMA], 9 Dec. Addr: 10 Regent Terrace / Edinburgh. PM: Chelsea, 9 Dec. 1875. MS: NLS 1778.121. Pbd: Shepherd, Carlyle 2:306–7 inc. Quot: Kaplan 523; John Morrow, Thomas Carlyle (2006) 198.
div3.head: TC TO DAVID MASSON

docBody.p: This of the Medal and formal Address of friendsSee TC to JAC, 4 Dec. was an altogether unexpected event to be received as a conspicuous and peculiar honour without example hitherto anywhere in my life.

Evidently you were the contriver, diligent promoter and essential Author of the work;The address had been drafted by Masson, and read: “Sir, / We beg leave, on this
interesting and memorable anniversary, to tender you the expression of our respectful good wishes. / Not a few of the voices which it would have been dearest to you to hear to-day are silent in death. There may perhaps be some compensation in the assurance of the reverent sympathy and affectionate gratitude of many thousands of living men and women, throughout the British Islands and elsewhere, who have derived delight and inspiration from the noble series of your writings, and who have noted also how powerfully the world has been influenced by your great personal example. A whole generation has elapsed since you described for us the Hero as a Man of Letters. We congratulate you and ourselves on the spacious fulness of years which has enabled you to sustain this rare dignity among mankind in all its possible splendour and completeness. It is a matter for general rejoicing that a teacher whose genius and achievements have lent radiance to his time still dwells amidst us; and our hope is that you may yet long continue in fair health, to feel how much you are loved and honoured, and to rest in the retrospect of a brave and illustrious life. / We request you to do us the honour to accept the accompanying copy of a Medal, designed by Mr. J. E. Boehm, which has been struck in commemoration of the day. / We remain, Sir, / Yours with deep respect.” There were 119 signatures (A. Carlyle, NL 2:323–24). to you therefore as to the centre of the affair, I address my thankful
acknowledgements, which surely are deep and sincere; and will beg you to convey the same to all the kind friends so beautifully concerned in it. Let no one of you be other than assured that the beautiful Transaction in result, management and intention was altogether gratifying welcome and honourable to me, and that I cordially thank one and all of you for what you have been pleased to do.

Your fine and noble gift shall remain among my precious possessions and be the symbol to me of something still more golden than itself on the part of my many dear and too generous friends so long as I continue in this world.

div3.sourceNote: TC-Prince B [PBI], 10 Dec. MS copy: NLS 1771.331. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:321–22; Wilson, Carlyle 6:374–75 inc. According to A. Carlyle (NL 2:321), the MS copy, in an elegant formal script, is an official transcript from the foreign office in Berlin. The version pbd. in Wilson, Carlyle is slightly different.
div3.head: TC TO PRINCE BISMARCK

docBody.p: On Saturday morning, which was my eightieth, and probably enough my last, Birthday, I was honoured with a Letter, by far the remarkablest, the least expected and the most agreeable that came to me on that occasion. This is the noble, wise, sincere and generous Letter which you have been pleased to write, and which I read with very great surprise and very great and lasting pleasure. Permit me to say that no honour could have been done to me, which I should have valued so much, or which shall live more brightly in my thoughts for the rest of my time in this world. What you deign to say of my poor History of your great King FriedrichSee TC to JAC, 4 Dec. seems to me the most pertinent and flattering utterance I have yet anywhere heard on that subject; and I am truly proud of it from such a quarter.

With very great sincerity, I warmly thank you for your goodness; and shall continue to wish for you, as I have long done, every prosperity in your great and noble career, and that God may grant you years and strength to fulfil, or carry beyond risk of failure, the grand and salutary enterprise in which you have already gone so far, in sight of all the world.
I have the honour to be and remain,

closer.salute: Sir, / Your obliged and obedient servant,

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 15 Dec. MS: NLS 528.46. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:322–23. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your welcome Letter came yesterday afternoon; and though hard up for time, I will not let this day pass without some answer to your kind enquiries. We have had one or two trifling events within doors here; which to so thin-skinned an individual as one of us is have not been without importance the first is, the slow and chaotic descent of 4 inches of snow upon us, which under the blundering management of London in such cases involved us in 3 weeks of abominable slush, slippery pavements & continual annoyance & which only disappeared altogether two days ago; a second small event was the sudden downbreak of our chief servant Ann,Ann, the new cook at Cheyne Row; see 49:246TC to JAC, 2 Oct. 1875; unidentified further. who, poor soul, after raising high expectations had suddenly to declare herself in an entirely unhealthy & almost dying state, out of long continued heart disease &c & request to be dismissed at once,—which Mary full of pity & anxiety managed by aid of Forster's brougham immediately to do; carried her, namely, all wrapped up to Kilburn to a Sisters,Kilburn, NW London; Ann's sister unidentified further. where we learn she is since for the present a little better. The interregnum of RoseRose, servant who had started the same time as Ann; unidentified further. our second servant who behaved like a heroine lasted only about a week; Mary two days ago introduced her new servant also a most promising person, a Swiss by nation, but familiar with England for the last 18 years;Unidentified further. still higher hopes are entertained of this new person; but of course all the adjustments are still to make & a fidgetty annoyance, insignificant for any one else is again the lot of the skinless old man. Saturday gone aweek may be named as the third event, a day of the most miserable agitation I can recollect in my life;— which item however I can now describe as entirely set at rest. The Noble & most unexpected Note from BismarckSee TC to JAC, 4 Dec. was the only really glad event of the day; the crowd of others, including even that of the Edinburgh Medal, was mere fuss & fret to me intrinsically of no value at all,—at least till one had time to recognise from the distance that kindness and goodwill had lain at the heart of every part of it among one's neighbours & fellow men;—all this has fretted & really hurt me; all the more as before any part of this a sad disturbance in my sleep had declared itself, namely the awakening a couple of hours before my time most mornings & of which with
all my blue pill &c I have not yet got the victory though I hope by judicious persistence to modify or conquer this also before long. Meantime of course I get no work done nor can expect any henceforth which is a steady sorrow to me as you may guess. My consolation is any bit of good reading. PlutarchSee TC to CEN, 2 Dec. at present is my chief resource & composes the ruffled hair of one's back in a sensible degree, as the speech of one wise clear & true man can smooth down the loud inanity of many fools & idiots when they are gone. As to the Edinr medal I understand only that there are to be silver medals at a guinea & bronze ditto at 5/ but where they are to be had or when I have no personal knowledge. Mary believes firmly that Mr George Morgan,See TC to JAC, 4 Dec. Morgan worked at the Royal Mint, London, and lived at 144 Finborough Rd.; a bronze impression of the medal presented to TC was exhibited at the Royal Academy of Arts in 1876. 144 Finboro’ Road London (the die sinker, whose name is on the case) if applied to, will give every information. People praise the medal, at least a little from the teeth outward; but I own myself at best indifferent to any merits it may have. Boehm it appears had nothing to do with it except furnishing the design in wax.

The answers to all that wheelbarrowful of Letters &c were undertaken by Mary (not a twentieth part of them answered at all) & are now completely off one's hands. The answer to Bismarck I with a gt effort painfully dictated as to his letter itself it is too big & too precious to me for sending you by post; but Mary undertakes to furnish you with a verbatim copy, intelligible to the last comma of it within this cover.

I have had a letter, as you see from Dushty;The Carlyles’ nickname for Baron Charles d’Eichthal from Munich; see 5:277TC to GE, 17 May 1831, and 47:87TC to JAC, 28 Oct. 1870. sent him, as required a photograph & two autographFor a signed photograph of TC by Charles B. Praetorius (1818–1900; see 49:72–73TC to JAC, 25 March 1874), taken around this time, see frontispiece. with the promise to forward the letter to you,—as herewith. Skelton's ingenious Book was the Jury trial of Mary Queen of Scots,Sir John Skelton (1831–97; ODNB), Scottish writer, The Impeachment of Mary Stuart Sometime Queen of Scots (Edinburgh, 1876); for a previous contact with Skelton, see 45:172TC to JSK, 21 Sept. 1868. of wh. I have not the least disposition to read a page, & indeed have given it to John Aitken,Their nephew John Aitken, Mary's brother, living in London. unless you want it.
This seems to be all the needful; & paper & time are both done. Adieu, dear Brother. God's blessing be on you & all the rest

div3.sourceNote: MA-CHH, 21 Dec. MS: Duke. Hitherto unpbd. Charles Henry Hart (1847–1918), Philadelphia lawyer, art historian and curator.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO C. H. HART

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle desires me to say with his compliments & best thanks that he has received your Letter and the official notification of his Hon. Membership of your Society,The Numismatic and Antiquarian Society of Pennsylvania; see 49:224–25MAI to CHH, 4 Aug. 1875, of which Hart was the historiographer. & that he begs you to continue to him the kind feelings which you express.
Mr Carlyle hopes you will excuse him for not answering your Letter in his own hand,—writing having become very difficult & troublesome to him in late years.

closer.salute: I remain / Dear Sir / Yours truly

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 23 Dec. MS: NLS 528.47. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I was about writing to you yesterday but unexpected impediments occurred. In the evening we had your letter which of course had its special interest for us, poor RussellMary Russell, old friend of JWC, d. 17 Dec. John A. Carlyle wrote, 19 Dec.: “Yesterday morning I daresay you would receive, as I did here, the announcement of Mrs Russell's death on Friday last…. One does not see how the poor Dr is to get on without her. They must have been husband & wife for at least fifty years.” being in all our thoughts. Some days ago we had got from DushtySee TC to JAC, 15 Dec. a second Letter, with multifarious photographs, connected with München, the whole of which I concluded were properly yours & ought to be sent to you, as they now are. Perhaps you are acquainted with the Schloss Egg;Schloss Egg [Egg Castle], in Bavaria, a moated fortress built in the 11th cent. and renovated in neo-Gothic style, 1838–42, by Count Joseph von Armansperg (1787–1853), lawyer and politician, whose grandson sold it to Charles d’Eichthal, 1871. or is it altogether a new erection, due to the actual Dushty? Only one or two of the others are known to me by name. Keep the photographs, so far
as you care for them at all; & please to write for me some time soon a word of thanks to Dushty.

We were all, as you may well fancy struck to the heart with the sudden calamity that had fallen on Holm Hill.John wrote again, 21 Dec., on his return from the funeral: “Mrs Russell … was apparently suffering only from a common cold…. But alarming symptoms came suddenly…. She grew worse & worse, but had little or no pain or apparent struggling & died … calmly & peaceably to all appearance.” Poor good old Russell; he has been a hundred times in my thoughts since the news came; and probably no man is sorrier for him, or knows better the stern loneliness that has now become his portion in this world. God help him; there is none of us that can do anything that will really help. I even abstain from sending any written condolence, knowing well how totally without help that is. On some calmer day you may express to him, if you like, what my feelings are. Alas, alas!

FroudeJames Anthony Froude, recently returned from South Africa; see 49:227TC to JAF, 6 Aug. 1875. called on Tuesday but without effect; he had come the day before, but went direct to Lord Carnarvons:Henry Howard Molyneux Herbert, 4th earl of Carnarvon, colonial sec. yesterday afternoon he appeared in person here, & I had a long & pleasant talk with him; and a more than usually comfortable walk. He believes himself to have left the affairs of the Cape in a comfortably prosperous condition, likely to ripen now into good arrangement, or at least into the best that is possible under Lord Carnarvon's own eye. Froude is writing a Report,See 49:249TC to JAC, 9 Oct. 1875. Froude's report to Lord Carnarvon, 10 Jan. 1876, was presented to the House of Commons in Feb. 1876. He continued to advocate Carnarvon's plan for an imperial federation in South Africa, although both the Cape ministry and the Dutch colonists distrusted his motives. In his conclusion Froude expressed confidence that a resolution to the dispute could be found: “A confederate South African Dominion, embracing all the states, both English and Dutch, under a common flag, may be expected as likely to follow, and perhaps at no very distant period. There is scarcely a person of intelligence in the entire country who does not desire it; and the object recommended alike by sentiment and interest can scarcely fail of realization. Suspicion will die out when the Imperial Policy is seen to be interested. Resentments will cease when the provocation no longer remains. But … the final consummation … can only be brought to wholesome maturity by the deliberate action of the South African communities themselves” (Parliamentary Command Papers, Feb. 1876, no. 1399, p. 83). to be presented when Parliament meets. He does not expect to be sent abroad again for a good while coming; & I expect a sensible improvement & new comfort from having him near me once more.

We have no farther news here; or none worth giving. My teeth are at present & are habitually in my mouth & I get a sensible benefit from them; and can even eat with them by taking great care.TC had been having trouble with his teeth, and had finally acquired a set of false teeth, but they had initially not proved very successful; see 49:257TC to JAC, 6 Nov. 1875. I think when you come next to
London you must let the artistTC's dentist was William R. Balland, 26 Manchester Sq.; TC's checkbook records: “30 Nov. 1875 / William Balland Esq. / Twenty-three Pounds, Two Shillings / £23.2.0” (TC's checkbook; MS: NLS 20752). examine you; if you have such a thing as a grinder tooth at the back of your jaw he will be certain to succeed with you; the imperfection in me is that I had nothing but a poor front tooth to take hold of. Forster, poor fellow has a sad fit of bile at present in addition to his usual miseries. I have not seen him for a week; but mean to try again today. He has sent me as birthday Gift a really excellent easy chair, not to be surpassed, I do believe in all London, so generous is the man in the middle of all his sufferings.Forster wrote, 21 Dec., thanking TC for calling to see how he was: “I am lifting up my face again—and shall be able to see you when next you come this way.” For a painting, by Helen Allingham, of TC reading in the chair that Forster gave him, see 142. Our weather is more like summer than Xmas, pleasant, but I know not whether wholesome or not. Kind regards from all of us to all. I ever am & remain
