div3.sourceNote: MA-MH [MP], 31 Dec. MS: Harry Ransom Lib., Univ. of Texas. Hitherto unpbd. Maria Ann Henshaw, b. Price (1839–1910; see JWC to KST, 7 Nov. 1865, and 43:biographical notes), da. of a Camberwell tailor, protégée of JWC's.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO MARIA ANN HENSHAW

docBody.p:
I was much pleased to receive your kind Xmas greeting; the only drawback to it was that I felt a pang of conscience on looking at your two pretty little cards and the friendly words that accompanied them. Any time for the last three or four months I have meant to write to you; but indeed I have had a great many excuses for not writing to anybody. I was not at all well all through the summer. Poor Miss WelshMaggie Welsh; see TC to CEN, 2 Dec. was coming up from Liverpool so as to set me free for a few weeks, when she very suddenly died after only a few days illness. It was very sad; she was always so bright and smiling that it was difficult to associate the thought of death with her; and it really was a great shock to us. Then Mrs WarrenSarah Warren, cook at 5 Cheyne Row since 1864. grew ill and had to go away, then there was the care of the house with a new servant who turned out badly;Presumably Ann, who fell ill; see TC to JAC, 15 Dec. & the care of two Uncles instead of one for my Uncle whom you know under the name of “ the Dr” was
here all the time; then we went to the countryJohn A. Carlyle stayed in Cheyne Row, May–Aug.; Mary and TC went to Keston, Aug.–Sept.; see TC to CEN, 2 Dec.— —and; but I wont inflict any more upon you in this strain.

My MotherJean Aitken arrived mid-Oct.; see TC to JAC, 4 Dec. came up to us about 8 weeks ago and is still here but returns home next week. She is pretty well; and sends her love to you, and says she is very sorry that she will not see you on this visit. My Uncle is in fairly good health; but good health even at 80 means a great deal of weakness & suffering. He asks to be most kindly remembered to you—& says he was much obliged for your kind birthday Note to him.

I should like to hear how you and yours are,Maria Price m., 1868, Henry Henshaw (1845–80), corn merchant; they had four children and lived in Biggleswade, Bedfordshire; see 43:27543:biographical notes. and how things are prospering with you. I shall be greatly pleased if you can come up for a two or three hours visit someday before very long; and we could then have a long exhaustive talk. I am hardly ever from home but a post card the day before would ensure my not being away anywhere. Excuse my long silence & excuse too this poor scrawl.

closer.salute:
With love and all good wishes, dear Friend
Affectionately yours

div3.sourceNote: MA-MW [MAI-MEW], 2 Jan. MS: NLS Acc. 9207. Hitherto unpbd. Meta Wellmer, German writer and teacher, regular correspondent of both TC and Mary Aitken. Mary misdated 1875.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO META WELLMER

docBody.p: Your kind present to my Uncle & the two welcome little notesWellmer wrote to both Mary and to TC, Nov. 1875, sending birthday greetings to TC, and saying that she was sending “einen Shawl oder cache-nez [muffler]” [ed.'s trans.], which she had knitted herself, for TC's daily walks (MS: NLS 1771.265). arrived a few days after instead of, as you intended, a few days before the Birthday and for all of them I take almost the first opportunity I have had to send you our cordial thanks. I have often intended to write to you; but have put off from week to week & month to month, as my habit and temperament make me prone to do, until I have grown too much ashamed even to offer an apology!

We were much surprized to hear of your being in Spain;Wellmer had been in Madrid since mid-Sept. as governess to the two das. of Sofia, b.
Troubetzkov (1836–98), duchess of Alburquerque, Charlotte (1858–83) and Mathilde (1863–1944). and hope you will like it as well at least as Switzerland.Wellmer wrote that she had gone to a vegetarian health resort in Switzerland in May for four months, where she had benefited from the healthy air, the bathing, and long walks. We were quite disappointed on the 4th Decr that there was no letter from you amongst the host that arrived for my Uncle, as we feared that you were perhaps too ill to write; but it all came right.

We here have been going on much as usual for the most part. My Uncle is really fairly well in health; able to walk about as usual,—indeed you would have been surprised to see him sally out when the snow was lying thick on the ground with a large pair of stockings drawn over his boots (to prevent his slipping) looking, as someone remarked, “like a gallant Zouave.”Zouaves were soldiers, usually from French light infantry regiments, who traditionally wore wide, baggy trousers with knee boots or leggings. He can read still for three or four hours at a sitting & his chief enjoyment is in a good book. He has generally friends to accompany him in his afternoon walks; but the misfortune is that they come like misfortunes themselves, “never singly but in battalions”;Cf. Hamlet 4.5. so that one day he has three or four & the next none at all.— My Mother (my Uncle's Sister) has been paying us a visit for the last two months; but she is just about returning home again.

You say that there may be a chance of your being in Brittany by & by;Wellmer wrote to Mary, Nov. 1875, that the “Duchess of Alburquerque owned a villa in Trouville [Brittany, N France] and travels with her family to stay there for a month every year” [ed.'s trans.], and she hoped that perhaps they might be able to meet (MS: NLS 1771.267). if you come to England I hope you will come & see us. We have never any visitors except an Uncle, Dr Carlyle, who sometimes stays for a month or two in summer. If you could put up with such entertainment as is possible here (for my time is so very much taken up with my Uncle that I have hardly any to spare for other concerns); I should be greatly pleased if you would pay us a visit for a week or two; and you could in this way see my Uncle & we could become further acquainted. What do you say to this? My only fear is that you will be disappointed if you should come; but at least you would like to see my Uncle.— — We did not go to Scotland this year; it is a long journey & my Uncle seemed rather to dread it. We went instead to a pretty little place in Kent,Keston Lodge; see TC to CEN, 2 Dec. 1875. only 14 miles from here, which with servants & all equipments was lent to him for as long as he liked & we there passed two months very quietly and pleasantly. We had a nice pony & small carriageSee 49:238TC to EF, 15 Sept. 1875. in which we drove
on an average about 16 miles a day (I being charioteer) & in this way we had many lovely drives in the beautiful country round about, which was all new to me & mostly new to my Uncle. I am sure it did him as much good as going to Scotland would have done, for he did not lose the strength he had gained by a long railway journey at the end of our visit.

My Uncle sends his best regards & many thanks for the pretty & most useful little muffler as well as for your kind Letter and with love from myself and many cordial new years wishes, dear Miss Wellmer I remain always

div3.sourceNote: TC-grand-duke of Weimar [GDW], 10 Jan. MS: Thüringisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Weimar. Hitherto unpbd. Charles Alexander (1818–1901), grand duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach 1853–1901, m., 1842, Princess Sophie of the Netherlands (1824–97); see 48:30TC to JAC, 20 Jan. 1872.
div3.head: TC TO THE GRAND-DUKE OF WEIMAR

docBody.p: Your Royal Highness has been so gracious as to honour me with a Letter from your own hand, in reference to those German congratulations on my poor 80th Birthday;The grand-duke wrote, 28 Dec. 1875, to congratulate TC on his 80th birthday: “I do it in fact and particularly at the end of a year which gathered round you the testimony of admiration and attachment of many German men of science”; see TC to JAC, 4 Dec. 1875. for which most kind procedure on Your Highness's part be pleased to accept my warmest thanks and acknowledgements. Surely it is a great honour and favour; and I may justly give it grateful welcome, coming from such a source. To Weimar and its high rulers I have owed many pleasant passages in my life;TC had first met Charles Alexander in Chelsea in 1847 (see 21:246–47TC to JCA, 30 Jun. 1847), and he had then visited his family in Weimar in 1852 (see 27:301–2TC to JWC, 25 Sept. 1852). Weimar for above fifty years has been dear and venerable to me beyond all German Cities;Charles Alexander continued: “Weimar has a right in my eyes to worship the author who feels so well the duties this name invokes, knowing so well its history.” Weimar is where Goethe had lived and worked for most of his life. and it may well continue so to the end of my life.

Kindest thanks to the high Lady, your Grand-Duchess, as well as to yourself; and may all good ever attend you and yours. Along with this I have sent a poor little Book,TC sent The Early Kings of Norway: Also an Essay on the Portraits of John Knox (1875). most probably the last I shall ever write, which I hope you
will persuade your amiable and illustrious Consort to accept, and perhaps to read in gentle remembrance of me.
I am and remain

closer.salute: Your faithful Ritter [Knight] and Obedient Servant,

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 15 Jan. MS: NLS 528.49. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: It seems a long time since I have written a special Letter to you; but indeed there has not latterly been anything special to say. Our weather is dark and miserable, continual cold and yet no right black frost ever seen through the winter, continual contributions of snow the streets kept in a perpetual state of slippery danger. Hitherto in fact to all weak old creatures, a dirty and miserable season. You can tell Jean,Jean Aitken had returned home to Dumfries early Jan.; see MAI to MEW, 2 Jan. however, that I seem to have got over the wretched habit of awakening about 6 a. m. into mere flutter of nerves; & now sleep in the old fashion a heavy nightmarish set of sleeps, seldom ending until after 8 oclock. For a week past I have given up my cold bath in the morning; I cannot yet say whether with much advantage or not; but if no new snow fall I mean to try it once again before long.

My reading has mainly been out of one Palacky's History of Bohemia,FrantiŠek Palacký (1798–1876), Czech historian and politician, Geschichte von Böhmen, Grösstentheils nach Urkunden und Standschriften [History of Bohemia, mostly based on Documents and Manuscripts], 4 vols. (Prague, 1845–60). concerning the Hussite warsThe Hussite wars, 1419–34, were sparked by the execution of Jan Hus (ca. 1372–1415), Czech theologian, philosopher, and religious reformer who denounced corruption in the church and the papacy, and who promoted the ideas of the English reformer John Wycliffe (ca. 1320s–84; ODNB). He was thus regarded as heretical and was excommunicated and finally burnt at the stake. The combined forces of the papacy, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Bohemian monarchy were unable to defeat the Hussite followers, and an eventual peaceful compromise was reached. there of which I could never get any clear idea at all before. Palacky (who wants to be called Pallatzky) is an aged Zech patriot, who has written this Book in 8 or 9 octavos by order of the Zech Parliament of Prague, & done many other Zech labours of an antiquarian kind, which he translates constantly into legible German, seems to be a very good painstaking old Gentleman; but dreadfully in need of being condensed into one Vol. instead of 9; &, it must be owned, is altogether wearisome reading & even
in the parts relating to Huss, is a dismal historical swamp with, here & there, bright islands of real historical importance intervening at great distances as the whole book by Harrison's stupidity &Palacky's has got bound three voll. into oneRobert Harrison (1820–97; ODNB), librarian of the London Library 1857–93; see 36:28136:biographical notes. The Catalogue of the London Library (1865) describes Palacký's book: “Vol. 1, 2. Urgeschichte bis 1306. Vol. 3. 3 Parts, 1378–1439. Vol. 4. Parts 1, 2, 1439–1471” (565); TC was presumably was mainly interested in vol. 3, which covered the period of the Hussite wars. the reading of it with rather margins in this dark weather with these bad eyes has been a work of difficulty: but in short I have got something out of it worth having & it has been better worth doing than nothing at all. There are still two books concerning Huss one with a preface by Luther, which I expect to get from the Library today.Jean Hus, Lettres de, écrits durant son Éxil et dans sa Prison, avec une Préface de Martin Luther, trad. du Latin en Français, et suivies d’une Notice sur les Œuvres de J. Hus, par É. de Bonnechose (1846); see Catalogue of the London Library (1865) 372. The other book was possibly Fr. Böhringer, Die Kirche Christi und ihre Zeugen, oder die Kirchengeschichte in Biographieen, vol. 1 bound in two parts, vol. 2 bound in five parts (Zurich, 1842–56). Part 5 includes a biography of Hus; see Catalogue of the London Library (1865) 84. These also I will read & these only. If I had still hands & eyes, which I haven’t, there might be fished out of this wide Dismal Swamp a really pretty bit of history. But alas, alas!— Copies of the Early Kings of Norway have been sent both to the Princess of Waldeck, who was very good to me at Mentone & sent a Telegram on Decr 4Helena Wilhelmine Henriette Pauline Marianne (1831–88), princess of Waldeck; see 44:150TC to JAF, 10 Feb. 1867, and 46:84TC to AT, 8 Oct. 1869; TC had met her in Menton, Dec. 1867. She sent TC a telegram, 4 Dec. 1875: “Receive for your eightieth birthday the warm congratulations from a friend whose deep gratitude for received kindness is everlasting and guiding words of wisdom and comfort the star and treasure of her life.” & to the Grand Duchess of Weimar, whose Grand Dukes autograph letter to me seemed to require some acknowledgement;See TC to GDW, 10 Jan.—it is here enclosed; though except its autograph character you will find little to distinguish it. I have also had to write to Tom WilsonThomas Wilson, old friend of TC, living in Weimar. & again a little note to the Grand Duke about introducing Henry Taylor's Son to the notabilities & curiosities there; about which Taylor himself seemed very anxious.Sir Henry Taylor (1800–86; ODNB), poet and diplomat, old friend of TC's; see 49:23TC to JAC, 22 Nov. 1873, and 37:27437:biographical notes; he wrote, early Jan.: “My boy Harry is going to Weimar there to remain for a few months & give his mind to German. Do you know any Germans there, & can you give him introductions? … He can speak German fluently, if not correctly, but he aspires to a more consummate knowledge of the language. He is a good fellow & people do not find him disagreeable.” He wrote again, 11 Jan., thanking TC for his help; he continued: “I am so glad that you remember Harry & that you liked him…. I hope we have made a good choice now in sending him to Weimar. We hear that the Grand Duke himself [see TC to GDW, 10 Jan.] & his Court & the society of the Town are of a literary turn & Harry has now I think learnt enough of the language to profit by it in conversation.” Harry Ashworth Taylor (ca. 1854–1907). Happily all that is now done & my hands washed of it Deo gratias. Of my acquaintances here I have seen less than usual, nor
indeed care to see. My usual companion has been Froude whom I generally see every alternate day & who is much the most interesting company I have & is always conspicuously kind & careful about me. Poor Forster is close confined to his house mostly to his bedroom & is rarely visible when I call. Probably not intrinsically worse I think; but dreadfully depressed in spirits by the dark snowy weather. No more at present but thanks to Jean for her Letter & my hearts blessing to one & all of you. We hope you got the 8 HedderlyJames Hedderly (1815–85), Chelsea photographer and sign painter, living at 21 Riley St. He published two photographs, Nov. 1875, taken from different points of view, of Joseph E. Boehm's terra-cotta statue of TC, which had been exhibited at the Royal Academy the previous summer; see 49:203TC to CEN, 1 April 1875. John A. Carlyle wrote, 21 Jan.: “I wrote to Mary at the beginning of this week to acknowledge receipt of the eight large photographs of Boehm's statue.” photographs or will soon get.
docBody.closer: Ever your affecte / T. Carlyle

postscript.p: Thanks for writing to Alick in Canada; alas poor Alick.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 29 Jan. MS: NLS 528.50. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your agreeable Letter has come this morning & in spite of the dark fog been read with pleasure. I agree altogether with your criticism on Lagarde,Paul Anton de Lagarde (1827–91), Biblical scholar and prof. of oriental languages at the Univ. of Göttingen, and leading nationalist and anti-Semite theorist; see 49:219TC to PL, 20 May 1875. John A. Carlyle wrote, 28 Jan.: “I return Lagarde's little book, as it occurs to me that you may wish to keep it along with the other which you got last year. I have read it all in spite of its fantastical orthography & short-headed fs, like ts, which are painful to old eyes. I think he takes too dark a view of every thing. There are many passages in the book which shew that he is a man of great acuteness & talent with all his peculiarities.” Lagarde wrote, 12 Dec. 1875: “Today I took the liberty of sending you a copy of my pamphlet on the present state of the German empire. As you love Germany, I trust you will read what I have written out from a heart full of sorrow. / Wishing that God may save your venerable life as a model to his children.” Lagarde, Ueber die gegenwärtige Lage des deutschen Reichs [On the Current Situation of the German Empire] (Göttingen, 1876). & will as you suggest have the two pamphlets stitched together;—the first of the two, I believe, was dissolved into types again before ever being sent to the public for reading.For Lagarde's previous book, Öber das Verhältnis des deutschen Staates zu Theologie, Kirche und Religion. Ein Versuch Nicht-Theologen zu orientieren [On the Relationship of the German States to Theology, Church and Religion: An Attempt at Orientation for Non-Theologians] (Göttingen, 1873), and its subsequent withdrawal, see 49:219TC to PL, 20 May 1875, and 221TC to WWE, 24 May 1875. Lagarde seems an impatient crotchetty person, probably
much of an IshmaeliteA descendant of Ishmael, eldest son of Abraham; a wanderer or outcast; see Gen. 16:11–12. about Gottingen perhaps he will get more wit as he gets on.— In the Medicine Book, vol 1,John wrote: “The Geschichte der Medicin [History of Medicine], a big book, & first volume, which Jean brought me from you, & wh had come from Göttingen too, was long-winded & intolerable as a whole; but by dexterous skipping I got through all the best parts & was much amused by many of them.” See TC to JAC, 29 April. I eagerly looked for some intelligible account of Paracelsus, the Father of Quacksilvers,Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, known as Paracelsus (ca. 1493–1541), German-Swiss physician and alchemist; he pioneered the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine, and from his studies of medieval alchemy believed mercury to be particularly important, along with sulphur and salt. TC is apparently punning on the words “quack” for doctor and “quicksilver,” the liquid form of mercury. I mean the first introducer of Mercury as a medicine; which indeed in my experience is pretty much the only medicine I ever got the least good of & certainly deserves the thanks of mankind: but of this truly remarkable human being I find neither in Vol i nor any where else the smallest intelligible account. In that old Book of yours which is now lost, or rather in your speech about it is the only glimmer of human tidings I have ever had of that notable son of Adam.

We had our visit from Jamie and his Grandson,Their brother Jamie had been visiting his widowed son-in-law, William Scott, in Birmingham, and was taking his grandson, John James Scott, home for a visit. which went off very well, all according to Jamie's own programme; for we pressed him to stay for a week; but he stuck firm to his project of two days Monday afternoon to Wednesday morning & was bent to be home again before Saturday night (that is, the night now coming): he looked well, much better than I expected; & talked in his own handfast, true & original manner about all sorts of Annandale things to me in a way I really liked. His Grandson is a good & clever little boy, but unfortunately seems weak of constitution; & will be difficult to bring up & educate in his unfortunately orphaned or quasi orphaned condition.His mother, Jenny Scott, d. 1 Feb. 1874; see 49:54MAI to JCHA, 3 Feb. 1874, and 57–58TC to JAC, 4 Feb. 1874. Jamie had a thought of taking him over to Scotsbrig for a month or two before the Bath School,The Bath Row School, Birmingham, initially called the Piggott School, one of several established after the Education Act of 1831 for the children of the poor; however the excellence of some of these schools meant that they were often oversubscribed by children from the middle classes. which seemed otherwise good & promising, were entered upon.

I am in great haste today hourly expecting poor Allingham with some rubbish translated from Goethe which he needs my help to prepare for presentation in his Magazine.Allingham recorded in his diary, 29 Jan.: “To C. 12.30, and stayed three hours, examining with him Goethe's Sprüche [Sayings], the original, and an English translation by a lady” (Allingham Diary 143); see 49:252TC to JAC, 26 Oct. 1875. Excerpts from Goethe's Sprüche in Prosa: Maximen und Reflexion (1833), translated by the German-born English poet and translator Mathilde Blind (1841–96), were pbd. as “Maxims and Reflections, from the German of Goethe,”
Fraser's Magazine 13 (March 1876): 338–48. But I hope to write shortly again and tell you more
minutely the insignificant “no news” we have. In fact after assuring you that we are in our usual state, going on without misadventure worthy of notice, there is nothing more that need be said. I have been reading a singular book or rather a book about highly singular things namely John Hus, Ziska & the terrible & wonderful Hussite Wars,Jan Žižka (ca. 1360–1424), Czech general and Hussite military leader; for Jan Hus and the Hussite wars, see TC to JAC, 15 Jan. which are far too little known to modern Europe. Our weather is damp & warm & so involved in mist & hideous London fog as I have not seen weather for years.— Give my love to Jean James & all the rest. Ever your affectionate Brother

div3.sourceNote: TC-JT [JTY], 31 Jan. Typescript: Royal Institution TYP/1.209. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN TYNDALL

docBody.p: Till the day before your letter came, I had heard no whisper of the glorious news:Tyndall wrote 27 Jan., announcing his forthcoming marriage: “During many a scramble in the Alps, during many a little excursion in England, during many an hour in her own home I have had occasion to observe the temper, character, and general qualities of body & soul of Louisa Hamilton, eldest daughter of Lord Claud Hamilton, and I thought, long before I took more than a theoretic interest in her, that I had never met a stronger, tenderer, more nobly self-renouncing nature than hers. She is not what you would call handsome, save when the light from within makes her far more than handsome. Well this noble girl has taken it into her head to prefer me to others, and she is willing to come and share my modest rooms at the Royal Institution.” you know of yourself what pleasure it would give me and how with my whole heart I congratulate you on so auspicious and fortunate an event. I have seen your excellent young lady several times but have not properly made any real acquaintance with her; I shall esteem it a great honour and pleasure if you will bring her down hither the first day that suits.Tyndall wrote: “You must allow me to bring her to see you some day.”
Invoking every blessing on you and her,
docBody.closer:
I remain / Ever affectionately and gratefully
Yours, / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 5 Feb. MS: 528.51. Pbd.: A. Carlyle, NL 2:325–26 inc. Quot: Wilson, Carlyle 6:380. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I am just returned from Kensal Green and poor Forster's funeral,John Forster d. at his home, Palace Gate House, 1 Feb. The Daily News reported, 7 Feb.: “The remains of the late Mr. John Forster were on Saturday morning, at ten o’clock, removed from Palace-Gate house, Kensington, for interment in Kensal-green Cemetery. The funeral cortège consisted of an unplumed hearse, four mourning coaches, and two private carriages. Among those who followed were:—Lord Lytton, Mr. Thomas Carlyle, Mr. J. A. Froude, Mr. Henry Dickens, Mr. Chitty…. [U]pon the procession being formed from the mortuary chapel to the grave, Mr. Carlyle walked side by side with the new Viceroy of India [Lytton]. The polished oak coffin, which was laden with flowers, was placed in the same tomb in which the remains of Mr. Forster's sister already reposed.” For Forster's sister Elizabeth, see TC to JAC, 1 March. Henry Fielding Dickens (1849–1933), sixth son of Charles Dickens. For a portrait of John Forster, see 22. which has occupied me in personal activity for all the morning (indeed a good part of the night); but which, thanks in great part to Mary's precautions & assiduities I dont think has done me any special damage great as have been the confusions, fasheries, and chaotic sorrows & reflections connected with it and him ever since his sudden removal from among us. Nobody I believe expected so sudden a death. I had called at the door on Sunday last & there met Dr QuainDr. Richard Quain (1816–98; ODNB), physician; see 45:101TC to JF, 2 March 1868. just stepping out, who told me cheerfully that Forster, who had been suffering much in previous days was today a shade better. Tuesday morning following Quain was sent for hurredly between 8 & 9; & before 12 he appeared here & by cautious degrees informed me, with considerable emotion of his own that poor Forster was no more. It is the end of a chapter in my life which had lasted, with unwearied kindness & helpfulness wherever possible on Forster's part, for above 40 years. Today, contrary to expectation, I found myself next after Lord Lytton,Edward Robert Bulwer Lytton, close friend of Forster's, recently appointed Viceroy of India. constituted chief mourner; I and the Lawyer ChittyJoseph William Chitty, one of the executors of Forster's will; Forster had studied under Chitty's father, Thomas Chitty, lawyer, legal writer, and teacher at Univ. Coll., London, 1828. along with Lytton heading the mournful procession, wh. was at an hour much too early for me. Mary, however, had provided every thing that was possible to secure me from trouble or injury; & I got home, accompanied by Froude, in Mrs Forster's own carriage about half past 12 & have now at least got into natural temperature again and hope there is no injury done. The event is really a
sorrowful one & practically a very considerable loss but as in all cases we have to adjust ourselves under it, & be thankful for what of human good there has been in it, without repining that it has come to an end. To poor Forster himself it has clearly been an immense deliverance from long years of pain & distress.
John Forster
Thomas Carlyle Papers, Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Columbia University in
the City of New York

Your kind Letter with the Canada enclosuresJohn A. Carlyle wrote, 3 Feb.: “I have this afternoon [received] the enclosed two letters from Canada…. Please return young Alick's when you have done with. Mrs Holden's [their niece] you need not send back.” Their nephew Alexander (Alick) Carlyle, son of Alick Carlyle in Canada. John had written, 21 Jan., that he was expecting letters from Canada, particularly from young Alick: “Alick is a member of the Senate of the Council in the Albert College, & I daresay he will have plenty of work there, & be happier than he has hitherto been as a schoolmaster.” See also 49:247TC to JAC, 2 Oct. 1875. came duly to hand; & I might have talked to you about several small incidents, & operations about reading &c; but I must forbear all that today. I was very glad of the Canada Letter. I am daily admonishing myself that I ought absolutely to dictate a word to our dear Alick in his sorrowful state. But my own mood is so gloomy & powerless, I have never yet got it accomplished. I end abruptly;—recommending myself to all my loving ones about you & sending them my blessing, if that could in the least avail them. Surely I will write to some of you in a few days.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 12 Feb. MS: NLS 528.52. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I must be content with a very short Letter to you today; Lady Derby is coming to me, which creates a certain disturbance in the house; & in the evening, by a rather sad inevitability of its kind we are to go and dine with Miss Bromley and her two Stanleys.Caroline Davenport Bromley; the “two Stanleys” were Col. John Constantine Stanley and his wife, Susan Mary Elizabeth, niece of Lady Ashburton, with whom Caroline Bromley was friendly; see 48:161TC to LLA, 11 Feb. 1873. The day is calm and bright, though with a strongish frost in the air, which is very hostile to one's poor old skin. Yesterday and indeed almost every alternate day of late we had a fog as dark as Egypt. Froude and I walked down the Embankment towards Millbank,Millbank, about 2 mi. (3 km.) E of Cheyne Row along the river. and all the way home nothing could be seen but the miserable fog-displaced lamps here and there the wall of the embankment, if one kept close to it as a continuous
guide post. We got home without the least mistake nevertheless though we had encountered various cabs & the like entirely devious & altogether lost in the black element.The Times reported, 12 Feb.: “The severe frost which set in in London on Thursday continued yesterday, and was accompanied by a dense fog. As a consequence, traffic in the streets was considerably retarded; personal locomotion was rendered very difficult and dangerous; the steamboat traffic on the river was suspended, and the service of trains on the various lines in and around London was only carried on with the utmost care.” I hear the frost is general, still stronger in Paris than here, and judge that we have to expect perhaps a considerable spell of it by way of second winter in return for the fair and clear Candlemas day we had. Brother Jamie strongly predicted this before leaving us,—by the by, we never have yet heard whether he brought home with him the little boy Scott or not.Jean Aitken wrote, 13 Feb.: “We too were wondering whether wee J. James had come on to Scotsbrig—but except the briefest of notes from James at Newlands have heard nothing.” She went on to say: “I wd like very much to ask Jamie to come up for a few days (which he seems rather to enjoy) but the Dr makes it impossible to do so with any comfort. He keeps up a constant racket, whereas Jamie likes best to be entirely let alone & left to entertain himself among the rest of us here & not be compelled to take long walks &c &c which he does not want.”

Since you last heard, there has nothing of the least note been passing with us and especially nothing that was sad or bad. Mary & I went up last Monday to Mrs Forster's but merely left cards. She herself was reported, poor lady, to have sunk down among her troubles & to be in worse health than usual, not yet able to see anybody. Nor have I heard anything about poor Forsters affairs (of all which Lord Lytton is left Trustee & Executor). Lytton himself did not know on the day of the funeral whether there was anything considerable or anything at all of the second vol. of Swift left written.Forster had been working on the second volume of The Life of Jonathan Swift; see 49:253–55TC to JAC, 26 Oct. 1875; for the first vol., see 49:225TC to JF, 4 Aug. 1875. Poor Forster, his death has left a great blank to me. For the last forty years he has been a continual item in our life here, always the kindest, helpfullest and cheeriest of men; & suddenly is called away and returns no more. I see plenty of people & might far more; but conversation with them does me little good & except Froude, I have little satisfaction in any company that comes about me. Lecky,William Edward Hartpole Lecky. poor fellow is extremely kind, knows all the news & punctually attends to me on our promenades but his sphere of thinking is altogether insignificant to me. Allingham comes seldomer; perpetually busy with Fraser & as I told himself long ago has a tendency to be a bore. Other company I seldom see except upon constraint. A Letter from NortonNorton wrote, 29 Jan., reporting a meeting with Ralph Waldo Emerson: “I told him that in your last letter you had asked for news of him, and he bade me, if I had occasion to write to you, to give you his love … and that he had come so to depend on his good daughter to write for him, that he had written no letters, otherwise he would surely have written to you…. His spirit is as young as ever, & his looks are not changed since you saw him.” has come this morning. I think it is the only one you will care to read.

Will you thank Jean for her Letter and ask her for a new one as soon as she can feel disposed. Tell her I should like to know if anything has been done about Sister Mary'sJohn A. Carlyle reported to their sister Janet Hanning, 15 Feb.: “Mary… is not very strong now, & has lost almost all her teeth” (MS: Yale). teeth, which often come into my head as a thing desirable. Poor Alick in Canada is daily among my thoughts. I intend, if it prove possible to me, to write to him next week. Adieu, dear Brother, I need not continue this weak stuff the rather as Mary is anxious to have done. I send my kindest love and my best blessings to you all I am & remain
docBody.closer: Ever your affectionate, / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-AC, 15 Feb. MS: MUL. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:326–27 inc; Marrs 786–87. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO ALEXANDER CARLYLE

docBody.p:
It is a long time since you have heard anything direct from me; indeed I more and more have given up the practice of writing altogether, my poor old hands quite refusing to serve me in that matter; and the business even by dictation becoming more, & more unpleasant and unsatisfactory to me. But you may depend upon it, dear Brother, there are few days in which you are not vividly present to my thoughts: and especially since that bodily disorder fell upon you,Alick suffered from asthma; see TC to JAC, 4 Dec. 1875. I and all of us, are anxious & interested about you. I figure you painfully as held down by your bodily sufferings & imprisoned in the house, under the fierce Canadian winter; and often & often ask myself how my poor old Alick is getting on, oppressed with burdens, from which even I am comparatively free. God be with him and assist him, is all I can say to myself! Winter agrees very ill with myself; and we have had rather an ugly time of it since the end of November last, snows & frosts always coming on us now & then, the latest of them hardly over even now. Your cold I figure to myself as far sharper & severer; but on the other hand your sky is oftenest perfectly free; and you have the blessing of pure light in abundance which many times [is] wanting here. The boys are very good in writing to us, especially Alick is, whom we much thank, and beg to continue the charitable process. His promotion & well doing in his new placeSee TC to JAC, 5 Feb.; see also A. Carlyle, Jottings 69–70. is the best tidings we have had from Canada for a long while. Tom,Alick's eldest son, Thomas; TC and his brother John had previously given him financial help; see 42:215TC to JAC, 2 Sept. 1865. also, wrote to me a clear & kind Letter several
months ago; him also thank from me. Good be with them all, poor young fellows; and may their life be worthy of the honest name they carry. I am thankful to Heaven that this implies what can be called a victorious future
for them.

Along with this, or perhaps a day or two before you will receive from the Bank a document bearing Adamson of the British Linen Co's.Samuel Adamson of the British Linen Co. Bank, Dumfries, where TC had an account. signature for the amount of £150,Mary Aitken noted in TC's checkbook: “11 February 1876 / Mr Alexr Carlyle / Bield / £150..0..0” (TC's checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). converted into dollars. This I beg you to accept as a small new year's Gift to the Brother who for so many scores of years has now been dear & true to me to yourself in your imprisonment I fear it cannot do much good but among your loved ones you may find beneficent use for it; & if there is anything of useful that it can procure for yourself right welcome is my dear Brother Alick to it and to much more. Please tell some of them to send me word in the shortest of letters that this poor little transaction is successfully
completed.

I am myself older than you & by nature ought to be weaker; & certainly I am grown as weak almost as if I were a second time a baby: but, by the great goodness of Heaven, I am, as it were quite free from bodily disease & have no illness upon me except simply what is implied in the word old age. Often enough I feel weary of the empty, painful & idle existence I now lead; but the suggestion is never far off; that God's will is the true will for us all in all things; & I look forward with my best patience for the hour that is ever drawing nigher, when the wearied soul shall be summoned to its rest, such “rest” as Gods holy will has appointed and as no man knows has known or ever will know. Perfect submission to that holy will, be it according to our own poor wishes or against them is for all mortals the one perfect rule.

I suppose the Dr sends you punctually enough all newsTheir brother John A. Carlyle, who kept all the family in touch with each other; see 49:192TC to AC, 4 March 1875. that occur amongst the few now interesting to you in Scotland; therefore at present I need not enter into that; indeed my time is done & I have had unexpected interruptions in this letter & am sorry it is on the whole so poor an expression of the feelings I had to put into words. I hope to try another time, if it be permitted me before very long. God ever bless you, my dear Brother. My love & blessing to one & all of you.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 1 March. MS: NLS 528.53. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Here is a Railway Paper which came the other day and might possibly enough have been burnt like other railway rubbish, but appears in reality to be worth £7 odd. I want you to take across to Adamson, and before parting with it to understand how & why it originates in this exceptional way.John A. Carlyle replied, 3 March: “I … have gone to the British Linen Co's Bank. The Gt Northern Railway paper you had enclosed is all right, & must have been sent to you instead of Adamson by mistake of some clerk. It is payable to him, & is the Dividend warrant for £7..10, which your £300 at 5 per cent, invested in that railway, produces for the half year ending 1st March 1876.” TC had been investing in railways for some years; see 45:48TC to JAC, 15 Oct. 1867, and 48:172TC to JAC, 7 March 1873. Mary says that it is some particular railway habit of now & then paying a surplus to Shareholders; & reminds me of what is a fact that a good few years since George CookeJohn George Cooke (1819–80; see 45:22445:biographical notes), stockbroker, and close friend of both TC and JWC. The anecdote of the £20 is untraced. saved for me a sum of some £20; which was in danger of the fire like this; and by your means I shall understand the thing.

Enclosed also today is the fair-Copy which I have not read over of Goethe's Geistes Epochen from the Communications of Hermann.For “Geistesepochen, nach Hermanns neusten Mitteilungen [Epochs of the Human Spirit, based on Hermann's Latest Theories]” (Goethe, Werke, 54 vols. [Stuttgart, 1833] 49:3–6), see 49:257TC to JAC, 6 Nov. 1875. John translated it for TC in Nov. 1875; see 49:260TC to JAC, 20 Nov. 1875. John replied, 3 March: “the ‘Spiritual Epochs,’ wh I return & have read carefully again, looks much better, now that the translation is corrected &fairly written out. But I cannot make out much of the meaning.” Johann Gottfried Hermann (1772–1848), German scholar and philologist, prof. of rhetoric and poetry at Leipzig Univ. The kind of Life of Hermann which I have diligently gone through has yielded me no light on that subject; neither can the Opuscula of Herman the first two volumes of which are for the present sunk irrecoverable out [of] the London Library which must have contained the only two Papers on Mythology that Hermann seems to have written.John wrote, 10 Nov. 1875:“In the old London Library Catalogue I find under Hermannus (Godof.) Opuscula 7 vol. 8 to & his ideas about old mythology might be in one of these vols” (MS: NLS 1775F.196). Hermann's Opuscula [minor literary works], 7 vols. (Leipzig, 1827–39), contains “De Mythologia Graecorum Antiquissima Dissertatio” (Opuscula 2:167–94) and “De Historiæ Graecae Primordiis Dissertatio” (Opuscula 2:195–216); the work is listed in the Catalogue of the London Library (1842) 55. HarrisonRobert Harrison; see TC to JAC, 15 Jan. maintains that they will yet be found
before long; but indeed I care not much whether or not for it seems highly improbable they should throw any light of the least importance on the matter.
Concerning the Tohu wa bohu,Tohu wa-bohu is a Hebrew phrase from Gen. 1:2 meaning desolate and formless, describing the condition of the earth immediately before the creation of light; see 49:257TC to JAC, 6 Nov. 1875. I think I must write to Max MüllerFriedrich Max Müller (1823–1900; ODNB), German-born Sanskritist and philologist, who moved to Britain in 1846; presumably TC wanted his expertise in Middle Eastern languages. or make Froude write. Max was in great gloom when Froude brought him to me for a walk six weeks ago; but no doubt you have heard since that he is to be retained in Oxford after all and so I daresay is pacified by this time.Müller held various positions in Oxford Univ. from 1851, and he was appointed chair of comparative philology in 1868. As a German Lutheran, Müller sometimes clashed with the high-church Oxford dons, and in 1875 he threatened to resign from his position and return to Germany. After considerable public controversy, he decided to remain at Oxford.

I had several other things to say but somebody has come in waiting for poor Mary down stairs and I must close. We are deeply sorry to hear of poor Aird's condition & fear that things may now be drawing to a close with him poor innocent soul. If you have any opportunity please express to him my deep and altogether friendly sympathies, with regret only that they can do him no good.Thomas Aird (1802–76; ODNB), poet and newspaper editor, longtime friend of the Carlyles; see 6:361TC to JAC, 29 March 1833, and 42:38TC to JWC, 24 May 1865. John replied, 3 March: “I have seen Aird this afternoon for a few minutes…. I found him looking weaker than at the beginning of this week. He looks quite resigned & even cheerful. I gave him your message which seemed to gratify him much.” I suppose he like the rest of us is content to be getting to the end of a weary lake of troubles.

I ought to have told you long before this that my new teeth after a good deal of training to their new home have turned out to be a complete success so far as artificial teeth can be. No doubt at all you ought to go to the same artist when you revisit London which I hope may not be a distant date. Remind Sister Jean of Mary's analagous case. I send my love to her and you and all the Hill household; and am ever, dear Brother,
docBody.closer: Your affectionate / T. Carlyle.

div3.sourceNote: MA-JR [MAI-JRU], 7 March. MS: Hilles. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO JOHN RUSKIN

docBody.p: My Uncle's little friend is a sparrow. I did not hear him tell the story about it on Sunday, but when I did, a day or two before, he said “it had been only a small speck of slobber”! He, too, thinks this is the word he used.Ruskin wrote to TC, 6 March: “Was it a sparrow, or robin, I forget, that you were watching the little eyes and ways and pleasures of, when the sense of its having been a bit of yellow jelly not a year before, and the miracle of it, came on you so? I wish I could recollect what you called the egg aspect of it—perhaps Mary can? it was infinitely better than my ‘bit of yellow jelly.’”

We have a good many birds here,—robins, sparrows, & some blackbirds; and last summer a nightingale used to make his “tender and strong” note heard quite close to us; a little robin built her nest in a tool house in the garden adjoining ours (our neighbours left the window open—so that she could always be free even when the door was closed); and thence she sent out nine little redbreasts to the world. They are disposed to be very friendly but we never become intimate because of the cat who usually follows me into the garden. If the poor little things ever reason about a personal devil, I am sure they must think of our Cat and have no doubt about his existence.

My Uncle was much interested in what you said about Humboldt.Alexander von Humboldt (1769–1859), Prussian explorer, naturalist, and geographer. He had missed the passage which you refer to.Ruskin wrote: “I’ve been looking at Humboldt. I see he ‘defines’ the vital force as ‘that which prevents the original affinities from acting’ Not at all which acts itself! What a lovely and cheerful view of life! (Mortal and other) God—as the Preventor of Original Affinities from acting—an omnipotent Drag upon Originality? isn’t it nice?” Ruskin possibly refers to: “Diejenige innere Kraft, welche die Bande der chemischen Verwandtschaft auflöft, und die freie Verbindung der Elemente in den Körpern hindert, nennen wir Lebenskraft [That inner force that breaks the bonds of chemical affinity and prevents the free combination of the elements, we call life force]” (Humboldt, Aphorismen aus den chemischen Physiologie der Pflanzen, trans. Gotthelf Fischer [Leipzig, 1794] 9). For TC's earlier views on Humboldt, see 21:165TC to TCH, 20 Feb. 1847.
My Uncle sends his love & I am always, dear Master and Teacher

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 11 March. MS: NLS 528.54. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: I designed a long letter for you today, but must be content with a very short one. Mary, it seems, has an engagement with the ChadwicksProbably Edwin Chadwick (1800–1890; ODNB), social reformer and retired civil servant, his wife, Rachel, b. Kennedy (1802–91), and da. Marion (1844–1928); known to TC since the early 1840s; see 43:14JWC to MR, 16 Oct. 1865. They lived at Park Cottage, East Sheen, Surrey. & will miss the train if she be not let go in a few minutes.

I am in tolerable ordinary health; nothing to complain of specially but total inability to get anything of the nature of work done, except it be mournfully musing in my own mind on the chaos of immensities & eternities with which one is surrounded in his closing years in this world. I read some hours every
day; but my books are seldom good for anything and the question often rise, Cui bono? I have been twice in Westminster Abbey on solemn enough occasions. First as Witness to Tyndall's marriageTyndall's wedding, 29 Feb.; see TC to JT, 31 Jan. Tyndall wrote, 25 Feb.: “The thought of you naturally associates itself with the most solemn act of my life. I dreamt of you looking on for 15 minutes in the Abbey on Tuesday. Is the dream realizable? My few friends—all of them your friends—start with me … at 2 P.M. walk to Henry VII's Chapel, where … Stanley will go through the brief ceremony. We have no breakfast, no speechifying,—nothing but the shortened service. What a delight it would be to both of us to have you there!” about ten days ago, Tyndall, you perhaps know, has made a great match, a Niece of the Duke of Abercorn's,Tyndall's bride was Louisa Hamilton, niece of James Hamilton (1811–85; ODNB), 1st duke of Abercorn. Tyndall himself being, as one hears, the son of a blacksmith in Carlo,Tyndall's father was John Tyndall (1792–1847), shoemaker and constable, of Leighlinbridge, co. Carlow, Ireland.—but possessed of a Genius! His Bride is a comely, bright kind of creature of about 30; he is himself 56. There is a great deal of good intrinsically I believe in both the parties. The marriage service as read by Dean StanleyThe ceremony took place in Westminster Abbey. The Morning Post reported, 1 March: “The marriage was celebrated by Dean Stanley, at his especial request, and as a mark of friendship for the learned professor the dean selected the chapel of Henry VII. for the rite. In addition to the parents of the bride and a few relatives and friends there were present Professor Huxley … Mr. Thomas Carlyle, Mr. Spottiswoode … &c.” Arthur Penrhyn Stanley, dean of Westminster. William Spottiswoode (1825–83; ODNB), mathematician and physicist; see 49:244–45TC to JAC, 18 Sept. 1875. was one of the most impressive things I ever heard. My second visit to Westminster Abbey, wh. occurred day before yesterday was of a far more solemn character & altogether mournful without any joy on any side: the funeral of Lady Augusta Stanley,Lady Augusta Stanley d. 1 March; the Times reported, 2 March: “Ever since [she] was attacked by fever at Paris, on her way home from a tour with Dean Stanley in Switzerland she never entirely recovered her health.” The funeral was 9 March. the poor Dean's Wife. I never saw such an assemblage. I think there must have been some 2000 of us in all; & we were kept processioning & wandering about for near two hours before ending in the southern extremity of Henry VII Chapel, where the lamented Lady was laid in her last resting place, a cell or vault of clear dry ashlar about 15 feet deep (with the top removed for the nonce). It is understood to have been by the Queen's precise order; & she herself, they say, was looking on at the conclusion from some private window.Lady Augusta had been lady of the bedchamber, secretary, and friend to Queen Victoria. The Times, 10 March, included a report dated 9 March: “The Queen, accompanied by [three of her daughters] went this morning to the Deanery at Westminster and had an interview with the Dean, and placed wreaths on the coffin of the lamented Lady Augusta Stanley. The Queen and Princesses were afterwards conducted to a private gallery in the Deanery, overlooking the nave of the Abbey, where they witnessed the funeral procession.” Among the many names listed as attending was “the venerable form of Thomas Carlyle.” We were a most miscellaneous, grave & serious assembly the Duke of ArgyllGeorge Douglas Campbell (1823–1900; ODNB), 8th duke of Argyll, politician.
& various Lords were visible in my neighbourhood, also a great many ladies seemingly of rank, with Browning MotleyRobert Browning, poet; John Lothrop Motley, American historian and diplomat. &c &c representative of literature. We heard half a score or more of anthems, without one word of intelligible to the audience, a great many prayers ditto, ditto;Alexander Macmillan (1818–96; ODNB), publisher, wrote to a friend, 11 March: “Carlyle sat next the Archbishop of Canterbury, who occasionally pointed out where in the service they were, and Carlyle peered down with apparent reverential interest” (Charles L. Graves, Life and Letters of Alexander Macmillan [1910] 335). Archibald Campbell Tait (1811–82; ODNB), archbishop of Canterbury 1868–82. & the last prayer of dismissal was pronounced by the poor Dean himself with an air & in a voice that can never be forgotten.

Of other things I will say only that they are all unimportant to me & I will not touch upon them at present. We are expecting to hear soon from you when you design a personal appearance here;John A. Carlyle replied, 13 March: “Some time when the weather becomes less oppressive I may think of going to see you again at Cheyne Row.” the weather is getting more & more endurable, now & then inviting & I can still walk about an hour or so & listen at all times to friendly & rational talk.
For the present accept my blessing one & all of you. Mary wrote to her Mother yesterday. My love may be added here.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 18 March. MS: NLS 528.55. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: We have as no news at all to send you, which at least means no bad news. Our weather has been wild and stormy, as no doubt your own has been and all other people's in this Island but it has now dried up again; and is distinguished by nothing very unpleasant except the high wind, always from the North & West, accompanied, however, by clear skies and copious possibilities or (where not interfered with) realities of March dust,—which should be equal to a King's ransom or to many of them if measured by pecks.

I have been, as it were, totally idle, doing nothing but read and my books
by no means of an inspiring quality. A new life of GodwinC. Kegan Paul, William Godwin, His Friends and Contemporaries, 2 vols. (1876). which Miss Bromley left me, & which is now wrapt up for returning has brought back vividly
enough the stony dull existence & ditto character of that remarkable and once very famous character,William Godwin (1756–1836; ODNB), philosopher and novelist; for TC's first meeting with him, on 15 Aug. 1831, see 5:337TC to JWC, 17 Aug. 1831. now fallen into such oblivion by the actual generation, a dull stony man, with a great deal of strong quality but in a most pedantic wearisome & dull form: the book, too, I found was altogether stupidly written; mostly consisting of dull letters shovelled together in seeming utter disorder & few of them worth reading again I think I got nothing out of it, except some new light and a glow of human pity about poor Mary WolstencroftMary Wollstonecraft (1759–97; ODNB), writer and feminist, author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792); she m. Godwin, 1797, and d. after giving birth to their da., Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin (1797–1851; ODNB), writer. Kegan Paul wrote: “She died in her prime, intellectual and physical…. Yet it may be hoped that in some degree what has here been written may give some a clearer view of the virtues, and a more tender pity for the failings and sorrows of Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin” (William Godwin, His Friends and Contemporaries 1:288).;—& a tragic new example shewn me of the boundless fluctuating nature of human stupidity and of its estimates as to human merit and worth intellectual or other. Another book I got engaged in by Allingham's bringing it to me, a Life of Hazlitt,Probably William Carew Hazlitt, Memoirs of William Hazlitt, 2 vols. (1867). William Carew Hazlitt (1834–19141913; ODNB), writer, grandson of William Hazlitt (1778–1830; ODNB), painter, journalist, critic, essayist.—a very stupid person & one of the worst written books I ever fell in with. The one attraction of it is in the dates of Hazlitts Life to which we ourselves have been contemporary. There is always a kind of wild half painful attraction at the sight of any incident and the dim recollection & what we ourselves were then doing & suffering.For TC's earlier estimation of Hazlitt, see 5:184TC to ADBM, 27 Oct. 1830; John A. Carlyle attended him in his final illness; see 5:163TC to JAC, 18 Sept. 1830, and Carlyle, Reminiscences 368–69. The first vol. of Memoirs covers the years 1778–1820, the second 1821–30. I did not think of reading the second volume at all, which Allingham was himself reading while I read the first, and did not bring me till the first was nearly or altogether done; but I decided at last to read it in what I call the stilting or seven-leagued-boots way & then to fling it out of hand and head for good. I am also engaged on a curious Swiss novel of the lowest rustic kind by a certain Clergyman called Bitzius,Albrecht Bitzius (1797–1854), Swiss pastor and novelist, Uli der Knecht [Ulric the Farm Servant] (Zurich, 1841) (TC's copy, 1854 edn.; Carlyle's House 79). Bitzius wrote under the pseudonym “Jeremias Gotthelf.” Ruskin had sent TC the first vol. of Bitzius's Oeuvres choisies (Paris, Genève, and Neuchâtel, 1859), Oct. 1870; see 47:80TC to JRU, 10 Oct. 1870. Ruskin wrote to Mary Aitken, 4 Feb.: “You should before now have received Ulric der Knecht, and I cannot tell you how very happy I am in the thought of your translating it, with occasionally a flash of guidance or sprinkle of salt from your uncle.— It will give three times the value to the book that it has been so done” (MS: NLS 556.111). near Berne, who died some twelve years ago, and is a great favourite with Ruskin. He is a most thick skinned, dull & potent Rhinoceros of a man & barely repays the
difficulty of reading him; but the solid practical sense & clear practical intellect which he has about a thing so new and strange carries one on in spite of his perpetual longeur. There has come also a biggish German book in celebration of the Philadelphia centenaryPossibly Welt-Austellung in Philadelphia 1876. Deutsche Abtheilung. Amtlicher Katalog [International Exhibition, Philadelphia,1876. German Department. Official Catalogue] (Berlin, 1876). The Centennial International Exhibition of 1876, to celebrate the signing of the American Declaration of Independence, was held in Philadelphia, 10 May–10 Nov. 1876. that is to be; but of this I have yet read nothing nor I think almost ever shall.TC indicated a new paragraph here.

Yesterday there came to me Motley the American ex-Excellency;John Lothrop Motley; he had been U.S. minister to Austria, 1861–67, and to Britain, 1869–70. and we had a long walk together down the embankment & circuitously on through the eligiblest streets to Hyde Park Corner; by no means very interesting for most of the talk was picked out of myself rather than otherwise; but to be roused up & forced to talk for an hour or so has its useful effects on a torpid old mind, too; Motley's bookMotley's most recent work was The Life and Death of John Barneveld, Advocate of Holland; with a view of the primary causes of the Thirty Years’ War, 2 vols. (1874). had more talent in it than I gave him credit for; but he is by no means a deep or a genial man, though lively enough in discourse & pretty well read both in German & other books. His health & spirits seem to be greatly improved since last year;Motley suffered from some form of paralysis; see 49:256–57TC to JAC, 6 Nov. 1875. but something of paralysis has again strangely appeared in one of his eyes which after a few minutes reading obstinately sinks blind & reduces him to the necessity of being read to, which he says he cannot stand at all; so that walking, wandering about & making calls has to be his main employment. I get but little good of him & indeed do not see him often. Mrs Forster is said to be getting into more & more
composure; but we have not seen her for the last ten days, though calling twice or thrice. The Kensington Museum fools have accepted the bequest of poor Forster's Library, which is worth many thousands of pounds; & are to build an apartment for it & comply with the conditions of the will.For Forster's bequest, see TC to JAC, 1 March. Froude strongly urges me to comply with a message of Lord Shaftesbury's & be one of a deputation to Home-Secretary Cross on the subject of Vivisection on Monday next.Following the publication of a report by a Royal Commission on Vivisection, 8 Jan. (see 49:229–30MAI to GHOG, 28 Aug. 1875), there was increased political pressure on the government to address the issue. A deputation, led by Lord Shaftesbury, president of the Victoria Street Society for the Protection of Animals Liable to Vivisection, was to meet Richard Assheton Cross (1823–1914; ODNB), home secretary 1874–80, on 20 March, to press for immediate action. Parliament passed the Cruelty to Animals Act, 15 Aug. 1876, which restricted the practise of vivisection and instituted a licensing system for animal experimentation. “Cardinal” Manning being one of the number I altogether
declineHenry Edward Manning (1808–92; ODNB), archbishop of Westminster 1865–92, cardinal 1875–92, head of the Catholic Church in England. Frances Power Cobbe (1822–1904; ODNB), feminist and leading antivivisectionist, wrote later: “Mr. Carlyle supported our Anti-vivisection Society from the outset, for which I was very grateful to him; but having promised to join our first important deputation to the Home Office [20 March], to urge the Government to bring in a Bill in accordance with the recommendations of the Royal Commission, he failed at the last moment to put in an appearance, having learned that Cardinal Manning was to be also present. I was told that he said he would not appear in public with the Cardinal, who was, he thought, ‘the chief emissary of Beelzebub in England!’” (Life of Frances Power Cobbe, by Herself, 2 vols. [1894] 2:165). & am peremptory upon it; but am to consider if I cannot write two or three words on the subject itself addressed to Lord Shaftesbury;—but am rather inclined to think I had perhaps better not.— — Poor Mary by some accident did not sleep last night or slept very badly & is suffering from headache &c as she writes so I will end here this most worthless of letters. Give my kindest love to Sister Jean who no doubt will write to me someday by & by; to James & all the rest,
docBody.closer:
I am & remain / dear Brother
Your ever affectionate / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 21 March. Addr: Care of General Stanton / H.B.M.'s Consul General /Cairo / Egypt. PM: Chelsea, 22 March 1876. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.p: Two days ago, I received your Letter, written at Denderah,Dendera, Egyptian town on the W bank of the Nile, about 37 mi. (60 km.) N of Luxor, site of a huge complex of ancient temples. 27 Feb. which was a great pleasure to me; all the more as it was a great rarity too. From time to time I have heard about you all through winter, but from your own hand nothing or next to nothing since you left Kent House solitary. It gratifies me much that you have had hitherto so prosperous & successful a journey, & most of all that it has so much improved your health, which indeed I think must have miserably suffered had you continued in these climates, through such a winter as we have had. In the end of May I will look forward to seeing you again much improved after all these far wanderings.Lady Ashburton had left Britain for Egypt, Nov. 1875, planning to be away for six months; see 49:255TC to JAC, 26 Oct. 1875. She returned early June; see TC to LLA, 16 Oct.

Poor Forster is indeed a great loss to me. For above forty years I had enjoyed his presence with me in the world, always friendly, kind & cheerful to both of us that were here & in the last ten years since I was left alone such a warm evercheerful wise & judicious help in all manner of things as one man rarely can afford to another. To the last I had not, naturally the least anticipation of surviving him; but so it has turned out, & I am again in many respects, especially in all that relates to business left alone. He was a man of great practical capacities & social good qualities,—a man full of skill in all that could be called business: his death is a very great loss to me as to yourself.Lady Ashburton wrote, 27 Feb.: “We are brothers in sorrow—having both lost what we never never can find again—most truly & tenderly do I mourn with you in the death of dear beloved Mr Forster—where shall I ever again find such generous, devoted friendship, such a tender heart, with such a strong wise heart— nowhere…. I fear to you also he will leave a blank that never can be filled.” Forster had helped Lady Ashburton in various ways, including supervising the building of Kent House; see 48:47. The thought of him comes up in strangely new figure before me, and mournfully occupies much of my time since I saw him laid in Kensal Green and for ever hidden from my eyes.— I called on Mrs Forster on Sunday last, and sat an hour with her after the two ChittysPresumably Joseph Chitty, one of Forster's executors (see TC to JAC, 5 Feb.), with either his father, Thomas, or his wife, Clara. who had been calling went away. She is gradually getting into a wholesome composure. She goes little out; tells me that she is saddest of all when driving about alone in the tumult of the Street; but has a great many pious employments & settlings and adjustings to do at home in memory of him she has lost, which yield her more of peace. She means by & by to sell her house and take a smaller oneEliza Forster put Palace Gate House up for auction, May 1876, but it failed to sell, and she continued to live there until her death; see Davies, John Forster 261. somewhere near these Chittys, who are her husbands's oldest friends.

Miss Bromley comes now & then to see me and has settled for a month or two in her new house, where I also have been (12 Montague Square) a comfortable, commodious looking house, which she likes well on trial. She suffers more or less from the winter colds, but is in much better spirits, I think, than when you left. Latterly she has purchased for herself a little villa somewhere near, or on, Banstead Downs;Banstead Downs, Surrey, about 7 mi. (11 km.) N of Reigate, 20 mi. (32 km.) S of London. not many miles from Reigate and about 22 from London thither she has at this time retired to get rid of a “face-ache” but promises to call here some day this week. She punctually enquires about you; but I think gets no direct intelligence more than I. The Stanley embryoMadeline Cecilia Carlyle Stanley, b. 2 July, da. of John and Susan Stanley; see TC to JSTA, 2 July. I heard of some time ago, I think almost from the first and am engaged as
Godfather, if I live so long. The “Emma Mine”John Constantine Stanley was appointed, Nov. 1871, one of three British directors of the Emma Silver Mine, Utah, a depleted resource that its promoters, Senator William Morris Stewart (1827–1909) of Nevada, and his business partner, James E. Lyon, tried to sell to London investors. They persuaded the U.S. ambassador to Britain, Robert Schenck (1809–90), also a director, to use his influence to persuade prominent members of the aristocracy and business community to join the board and purchase shares. The Emma Mine scandal was eventually exposed by a United States congressional investigation in 1876, and British participants lost the bulk of their investments. still hangs theoretically about Stanley more or less; but he seems to understand that practically he is out of it. It is currently reported also that the scandalous Baron GrantThe scheme was promoted by Albert Grant, born Abraham Gottheimer (1831–99; ODNB), financier and company promoter, regularly accused of fraud and corruption, who issued a prospectus that estimated profits of £800,000 a year. He had been awarded the title of Baron in the Italian nobility, 1868; see 49:125TC to JRU, 15 July 1874. is actually to be exploded in regard to that and perhaps some of his other dealings, which will be a real comfort to me, I should think & to all that remains honest in England.

My own physical sufferings from the fitful and capricious winter which gives us hard frost & new showers of snow or sleet with boisterous winds, even at this late date of March; but I cannot trace any specific disease that has come to afflict me, nothing but ever-increasing weakness, the inseparable attendant of ever-increasing old age. I am still able to walk a mile or two, go every morning when the roads are not slippery with frost to the end of the embankment & back before breakfast then latish in the afternoon about as far as Kent House, though seldom exactly past that, and thence home again before dinner and afternoon sleep; this is what they call Euthanasia I believe, and one ought to be thankful for it, more I fear than I am; but I do endeavour to possess my soul in patience & wait until the solemn signal is given: God be with us all. Allah akbar: God is great that is an everlasting truth & the religion that never can grow doubtful to the wise of mankind.

I was at Tyndall's wedding in Westminster AbbeySee TC to JAC, 11 March. & found it, contrary to expectation a very grand and solemn Church service, as read by the Dean, solemnly accepted even by the heterodox Tyndall much more by his loving Spouse; Lord ClaudLord Claud Hamilton, Louisa's father. himself who gave her away was almost at the crying. Since then I have been at an opposite kind of ceremony, the funeral of Lady Augusta StanleySee TC to JAC, 11 March. in the same place. Never in my life did I witness such a ceremony or symbolic solemnity. We were above 2000 in number & were kept processioning & antheming & chanting hither, thither, through all parts of the sublime edifice for about two hours long; then dismissed at the outer or
eastern end; the Dean himself pronouncing in a most sonorous, strong & heavy laden voice the blessing of dismissal,—& the Queen's Majesty looking privately in upon it, it was said, from a window above. She herself I believe was Authoress of the whole ceremonial, which everyone seemed to consider with disfavour rather than otherwise.

Mary's JournalMary Florence Baring, Lady Ashburton's da., was keeping a diary of her Egyptian travels. will be very interesting to me if I live to read it. No doubt Egypt must have cast a great deal of seeds various in kind over that fertile young mind of hers: May they be blessedly instructive to her & fruitfully productive in the years that are to come. My best love to her and to her dear Mama, who I hope will keep her appointment to be here before May end.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 25 March. MS: NLS 528.56. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:436. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Thanks for your punctuality in finishing off that Helen BrownPossibly Helen Hastie, b. Brown (ca. 1801–86), wife of Robert Hastie (ca. 1802–78), carter. bit of charity. I meant to send you the £5 which is my share of it this very day; but Mary reminds me that there is not only the price of my new slippers (which are very welcome to me & a perfect fit) still due to somebody at The Hill; but also of “four shirts” which I have heard of for some time as being to come “next week”;John A. Carlyle wrote, 20 March: “By this post a pair of slippers wh you have long been expecting will be sent off to you.” John then replied, 27 March; “Maggie wrote yesterday to Mary & would tell her for what reason your shirts had been delayed by Mrs Gordon.” Mrs Gordon unidentified further. so soon as these arrive, I can liquidate the whole matter, with only one signature instead of two or perhaps more. Helen Brown appears to be a very feckless, useless creature I remember her, as a foolish young lassie; and her Mother before her was very far from wise.Helen was the da. of their cousin Nell Brown (see 13:174TC to JWC, 8 July [1841]); for a previous instance of John and TC providing her with financial assistance, where she is more favorably described, see 45:45TC to JAC, 7 Oct. 1867. We can only hope the miserable ineffectual Helen will keep her word & that we may be troubled with her no more.

Our weather here is still very blusterous a violent East wind blowing this morning so that I could not venture down the Embankment for fear of losing
my hat and had to go by the world's end“The World's End” is a historic tavern at the W end of King's Rd., Chelsea, and gives its name to the surrounding area. & other intricate places to get shelter of the streets. Meanwhile there is a strong sun shining, which we generally have for some days past & March whether as lion or lamb must now very soon come to a conclusion. You will find your room here a much more trim and handsome article than it used to be or than Jean found it while here so soon as you can resolve to lift anchor you will find all ready for you,—& can be pretty certain withal that there awaits you an effective set of artificial teeth the like of which I find to be a sensible convenience for my own part.John A. Carlyle wrote, 13 March: “I … have lost nearly all my old teeth, & contrive to exist without them…. I may think of … trying to get some substitutes for them, though I don’t expect much aid from any dentist.” No answer comes from Alick in Canada, though I had been confidently expecting one almost by return of post;See TC to AC, 15 Feb. but in the meanwhile there are newspapers from young Alick and other Canada indications, which give me room to believe that nothing has gone far wrong since we expressly heard. Poor old Alick, I have his photographFor a photograph of Alexander and his wife, Janet, see 42:222TC to JAC, 14 Sept. 1865. in my dressing closet upstairs; and often enough think of him & his bodily & other griefs!— —

For the rest I have been as idle as usual, alas, doomed to idleness seemingly. My work all done & my strength along with it; but we must not complain. I have about finished that wearisome long-winded, vulgar; but strangely graphic and vivacious Swiss Gotthelf: I know not if you could have the patience to read it. There is a large element of Berne dialect in it; but after a little it is not difficult [to] understand & the man I believe had, &, though now 12 years dead now has a solid reputation in his country. Say if you would like to have it.See TC to JAC, 18 March. John replied, 27 March: “if you think that Swiss book of Ruskin's is in such a state that it can be safely sent by post I should like to see it.” He then wrote, 30 March: “The little Swiss book arrived here this day all safe, & I have already begun to read it, & find that I can make out the most of it clearly enough, & I think it very interesting.” The Book is Ruskin's; but there is no possibility of Mary's translating it for him;Mary Aitken wrote to Ruskin, 6 June: “I hardly know how to put into words the awful fact I have to communicate. I have failed utterly and ignominiously in my attempt to translate Uli into English. I have tried over and over again and can’t get on at all. It is written in cramped, foreign German, largely interspersed with Swiss words, which no dictionary will explain. My uncle had goaded me on with cruel jibes; but he read the book himself, and says now that he could at no period of his life have translated it. I need say no more, except that I am much grieved to find what would have been a great pleasure to me so far beyond my very small powers” (Ruskin's Works 32:344). The book was eventually translated for Ruskin by Julia Firth, 1886–88, and reissued, revised, edited, and annotated by Ruskin (Orpington, 1888). and at any rate the vol. specially in its present loose state is worth very
little. Godwin's Life & Hazlitts ditto, I have, happily altogether done with coarse stupid books both of them, especially the latter which I think is as ill-written a book as ever came before me;See TC to JAC, 18 March. a book of Emersons,Ralph Waldo Emerson, Letters and Social Aims (Boston, 1876). the exact title of which I forget has been lent by me to Froude these 5 or 6 weeks; but I think he will never read it; if you have the least notion to try it, it shall be sent you. I myself read it over with a kind of agreeable stimulus that Emerson's fragmentary glitterings generally yield; but I learnt nothing from it, strictly speaking; nor I doubt will you beyond what we already know of him. Yesterday morning I got from Trevellyan in 2 heavy volumes a Life of his Uncle T. B. Macaulay,George Otto Trevelyan, The Life and Letters of Lord Macaulay, 2 vols. (1876). George Otto Trevelyan (1838–1928; ODNB), politician and author, nephew of Thomas Babington Macaulay (1800–1859; ODNB), historian and poet. which is much better reading, at least much easier, & promises to give a kind of recognisable likeness of the great Thomas Babington,—whom, to say truth, I never could any way deeply admire or at all believe in except to a very shallow depth. You remember bringing up his first Edinburgh Review Essay one night from Annan to the Hill & reading it with me before going to bed. That I think was the only thing of his I ever read with lively satisfaction, due principally I suppose to the surprise & entire mystery of authorship which was attached to it.Macaulay's essay “Milton,” Edinburgh Review 42 (Aug. 1825): 304–46. John wrote to TC, 21 Nov. 1825, shortly after leaving Hoddam Hill where TC was living at the time, identifying Macaulay as the author of the article which they had apparently both recently read; see 3:421TC to JAC, 1 Dec. 1825. Did you know that Macaulay is understood by T. B & others to signify the son of Olaf & that aulay Macaulay means simply Olau (or Olaf) son of ditto.The Macaulay family came from the outer Hebrides, descended from Norse invaders. Writing of Macaulay's early childhood, Trevelyan noted: “Of all [his] performances, that which attracted most attention at the time was undertaken for the purpose of immortalizing Olaus Magnus, King of Norway, from whom the clan to which [he] belonged was supposed to derive its name” (The Life and Letters of Lord Macaulay 1:31–32). Trevelyan also recalled that “Mr. Carlyle, during a visit to the late Lord Ashburton at the Grange, caught sight of Macaulay's face in unwonted repose, as he was turning over the pages of a book. ‘I noticed,’ said he, ‘the homely Norse features that you find everywhere in the Western Isles, and I thought to myself ‘Well, anyone can see that you are an honest good sort of fellow, made out of oatmeal’” (The Life and Letters of Lord Macaulay 1:7). For Macaulay's Norse lineage, see W. C. Mackenzie, “Lord Macaulay's Ancestors,” Gentleman's Magazine 285 (July–Dec. 1898): 128–36. Olaf Tryggveson would surely be much surprised to
see some of the descendants he has had!Olaf Tryggveson (d. 1000), king of Norway 995–1000; see Early Kings of Norway (1875), Carlyle, Works 30:230–47. See also 49:239–40TC to EF, 15 Sept. 1875. If you would like to have this Book, so soon as I am done with it you are of course welcome to it:John replied, 27 March: “I have seen long extracts from Trevyllian's Life of his uncle Macaulay, in the newspapers & can wait till I get back to London for the rest of it. And of Godwin & Hazlitt I know enough already to make [me] rather indifferent about further details concerning them.” but I must not call it interesting in any but a shallow sense, indeed the essential shallowness &c, as it were, sublime of commonplace both in subject & author are its most conspicuous features.

Froude is gone to Oxford for a few days on visit to Max Mülller.
