Max, whom I saw some weeks ago, angry & unhappy & determined to flit to Germany in few months has got all made straight for him in Oxford; & is now cheerfully determined to continue there in the way of sinecure, with such opulent provision supply.See TC to JAC, 1 March. In which I cannot but praise him both for his prudence and good luck. I ought not quite to forget (though I had all but done so) to inform you that the Royal Irish Academy has voted me an honorary membershipSee TC to EPW, 28 March. (see the Letter enclosed from which I think it will be difficult for me to extract anything but the small increase of fash caused by saying “thank you, thank you.” Oh dear, Oh dear, Vanitas vanitatum omnia vanitas.

The Lady that writes about Vivisection Mary guesses to be the person with whom your friend Miss Hutchison is used to stay:John replied, 27 March: “The Miss Marston who wrote to you from Hans Place is, as Mary conjectures, the lady whom Miss Hutchison visits every year. She is wealthy & very charitable, but strict in investigating the circumstances of all who seek assistance from her. I have known her for some twenty years. She is very modest, & it must have cost her a great effort to ask you to make any second direct or indirect demonstration at the Chelsea Vivisection meeting. Of course you could not stir further in the matter.” Ann Marston, founder of the London Anti-Vivisection Society; Miss Hutchison had been the bridesmaid at John's wedding, Nov. 1852; see 28:188JWC to TC, 8 July 1853. I cannot afford to be bothered any more with vivisection. My opinion upon it has been clearly made known & to preach upon it for a single instant farther would be unsuitable and disagreeable.
Well here is enough of inanity for you once more, dear Brother. Give my loving regards to Jean & James and the two lassies & believe me ever

div3.sourceNote: TC-EPW, 28 March. MS: offered for sale by David J. Holmes Autographs, Collingswood, New Jersey, Jan. 2001; text from photocopy. Pbd: J. K. Ingram, Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy (1875–77) 2:cxxix–cxxx. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Edward Perceval Wright (1834–1910; ODNB), M.D., naturalist, prof. of botany at Dublin Univ. 1869–1904 and sec. of the Royal Irish Academy 1874–77.
div3.head: TC TO EDWARD PERCEVAL WRIGHT

docBody.p:
About a week ago I received the agreeable and most unexpected announcement from you that I had been elected an honorary Member of the Royal Irish Academy,Wright wrote, 22 March: “I have the honour to inform you that you have been elected an Honorary Member of the Academy in the Department of Polite Literature and that I shall forward you a Certificate of the same in the course of a few days.” an Institution which I have always much respected. To this your official announcement there was added on another sheet some extremely kind words in your private capacity,Wright wrote, 20 March: “I am not able to send you the enclosed formal notice of your election [to the Royal Irish Academy], without at the same time telling you with what feelings of joy the event has been received…. It is true the Honour is a tardily paid one, but if your great merits dawned but slowly on our minds, they are, by the slowness of that growth now all the more deeply planted. / Ireland is so separated in thought from England, that you may not have known that you had here so many friends. I trust therefore that you will not consider this quite unofficial note as either intrusive or impertinent.” from which also I derived great satisfaction and beg to thank you accordingly. By this morning's post, there arrived, accompanying your second Note, the Official Diploma or Certificate of my election:Wright then wrote, 25 March, that he was forwarding the certificate by that day's post; certificate untraced. and it now only remains that I request you to express to the Gentlemen Members who have done me this conspicuous honour my grateful sense of their kindness and my loyal feeling towards the Institution of which I am henceforth a Member. Some five and twenty years ago I passed a very pleasant & instructive day in your MuseumTC visited the Royal Irish Academy in Dublin, 7 July 1849, during his visit to Ireland that summer; see 24:106TC to JWC, 8 July 1849. and do not remember that I ever had so much satisfaction on any visit to a similar collection. Regretting only that I am now too old to assist in your labours at all except by good wishes, if
there could lie the least help in these, I have the honour to remain yours
sincerely,

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 30 March. MS: NLS 528.57. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:436; Stuart Wallace, “‘ Blethering Blackie’ and Thomas Carlyle,” CSA 23 (2007): 178. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: This morning there arrived a letter from one of our poor Alick's daughters,The letter was from Alick's da. Margaret; see TC to JAC, 29 April. which has made me very sad to read. Poor Alick, it appears, is gradually losing head, as well as suffering from asthma & other complaints. This is an altogether mournful way of ending the long journey we are all near the end of. My heart is very sad about him; &, alas, what can we help in any respect of the least importance. What I wish you to do is to write a letter of punctual enquiry to TomThomas, Alick's eldest son. John A. Carlyle wrote, 30 March, forwarding a letter from Alick's son James: “the account it gives of poor Alick's condition is little or no better. By this day's mail you may perhaps have a letter from James, of wh he speaks in mine, as acknowledging the £150 you had sent.” TC had recently sent Alick £150; see TC to AC, 5 Feb. John wrote again, 3 April: “Last week I wrote to James Carlyle at Cedar Valley asking him for a fuller account of his father's illness.” James had recently acquired a farm at Cedar Valley, about 16 mi. (26 km.) N of Brantford, Ontario; TC and John A. Carlyle had offered to help him with money to buy the farm; see 48:184TC to JAC, 29 March 1873, and 49:15TC to JAC, 5 Nov. 1873. who lives not far off Bield and earnestly ask him for correct and precise details and to ask if in any respect we can be of the least use. This is all we can make of it for the moment: but one's thoughts will dwell on the scene over yonder as the saddest item of our position at present.

I send today the £5 owing you by me in re Ellen Brown; & £5 more for the two pairs of slippers, one pair of them arrived, the other slowly coming, with the four shirts which also I understand to be under way.See TC to JAC, 25 March. Tell Jean that there is no specific hurry about the shirts nor about the second pair of slippers either; but I wished to have done with the money settlement which you can complete whenever the articles get actually sent; the small change, if any, you can bring up with you when you yourself come, which I think ought now to
be soon.

BlackieJohn Stuart Blackie, prof. of Greek at Edinburgh Univ.; he was also a tireless advocate for Gaelic language and culture, and was campaigning to raise funds for a Chair of Celtic at the Univ. of Edinburgh; see CSA 23 (2007): 178. has sent me this morning the enclosed blash of a letter, which is worth nothing at all, & may be burnt immediately. It was accompanied by a number of papers about the “Celtic professorship” which Blackie is endeavouring to found. I send you his list of subscribers, which amounts he says to
£8000. The only one of said papers which can be of the least interest as throwing light on the posture of the matter. The subscriptions are nearly altogether from Highland Lairds & dignitaries; & I have not for the moment opened my purse on the affair at all; but perhaps shall, if people take it up. There came also in a Scotsman (of Tuesday last) which probably you have seen a loose blether of a letter about the cultivation of Scotch Music in schools,Blackie was involved in a correspondence about Scottish music, prompted by the annual concert of the Univ. Musical Society, 22 March. In a letter to the Scotsman, 27 March, he complained that “our national music in the majority even of what are accounted our best schools does not receive that systematic attention to which, whether on grounds of educational philosophy or of social polity, it is pre-eminently entitled.” He attributed the ignorance of Scottish music to “a false idea of culture … prevalent in the upper and upper middle classes of this country … and the notion that the Scotch language and everything Scotch means vulgarity, and that English, with a little dabbling in French and German and Italian accomplishment, means gentility” (Scotsman, 28 March). which is a subject that I wish could find a better advocate than blethering Blackie, to whom I mean no answer at all for the present.

The Swiss Novel was sent away yesterday; but I fear you will find it intolerably cramp & wearisome:See TC to JAC, 25 March. John replied, 3 April, that he had found the book interesting: “It looks like a small book, but contains far more than any novel of three volumes, & is most carefully & earnestly written … & seems entirely sincere & true.” if so, do not scruple to lay it down at once & return it hither; it is Ruskin's book; and Mary is bound to return it him, with protest I suppose against her trying to translate it for him.

March seems to be intending to go out like a lamb after all; this is one of the finest spring days; and the walk down the embankment & back is the most medicinal element in my affairs at present. I hope you will now soon think of making hitherward again; opportunities of meeting are now getting fewer & fewer & before long there will be none at all. Macaulay is a most singular biography & psychologically may be considered the most curious ever written. No man known to me in present or past ages ever had, with a peaceable composure, too, so infinite a stock of good conceit of himself.

I am not in very good order today, having considerably lost my sleep last night: but I know what the reason of it was and hope to avoid it tonight and afterwards. I will add no more at any rate;—except indeed that I have a Book of Emersons for you which probably will go tomorrow and may be a substitute for Uli the Knecht if you find him too leaden. I send my love to one & all of you & am always

div3.sourceNote: TC-UC, 30 March. Pbd: Froude, Carlyle 4:437–38. Froude introduced the letter: “Many letters have been sent to me from unknown correspondents—young men probably who had been diverted from clericalism by reading his books—and had consulted Carlyle in their choice of a life. Here is one. I would give many more had I room for them, for they are all kind and wise” (Froude, Carlyle 437).
div3.head: TC TO AN UNIDENTIFIED CORRESPONDENT

docBody.p: I respect your conscientious scruples in regard to choosing a profession, and wish much I had the power of giving you advice that would be of the least service. But that, I fear, in my total ignorance of yourself and the posture of your affairs, is pretty nearly impossible. The profession of the law is in many respects a most honourable one, and has this to recommend it, that a man succeeds there, if he succeeds at all, in an independent and manful manner, by force of his own talent and behaviour, without needing to seek patronage from anybody. As to ambition, that is, no doubt, a thing to be carefully discouraged in oneself; but it does not necessarily inhere in the barrister's profession more than in many others, and I have known one or two who, by quiet fidelity in promoting justice, and by keeping down litigation, had acquired the epithet of the “honest lawyer,” which appeared to me altogether human and beautiful.

Literature, as a profession, is what I would counsel no faithful man to be concerned with, except when absolutely forced into it, under penalty, as it were, of death. The pursuit of culture, too, is in the highest degree recommendable to every human soul, and may be successfully achieved in almost any honest employment that has wages paid for it. No doubt, too, the Church seems to offer facilities in this respect; but I will by no means advise you to overcome your reluctance against seeking refuge there. On the whole there is nothing strikes me as likelier for one of your disposition than the profession of teacher, which is rising into higher request every day, and has scope in it for the grandest endowments of human faculties (could such hitherto be got to enter it), and of all useful and fruitful employments may be defined as the usefullest, fruitfullest, and also indispensablest in these days of ours.
Regretting much that I can help you so infinitely little, bidding you take pious and patient counsel with your own soul, and wishing you with great truth a happy result,
docBody.closer: I remain, dear Sir, / Faithfully yours, / T. Carlyle.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 8 April. MS: NLS 528.58. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: We received your Letter duly, and were glad to read it. There is nothing in the least particular to tell you today; but I should regret to end the week without a few lines sent your way.

April has come in upon us in the most mild and inoffensive way. No “borrowing days”The “borrowing days” are the last three days of March and the first three days of April, when the weather is often very bad just before the warmer weather arrives; from an old Scottish proverb; see 36:97–99TC to LS, 19 April 1860. nor other trouble of the elements; several days of warm dim mist, which now have become bright and sunshiny and hitherto no rain at all. I do not feel very well or courageous for walking in the sudden change of temperature but I do daily get down to the end of the embankment before breakfast and again in the afternoon, with or without company (oftenest with,—more than I desire). I go out again into Hyde Park or Battersea Park where already the grass is very green, and the strange pathetic prophecy of spring, which has always made me pensive and softly sad, meets me on all hands. Froude is the company I like best and oftenest have. He puts me into an omnibus in Piccadilly if I have already had enough of walking and I come passively rumbling home where Mary is always in her place to receive me. The rest of the night is reading and sleeping,—attended with much irremediable dyspepsia; but ending generally in a tolerable extent of sleep, however bad its kind. I have finished MacaulaySee TC to JAC, 25 March. above a week ago; & written my eulogy upon TrevelyanPresumably TC wrote to Trevelyan to thank him for the book; letter untraced. TC's copy of the work is listed in Sotheby's catalog as containing two letters from the author to TC, in the second of which, dated 4 April 1876, Trevelyan “acknowledges help and encouragement in writing the book” (Sotheby's [1932] 133). the biographer, who indeed has done his task very cleverly & well. I got a good deal of something like entertainment out of the book & finished it with rather an increase of pity and human regard & a sensible increase of wonder at the natural character of him but with a clearer view than ever of the limited nature of his world-admired talent; which I take it will be the general impression among the best kind of readers. By the way there is a very superior article not on the Biography but on Macaulay himself in the last No of the Fortnightly Review,John Morley (1838–1923; ODNB), politician and writer, “Macaulay,” Fortnightly Review 112 (1 April 1876): 494–513. John replied, 14 April: “I got the Fortnightly Review from the library here, & read the article on Macaulay which seemed to me very good & quite clear & effectual.”
Dr RussellDr. James Russell; John wrote, 14 April, that he was going to visit Russell the following day. has it for several days back & no doubt could send it down to you with little or no trouble but perhaps you have the Fortnightly at any rate from the Circulating Library & have already read the piece in question. If you want to read the Book, we could in the course of a day or two easily send it you; but as you are due here yourself about the beginning of next month perhaps you will prefer to wait. I have for myself got into a book of Michelet's, 3 voll.,Jules Michelet, Histoire du XIXe siècle, 3 vols. (Paris, 1872–75). the last he wrote, all dealing with the early history of Bonaparte; whom he considers a rather diabolic and dirty kind of creature, and wearisomely hunts (in a, to me, very dubious manner) through all his underground intrigues and treacheries & Heigho! Reading is but a poor resource after all, especially where it is not the best of books that one gets hold of, but often enough rather the opposite kind.

VigfussonGudbrand Vigfusson, scholar of Icelandic literature, now living in Oxford; see 49:7TC to JAC, 18 Oct. 1873. has been twice here this week, and was rather interesting to see. He is here taking a little holiday and lodged near the British Museum where doubtless he is consulting books. He looks well and hearty, complains a little of his solitude at Oxford but appears to be getting on at a fair pace with the printing of his Sagas:Vigfusson was currently working on scholarly edns. of the Orkney Saga and the Hakonar Saga. he much celebrated his little tour in Scotland of last year, especially the two days he had spent at Dumfries. I find him a sensible and solid man, but have some difficulty in making out what he says more particularly when there are other people by. Perhaps he will call again before going; and I think he said yesterday that he was intending to write to you without delay. Lowe,Possibly Robert Lowe (1811–92, ODNB), politician; otherwise unidentified. he has not called upon this time, finding that he was “a man of crotchets” & did not keep his promises.

Naturally I am often thinking and anxiously wondering about poor Alick; when the news comes which you have asked from JamesSee TC to JAC, 30 March. of course I shall be eager to hear it. But, alas, alas, I fear there is no clear hope of any solid improvement.

Adieu, dear Brother, there will probably be some interruption before long at any rate it is time I should conclude. Tell Jean that she has not written a word hither for a long time. If I had fingers of my own I would write oftener to her than I do. Give my love and blessing to her and all the household. I ever am your affectionate Brother,

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 15 April. MS: NLS 528.59. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
We received your letter this morning not by the first post but by the second and were very glad to find by it that things were going on pretty much as usual among you. We have had a week of very bad weather here; nothing but wild storms of wind, continual showers of snow, sleet and one whole day of rain: in fact if one count by old style these are the borrowing days of March & AprilTC refers to the old-style dating under the Julian calendar, when 15 April would have been 4 April (see also 48:26TC to AC, 16 Dec. 1871); for the borrowing days, see TC to JAC, 8 April. & they faithfully keep their old character. Happily since yesterday about noon the sky is bright & even sunny, though still with a strong South-east wind which is rather sharply cold. I have been busy as usual with nothing at all; that is, with mere reading of insignificant books & taking care of the mean necessities which the possession of a body keeps all men and still more especially all old and weak men subject to and bound to fulfil at their peril. In fact one of the most important acts of a common day with me is that of the cold bath in the morning which I judge to have a really good effect & which, followed by the briskest walk I can now get up (by no means very brisk to the foot of the embankment and back any clear thoughts I have are apt to be at their clearest during this process. Froude is off to Hertfordshire keeping Easter with Henry Cooper & the Dowager Lady Cooper,Henry Frederick Cowper and his mother, Anne Florence, dowager Countess Cowper; the family estate was at Panshanger in Hertfordshire.—and privately writing, I believe a criticism on MacaulayFroude, “Lord Macaulay,” Fraser's Magazine 13 (June 1876): 675–94. which may very possibly be well worth reading. I go and walk duly at four oclock and for an hour after; & generally there is company attending me; but it is for most part of little use and rather bothers me with the obligation to talk instead of strolling on in free communication with my own moody thoughts and humours. The loss of poor Forster is much felt by me & the thought of this opens up old wounds as every mournful event is apt to do. His widow comes little out but is getting gradually into composure; settling & adjusting within doors for her now altered life; and seems always glad to see me or Mary and me when we decide to make an effort & call there. I have finished Michelet's Book called Les origines de BonaparteMichelet, Histoire du XIXe siècle; see TC to JAC, 8 April; “Origine de Bonaparte” was the subtitle of the first vol. (three voll. octavo) published since his death
which is full of wild flights and fantasticalities on his part, but contains also some curious glances of insight. Along with this letter comes a tawdry little French Pamphlet of which I have read little and of the “poetic” parts nothing at all: a foolish flimsy kind of man I can perceive; but who may perhaps entice you for a half hour here and there I learnt yesterday is just dead.Pamphlet and writer both unidentified further.— —
Thank Jean very much for her Letter. I send my love & blessings to her & to you all.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 22 April. MS: NLS 528.60. Pbd: A. Carlyle NL 2:328–29 inc. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:438–39 inc. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Your letter came to us yesterday, with accounts from all the Annandale kindred and the cheerful prediction that you are coming to us very soon. We wanted to know what it was that ailed poor Jessie Grierson.John A. Carlyle wrote, 20 April, that he intended to come to London in a week or two. He continued: “Today Jean & I have been to the Gill to see poor Mary, who had had bad news of her daughter Jessie in Canada, as we heard yesterday from James Austin…. On reading the letter from Jessie's husband I found that James had rather exaggerated the case, though serious enough.” He replied, 24 April: “Mary was unable to tell me any thing about the nature of the disease her daughter Jessie had been suffering from, & Jessie's husband, in the letter which brought the bad news, gave no particulars.” You did not seem to think it so dangerous as the rest; but we know not what it specially is. This morning the enclosed letter from Hawick came;John replied, 24 April: “The printed letter from Hawick is a memorial of Lucy Cruickshank a good quakeress I knew of old in Edinburgh, who died a year ago.” Lucy Cruickshank (1810–75), member of a prominent Edinburgh Quaker family. the black edges of which somewhat alarmed till Mary gave her opinion that on that symptom there was probably nothing dangerous.

We are all here in our common way, nothing worth reporting except what already has made you all sad the mournful news from Canada.Their brother Alick d. 30 March. Poor Alick, he is cut away from us; and we shall behold his face no more nor think of him as being of the earth any more; the much struggling, ever-true and valiant Brother is forever gone. To himself in the state he was in it can be considered only as a blessed relief, but it strikes me heavily that he is gone before myself, that I who should
in the course of natureSee TC to JAC, 4 Dec. 1875. have gone before him am left among the mourners, instead being the mourned. Young Alick's account of his death is altogether interesting & brings one as it were present to the scene. A scene of sublime simplicity great and solemn under the humblest forms. That question of his when his eyes were already shut and his mind wavering before the last finis of all “Is Tom coming from Edinburgh the morn?”From autumn 1816 until early 1824 TC lived first in Kirkcaldy and then mostly in Edinburgh; his usual route to and from Dumfriesshire was by coach, and Alick would take him or pick him up somewhere along the route near Moffat; see for instance 1:287. will never leave me should I live for a hundred years. Poor Alick, my ever-faithful Brother come back across wide oceans and long decades of time to the scenes of brotherly companionship with me; & going out of the world, as it were, with his hand in mine. Many times he convoyed me to meet the Dumfries Coach or to bring me home from it and full of bright and perfect affection always were those meetings and partings of ours. It is a strange thing to me that little question of his and comes up continually on me, not with common sorrow only but with a tenderness and strangeness which much affects me. Be sure you send us back safely the letter of young Alick; the hasty notices in it are and will continue very precious.John replied, 24 April: “I must at once send back young Alick's letter. I read it to all at Scotsbrig & Newlands, & none of them had got any notice of dear Alick's decease before my arrival.”

There is nothing else that I can think worthy of writing about today. Our weather has brightened up suddenly into the complexion of very summer, which of course is welcome, though it will have pauses and retrogressions. There is nothing yet fully in leaf with us but all is getting greenish & some of the fruit blossoms were out (& I doubt got greatly injured) before the late ten days of sleet and puddle. One singular Letter,This is probably the eight-page letter, undated but postmarked 12 April, and signed only “An old Tory,” railing against Queen Victoria taking the title Empress of India, on the grounds of Britain being a constitutional monarchy; he ended his letter: “We do not want an Empress! Why should they?” TC wrote on the envelope: “‘Old Tory’ (on Title of ‘Empress’).” Benjamin Disraeli, the prime minister, had suggested that Victoria should take the title, which she was very happy to do, as several of her children were marrying into other European imperial
families. She was proclaimed empress of India in Delhi, 1 Jan. 1877. It was intended that she should only use the title in her dealings with India, but it soon became her normal style. wh. may be worth your reading I enclose, 6 or 7 others rather the reverse I will not trouble you with.
My sorrowful sympathies & ever affectionate good wishes & regards to Jean & all of you.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 29 April. MS: NLS 528.61. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: We are rather short for time today; and I have latterly had some misventures with my sleep, so that we must be content with a brief and hasty letter for the present. Your welcome Note came yesterday, with the sad news in it of poor Aird's departure;Thomas Aird; see TC to JAC, 1 March; he d. 25 April. John A. Carlyle had been visiting him regularly during his illness. He wrote, 27 April: “On the Tuesday I called at Aird's & found that he had violent diarrhea, was much worse & could not see me at the time, & I had not the heart to try to see him in the evening of that day again; & next morning … we learnt that he had died on the Tuesday evening at ten o’clock.” He then wrote, 30 April: “Aird's funeral is to take place … tomorrow afternoon…. It is to be a publick funeral, & I know not whether James or I will go to it … as we both dislike such displays.” The Scotsman reported the funeral, 2 May, and included “Dr James Carlyle” among the many mourners. a thing that clothes one's mind in sorrow; but for poor Aird's sake is a matter rather of thankfulness that his miserable pain is at an end. Poor Aird, no more innocent man has been known to me; and for 50 years he has been a wholesome, simple-hearted and affectionate fellow traveller, who has now got to the goal we are all walking towards.

Your account of Maggie,Their niece Maggie Aitken; John wrote, 24 April: “I am sorry to say, Maggie has been unwell since … Saturday, & is now confined to bed. Her disease is a threatening of rheumatic fever.” He wrote again, 30 April: “I am glad to say that Maggie is great deal better, has had an unusually good night's rest, is now almost free from pain, & able to take food.” about whom we are much interested and anxious was very welcome; and we beg from some of you at The Hill the most frequent tidings you can send on that head: Annie'sTheir niece Anne Aitken. Letter this morning, which seemed to express a continued improvement of symptoms, slow but evident, gave us great satisfaction. There was nothing said in your letter about the appointment of a day for arriving here; but we hope very soon to hear of your packing up & appearance here.John replied, 30 April: “Tomorrow we are to have a great change of London trains…. I have not yet got the Time Table … & I think it better to wait till a few journies have been made…. I have got most of my things ready, & shall hope to see you about the end of this or beginning of next week.” The weather is now fairly turned into summer, warm often sun-shiny with fine doses of soft April rain: the embankment every morning is very quiet very clean & pleasant and almost the best physical comfort I have. Every thing is swept & garnished for you here or can be in the space of three or four days after warning comes. Let us have warning then, dear Brother; and see you once
more in this world. Our dear Alick's disappearance from among us here dwells strangely in my thoughts day after day: I read over the two Canada letters you sentJohn wrote, 27 April: “The enclosed letter from young James has come this afternoon, & I send it on at once though it contains nothing new.” He had also sent a letter from young James, 30 March; see TC to JAC, 8 April. and remembered that there was another by his Margaret,For Margaret's letter to TC, see TC to JAC, 30 March. John replied, 30 April: “The letter from Alick's daughter Margaret, as I see by yours in which it was enclosed, reached me on 30th March. I took it with me on that day to the Gill & read it to Mary; & then returned it to you so far as I can remember that same day by our evening mail.” John is apparently misremembering; he wrote, 3 April: “On Friday [31 March] I forwarded the Bield letter to Scotsbrig, & also an account of what I had heard about poor Alick from his son James.” The Bield letter was presumably the one from Margaret, as she lived there with her father. which I hope is still in existence at Dumfries. Pray by all means send that on if it is still in existence as I earnestly hope. That strange question several times repeated “Is Tom coming from Edinburgh tomorrow?” is continually present to me as a most singular and heart-affecting thing. Some of us ought to write to Nephew Tom without delay. I have always a notion of doing so, and will surely one of these days; but having so many loads upon me and no fingers of my own, I am always in a great indisposition to write.— The letter of that German Medical being was sent you with his Pamphlet.John wrote, 27 April: “I have looked into the Göttingen pamphlet, & like it still worse than the empty Geschichte der Arzney Kunde [Kurt Sprengel, History of Medical Science; see TC to JAC, 29 Jan.]. Better perhaps to send no notice of them to the Author? He is evidently a very conceited self-sufficient personage.” He had written, 24 April: “I did not write to the German at Göttingen, author of the Hist. of medicine you sent me…. I found his History very declamatory & long winded, & could not read much of it, & Dr Hunter liked it even worse.” Dr. Jacob Dickson Hunter, friend of John A. Carlyle. I believe & I feel always there should be a few words written to him. If you will send me back his address I could do here what little is necessary on that head,—very little indeed.John replied, 30 April: “I enclose the German Professor's letter…. [Y]our few words will satisfy him completely, which any from me could hardly have done so well.” The man is not entirely a fool; I even read through the Pamphlet he sent which is not without a scrambling sense & German practicality in it: on the whole all I had to tell him that his book had come; & had been sent away among “Medical readers” (hiding from him that they are only two) & that I thank him for his attention.

The Lord Mayor has determined this year to give the Authors of London a dinner at the Mansion House this day week; & being anxious to have some kind of attendance upon it asked me to come as principal guestWilliam James Richmond Cotton (1822–1902; ODNB), businessman, politician, M.P. for the City of London 1874–85, lord mayor of London 1875–76. He wrote, 19 April: “On the 6th of May next I intend, as Lord Mayor, to receive here the representatives of Literature at dinner, and, in the first place, I address you in the sincere hope that one of the greatest and most honoured of English writers will favour me by becoming the guest of the Evening and the Citizens of London by his presence.” (which Mary
says you know already). I naturally refused; but on the Sunday following he came attended with DilberoglueStavros Dilberoglue, Greek businessman resident in London, old friend of TC, and friend and colleague of William Cotton. & considerable state to press the matter farther. Being tired of his urgencies, his offers to bring me & fetch me back &c &c, I at length answered—Well I will not say No; but we will keep it open—if you can permit me till the time itself come. My Lord completely contented hereupon at once acceded, has put it in the Newspapers I understand that I am conditionally coming and is inviting all round.The Evening Standard reported, 24 April: “The Lord Mayor of London and the Lady Mayoress are issuing invitations to a grand banquet to the representatives of literature and journalism at the Mansion House on Saturday, May 6th, at which, it is expected, the Prime Minister, Mr. Tennyson, Mr. Carlyle, the Duke of Argyll, Mr. Froude, and other distinguished literary personages will be present.” The Mansion House is the official residence of the lord mayor. On Friday next we will therefore write to his Civic Highness that I am not coming;See TC to WC, 6 May; John wrote, 4 May: “We hope you will succeed in avoiding that Lord Mayor's banquet tomorrow evening.” and so let us trust the Mansion House matter will comfortably melt into air. A wearisome visitorUnidentified. is waiting for more than the last page,—and there seems another rapping at the door; so in the most abrupt manner I must perforce terminate.
With my love & blessing to you all and hoping to hear of poor Maggie's continued improvement, if Heaven so grant—

div3.sourceNote: TC-TC [TCA], 4 May. MS: Manchester Univ. Lib. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:329–31 inc. Thomas Carlyle, TC's nephew, son of Alick Carlyle in Canada.
div3.head: TC TO THOMAS CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Yesterday morning your sad Letter reached me; and today in spite of my weakness I must write to you a word of sympathy and mournful affection. For a good many weeks past, ever since your Maggie's LetterSee TC to JAC, 30 March. to me here, I had a sad and painful assurance in me, which was shared by us all, that the fatal end could not be distant. We hoped, liked [sic] you, that, the gloom of winter being nearly over, the Spring with its sunshine might produce some
temporary alleviation; but ever from that day your Father's sad image fixed itself in my mind, and a thousand thoughts and tender recollections of him were my continual companions. At last unexpectedly, on the 20th of April last, your Brother Alick's Letter came to his Cousin Mary, with the news that all was now ended; and that the kindest and truest hearted of brothers was gone forever. For himself, so loaded with pain, one could only regard the event as a benificent deliverance; but the shock we all had from it was heavy and sore. There never was a kinder Brother than he from his earliest years, and without break through life was to me. True as steel he ever was, and with a fund of tenderness, strange in one of so fiery a temper; a man of infinite talent, too, had it been developed by friendly fortune; I never knew a more faithful, ingenious and valiant man. He was, withal, the first human being I ever came to friendship and familiarity with in this world; and our hearts were knit together by a thousand ties. Very beautiful, very sad and tender are the endless recollections I have of him, which must continue with me as companions while I live. No doubts similar thoughts dwelt in his mind about me, and it seems were even present with him. Nothing has affected me more than what Alick mentions in his letter, that in the wanderings of mind in the last hours of his life your Father asked repeatedly “If Brother Tom were not coming from Edinburgh tomorrow.” Ah me, ah me, can I ever forget these words? He always escorted me out to meet the Dumfries Coach near Moffat, and back again generally from Moffat, when I was returning,See TC to JAC, 22 April. a right glad man on these latter occasions; a quietly sad but always helpful one on the former. You will oblige me very much dear Tom, if you can, by strict inquiry accurately make out for me on which of the two days, Tuesday or Wednesday 28th, 29th March my beloved Brother Alick spoke these words. I have read both the Letters, James's too, again and again, but cannot with certainty ascertain: and to me more than to any other it is a point of vital interest.

Your Letter has gone to Dumfries & Annandale, where all hearts are struck by the sad event that had come. I will beg you now farther to send me some lucid account of family affairs at Bield and what new arrangements and settlements are made or contemplated in this great change. Make my loving regards to your poor Mother;Janet Carlyle. be gentle & good to her, all of you,—I need not bid you. Your Sister JaneTom's sister, Jane Sims. has not written to me for a long while. Tell her, too, I wish she would. With my best blessings on you all, & prayers that your lives may be worthy of him who has gone,
docBody.closer: Ever your affectionate / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-WC [WJRC], 5 May. Addr: The Mansion House / E. C. MS: John Wilson Autograph Letters and Historical Documents, London. Pbd: The Evening Standard, 8 May 1876. For William Cotton, see TC to JAC, 29 April.
div3.head: TC TO WILLIAM J. R. COTTON

docBody.p: I regret that after all, it is not practicable for me to be present at the Banquet at the Mansion House this evening. My regret is the greater on considering your kindness and conspicuous courtesy to myself in this matter, as well as the honour you are doing to the profession of which I am a member.
Pray present my best compliments and apologies to the Lady Mayoress.
With many good wishes and regards, I remain,
docBody.note: Cotton replied, 5 May, regretting that TC could not attend; he continued: “I have now to ask a double favour, first, that you will kindly allow your good niece Miss Aitkin to be present, Mr Dilberoglue undertaking her charge. Secondly, to ask by way of consolation to the Lady Mayoress, myself and the company the favour of a few lines at your own dictation to be read.” Cotton's wife was Caroline, b. Pottinger (1828–1901). It would seem that TC did not write anything further; the Standard, reporting details of the banquet, 8 May, noted: “The Lord Mayor said—I should like to claim your silence for a few moments in particular while I read to you a letter which I have had the honour to receive from that great man Thomas Carlyle (cheers). Up to yesterday I entertained the hope, and I know that he had the most earnest desire to be present to night, but the wishes of the octogenarian are sometimes destroyed by want of a physique in the frame.” He then read TC's letter, concluding: “Mr. Froude, who sits on my right … says that it is the firmest signature he has seen of Mr. Carlyle's for some time.”

div3.sourceNote: MA-MW [MAI-MEW], 20 May. MS: NLS Acc. 9207. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO META WELLMER

docBody.p:
Many thanks for your kind & welcome note. I am very glad that there is a prospect of seeing you so early.Meta Wellmer was planning to visit, presumably while the family of the duchess of Alburquerque were on holiday in Brittany; see MAI to MEW, 2 Jan. I regret very much that I have not a spare bedroom here to give you,—as my Uncle's brotherJohn A. Carlyle; he arrived 8 May. is on a visit to us; but you shall still come as our guest and I shall take charge of finding a comfortable room for you quite near to us. We are rather a sick household & perhaps this arrangement is after all the best for our hours & plans are so uncertain that you will have more freedom & yet we can feel that you belong to us for the
week or two I hope you will stay. You will of course come direct to us a day's warning will be quite sufficient I write in very great haste which pray excuse; but am with best regards from us both.

bibl.person: THE COMMITTEE OF THE ROYAL LITERARY FUND

div3.sourceNote: MA-RLF Committee [GCRLF], 7 June. MS: Royal Literary Fund, London. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO THE COMMITTEE OF THE ROYAL LITERARY FUND

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea, S.W.
7 June 1876.
docBody.p: Mr Carlyle bids me state that Mr Bentheim,TC recommended a Mr. Bentheim as tutor to Mary Rich (1789–1876; see 10:35JWC to FW, 7 March 1838) in Dec. 1840; see 12:344–45TC to MRI, 5 Dec. 1840. then a man of letters and an intimate friend of Professor Bernay's of King's College,Adolphus Bernays (1794–1864; ODNB), German scholar, settled in London in 1816, prof. of German at King's Coll., London, 1831–63. was known to him more than twenty years ago. In late years he has seen nothing of him. He is very sorry to hear of Mr Bentheim's necessitous circumstances; he begs to recommend him to the kind consideration of the Committee of the Royal Literary Fund.William Bentheim is listed as an applicant to the Royal Literary Fund, June 1876; unidentified further.
docBody.closer:
I remain,
My Lord and Gentlemen
Your faithful Servant
Mary Carlyle Aitken

div3.sourceNote: MA-MW [MAI-MEW], 14 June. MS: NLS Acc. 9207. Hitherto unpbd. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO META WELLMER

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
14 June 1876.
docBody.p:
I deferred answering your kind Note till I could tell you more definitely what our plans were likely to be. But my Uncle is still so poorly that we are
pretty sure to go out of London for a change of air before long; so I think all things considered, it will be better if equally convenient to you if you can come off to us at once. I am sorry to think that you will have a very dull time here and perhaps not see much of my Uncle; but since you are so brave a hero-worshipper I will say nothing more than that I shall do all I can to make you comfortable. So I shall look for a few lines to say when we may expect you,—the sooner the better. My Uncle, Dr Carlyle, is still with us; but I shall find a comfortable room for you quite near to us; so that you can be here all day and only sleep there.

You must tell me what Brod u. Obst [bread and fruit] you like; for although I am not much of a Cannibal myself, I shall be much exercised lest I starve you altogether in my ignorance!Wellmer was a vegetarian; see MAI to MEW, 2 Jan.

div3.sourceNote: MA-P&S [MAI-MPS], 25 June. Quot: R. Atkinson Autographs. Puttick & Simpson was an auction house, founded 1794, currently at 47 Leicester Sq.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO MESSRS. PUTTICK & SIMPSON

docBody.p: did not doubt that the two signatures were in Cromwell's own hand.Presumably they were selling documents purportedly signed by Oliver Cromwell and had asked TC to verify the signatures. For a previous Cromwell letter sold by them, see 28:301TC to CHC, 30 Oct. 1853.…The sentiment he thinks is unlike Cromwell.

div3.sourceNote: MA-MW [MAI-MEW], 26 June. MS: NLS Acc. 9207. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO META WELLMER

docBody.p: You will be surprized to see that we are still here at the above address. We are hoping to hear of your safe arrival in Paris and that you did not suffer in the passage.

My Uncle is just the same as when you went away—very weak & poorly; and he has decided not to leave home for a few days yet, till he has a chance to get a little better. Our latest plan is to go next Thursday or Friday to my Uncle's Sister in Scotland, about 12 miles from Dumfries.Presumably Mary Austin, at the Gill; however TC rarely stayed long at the Gill, as the train passed close to the farm and he found the train whistles very disturbing (see 47:22TC to JCA, 8 June 1870), and within the week they were at Jean Aitken's house in Dumfries. John A. Carlyle, who had stayed for a further week or so in London, wrote to his nephew James Carlyle Jr., 7 July, to say he was returning to Scotland the following day. He continued: “Letter today from Dumfries reporting all pretty well there, though your uncle has not got back to his usual sleep. He & Mary take long drives every day, & the weather had been fine for it” (MS: NLS Acc. 9086). I hope he will not draw back;
and that if we go the change will do him good. You will be pleased to know that the supply of the essence of beef is for the present quite exhausted. Have I read the 24 reasonsUnexplained. to my Uncle yet? Well, no, not yet, but I surely will do so. “The Dr” has for the present taken possession of them & I have not seen them until today.— — My Uncle has got on his new “Jacket” & he finds it most satisfactory & comfortable. As to me I have been wearing the pretty little shawl & it is very nice—for it has been almost cold these two days.— — You were very good & kind to us all, especially to my unworthy self; & I can only repeat to you that I am very sorry I could do so extremely little to recompense you for the great trouble you had in making your long pilgrimage to my Uncle's shrine.

I send enclosed a letter which came for you on Friday night. I thought I should keep it until I had time to send a small letter as accompaniment to it. Both my Uncles unite with me in best regards and many good wishes. TibTib, Cheyne Row cat; see MAI to MEW, 25 June 1877. ventures to send his duty; and I am dear Miss Wellmer

div3.sourceNote: TC-JS [JSTA], 2 July. Pbd: Susan Mary Elizabeth Jeune, Lady St. Helier, Memories of Fifty Years (1909) 153. Lady St. Helier was the wife of John Constantine Stanley; after his death she m., 1881, Francis Henry Jeune (1843–1905), Baron St. Helier; she misdated the letter 1878.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN STANLEY

docBody.p: I am much touched at your letter, and the wish expressed that I should undertake that god-fatherly enterprise which you propose.John Constantine Stanley had asked TC to be godfather to their first child, Madeline Cecilia Carlyle, b. 2 July.

If you wish it, I am agreeable, only would you not like to wait for another time, when the boy you want may perchance make his tardy entry? I will do as you wish, and will endeavour to be present at the ceremony, and I hope to send an appropriate gift to the young lady from her godfather.Lady Helier commented: “He did not come to the christening, but he sent her a mug with an engraved inscription in his own peculiar handwriting round the top of it” (Memories of Fifty Years [1909] 153).
docBody.closer: Yours, / T. Carlyle.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 7 Sept. MS: NLS 528.62. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
7 Sep 1876.
docBody.p: We did exactly as you advised with our Caledonian Railway paper, understanding it quite well, by your explanation:John A. Carlyle wrote, 4 Sept: “Today I got Mary's letter about Caledonian R. W. Stock with new receipt for £3125 Guaranteed belonging to you, & on Friday last got similar receipts for stock of my own—which I did not understand the meaning of at first. I now see that in order to simplify the calculation of dividends twice a year, these dividends are to be made the same for all sorts of Stock. Thus: You held of 5 per cent Preference Stock £2500, & now get instead of it £3125 of 4 per cent Preference which amounts exactly to the same thing in value…. The object of the change must be the saving of labour in calculating dividends twice yearly. / You have only to date & sign the second leaf of that enclosed paper & return it … as I have done mine today…. It is all quite right whether you take the trouble of understanding it or not.” we suppose there is no need of apprising Adamson or meddling with him on the subject.

I have nothing new to report about my health; I generally get some three hours of a shallow but quiet sleep in the course of the night, often at the very beginning of it; but am sadly tossed and agitated on awakening, sometimes not always getting by way of finis before the morning quite come a little touch farther of very heavy half-sleep;—and in short I begin to feel that the prickly agitation of wakefulness will probably never leave me; but is appointed to be my way of ending in this world. God's will be done.

Our weather here is usually temperate enough, but beyond measure fickle. One goes out with light clothing for the sun-shiny streets and probably enough there will be a small plump of gradual drizzle of rain before one gets home. We generally for exercise walk up into the Brompton Road, get hold of a Brompton omnibus and drive in it for “carriage” exercise to the crossing at Oxford St. Circus, walk up there in the shade into Portland Place and back still in the shade, down to Piccadilly Circus, after which, get into a Chelsea omnibus; and so get home somewhere about half past four, a dreary enough operation but the best we can contrive hitherto. This and the morning walk on the embankment is mostly all of exercise I get. We called one day on DarwinErasmus Darwin. and another on BlakistonDr. Peyton Blakiston; he and his wife, Bessy, were old friends of the Carlyles, from St. Leonards; they moved to London toward the end of 1871, now living at 55 Victoria St., Westminster. who declares he could cure me completely if we would but apply to pepsinePepsin, a commercial remedy for dyspepsia. JWC first heard of pepsin in 1857; see 33:104–5JWC to AHO, [24 Oct. 1857]; Dr. Blakiston prescribed it for both her and TC in 1863; see 39:145JWC to TC, 9 June 1863, and 149JWC to LAI, 11 June 1863. and a more effective diet;—which I have complied with by way of keeping the peace, tho’ there has otherwise no definite result appeared.

I am sorry to hear of Jean's foot threatening to be a tedious affairJohn wrote, 4 Sept.: “Jean's sore toe is getting better slowly, but will still require considerable time & patience.”: alas, I can do nothing for her or for any one, can only send my heart's wishes, my love and perpetual blessings if they were good for anything. AllinghamAllingham reported a visit from TC and Mary Aitken, 6 Sept.: “C. looking well and very neatly dressed—a long dark frock-coat and a straw hat dyed black. Says he is rather better than he was. Goes out every day about two, takes an omnibus to the top of Regent Street, walks along Portland Place and back again southward, and takes a Brompton omnibus back again. To-day he wished to walk with me. We went through S[outh] K[ensington] station and up through Brompton Churchyard to Hyde Park, and by his favourite road, that between the Ride and the Serpentine, sitting down a while on a free bench” (Allingham Diary 251). & Lecky are both come back and diligent enough in calling. But, alas, I can get small good of them or anyone, by conversation & am merely thankful for their good will. Adieu, my dear Brother, Kindest love to all of you. I ever am your affecte Brother

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 23 Sept. MS: NLS 528.63. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
23 Sep 1876.
docBody.p:
Today I must send you a few words in return for your kind and punctual notes and keep you at least from imagining that anything worse than usual is going on here. I continue daily to get my two dinner sleeps on tolerable terms, and every night, under various conditions a modicum of welcome sleep, usually followed by the prickly nervous vigilance, which there is generally no way of absolutely stilling; in fact I begin to see that this miserable afterclass of wakefulness is not likely to leave me or be cured by prescriptions, as Blakiston had prophecied but will in all probability continue with me so long as I myself continue here. Through the forenoon and through the interval
between after dinner sleep and bedtime I generally read (very ill off for suitable books); am reading much in SwiftJonathan Swift (1667–1745; ODNB), writer, dean of St. Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin, 1713–45. William Edward Hartpole Lecky wrote to his wife, 21 Sept.: “I was yesterday … a long omnibus and walking expedition with Carlyle, who seemed very well, is deep in Swift, was much pleased with some more books I have got him about Swift” (Elisabeth Lecky, A Memoir of the Right Hon. William Edward Hartpole Lecky [1909] 113). latterly and wondering much at the inscrutable man (with his Stellas and VanessasEsther Johnson (1681–1728; ODNB), friend of Swift, whom he called “Stella,” subject of his Journal to Stella (1784), and Esther Van Homrigh (ca. 1688–1723; ODNB), friend and possible lover of Swift, known as “Vanessa,” fictionalized in his Cadenus and Vanessa (1726); see also 49:225–26TC to JF, 4 Aug. 1875. & strange imperious character, and at last insufferable miseries);—but am yet far from satisfied with my poor choice of books.

We had a visit one night, as you probably know, from Henry WattHenry Watt, one of John A. Carlyle's stepsons; John replied, 25 Sept.: “Harry Watt wrote to me after seeing you in London, & thought you were looking better than when he had seen you before.” who surprised me much by the quantity of Scotch there had grown into his dialect. Another night pretty late (the night Mary was at BrightonMary was probably visiting Clementia Taylor, b. Doughty (1810–1908; ODNB), women's activist, and her husband, m. 1842, Peter Alfred Taylor (1819–91; ODNB), politician and radical. Mary worked for them at their school, Aubrey House in London, as teacher and secretary,Jan.–July 1873; see 48:63–64TC to JAC, 29 May 1872. Due to Peter's ill health they had moved to Eaton Place in Brighton. and not expected to
return till next day) Tom Wilson and WifeThomas Wilson; see TC to JAC, 15 Jan. suddenly announced themselves, but I was in too low spirits to accept and they went away bound for Weimar again on the morrow. I take no share in the violent emotion about Servia,Servia, old name for Serbia, which had been struggling for independence from the Ottoman empire since the beginning of the century; joining with Christian uprisings in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Bulgaria, Serbia declared war on Turkey, June 1876; see TC to GEH, 24 Nov. and make no answer when called upon to attend this or the other meeting on the subject, apprehending that any answer whatever from me would get printed. Fredrick Chapman has decided to have the two pieces, Norway Kings and Knox forthwith set up in stereotype to be the 32nd vol of our people's edition.Early Kings of Norway and The Portraits of John Knox were pbd. together as vol. 39 in the people's edn. of TC's Complete Works,1878. TC's nephew John Aitken had been working for Chapman & Hall since 1871, but had apparently recently left; John A. Carlyle wrote, 25 Sept.: “Last Saturday John had a letter from Chapman, stating that he would not expect him again in the office at Piccadilly. [We] were rather glad to hear that he is to have nothing more to do with Chapman, who is a … rather unscrupulous man in many respects & needs to be served by people of the same sort.” I am rather glad of this, though it will give me the trouble of carefully correcting. The paper is done & I can only send my poor blessing to you all & remain everThe Edinburgh Evening News reported, 25 Sept.: “Stupid Hoax about Mr Carlyle.” The report told that TC “was made the victim of a singularly idiotic mistake on Saturday [23 Sept.]. On that evening … literary circles in London were thrilled to the very core by a report that the illustrious sage of Chelsea had cut his throat. You may imagine the excitement the story caused, and you would scarcely believe that it was widely credited…. I need hardly say that the whole story was a ridiculous falsehood. I have seen a letter from Miss Aitkin … not only contradicting the story, but explaining how it originated. There lives near their house in ‘Carlyle’ Square an eccentric old man who actually did commit suicide. Somebody happening to mention the fact that Mr——cut his throat in Carlyle Square to a foolish reporter, he, in the excitement of getting a ‘good item,’ mistook his informant to say that Mr Carlyle himself had cut his throat. The tidings were sent to the late editions of the evening papers, and leaked out in this way. Poor Miss Aitkin's life has been made a burden to her ever since. People are calling in shoals to ask about the matter. Letters in heaps are coming asking if Mr Carlyle really made away with himself. As the old gentleman has wrathfully forbidden any contradiction to be sent to the London papers, his niece had to see these callers and to reply to these letters. Though Mr Carlyle is in splendid health, he is too feeble to write himself now, and this lady acts as his secretary. For the next few days her task will be an extremely heavy one.” The Morning Post reported, 25 Sept., that the suicide was Mr. George Wood of King's Road, retired army officer, unidentified further.
docBody.closer: Your Affectionate / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-Lady A [LLA], 16 Oct. MS: NLS Acc. 11388. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO LADY ASHBURTON

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
16 Oct. 1876
docBody.p:
It will be a great act of charity, if you now write to me, and be so benificent as send me your address, and predict for me when there is any chance of seeing you. It is a miserably long while since I heard from you or wrote to you; and, alas, the excuse of it, if any is itself a somewhat melancholy thing. Ever since the morning I parted with MaryMary Florence Baring, Lady Ashburton's da.; they had been traveling in Egypt; see TC to LLA, 21 March, but returned to Britain early June and would presumably have visited TC soon after. and you I have been tossing about with much suffering, continual want of sleep for one thing; in addition to which I learnt somewhere and understood as certain that you had let Loch LuichartKinlochluichart, Lady Ashburton's Highland estate, about 34½ mi. (60 km.) NW of Inverness. and were yourself away, I could not learn where; and not till after my return to London and various attempts there, your nephew and nieceLady Ashburton had many nieces and nephews, the most likely being some of the nine surviving children of her sister Mary Frances Anstruther; see 38:273–7438:biographical notes. The Carlyles had been friendly with Mary Anstruther and her da. Annie Nairn Stewart, b. Anstruther (1843–1931) during the early 1860s. being absent, did it strike me that to enquire at KentTC possibly refers to Lady Ashburton's estate at Addiscombe in Surrey; he presumably does not mean her London home at Kent House, as he says he has already looked for her in London. clearly offered a chance,—which I now make use of. All this is very stupid and unfortunate & I can only come upon your mercy and hope to be forgiven and at once answered. I am truly in great difficulties continually and though I went driving daily for a month amid the Highland breezes, under the kind guidance of the Mrs James Anstruther,Annabella Anstruther, widow of James Anstruther, living at Old Ballikinrain, Stirlingshire; for a photograph of Anstruther, see opp. She had first called on TC in 1874 (Wilson, Carlyle 6:328–33), and the following year she had invited him to visit her in Scotland. She called again, June 1876, and this time he agreed to visit. TC and Mary Aitken arrived at her home, 10 July. D. A. Wilson used passages from Anstruther's private journal to recount details of the visit: “She found [TC] an appreciative, as well as a singularly observant guest, remarking how strange it was that he should be here in her house, although two years before they had been totally unknown to each other. ‘But I felt such confidence in you,’ he added, ‘that I resolved to take the journey. There is not another house in the kingdom to which I would have gone.’ … They found that he could take unlimited ‘driving exercise, as fast as possible, along the roughest roads,’ and accordingly they were out a great deal…. They … saw, besides Loch Lomond, Loch Ard, the Lake of Menteith, Stirling … [and] the field of Bannockburn, where he ‘reconstituted the battle in the most vigorous and inspiring language.’ … On the day he left Ballikinrain, Mrs. Anstruther accompanied him to Glasgow, to go to the Cathedral and see Irving's tomb…. [From] Dumfries, he sent his hostess a complete set of his works, with an inscription in his own handwriting, sadly shaky now” (Wilson, Carlyle 6:386–90). Edward Irving, TC's great friend, buried in the crypt of Glasgow Cathedral. TC and Mary then stayed in Dumfries till mid-Aug.
whom you know, and did everything I could, there is no steady improvement even yet; and I conclude generally that this miserable affliction and want of sleep must continue my companion henceforth. All which I know you will pity and allow to plead with you.
Annabella Anstruther
Thomas Carlyle Papers, Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Columbia University in
the City of New York

I have seen nobody you are interested in; I yesterday missed Colonel John Stanley,See TC to JSTA, 2 July. from whom I might have heard something; and in short I have nothing to say that can interest you; and simply leave my case in your hands. Miss Bromley has twice called, but I have missed her each time. She is now in her new cottage at Walton-on-the-hill in the Epsom country,Walton-on-the-Hill, village 4½ mi. (7 km.) S of Epsom, near Banstead Downs; see TC to LLA, 21 March. but has made no answer since my note to her about a month ago.
I send my kindest regards and confident hopes to your dear Mary and am ever,

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 21 Oct. MS: NLS 528.64. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea S.W.
21 October 1876
docBody.p:
Your letters to myself and to Mary came all to hand and were thankfully received. I have been considerably tossed about, and steadily below par since you last heard from me. I generally get three or two hours of sleep at the beginning of each night, but am wofully, for most part, tormented with my nerves in my waking time though sometimes again too I fall asleep or half asleep. In short, I struggle on and do the best I can, but without hope of getting rid of this new kind of sorrow. There has been a vague speculation of our
going to MadeiraArchipelago in the North Atlantic, ruled by Portugal, about 320 mi. (520 km.) W of Morocco. through the winter wh. Froude strongly recommends for a fine sunny climate &c &c but I think on the whole there will nothing practically come of it. It is fairly cold at present wind sharp from East; and we must try to do our best with it when far colder, as it is like to grow.

But the thing I had to say is, specially, that if your mind at all encourage you to come now is as good a time as there is like to be; and I shall be glad to hear of such a purpose in you. We are all three I believe desirious to have the thing made feasible and agreeable but till you practically appear and try it for a month,John A. Carlyle wrote to Mary Aitken, 9 Oct.: “Later in the year I may be able to go to London … & I daresay some suitable lodging might be got for me not far from Cheyne Row…. I should be very sorry if you lost Mrs Canning who is so quiet & respectable, & has now learnt to cook successfully for you both. She had no fair chance when I was with you & everything was new to her including your Uncle's & my own still more complete want of teeth” (MS: NLS 1775G.61). He then wrote to TC, 13 Oct.: “What you say about my going to London to see you again is all kind & welcome as usual. I don’t think of starting for some time, but could be ready to do so at once if called upon.” He replied, 23 Oct.: “I never was so ill & uncomfortable as I have been for the last ten days, & I feel sure that I could do no good by starting for London just now…. Jean … also thinks I ought to remain here for the present at least. So I have reluctantly & after mature consideration given up the idea of going, as I could only be a burden to you & Mary under such circumstances.” Mrs. Canning, the new cook, unidentified further; see also TC to JAC, 15 Dec. 1875. I shall not clearly see how all is to be adjusted.

Froude is commonly the chief company I have for my walks and even he is not much of a heartfelt comfort: but at the end of next week, he intends for Edinburgh; and then I am reduced to Allingham, Lecky Fitz-James StephenJames Fitzjames Stephen. &c, who are of inferior value.

Yesterday I sent you two books, a German and an English, wh. you need not read unless you like;—I have taken no notice of, nor intend to take all. A whole book of German Lectures upon Hamlet is not inviting, and Dobell's Maxims, where I glance into them are not credible to me for most part.Possibly Henryk Struve (1840–1912), prof. of philosophy at Warsaw Univ., Hamlet eine Charakterstudie (Weimar, 1876); and Sydney Thompson Dobell (1824–74; ODNB), poet and scholar, Thoughts on Art, Philosophy, and Religion: Selected from the Unpublished Papers of Sydney Dobell, ed. John Nichol (1876). For TC's earlier contact with Dobell, see 26:209TC to SD, 17 Oct. 1851, and 29326:biographical notes. John replied, 23 Oct.: “I got the two books safely—Dobell's & the German one on Hamlet. Dobell's I find difficult to read & unsatisfactory; & the Hamlet one is too long for such a subject.” But enough of all this. It is no use continuing to write at present. I send my heart's affection to you all, Sister Jean to begin with; and am ever your affecte Brother,

div3.sourceNote: TC-GH [GEH], 24 Nov. Pbd: The Daily News, 28 Nov. 1876; Times, 28 Nov. 1876; H. J. Nicoll, Thomas Carlyle (1881) 241–44. Quot: Dunn, Froude 449; Wilson, Carlyle 6:392–93. Many other newspapers around that date also carried TC's letter. Text from the Daily News.
div3.head: TC TO GEORGE HOWARD

docBody.p: It by no means seems so evident to me as it does to you and your friends that an utterance of my opinion on the Eastern CrisisThe Eastern Crisis was caused by a combination of increasing nationalism, and resentment at the treatment of the Christian populations, in several of the countries in the European side of the Ottoman Empire. Uprisings in Serbia, Bosnia, and Herzegovina began in summer 1875, Bulgarian nationalists launched an insurrection in April 1876; then Serbia and Montenegro declared war on Turkey in June. The Eastern powers of Russia, Germany, and Austria-Hungary, mostly supporting the claims of the Balkan nationalists, and particularly wishing to support the Christian populations, met in Berlin, May 1876, to try to work out a resolution. could be important; but since you assure me that it might be of service to many persons now in doubt on that matter,Howard was a secretary of the National Conference on the Eastern Question, to be held 8 Dec. at St. James's Hall, and addressed by William Gladstone among others. Howard invited leading literary and scientific figures, including Carlyle, to write letters on the subject that would be read out at the meeting. “The Eastern Question Association” was formed at the conference “for the purpose of watching events in the East, giving expression to public opinion, and spreading useful information” (The Eastern Question Association: Papers on the Eastern Question [1877] preface). I overcome the very great reluctance I had to speak of the subject at all, & will try to indicate summarily what my own poor private views upon it are.

In the first place then, for fifty years back my clear belief about the Russians has been that they are a good and even noble element in Europe. Conspicuously they possess the talent of obedience, of silently following orders given;See, for instance, TC's letter to Alexander Herzen (1812–70), Russian writer and thinker, 13 April 1855: “In your vast Country … there is evident, down to this time, one talent in which it has the preeminence, giving it potency far beyond any other Nation … the talent of obeying,—which is much out of vogue in other quarters just now!” (CL 29:288). which, in the universal celebration of ballot-box, divine freedom, &c, will be found an invaluable and peculiar gift. Ever since Peter the Great'sPeter the Great (1672–1725), czar of Russia 1682–1725. appearance among them, they have been in steady progress of development. In our own time they have done signal service to God and man in drilling into order & peace anarchic populations all over their side of the world. The present Czar of RussiaAlexander II (1818–81), czar of Russia 1855–81. I judge to be a strictly honest and just man:—and in
short my belief is that the Russians are called to do great things in the world, and to be a conspicuous benefit, directly and indirectly, to their fellow men.

To undertake a war against Russia on behalf of the Turk, it is evident to me would be nothing short of insanity; and has become, we may fondly hope, impossible for any Minister, or Prime Minister, that exists among us.Disraeli, now Lord Beaconsfield, was in favor of supporting Turkey against both its insurgents and their Russian supporters. Twenty years ago we already had a mad war in defence of the Turk;The Crimean War 1853–56; for TC's views on that war, see 29:178TC to JC, 26 Oct. 1854. a mass of the most hideous and tragic stupidity, mismanagement and disaster (in spite of bravest fighting) that England was ever concerned in since I knew it; a hundred millions of money and above sixty thousand valiant lives were spent in the enterprise. By Treaties of Paris, &c., the Turk was preserved intact; binding himself only to reform his system of government,The Treaty of Paris, 30 March 1856, ended the Crimean War, restoring the pre-war borders between Russia and the Ottoman Empire, and demilitarizing the Black Sea, thus improving trade while weakening Russian influence. All the powers pledged to maintain the integrity of the Ottoman empire, which itself pledged to improve the conditions of its constituent provinces, and particularly of its Christian subjects. which certainly of all things in the world needed reform. And now, after twenty years of waiting, the Turk is found to have reformed nothing, nor attempted to reform anything. Not to add that by bankrupt finance he has swallowed a disastrous tribute of many new millions from the widows and orphans of England.The Ottoman Empire had taken out loans from Britain and France (its supporters at the time) at high interest rates, both to finance the Crimean War and for internal infrastructure projects. In Oct. 1875 the Ottoman government announced it was defaulting on part of the debt, and in March 1876 it suspended all cash repayments. As finis to all which, he has wound up by the horrors of Bulgaria, and such savageries as are without a parallel.The Daily News, 23 June, reported mass atrocities being carried out by Turkish irregulars against the Christian population in southern Bulgaria. Gladstone pbd. The Bulgarian Horrors and the Question of the East, 5 Sept.: “We now know in detail that there have been perpetrated, under the immediate authority of a Government to which all the time we have been giving the strongest moral, and for part of the time even material support, crimes and outrages, so vast in scale as to exceed all modern example, and so unutterably vile as well as fierce in character, that it passes the power of heart to conceive, and of tongue and pen adequately to describe them” (Bulgarian Horrors 9–10). With these weighty aggravations, the Turkish Question returns upon us anew, and demands a solution.Gladstone wanted the British government to drop its traditional hostility to Russia and begin negotiations with both Russia and the principal European powers to promote greater political autonomy for the Balkan states. However, Disraeli, fearful that a Russian invasion of Constantinople would threaten British trade routes to the Suez Canal and India, believed British support for Turkey was necessary for the security of the British empire.

It seems to me that something very different from war on his behalf is what the Turk now pressingly needs from England and from all the world; namely,
to be peremptorily informed that we can stand no more of his attempts to govern in Europe, and that he must quàm primùm turn his face to the eastward, forever quit this side of the Hellespont,Hellespont, classical name for the Dardanelles, a narrow strait connecting the Mediterranean to the Black Sea, and forming the boundary between European and Asian Turkey. and give up his arrogant ideas of governing anybody but himself.

Such immediate and summary expulsion of the Turk from Europe may appear to many a too drastic remedy; but to my mind it is the only one of any real validity under the circumstances. Improved management of these unhappy countries might begin on the morrow after this long-continued curse was withdrawn, and the ground left free for wise and honest human effort. The peaceful Mongol inhabitants would, of course, be left in peace, and treated with perfect equity, and even friendly consideration; but the governing Turk, with all his Pachas and Bashi-Bazouks,Pachas, high-ranking officials of the Ottoman empire, civil or military; Bashi-Bazouks, irregular Turkish troops particularly responsible for the Bulgarian atrocities. should at once be ordered to disappear from Europe and never to return.
This result is in the long run inevitable, and it were better to set about it now than to temporise and haggle in the vain hope of doing it cheaper some other time.

As to the temporary or preparatory government of the recovered provinces, cleared of their unspeakable Turk (government for twenty, or say any other term of years), our own experience in India may prove that it is possible, and in a few faifthful and skilful hands is even easy. Nor in the temper of the Czar and of the Austrian Emperor need the fair partition of these recovered territories be a cause of quarrel. Austria must expect to become more and more a Sclavic and Hungarian Empire, her nine millions of Germans more and more gravitating towards their countrymen of the great German Empire. The Czar, whose serious task it is to protect the Christian subjects in Turkey proper, will justly have a claim to territorial footing in the recovered country. To England there is one vital interest, and one only, that of securing its road to India, which depends on Egypt and the Suez Canal.

The thing to be desired is concord among the three Great Powers;Russia, Germany, and Austria-Hungary. and if, as we do hope, there is a mutual trust grounded on honesty of intention on the part of each, none claiming more than in the nature of things belongs to him, we may confidently expect that the difficulties of the business cannot prove insuperable. It seems to me the advice of Prince Bismarck, a magnanimous, noble and deep-seeing man, who has no national aims or interests in the matter, might be very valuable; nay, were he appointed arbiter where difficult
dissidences arose, what but benefit would be likely to result?Robert Gascoyne-Cecil (1830–1903; ODNB), 3d marquess of Salisbury, politician, sec. of state for India 1874–78, met Bismarck in Berlin, 23 Nov. Bismarck assured him that in the event of a war between Russia and Turkey, Germany intended to remain neutral, and he offered to serve as a mediator if relations deteriorated between Britain and Russia to the point of war. The Times reported, 27 Nov.: “Lord Salisbury's long conversation with Prince Bismarck has produced a mutual impression which will be favourable to the maintenance of peace. The accord will be effected by means of serious improvement firmly guaranteed in favour of the Christians of Turkey. The military preparations of Russia do not signify war in any circumstances.” But on this portion of the subject I am not called to write.

The only clear advice I have to give is, as I have stated, that the unspeakable Turk should be immediately struck out of the question, and the country left to honest European guidance; delaying which can be profitable or agreeable only to gamblers on the Stock Exchange, but distressing and unprofitable to all other men.—I remain always, dear Howard,
docBody.closer: Yours truly, / T. Carlyle.John Tyndall wrote to Mary Aitken, 5 Dec.: “A Russian Lady—Madame de Novikoff who lost a brother some time ago in Servia,—writes to me thus:—’I ask now a service from you. Since Mr Carlyle's letter about the Eastern question there is nothing that I should like more than to thank him personally for the great service he rendered to a cause extremely dear to me. Could you arrange that for me? But I hope I need not add, that, if you think my request would be unpleasant to your generous and noble friend, my desire will have no further development’” (MS: Royal Institution JT/1/T/92). Her brother Nicholas Kiréev d. July 1876, fighting as a volunteer for Serbia against Turkey. For a portrait of Novikov, see 73.

div3.sourceNote: MA-TC [MAI-TCA], 13 Dec. Pbd: Marrs 789–90. Thomas Carlyle, TC's nephew.
div3.head: TC TO MARY AITKEN TO THOMAS CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row, Chelsea. S.W.
13 Decr. 1876
docBody.p: My Uncle bids me send to you the enclosed inscription which he has written for your Father's tombstone.The enclosed inscription is missing; Edwin Marrs noted: “Missing. And all that is legible on Alexander's gravestone in Greenwood Cemetery, Brantford, are his name, the date of his death, and a portion of these three lines: A Man of Excellent Natural Calm Mind Full of / Valour, Affection, and [about four words illegible] and / Most Loving of Friends” (Marrs 790). He has thought on the subject very much and can think of nothing more appropriate for it. We are sorry that we have not been able to ascertain the dates; but no doubt it will be possible for you to find them out.

My Uncle is in pretty good health. The winter hitherto has been very mild and pleasant; and he has not yet suffered much from cold. The Dr who is here at presentJohn A. Carlyle had been staying in Cheyne Row since mid-Nov. is well and from Scotland the accounts are quite satisfactory.
docBody.closer: With love from us all, Yours very truly / Mary Carlyle Aitken
