div3.sourceNote: TC-CGD, 30 Dec. Pbd: Sir Charles Gavan Duffy, Conversations with Carlyle (1892) 251–52.
div3.head: TC TO CHARLES GAVAN DUFFY

docBody.dateline:
5 Great Cheyne Row, Chelsea, S.W.
Dec. 30, 1876.
docBody.p: Till the arrival, about a week ago, of the Melbourne Review,Charles Gavan Duffy, “Port Phillip: A Preliminary Chapter in the Political History of Victoria,” The Melbourne Review 4 (Oct. 1876): 385–409. with your article, addressed to me, which was very welcome, both as personal memento, and also as a bit of pretty enough reading, I had seen no trace of you, nor heard any rumour of news. Singularly enough, within the last three days, I have received from Melbourne, from a poor neighbourNeighbor unidentified further; Duffy described him as “a young man whom [TC] thought deserving, or, at any rate, in much need of help” (Duffy 250–51). of yours there, a feeble but pathetic request, which, on reading it, I decided to send you, with two enclosures that were in it, which are now by mistake burnt, in hopes you might be able to do something for the unfortunate writer who has thus sent his message to you, written within a stone's throw of your own door, but obliged to go round the world before it could get entrance! Pray, for my sake, read with attention; understand, too, that the bits of mildly satirical verse, once printed in the Melbourne Punch,The Melbourne Punch (1855–1900); verses untraced. were not without some decided indications of a superior talent that way. These unhappily are burnt, and you must take my word for them. The poor creature's letter, as you will observe, expresses a kind of feeble hope that you, by some way or another, might find some employment for him to supplement his miserable £40 a year—if you had been in office, and if he, poor wretch, had not been on the free trade side of politics!Duffy had held various political positions in Victoria, including premier and chief secretary 1871–72; see 48:21TC to CGD, 12 Dec. 1871, and 166TC to JAC, 19 Feb. 1873. Duffy himself was at least partially in favor of free trade.

The thing I do desire of you, dear Duffy, is that you would see this poor deformed creature, and examine him with your own eyes, and in right and brotherly pity and desire to help. To me it would give a real pleasure if you
could in any way help him. And that is all my message; and so I leave it in your hands.

Of myself I have only to say that, being now in my 82nd year, I feel more completely invalided than ever before, and have no strength left for work of any kind. But, except langour and laziness, I feel no decay of spiritual faculty; and I have in the late months read with enjoyment the whole of Shakespeare, and am now reading, still with a kind of real enjoyment and wonder, Brumoy's “Théâtre des Grecs,”Pierre Brumoy (1688–1742), Le Théâtre des Grecs, 3 vols. (1730); TC owned the first vol. of the 1785 edn.; see Carlyle's House 39. The work consisted of translations, discussions, and analyses of seven Greek tragedies. of which I have finished prosperously about the fourth part. Adieu, dear Duffy; may good ever be with you, and the blessing of an old friend, if that be of any value.— Yours, ever truly,

div3.sourceNote: MA [MAI]-[AB], 14 Jan. MS: Hornel. Hitherto unpbd. Recipient identified as most likely Amalie Charlotte Elise Marianne Bölte (1811–91), German feminist and writer. She worked in England as a governess, 1839–51, when she became friendly with the Carlyles; see JWC to HW, 15 July [1847]. TC's last recorded contact with her was in July 1856; see TC to AB, 5 July 1856.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO [AMALIE BÖLTE]

docBody.dateline:
14 Jan. 1877
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
docBody.p: Mr Carlyle bids me say, that he has received the Frauen Brevier,This was presumably Bölte's Neues Frauenbrevier (Leipzig, 1876); she had earlier pbd. Frauen-Brevier (Leipzig, 1862). which you have kindly sent him. He has been reading it and he thinks very well of it.— He was much pleased to hear of you after such a long interval of silence on your part. He hopes that you will excuse his not writing to you with his own hand, which has lately become so shaky that writing is very unpleasant to him, indeed next to impossible. You will be glad to know, however, that he is in very tolerable health, able to walk for a mile or two every day no matter what the weather may be, and able to enjoy his books as well as ever.
He is very sorry to hear that your health has been and still is so unsatisfactory. He sends his best wishes and many cordial remembrances; and I remain

postscript.p: I may mention that I am Mr Carlyle's niece; and have been living with him for the last 8 years.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 28 April. MS: NLS 528.66. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 4:441. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
24 Cheyne RowTC's house had recently been renumbered 24 Cheyne Row; Mary used the old “5 Great Cheyne Row” headed paper, crossing out the “5 Great” and replacing with “24.”,
Chelsea. S.W.
28 April 1877.
docBody.p: A few words to you today will be a kind of comfort to me. I can inform you withal by the same operation of our general condition here and any adventures we have had if indeed there be any such worthy of pen and ink, which indeed may be doubted.

One thing I can say with certainty that we have had a great miss of you in these two weeks since you went away.John A. Carlyle had been staying at Cheyne Row since mid-Nov. 1876, returning to Dumfries early April. I remember always the look of your face from the dressing room window,—a face not quiet & cheerful as you smoked & played with the cat; but looking out seriously, anxious and sad, as you thought of the journey before you. I look out now and find only a mournful remembrance that the Dr is away. I can only wish that some new impulse may rise in you to return. We have no long time to be together in this same world, and nature herself seems to prompt that as far as rationally feasible, we may be in speaking communication while time yet is.

I have not been usually worse in health since you went away but rather in general visibly improved in point of sleep especially. I generally fall asleep soon after going to bed and lie there unconscious till after five o’clock sometimes till half past six and get through my morning's washings and dressings in a gloomy but a quiet mood of mind scarcely above one night of very bad sleep and not one or none at all have I had since we parted.

Mary and I have both been with the dentist,William R. Balland; see TC to JAC, 23 Dec. 1876. who has supplied me with a kind of under jaw as well as could have been expected; filling up the gap of the two loose fore-teeth & fitting as well as could be expected. I can when in good luck masticate a thin piece of roast mutton; beef is rather more dubious and yesterday I broke away one of my false front teeth in that very operation. On the whole I don’t expect to be much benefited by this new teeth adventure but it will do me at least no ill & keeps the mouth in a more solid and shapely condition.

The Leckys, Froude, Henry CooperHenry Frederick Cowper. &c come about me as usual and the commonest adventure is what you and I were used to a mixed drive and walk to the top of Portland Place or sometimes, though rarely, as yesterday a walk down to Charing Cross where Froude wanted a Turkish Map,Presumably to Stanford's, 7–8 Charing Cross, specialist map shop, est. 1853 by Edward Stanford (1827–1904; ODNB), mapmaker and publisher. after which a Chelsea bus is the regular conveyance. The evening passes in reading (not one very eligible book has yet fallen to my share). Between 11 & 12 the old puff of smoking, but, alas, there is no Dr now there, and then downstairs to the solitary promenade and summing up of the day's poor transactions. DarwinErasmus Darwin. I have seen once since you went, hardly any other worth noting. On the whole I have no intimate here and feel my visitors especially stray visitors to be a labour, little else. I have got no books worth sending you today, a quantity of
Magazines are dropping in especially the “ 19th Century”The Nineteenth Century (1877–1972), a monthly literary magazine, founded by James Thomas Knowles (1831–1908; ODNB), editor and architect. The first issue, pbd. March, sold over 20,000 copies. Knowles was previously ed. of the Contemporary Review, but following a dispute with its new owners, he resigned and launched a new periodical, providing a venue for impartial commentary that was open to writers of all parties and opinions. decidedly rather worthless, though of huge sale (25,000 they said of No 1). No 3 shall be with you in the course of next week, if you care to see it.

Dismal rumoursApparently Lord Carnarvon, the colonial sec. and a critic of Disraeli's policies, had leaked details of a recent cabinet meeting to Froude, who in turn conveyed them to TC; see TC to EOT, 4 May. are afloat that Dizzy secretly intends to break in upon the Russian Turk WarSee TC to GEH, 24 Nov. 1876. At the conference of great powers in Constantinople, Dec. 1876–Jan. 1877, Russia, Germany, and Britain demanded that Turkey institute reforms and make peace with Serbia, and that Bosnia and Bulgaria be declared autonomous. The Ottoman government prevaricated, and this prompted Russia to declare war, 24 April. The British government adopted a position of conditional neutrality, based on the demands that free passage was preserved with the East through the Suez Canal, Egyptian sovereignty was respected, and Constantinople was not invaded. However, Lord Beaconsfield remained deeply suspicious of Russia's intentions, and did not rule out military intervention. and supporting himself by his 100 Irish Home RulersIn the general election of 1874, out of the 101 Irish seats in the House of Commons, 60 were taken by members of the Irish Home Rule League, led by Isaac Butt (1813–79; ODNB), lawyer and politician, M.P. for Limerick 1871–79, who instituted themselves a separate party, not affiliated with either conservatives or liberals; 31 of the other Irish M.P.s were conservatives. a great troop of commonplaces Tories JewsThe Anglo-Jewish Association, founded in 1871, campaigned against the persecution of Jews in Russia, Serbia, and Bulgaria. John Simon (1818–1897; ODNB), serjeant-at-law, Liberal M.P. for Dewsbury 1868–88, wrote to the Evening Standard, 20 Jan.: “[In Russia] the Jews are as much oppressed as the Christians of the Turkish provinces whose sufferings have so touched Russian hearts, and made Russia their chivalrous champions. The Jews there are not in a condition to speak or act, or even to form an opinion upon any public question.” &c &c suddenly get parliament to support him in a new philo-Turk War against Russia the maddest thing the human imagination could well conceive. I am strongly urged to write something farther upon it; but cannot feel that I have anything new to say. Froude seems really persuaded that the purpose of Dizzy is steady in his mind; I advised that the “Conference”The National Conference on the Eastern Question; see TC to GEH, 24 Nov. 1876. (G. Howards) should hold another meeting and rouse the spirit of England to declare itself. This I hope they will find it possible to do.

Our weather has been a series of stormy east winds, several times
very violent, but always at least dry; except for their noise, they are not unwelcome.

Allingham's poor Wife is we hope slowly recovering but there is still said to be constant danger.Helen Allingham had given birth to a da., Eva Margaret, 21 Feb., and was ill for several months. Allingham noted, 11 April: “C. very sympathetic about H.'s serious illness” (Allingham Diary 255). MillaisJohn Everett Millais; he had arranged to paint TC's portrait. has not sent his message but it is now likely from day to day. I shall be right glad to have it over and that is nearly all my hope about it and all my care.

Thanks for the punctual news you send us about our kindred. Scotsbrig John duly announced that a 6th childJohn and Margaret Carlyle's son Thomas. was born to him and that all was going well. Do you think Jamie has any notion of Birmingham this summer. If so tell him he is confidently expected here and not in such a hurry as he usually is.Their brother James's son-in-law, William Scott, and his family, lived in Birmingham; James's last visit to TC had been very short; see TC to JAC, 29 Jan. 1876.

I will now terminate with my kind regards to every one in the Hill, Jean especially I could wish much to hear from. Tell me particularly how she is.John replied, 4 May: “Jean does not look worse than last year, but she generally breakfasts in bed, & hardly ever goes out for any exercise…. I hope she will get out whenever we have warmer weather. She often goes to look after things in the garden, & is now busy superintending the removal of the henhouse, getting the walk smoothed behind the house & placing a garden seat established there.” And so adieu for this day.

div3.sourceNote: TC-editor of the Times [EOT], 4 May. Pbd: Times, 5 May 1877; Shepherd, Carlyle 312–13; J. H. Nicoll, Thomas Carlyle (1881) 245–46; Wilson, Carlyle 6:399.
div3.head: TC TO THE EDITOR OF THE TIMES

docBody.p:
A rumour everywhere prevails that our miraculous Premier, in spite of his Queen's Proclamation of Neutrality, intends, under cover of “care for British interests,” to send the English Fleet to the Baltic,TC had apparently heard details of a recent cabinet meeting from Froude; see TC to JAC, 28 April. The London correspondent of the Southern Reporter wrote, 31 May: “The story of Thomas Carlyle's letter to the Times which caused so much stir the other day has oozed out. I have it on unimpeachable authority that at the Cabinet meeting held just before the letter was written, Lord Beaconsfield proposed a certain movement of the British fleet, which other members of the Cabinet opposed, on the ground that it would be deemed by the Russians equivalent to a declaration of war. A long and rather warm discussion ensued, and finally the idea of the Premier was abandoned. The Earl of Carnarvon, who strongly reprobated the views advanced by Lord Beaconsfield, told the whole affair to Mr Froude, the historian, whom he met shortly after the meeting. Mr Froude in his turn conveyed the news to the sage of Chelsea, and the latter could not forbear the opportunity of giving the ‘miraculous Premier’ and the ‘unspeakable Turk’ a rap on the knuckles.” Lord Derby, the foreign sec., noted in his diary, 1 May: “In cabinet, we began by a discussion on the strength of the Russian fleet: which Disraeli either really believes, or affects to suppose, to be very strong: but all our information shows that they have few ships, and those defective. [Disraeli] pressed very eagerly for the strengthening of our own navy…. The lines of defence in front of Constantinople would require 50,000 men, and six weeks to prepare them. On the whole it seemed clear from [the] evidence that any expedition intended to land troops and hold a position would be a serious business, involving much preparation and expense” (Derby Diaries, 1869–78, ed. John Vincent [1994] 396–97). Since the Crimean War, British policy in the Baltic had been to keep Russia out of the north Atlantic and the North Sea, but Disraeli's government had no specific plans to launch a naval expedition in the region. or do some other
feat which shall compel Russia to declare war against England. Latterly the rumour has shifted from the Baltic and become still more sinister, on the eastern side of the scene, where a feat is contemplated that will force not Russia only, but all Europe, to declare war against us. This latter I have come to know as an indisputable fact; in our present affairs and outlooks surely a grave one.

As to “British interests,” there is none visible or conceivable to me, except taking strict charge of our route to India by Suez and Egypt; and, for the rest, resolutely steering altogether clear of any co-partnery with the Turk in regard to this or any other “British interest” whatever. It should be felt by England as a real ignominy to be connected with such a Turk at all. Nay, if we still had, as, in fact, all ought to have, a wish to save him from perdition and annihilation in God's world, the one future for him that has any hope in it is even now that of being conquered by the Russians and gradually schooled and drilled into peaceable attempt at learning to be himself governed. The newspaper outcry against RussiaAfter Russia declared war on 24 April, there was widespread opposition in both the British government and the British press to Russia's action, on the grounds that military action would only create further hostility among the Turks, and exacerbate the problems particularly of the Christian population. The Pall Mall Gazette commented, 7 May: “Russia long since pledged herself to a concurrent course of diplomatic ‘bounce’ and military bullying. Such conduct could have only one result, as was long since forseen. And it is a melancholy reflection that this course of conduct … would never have been adopted if certain English orators and newspaper-writers had not persuaded the Czar and his Ministers that the ‘great heart of England’ sanctioned it, rejoiced at it.” is no more respectable to me than the howling of Bedlam, proceeding, as it does, from the deepest ignorance, egoism, and paltry national jealousy.

These things I write not on hearsay, but on accurate knowledge, and to all friends of their country will recommend immediate attention to them while there is yet time, lest in a few weeks the maddest and most criminal thing that a British Government could do should be done, and all Europe kindle into flames of war. I am, &c,

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 5 May. MS: NLS 528.67. Quot: Froude, Carlyle 2:442. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Many thanks for your letter. I have nothing to return to you that is worth much attention. Enclosed is the ChorleyWilliam Brownsword Chorley (1804–79), M.D., brother of TC's friend John Rutter Chorley (1806–67; ODNB; see 19:135TC to JWC, early Aug. 1845, and 22:30TC to WEF, 9 Aug. 1847). He was often in financial trouble; see 45:6–7TC to HFC, 11 July 1867. John A. Carlyle wrote, 4 May, enclosing a letter to himself from Chorley: “He had written on Sunday last to me asking in desperate circumstances for the small sum he acknowledges, & had forgotten that there is no London Sunday post & he could not by any possibility get the money on Monday…. He is a very curious, wiry, half-distracted man; but seems now really to have some chance of getting over his difficulties for the time at least.” John and William B. Chorley had been friendly for many years; see 44:217TC to HFC, 19 June 1867. Letter. He says nothing to me about his application to you: it appears therefore he has got a double Allowance to liberate his goods. He is a distracted dud of whom one wishes to hear nothing more for a great while.

Poor Elizabeth Welsh!Elizabeth Welsh, d. 4 May; she was one of JWC's aunts, living in Edinburgh. She is out of all her troubles. She was the best of all her family that I was acquainted with. I cannot guess who wrote that fatal announcement. If you have any hold of Dr Hunter I should like much to hear from him what is becoming of poor Ann Welsh.Jean Aitken wrote, 6 May: “The Dr has just been down & bids me tell you that he has written to Dr Hunter today to see what he says about poor Miss Anne Welsh…. She is much to be pitied the poor Sister who is left, but I think she is not likely to survive her Sister long. They were both alike frail when I last saw them but that is more than a year since.” Dr. Jacob Dickson Hunter, friend of John A. Carlyle's, and physician to the Welsh sisters.
I have not been worse since you last heard but rather better. But today Mary feels very poorly having caught a violent cold & sore throat, which incapacitates her from much writing.

The only bit of news worth sending is that after much urgency & with
a dead-lift effort against my burdens & incumbrances I have this day got issued through the Times a small indespensible deliverance on the Turk & Dizzy questionSee TC to EOT, 4 May. Jean wrote, 6 May: “I hope we may get a sight of your letter it will surely appear in some of our papers tomorrow. What a fool Dizzie must be!” wh. you shall see by the next post. Dizzy it appears to the horror of those who have any interest in him and his proceeding has decided to have a new war for the Turk against all mankind and this Letter hopes to drive a nail through his mad & maddest speculation on that side.— Time is so run
out & Mary so streaming with cold that I will not add another word except my constant love to Jean & to you all. Blessings be with you ever

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 12 May. MS: NLS 528.68. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Your letter I took out with me this morning & endeavoured with my shaky fingers anxiously to pick out what the fatal purport of it was, the death of my two poor AuntsAnn Welsh d. 10 May, six days after her sister Elizabeth; see TC to JAC, 5 May. John A. Carlyle wrote, 11 May: “The enclosed telegram, along with Dr Hunter's small scrap, came to me this morning … & my first impulse was to send you a telegram, but Jean & all the rest thought it would be better not to agitate you by doing so…. [Dr. Hunter] had known all the three sisters very intimately from his childhood, & always attended them in their illnesses, much to their satisfaction.” The telegram announcing Ann Welsh's death had been sent to Dr. Hunter by Mary May Craven, b. Welsh (1829–85; see 39:27139:biographical notes), da. of JWC's paternal uncle Robert Welsh (ca. 1786–1841; see 14:217JWC to MW, [8 July 1842]). She was one of the few surviving Welsh family members (see 43:94–95JWC to BB, 28 Dec. 1865) and had presumably been staying with her aunt. coming down precipitously upon me thus without a word of farewell to either of them has saddened my very heart. Poor good souls gone at once the road we have all to go!— I shall be anxious to hear whatever word Dr. HunterDr. Hunter had promised to send further details; see TC to JAC, 29 May. may say on the subject.

For the last three or four days I have been in the gulph of blue pill greatly deranged in my inner works but at last fairly seeming a little better. I get a great deal of sleep considering everything but of a rather miserable quality. Nothing new has happened here except it be that Froude has gone into the country for a week. Three days ago I had a visit from Paterson Erskine of LinlathenJames Paterson, nephew of TC's old friend Thomas Erskine; he took the surname Erskine on inheriting the Linlathen Estate in 1870; see 48:4TC to JCA, 13 Oct. 1871, and 23648:biographical notes. & the day before yesterday his wife & a half-blind SisterPaterson Erskine's wife was Mary Jane, and her sister was probably Charlotte Elizabeth Dick Maitland, b. Macnab (1828–92), widow of William Fuller Maitland (1813–76). came in & sat a long while good women both but rather wearisome to me. I had seen them last as bright little girls by name McNab. The younger of them & at that time the smarter is now a forlorn widow in real danger of losing her sight altogether. The left eye is irrevocably shut up from total loss of power about the eyelids & the other she is much afraid will go the same road. The second
vol. of the Erskine letters is to come about the end of Oct.Letters of Thomas Erskine of Linlathan, ed. William Hanna, 2 vols. (Edinburgh, 1877). John wrote, 17 April: “Today a copy of the Erskine letters … came for me from Erskine's nephew…. And your copy, wh Mary forwarded, also had come punctually and was immediately handed to her mother.” TC had sent his letters from Thomas Erskine to Paterson Erskine in Oct. 1871 for inclusion in the volume; see 48:4TC to JCA, 13 Oct. 1871. Patterson Erskine had seen lately Stirling of Kier whose new WifeSir William Stirling Maxwell; he m., 1 March, his longtime friend Caroline Norton, at her home, 10 Upper Grosvenor St. is totally crippled was married in her chair and never stirred except as wheeled in and out in that sad vehicle. Poor souls both; only that Stirling has still his strength & I think two promising boys.Stirling Maxwell had two sons, John and Archibald, from his first marriage, to Anna Maria Leslie Melville.

The DeQuincey's LifeH. A. Page, Thomas de Quincey: His Life and Writings, 2 vols. (1877). H. A. Page was one of several pseudonyms used by Alexander Hay Japp (1836–1905; ODNB), Scottish author, editor, journalist, and publisher. Jean wrote, [27 May]: “Thank you very much for De Quincey's Life the Editor is a muddlehead but there are many interesting things in the Bk in spite of the helpless style of the Editor. I had to lend it to the Dr & have not got back for second volume. But I have been reading some of Mr Erskine's letters today instead.” Thomas Penson de Quincey (1785–1859; ODNB), essayist; friendly with the Carlyles in the late 1820s; see 4:282–83TC to ADBM, 20 Nov. 1827, and 291TC to JAC, 29 Nov. 1827; see also Carlyle, Reminiscences 303. wh. Mary has directed to her Mother will I doubt much weary you both. It is wretchedly ill done by the flaccid ever-reitterating editor but there is a straggling likeness of DeQ. himself glittering through at intervals & he is if not a great a very singular specimen of humanity. Next week I shall have another bit of biography to send you, which perhaps may prove more entertaining.Probably James Brown, Life of a Scottish Probationer, Being a Memoir of Thomas Davidson (Glasgow, 1877); see TC to JAC, 19 May. Not another word from me except my loving farewell to you all and best blessing if it were worth anything all round.
docBody.closer: Ever your affecte / T. Carlyle.

div3.sourceNote: MA [MAI]-DD, 17 May. Pbd: David Davidson, Memories of a Long Life (Edinburgh, 1890) 327. David Davidson (1811–1900), army engineer and inventor, childhood friend of JWC's; see 35:biographical notes. He lived in Edinburgh and regularly visited the Welsh sisters.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO DAVID DAVIDSON

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
17th May 1877.
docBody.p:
My Uncle is very much obliged to you for your kindness in writing to him. But for your thoughtful attention, he would have heard no
particulars at all of the death of his poor aunts,Davidson wrote, 8 May, telling TC that both Welsh sisters had been ill all winter, that Elizabeth Welsh had died, and he did not expect Ann to live much longer: “[I]t would be almost a mercy were she taken to glory, there unexpectedly to find her dear sister just entered before her, and dear Grace too, from whose death Ann told me a few weeks ago, she had never recovered!” Davidson wrote again, 15 May: “I have just returned from helping to lay dear Anne Welsh by her two sisters. She was hardly conscious after I took leave of her [5 May], and just a week after her sister, passed so quietly into the unseen, that they scarce knew when she ceased to breathe.” Their sister Grace d. 1867; see 44:160–61TC to JCA, 24 Feb. 1867. and he was very anxious to have them. You will easily guess how sad my uncle is to think that he has lost his old friends; but he is glad to think that poor Miss Ann did not live to realize the heavy sorrow that was waiting her in the death of her sister.— My uncle begs you to accept his grateful thanks and regards.—

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 19 May. MS: NLS 528.69. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:331–32. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
19 May 1877
docBody.p: The second Letter of Col. Davidson which comes to you here is the only one worth sending, out of hatfuls of all insignificant complexions which are not worth your looking at.

This week I have been rather ill off; once or twice extremely so with the affair of sleep. But last night by the special blessing of Heaven I had once more a right human sleep of six hours; & feel much better if there were any good use that I could make of my restored capacities. The fact is I was making an attack of the “blue pill” kind which I find now & then to be the only medical appliance of the least avail to me & this time it had to be applied twice and the good results of it, if they are really come, are only clearly this day visible. I have had a great many miscellaneous & mostly come-of-will visitors. They & even the customary sort are nearly altogether a sorrow and an encumbrance to me. The earth grows very solitary when all our loved ones are faded away to the unseen Land. Yesterday Lady Ashburton was here, her Mary & she in good trimLady Ashburton and her da., Mary, had recently been traveling in Europe. She wrote from Kent House, [14 May]: “One line today that through God's great goodness to us we are arrived this evening, home again, safe & well…. When will you come & see us I wonder?— Before many hours won’t you?” & exceedingly kind; Miss Bromley has a capricious SisterProbably Caroline Bromley's younger sister, Louisa Cecilia Bromley Davenport. under
bronchitis whom she is continually obliged to watch over so that I have not seen her for a couple of weeks. Froude has been away “fishing” for a week, to be out of the way of questions about the “torpedo” which you read in The Times.TC presumably refers to his letter to the Times, 4 May, which was widely believed to be based on information from Froude about a cabinet meeting; see TC to EOT 4 May There seems to be a hope for the present that Dizzy is crippled in regard to his Turk war or war of any kind: he is said to be in goutDisraeli suffered from a variety of ailments in the mid-1870s, including gout, asthma, and bronchitis. & in perpetual flirtation with some Lady Radford;Selina Louisa Bridgeman, b. Weld-Forester (1819–94; ODNB), countess of Bradford; after the death of his wife, Mary Anne, 1872, Disraeli began an epistolary romance with Lady Bradford, 1873, as well as with her sister Anne Elizabeth Stanhope, b. Forester (1802–85; ODNB), countess of Chesterfield. for certain he refuses altogether to speak in the House of Lords & one sometimes hears that he is losing his memory &c; & in brief that there is no chance of his ever trying to become a ChathamWilliam Pitt (1708–1778; ODNB), 1st earl of Chatham, prime minister of Great Britain 1766–68. He was leader of the House of Commons during much of the Seven Years’ War, 1756–63, and was widely credited with its successful conclusion. in this world to which he has long been a disgrace in all wise men's opinion & is now what may be called a continually minatory terror & curse.
Our weather is becoming warm & friendly to growth of all kinds,—the latter result partly owing to continual showers & drippings which are not so handy.

Please send back the Davidson Letter. There is one phrase in it which is deeply pathetic, under a coarse form,—that of his always in killing off his lambs taking the last two of them together.See MAI to DD, 17 May; Davidson wrote, 15 May: “When we come to the end of the flock we have in our little field here, we take the last two together— Thus has the Good Shepherd done with the last two of this large family.” Daily I think of my two poor Aunts lying silent together in their new grave & ending for me the Craigenputtock genealogy,The farm of Craigenputtoch had belonged to JWC's paternal grandfather, John Welsh (1757–1823); see Carlyle, Reminiscences 114–15. Ann and Elizabeth Welsh were almost the last of his descendants; see TC to JAC, 12 May. you may well think with boundless reflections on my part.

The bookProbably James Brown, Life of a Scottish Probationer, Being a Memoir of Thomas Davidson (Glasgow, 1877); Thomas Davidson (1838–90), preacher and poet. John A. Carlyle wrote, 27 May: “[Jean] has read more than the half of that ‘Life of a Scottish Probationer’ since the morning…. He certainly was one of the most wonderful probationers ever heard of…. The story of his life circumstances is very well told, & is most interesting.” you get with this has given us great satisfaction here, far beyond what was expected, a beautiful, tender & melodious self-drawn picture of a Scottish human soul whom one finds to be both humble & high & on the
whole pathetically welcome to one's heart. The DeQuincey book,See TC to JAC, 12 May. I find is totally unknown here & indeed I think is never likely to circulate much nor DeQuincey himself with his strange organization, pretty faculties to come generally into vogue again, truly the present biographer in general is one of the worst that could put pen to paper.

Thank Sister Jean for the kind little letter she wrote me some time ago. If a new charitable thought of the kind arise in her try to forward it by all means in your power.TC means he regards Jean writing to him as a charitable act, and wishes John to encourage it. Jean wrote, 6 May, that John continually interrupted her while she was writing to him: “The Dr has been in three or four times since I began & spoilt my chance of making a feasible letter…. He is very queer whenever he sees me writing he delights in bothering me, tho’ I daresay he means no harm.” To her always my special love & regards. Tell me about Mary's daughter & her wedding at the Gill. Do you know anything about the bridegroom.Mary Austin's da. Isabella was to marry Robert Hoggan, farmer at Gillbrae, Dalton. Jean wrote, [27] May: “Two of the lasses from the Gill came up here…. They told us about Isabella's intended marrying in June…. It seems they have been engaged for the last six years, but cd not well see their way, the Father of young Hogan being very old & helpless the Mother also is still alive tho’ from the little they said one was led to believe she also was in ‘a weak nervous state & needed to be taken care of.’ There are also two maiden sisters living in the house…. The young people seem to have seen no end of waiting. The two sisters of Hogan being against their brother marrying at all…. This is the only son & will I suppose continue to manage the Farm as he has been doing for a number of years past.” I hope it will be a benifit & blessing to all parties concerned. I have a book here for James Aitken but it cannot come off till next week. Here has Mrs LeckyCatharina Elisabeth Lecky. come in. I must end at once. With my kindest love to one & all of you

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 29 May. MS: NLS 528.70. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:332–33 inc. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper, with “5, Great” crossed out and “24” superimposed.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I confidently meant to have written on Saturday last but found myself in the hands of Millais the painterSee TC to JAC, 28 April. Millais wrote, 22 May: “Can you give me a sitting any morning this week? I am quite ready 11 o’clock.” and without time for that or any such operation. Millais still keeps hold of me for four days now, this and Sunday my only
holidays from him hitherto and I see not yet what will be the day of my deliverance. Millais seems to be in a state of almost frenzy about finishing with the extremest perfection his surprising and difficult task; evidently a worthy man. Mary went with me yesterdayMillais had recently moved to a new house built for him in a palatial, Italianate style at 2 Palace Gate, Kensington. William Bell Scott (1811–1890; ODNB; see 23:3TC to WBS, [3 April 1848]), poet and painter, recalled that “[Millais] had had Carlyle for two sittings to paint his portrait [26 and 28 May]. The philosopher of Chelsea turned round upon him on the stair of his new house, which is said to be quite a scala dei giganti, and inquired, ‘Has paint done all this, Mr. Millais?’ On being answered, with a laugh, in the affirmative, Carlyle continued, ‘Ah, well, it shows what a number of fools there are in the world!’” (Autobiographical Notes of the Life of William Bell Scott, ed. W. Minto [New York, 1892] 2:223). to see and had doubts privately as to what the success would be; but indeed it can, with my complete acquiescence be what it will. For the third and last time I am in the hands of a best painter in England (Watts,George Frederic Watts (1817–1904; ODNB) had painted three portraits of TC in 1867–68, but only finished two; see 45:142TC to JAC, 30 May 1868, and 195TC to JAC, 4 Nov. 1868; for the portraits, see 45:frontispiece and 140TC to JAC, 30 May 1868. Legros,Alphonse Legros (1837–1911; ODNB), French painter and etcher, living in London from 1863. He was commissioned by Stavros Dilberoglue to paint TC, Feb. 1877; Legros replied to Dilberoglue, 2 March: “Votre proposition me sourit d’autant plus qu’il y a longtemps que je désire faire le portrait de Carlyle [Your proposal makes me smile especially as I have long wanted to do a portrait of Carlyle]” (MS: Bancroft Lib., Univ. of California, Berkeley). TC does not mention sitting for Legros in his letters; “Of Carlyle … Legros spoke with veneration. The gentler side of the old sage's nature was borne in upon him as he watched the sad yet beautiful face take on tenderness while listening to his niece reading Scottish poetry during the sittings” (Charles Holroyd and Thomas Okey, “Alphonse Legros: Some Personal Reminiscences,” Burlington Magazine 20 [1912]: 276). Millais) and with that I will consider the smallest quasi-
duty of leaving some conceivable likeness of myself as altogether finished.

You asked me lately as to my election of a place of burial.John A. Carlyle wrote, 20 May: “Many a time during the winter when we were walking together … I wished to ask you what you thought of interment amongst the crowd in Westminster Abbey, & whether in any case you would prefer resting there to resting at Ecclefechan beside your Father & Mother & the others of us…. [It] might be well to write down in a few words what your wishes are.” For TC's instructions about his burial in his will, see 48:151–52TC's Will. A good many years ago that was done & it is marked in my Will that I am to rest in the Kirkyard of Ecclefechan, as near as possible to my Father & Mother.— The only other thing that haunts me with a sense of incumbency as a thing yet to do is that of writing something about poor ForsterEliza Ann Forster wrote, 1 June, enclosing a copy of the inscription for her husband's tombstone: “In Memory / of / John Forster Esqre / Historian, Biographer, Critic / Noted in private life / for the robustness of his character, and the warmth / of his affections; / for his ceaseless industry in literature and business, / and the lavish services which in the midst of / his crowded life, he rendered to friends; / for his keen appreciation of every species of excellence, / and the generosity of his judgments on / books and men.” TC did not write anything about Forster. in memory of his great kindnesses to me ever since I was left alone in the world; but I find it extremely difficult;—owing considerably to my total want of hand power! This
is perfectly true; and you know not, dear Brother, what a treasure you still have which I have altogether lost. Forster's bequest to the Kensington Museum has been formally put in order & set forth to the public;The Times reported, 21 May: “To-day visitors to the South Kensington Museum will see the bequest to the nation of the late Mr. John Forster…. Of the printed books, some 20,000 in number, the mere enumeration of the titles of the books, briefly described, fills 272 closely-printed octavo pages…. The collection of tracts and pamphlets, proclamations, broadsheets, and chapbooks is of rare and varied interest…. Among the books are many presentation copies, and volumes enriched with autographs, letters, and notes; books that have belonged to men of mark or formed part of other famous collections; original editions, rare and privately printed books, illustrated books, and books on art.” For Forster's bequest, see TC to JAC, 1 March 1876. I missed going to the private view in spite of Mary's urgently representing the great desire of Mrs Forster I could not manage it that day.

The death of my poor Edinr Aunts still haunts me daily. The details in Dr Hunter's Letter represent one of the most tragic scenes.John A. Carlyle wrote, 20 May: “By this morning's post the expected letter from Dr Hunter has arrived, & gives a very clear account of the illnesses & death of our friends at Craigen Villa. There is something very sad & solemn about it, the inevitable time having come; but on the whole the end of both was peaceful…. And there were kind friends at hand to give what help was possible in the case to the very last.” Dr. Hunter wrote to John A. Carlyle, 18 May, with a long and detailed account of the illness and death of both sisters. We heard incidentally yesterday from their man of business enclosing an enquiry to me of some ladyNeither identified further. at Stirling or Bridge of Allan about a certain miserable widow of poor Benjamin Welsh,Benjamin Welsh (1796–1822), youngest brother of the Welsh sisters; see Carlyle, Reminiscences 115; his wife was regarded as “a woman worse than an idiot” (see 2:181JBW to TC, [24 Oct. 1822]); unidentified further.—a very unworthy “life-companion” to him, who indeed was clearly the cause of his death: the Stirling lady wished to enquire whether the Miss Welshs had left no legacy to this poor woman; to which we cd only answer that we had no information whatever. Later in the day we did learn accidentally from Mrs George WelshMargaret Welsh, b. Kissock (1803–88; see 43:28043:biographicaL notes), widow of JWC's paternal uncle George (1799–1835), living at 19 St. John's Grove, Richmond. JWC had visited her regularly, her last visit only two days before her death; see 43:206JWC to TC, 19 April 1866. TC apparently kept in contact, sending her £50, Oct. 1874; see 49:157TC to MW, 29 Oct. 1874. that their property would amount to some £10,000 & that they had left £2,000 of it to the Free KirkFree Church of Scotland; the Welsh sisters were very involved with the church, to an extent which JWC had often found rather overwhelming; see for instance 31:188 and 33:38. & the remainder of it altogether to a Mrs Craven, Robert Welsh's daughter now married to somebody either in YorkshireMary May Craven; see TC to JAC, 12 May; her husband, m. 1859 as his second wife, was Dr. Robert Martin Craven (1824–1903), surgeon at Hull General Infirmary, Yorkshire. or in Ayrshire & no legacy to anybody else whatever not even to Dr Hunter, who has been so perpetually kind to them, nor to the two sisters-in-law Mrs George nor Mrs Benjamin which
latter seems to be in great poverty; her one son having died mad long ago & of his property nothing but the widow's third fallen to her.In Scots law a widow with children is entitled to one third of her husband's movable estate. Ah me! ah me! how many things are winded up in this grim finis.—

I send today two Books, one for Jean a miserably bad narrative of two great men's biographies, which in spite of their languor and pedantic feebleness, I think, she will contrive to read. The other is marked for James, who, I hope, may find something in it. A miserable little pamphlet just come from America may amuse you for a few minutes.Books and pamphlet unidentified further; James Aitken, Jean's husband. Today I have a drive to Portland Place, such as we were used to.An outing TC and John often made together when John was staying in Chelsea during the winter; see TC to JAC, 28 April. Both Mary & I were in a baddish condition of stomach &c yesterday; but today are both of us better. I will write to Jean so soon as Millais has let me go. My kindest love to her and to you all

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 9 June. MS: NLS 528.71. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S. W.
9 June 1877.
docBody.p: Millais some eight days ago dismissed me from the present task of sitting to him, but bargained that I was to come back in ten days, when he would have the picture frame and require two more brief sittings and so end. Accordingly I am to go again on Monday and give him the first of the said two sittings and so I earnestly hope & expect dismiss the matter from my mind for evermore. Whether the picture will really prove good or not I have no clear notion nor even any definite guess: enough for me that I have done all that I could to get some likeness of myself by the best methods there were. And having got done with it, I shall as near as possible think nothing whatever on the subject. Heigh ho!

We have beautiful June weather and I am not worse in health than usual. Perhaps rather a degree better; but am only as usual dreadfully ill-off for any real work. Reading fills up my time but to no advantage; so utterly bad and stupid is my reading. The last thing I had was a wildly miserable burlesque of
present opinions and speculations, called “The New Republic”William Hurrell Mallock (1849–1923; ODNB), The New Republic; or Culture, Faith, and Philosophy in an English Country House (1877). Mallock was the son of Froude's sister Margaret (1808–83), and his satirical novel took the form of a symposium, held at a country-house party, on issues of religion, philosophy, and morality, in which he parodied the views of leading Victorian intellectuals, including Matthew Arnold (1822–88; ODNB), Benjamin Jowett (1817–93; ODNB), Walter Horatio Pater (1839–94; ODNB), Edward Bouverie Pusey (1800–82; ODNB), Thomas Huxley, John Ruskin, John Tyndall, and TC. which I strode through not without some amusement as through a wild Atlantic of seething nonsense, the two chief ridiculed figures in which are Jowett & Matthew Arnold. Along with this letter today come three little books, the two French onesFrench books unidentified further. sent to me from Poitiers are hardly worth reading but may be read under more or less of protest. Of the third I have only to say that it is by the paltry gomeril whom I used to call Peesweep,Frederick Martin (1830–83; ODNB; see 32:25332:biographical notes), Swiss-born writer and editor, whom TC hired as an assistant Oct. 1856–June 1857; see 32:12–13TC to FEMA, 15 Oct. 1856. TC took to calling him Peesweep, Scottish name for the lapwing, claiming that his ceaseless complaining resembled the wailing cry of the bird; see 32:99TC to LA, 9 March 1857. He was now living at 7 Fortess Ter., Kentish Town, London. & that of all the “Lives” ever written of me, it is the most utterly erroneous, false, imaginary and absurd.Martin pbd. “Thomas Carlyle: A Biography with Autobiographical Notes. Chapter I: Ecclefechan,” The Biographical Magazine, June 1877; excerpts from the chapter were serialized in a number of newspapers. Francis Espinasse (1823–1912), journalist and writer who had known the Carlyles since 1841 (see 13:227TC to FEHD, 28 Aug. 1841), later wrote: “[Martin's] parading ‘autobiographical notes’ was decidedly deceptive, and might well irritate Carlyle, as seeming to promise not only his sanction but his co-operation. They consisted wholly of a translation by Martin of the German places and persons in Teufelsdröckh's early autobiography [see Carlyle, Sartor Resartus] into the supposed Scottish originals” (Francis Espinasse, Literary Recollections and Sketches [1893] 261–62). John A. Carlyle replied, 11 June: “The Biographical Magazine I read yesterday. Its first article on you seems to me quite unworthy of any attention.” I wish you not to communicate it to anybody nor to speak to anybody about it (except indeed that you may tell Jean quietly what it is). I believe there is to be a great deal more of it from which nothing can save me,—except the total downbreak of the Magazine,—Peesweep's own intention I learn is to publish it in a book in two or more volumes. Mary went to TrübnerThe Biographical Magazine was pbd. by Nicholas Trübner (1817–84; ODNB), philologist and publisher, Ludgate Hill; see 42:114TC to NT, 8 July 1865; no further issues of the magazine were pbd., nor any further chapters of Martin's biography (see Espinasse 260–63). who is a respectable man & well affected to me. She also saw in his presence the agitated Peesweep & appeared to have driven him nearly delirious; but though both he and Trubner professed themselves ready to correct to all lengths according to her orders, I judged the only safe course for us to be that of being dumb altogether & allow the brutish gush of nonsense to go its own course & end
in the bottomless cesspool in its own sweet way. I cannot say that it gives me at bottom almost any pain & my course all along has been, to leave all newspapers, Peesweeps & blockheads to sing or say of me whatsoever they found good. Mary found that Peesweep himself had never himself spoken to Easton or to Mrs MulliganWilliam Easton, “a hale old man approaching ninety” (Biographical Magazine 2) had been apprentice to TC's father; see 19:190TC to JWC, 13 Sept. 1845; he was still working in 1845; see 19:230TC to AC, 30 Sept. 1845. Mrs. Mulligan, or Milligan, “an old lady, past ninety, yet still full of intelligence and vivacity” (Biographical Magazine 4), identified as a girl “some years [TC's] senior” (Wilson, Carlyle 1:19). (whoever she may be), but that his oracle was an ass called WellsJohn Thomas Wells (d. 1909), b. in Waterbeck, 4 mi. (6.5 km.) S of Ecclefechan; he became a temperance preacher and slum worker in Edinburgh. Wells was an extensive collector of Carlyle memorabilia and anecdotes (Wilson, Carlyle 1:x). He apparently loaned Martin his notes on TC, including woodcuts by a local gardener, J. Leslie. Martin used Wells's material without acknowledgement and did not return it to him. Wells later pbd. Thomas Carlyle: His Religious Experiences as Reflected in Sartor Resartus (Edinburgh, 1899). (Son I suppose of stupid Samuel WellsD. A. Wilson mentions a Samuel Wells (or Wolls) (d. 1895; Wilson, Carlyle 2:144) and a William Wells (Wull Wolls) (b. ca. 1811; Wilson, Carlyle 1:401), agricultural laborers who worked for TC's father; they were presumably related, and cousins of John Thomas Wells's father (Wilson, Carlyle 2:144). & it seems now a shopman to Carlyle of Waterbeck).TC confuses John Thomas Wells with John T. Wells (d. 1921), a partner in the firm of Thomas Johnston Carlyle (1810–93) and Robert Carlyle (1813–1902), grocers, drapers, ironmongers, and seed merchants in Waterbeck. Enough of him and of his foul jawhole.

Poor Edward Sterling, eldest son of my SterlingEdward Coningham Sterling, eldest son of TC's great friend John Sterling, d. 3 June. went away into Switzerland, till a new house here were built, last year I thought at the time it was likely I should never see him more, but he did return some little while ago, but had not yet got down to see me when all on a sudden he broke a blood vessel in the stomach and in the course of few hours, half an hour before his poor brother JohnJohn Barton Sterling, captain in the Coldstream Guards. could arrive from the country was lying dead. Poor fellow, he was a very amiable, very intelligent and blameless young man. There are now only two young women, who live at FalmouthJulia Maria and Hester Isabella Sterling, living in Falmouth, Cornwall. Both John and Julia Sterling wrote, 6 June, telling TC of Edward's death. & this Captain John in London who represent my old friend now at rest at Bonchurch.John Sterling was buried in the churchyard of Bonchurch church, nr. Ventnor, Isle of Wight.
Farewell, dear Brother, I hope I shall have something more comfortable to tell you of next week. At present I have no capacity to write at all.

I received James Aitken's cheerful and obliging letter. Tell Jean I have not forgotten my debt to her. I intend a little gift to Mary's new-wedded daughter.
Can you tell me when her husband and she are to come home again from Liverpool.See TC to JAC, 19 May; John wrote, 11 June: “Mary's new-wedded daughter Isabella is probably returned already from Liverpool…. The wedding had been got through very quietly & comfortably…. She is to stay for some time at the Gill, & her husband … at his old home till they get arrangements made…. I think she is the cleverest of the family, & likely to get on well.” Tell me if you easily can.
I send my kindest love and poor blessing to one and all of you. I ever am

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 16 June. MS: NLS 528.72. Quot: Wilson, Carlyle 6:406. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
16 June 1877
docBody.p: Many thanks for the letter that arrived this morning. You are duly minute about everything; and old and young from Brother Jamie down to poor little “Thomas”Letter from John A. Carlyle untraced; TC presumably refers to John and Margaret Carlyle's son Alexander, b. April; see TC to JAC, 28 April. of whom I hear for the first time everyone is brought clearly before me.

Yesterday I sent off a poor £50, with greeting to Mary, & enclosed in a note to her,—a feeble marriage gift to the young Mrs Hoggan.TC sent a check for Mary Austin's da. Isabella: “15 June 1877 / Mrs Isabella Hoggan (for The Gill) / £50..0..0” (TC's checkbook; MS: NLS 20753); see TC to JAC, 9 June. This is really nearly all that I can specify as my history of last week. I did finish off with Millais the day before yesterday I trust for good and all. He is merely to have my coat when he sends for it to be put upon a model & enable him to finish out the figure, wh. he could rarely be persuaded to touch, such his eagerness for ultra perfection in the face. I never in my life saw such burning eagerness of effort as poor Millais showed all along. A rational enough kind of man, with plenty of common sense, whom I did not at all dislike. The picture I think does not please Mary, nor in fact myself altogether; but it is surely strikingly like in every featureCiting passages from Annabella Anstruther's private journal (see TC to LLA, 16 Oct. 1876), D. A. Wilson wrote: “Mrs. Anstruther and Mary drove to the studio to meet Carlyle and take him for a drive. Unfortunately, he had just left, but Mary sent up her card, requesting permission to see the picture…. [Anstruther wrote:] ‘The picture was in Millais’ usual style,—hard, clever, forcible painting. The outline, the features, all correctly given, and with great power of brush. But merely the mask; no soul, no spirit behind. I said it looked modern, and in fact I did not like it’” (Wilson, Carlyle 6:405). For Millais’ portrait of TC, see above. & the fundamental condition was that Millais should paint what
he himself was able to see there. I am thankful at least to be assured that all that could be demanded of me in regard to pictures is now completely done.
Thomas Carlyle, 1877, painting by John Everett Millais
© National Portrait Gallery, London
The PeesweepFrederick Martin. has written again to Mary willing & eager to be corrected &c
&c but the rule is and is to be Leave Peesweep to his own fate in this enterprise & forget altogether that such platitude has ever existed. Mrs Anstruther who is here for perhaps a fortnight yet has given us two excellent & extensive drives in the country perhaps another of these and a short interview with Mr CairdJames Caird (1816–92; ODNB), agriculturalist and writer; his home was at Cassencarie (Castle Cary) Creetown, Dumfries and Galloway, but he had interests in the home counties; Annabella Anstruther's mother was his sister. the high-class farmer, who is a Galloway man, her Uncle, will make up what we have to hope from her at present. She is passionately eager that we should come to her place again this summer;Ballikinrain, Anstruther's home in Stirlingshire; TC and Mary stayed there for a few weeks in July 1876; see TC to LLA, 16 Oct. 1876. but that is a thing I have never had any thought of yet.

I cordially meant to write a word to Sister Jean this day before your letter came. Now that I have done with Millais my promise to her becomes valid & I will faithfully fulfil it soon but today all that I can do is to send her this book in token of this purpose,—a book, too, wh. I think she will rather like. It is certainly the record of a mild, gentle hearted, wise and worthy kind of man: he was elder Brother of the man they call “Cussandra Greg,” whom I did not like nearly as well.A Layman's Legacy in Prose and Verse: Selections from the Papers of Samuel Greg with a Biographical Memoir, ed. Arthur Penrhyn Stanley (1877). Samuel Greg (1804–1876; ODNB), mill owner and philanthropist; he owned Lower House Mill, nr. Bollington, Cheshire, 1832–54, where he introduced a number of reforms, including a gymnasium, baths, libraries, and art and singing classes; his introduction of new machinery for stretching cloth antagonized his workers and forced him to retire in relative poverty. Greg's younger brother, William Rathbone Greg (1809–81; ODNB), industrialist and writer, was initially a political radical, but he became increasingly conservative, writing against democracy and populism in works such as Rocks Ahead; or the Warnings of Cassandra (1874). For TC's memory of him see 29:283TC to JN, 5 April 1855. Their father, Samuel Greg (1758–1834; ODNB), was a pioneer of the industrial revolution and a prominent Manchester nonconformist. They were shining cotton manufacturers in Cheshire; but came to grief & could not complete what they had strenuously begun, the new modelling and thoroughly improving of their work people, which I used to hear talked of about thirty years ago.
Lady Ashburton is to send her carriage for me in less than five minutes so I must end.
We have brilliant summer weather, sunshine generally with, occasionally, strong east wind.— — I send my love & blessing to you all.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 22 [23] June. MS: NLS 528.73. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Letter misdated.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: The day before yesterday I had sat down with the fixed intention of writing to Jean but as Mary assured me that her Mother was at NewfieldJohn A. Carlyle wrote, 22 June: “Jean & Annie went off to Newfield on the Tuesday, & are still there.” Newfield farm, 2½ mi. (4 km.) W of Scotsbrig, farmed by sisters Helen and George Currie; their sister Mary d. early 1876 (see 49:194TC to AC, 4 March 1875), and their brother John was staying with an invalid friend. (as your letter of this morning further assured me) I had to give up the enterprise. This mornings Letter from you contains ample details about our Dumfriesshire friends and would at any rate have set me upon winding up the week by sending a few words to yourself. The only thing of moment I had to say was the agreeable intelligence that Peesweep has entirely given up his attempt at writing any “Biography” of me and that he and his distracted attempt have completely vanished and to all human appearance will not trouble us any more. The “Biographical Magazine” of which the distracted article Carlyle was to have been the piÃ?ce de resistance has likewise vanished forever.Martin wrote to the Athenaeum, 12 Sept.: “In the Athenaeum of August 25 there appeared a paragraph, referring chiefly to the Biographical Magazine, but mentioning, inter alia that I had the ‘consent’ of Mr. Thomas Carlyle to write his biography. Will you kindly allow me, in justice to the venerable author, to state the facts of the case? Having been for a great many years engaged in collecting materials for a Life of Mr. Thomas Carlyle, I published the first portion of my researches, consisting of an elucidation of the autobiographical mystery of ‘Sartor Resartus’ in No. 1 of the Biographical Magazine. A ‘proof’ of my article was sent to Mr. Carlyle, but by some mishap, explained to me, did not get into his hands. A week after publication, a near relative of Mr. Carlyle, residing with him, called on me, and I was told that Mr. Carlyle had seen with displeasure what I had written about ‘Sartor Resartus.’ Thereupon I consulted with friends, among them a leading London publisher [Trübner], and the resolution come to was that I should discontinue my articles, for the satisfaction of Mr. Carlyle. My articles stopped, and with them the Biographical Magazine, at what pecuniary loss I need not say. But it earned me the warm thanks of the relative previously referred to.” The Athenaeum then announced, 15 Sept.: “We have received from Mr. Carlyle a letter, in which he states that Mr. F. Martin has not his authority to write his life.” I heard from DarwinErasmus Darwin. with considerable provocation that the book was eagerly grasped at by an idle public but it did not tempt me to take the least public notice of it; for which I am now decidedly thankful. Mary has been very diligent & dexterous upon this matter. It is she properly that suppressed the whole affair & she encloses the Peesweep Letters; the end of the most futile chimera to which now adieu for evermore.

We had no thunder like you but we had a welcome shower or almost whole night of rain & today again the weather is not only cooler but there is a wavering attempt at something like North in the wind & the sky is quietly grey.

I have lost both Lecky & his Wife who are gone to bury the queen of HollandWilliam and Catharina Lecky were attending the funeral of Sophie of Württemberg (1818–3 June 1877), queen of the Netherlands 1849–77; wife, m. 1839, of William III (1817–90), king of the Netherlands 1849–90. Catharina Lecky had been a lady-in-waiting to Queen Sophia before her marriage. & thence to Switzerland &c. I also see less of Froude & of FitzJames Stephen than common; but on the whole lack of company is not what I suffer from, the mournful company of myself is often not so unwelcome as that of almost any other fellow creature who forces me to talk when there is nothing worth uttering. I am very weak but could almost say I have less of pain & more of sleep than at the time you were here. The question where we are to go & especially where I am to go as the season culminates is very vague & intricate & I cannot hitherto form the least resolution. Ballikinrain, the Lady of wh. is hospitably urgent, does not much smile on me, or hardly at all. The Howards have zealously asked me to NaworthGeorge James Howard; see TC to GEH, 24 Nov. 1876, and his wife, Rosalind Frances, living at Naworth Castle, Cumberland; they had previously invited TC to visit, Sept. 1871; see 47:224–25TC to GEH, 23 Aug. 1871. a place only 10 miles eastward of Carlisle but that also does not much smile on me. One consideration also is continually present, That Mary ought to get away for health's sake, a six weeks to her Mother, whither, alas, I cannot follow. A sail might do me good, but on that she cannot attend me with any success, being always sea-sick. What do you purpose for your own behoof.John replied, 28 June: “I have thought about your plans for the summer … & should have been most ready to second you in any of them. But I have been suffering much from dyspepsia since the hot weather began … & do not see much prospect of being able to leave home so long as it lasts. The hernia troubles me much at times, in spite of all trusses, when the bowels are in disorder, & might of itself hinder me from travelling.” I often wish you could take a notion of coming up hitherward again! Tell me what your thoughts are, if they have yet got any shape.

I was glad to hear of poor RussellDr. James Russell of Holmhill; John wrote, 22 June: “[I] found Dr Russell looking measurably well, & even cheerful…. He cannot walk to any distance, for his toes that were once dangerously gangrenous would at once become gangrenous again if he took any walking exercise. We drove to the Closeburn churchyard where his wife is buried…. He had been ill most of the winter, & often confined to bed, but since the beginning of May is well…. He talked of retiring from the Bank … but I advised him to retain his place & go daily as usual.” For Mary Russell's death, see TC to JAC, 23 Dec. 1875. & that he bears his heavy burden so well. Masson,David Masson, who was working on The Life of John Milton: Narrated in Connexion with the Political, Ecclesiastical, and Literary History of His Time, 7 vols. (1859–81); see 49:43TC to JAC, 1 Jan. 1874. did I tell you, was here for three weeks lately & we parted on
Sunday last. He calculates on finishing his last volume by the time his College
work begins.— We have got two or three fine wholesome drives from Mrs Anstruther chiefly the three or four hours of green country are wholesome & refreshing.D. A. Wilson wrote: “Mrs. Anstruther took Carlyle out for a drive to Kew Gardens, and on subsequent days they had many drives together, to Richmond Park, Wimbledon Common, Ham Common, and other places, where they could leave the carriage and enjoy the fresh air and the view” (Wilson, Carlyle 6:403). I am reading Gibbon; a repetition after above fifty years. My esteem of Gibbon rather sinks in comparison; but is still considerable & peculiar.Edward Gibbon (1737–94; ODNB), historian, Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (1776–88). Allingham recorded in his Diary, 24 June: “Carlyle is going through Gibbon's Decline and Fall (not read since his youth). ‘I find it entirely below my expectations, the style is laboriously antithetical—and he doesn’t lay out his history well; there are many chapters where a mere tabular statement ought to have sufficed. I should have liked him also to hang out more frequent general elucidations in the way of dates. On the whole, it is very disappointing.’ I reminded C. that Gibbon was one of the writers whom he strongly recommended to me, many years ago, saying, ‘Gibbon is always worth meeting.’ He replied, ‘Oh, one must read Gibbon to get any insight into this wild history of mankind’” (Allingham Diary 256). For TC's advice to Allingham, see 25:193TC to WA, 4 Sept. 1850; for TC's first reading of Gibbon, borrowed from Edward Irving's library in Kirkcaldy 1817–18, see 1:120–21TC to RM, 16 Feb. 1818, and Carlyle, Reminiscences 219.— I will not add another word to this poor rigmarole; but send my blessing to all friends & ever remain,

div3.sourceNote: MA-MW [MAI-MEW], 25 June. MS: NLS Acc. 9207. Hitherto unpbd.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO META WELLMER

docBody.p: I have been a wretch never to answer your kind letter, to tell you that I have behaved even worse to other correspondents would perhaps scarcely be an excuse so I will not trouble you with it.

I have not been well this last winter. I have tried vegetarian diet too, but I gave it up, for I became so weak that the wind could almost have bowled me over. I should like to write a book upon Vegetarianism. For some people I am sure it is most salutary & wholesome for others it is equally unwholesome.

My Uncle is considerably better than he was last year, though I am afraid he is not much stronger. He is now busy reading Gibbon's Decline & Fall of the Roman Empire. For Uncle John, he was here for six months and went back to
Dumfries early in April.John A. Carlyle stayed in Cheyne Row early Nov. 1876–early April 1877. He wrote to Wellmer from Cheyne Row, 12 Feb.: “My niece Mary … had some attacks of illness. She often spoke of writing to you…. She bids me tell you with kindest regards, that she is very sorry for having put off so long.” The weather here is not specially hot at present; my Uncle has got a curious Dutch chair given to him, with a hood of wicker work over itProbably a traditional north European hooded chair, described by Annabella Anstruther as an “odd-looking wicker chair some admirer had sent him from Holland” (Wilson, Carlyle 6:403). & in it he sits out of doors nearly all day. We have not yet fixed on any place to go to for the hot months, but I hope we shall get away before very long somewhither. I shall be delighted to receive your kleine pÃ?dagogische Schrift“Small educational work”; possibly a book or article by Wellmer, otherwise unidentified. & thank you for your promise to send it.

RoseRose, Cheyne Row servant; see TC to JAC, 15 Dec. 1875. after whom you ask is very flourishing; she is engaged to be married to a young man I have never seen; but who I believe is a respectable man. He is a “French polisher.” At first they decided to marry off hand, but now they seem to be in no violent haste about it. The CatCheyne Row cat, named Tib. is all right. He and I are on the most intimate and affectionate terms. He allows me to carry him about in my arms now, although he never used to be able to bear being touched. It is a cat without intellect, I am afraid. Excuse this poor scrap I am so ashamed of not having written that I feel myself quite constrained and stiff. Next time I hope to do better.
Uncle sends his best regards with mine.
docBody.closer: Affectly yours / Mary Carlyle Aitken

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 30 June. MS: NLS 528.74. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
30 June 1877.
docBody.p:
Yesterday your letter pleasantly surprised and entertained us & gave a clear sketch of the state of affairs in our native circle. Dickson's LetterJohn A. Carlyle wrote, 28 June: “Yesterday I had a letter from Judge Dickson of Cincinnati…. He is the grandson of old Mr Dickson minister of Mouswald, whom you once saw at my rooms in George Street, in 1866…. Like Dr Hunter he was a cousin of the Miss Welshes & used to be a visitor at Craigen Villa.” William Martin Dickson (1827–89), U.S. lawyer and judge; his grandfather was Rev. Jacob Dickson (d. 1824), Presbyterian minister at Mouswald, nr. Dumfries. TC visited John at his rooms in George St., Edinburgh, when he was in Edinburgh for his rectorial address, 31 March–7 April 1866; see 43:156–57TC to JWC, 3 April 1866, although there is no mention of meeting Judge Dickson. I found very
good and interesting & I now return it as worthy of being in the meanwhile preserved.

We are both well here; at least in our usual degrees of wellness, though both of us are very weak vessels; and Mary has seemed to me for months to have real need to get away for a rest & holiday for a month or six weeks to get braced up again. I myself get visibly a greater allowance of sleep, though the stomachic part goes rather worse than before & in walking I naturally grow more & more feckless. Besides NaworthSee TC to JAC, 22 June. & altogether independent of it Henry Cooper, who purposes to be at home in the great house called Brocket,Henry Frederick Cowper. wh. was once Lord Melbourne's,Brocket Hall, Hertfordshire, built in 1760 for Sir Matthew Lamb (1705–68), 1st Baronet Lamb, was inherited by his grandson William Lamb (1779–1848; ODNB), 2d Viscount Melbourne, prime minister 1834 and 1835–41; it now belonged to his great nephew Francis, 7th Earl Cowper, Henry's older brother. & altogether by himself asks me to go to him & be his solitary companion there, so soon as the parliament rises. The place is only a twenty miles bit of railway in a pleasant fruitful country & Henry himself is a most excellent, sincere & quiet man worthy to be a kinsman of the poet CowperWilliam Cowper (1731–1800; ODNB), poet and letter-writer; he was the great-nephew of William Cowper (1665–1723), 1st Earl Cowper. For TC's opinion of the poet, see for instance 5:49. & much liked by me. Mrs Anstruther is still very urgent about Stirlingshire but I have never had, nor have yet any notion thitherward for this year. Cooper gave me a long, airy and pleasant enough drive in his brougham over the Clapham & Southern verdant regions setting me down at home here by the stroke of 5 oclock, wh. I supposed would be at least equivalent to the customary Portland Place expedition by omnibus combined with walking, which you & I were so well acquainted with in winter. Mrs Anstruther also gave Mary & me a long and beautiful drive thro’ Richmond Park Kew Green &c &c which had a wholesome character in it. On Monday last we had a sublime visit from the Princess Louise, escorted by his Grace of Argyll;Princess Louise (1848–1939; ODNB), marchioness of Lorne, 4th da. of Queen Victoria; she was a friend of Lady Ashburton's; see 49:243TC to JAC, 18 Sept. 1875. She was accompanied by the duke of Argyll (see TC to JAC, 11 March 1876), father of her husband, m. 1871, John George Edward Henry Douglas Sutherland Campbell (1845–1914; ODNB), marquis of Lorne. both of whom, especially the Princess were beautifully civil—only unluckily I was ill slept that day dyspeptic & abundantly miserable.

I send you today two of the crowd of stupid Magazines that have come to me, hoping you might find some trifle in them worth reading. In the ContemporaryThe Contemporary Review. are several things worth glancing at & in the Fortnightly there is at least one short Article that by Laveleye on the Eastern question,Emile de Laveleye, “British Interests in the Present Crisis,” Fortnightly Review 22 (July 1877): 25–34. which I considered altogether wise and true. The Fortnightly you understand is meant for Russell, the other for Walter Welsh.Rev. Walter Welsh, living at Auchtertool Manse, Fife; TC regularly sent him magazines. If this method is quite useless or even a bore for you, be so good as just say so & I will discontinue it. My kind regards to the good old Russell; there is another magazine for Jean; but we just hear from Maggie that she is still at Newfield.John wrote, 28 June: “Jean and [Annie] are still at Newfield with the Miss Curries, & will perhaps stay till next week, if Jean continues to get on as well as she has hitherto done.”

Mary's lunch, it appears, has come up for her & I, without more waiting will conclude this blash. The sooner a new letter comes from you of course it will be the better but dont burden yourself with it either. I am grieved to hear of your stomachic &c botherations but, alas, alas, what can we now do at this stage of our affairs. I send my kindest love to one & all of you & am ever

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 21 July. MS: NLS 528.75. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row, Chelsea. S.W.
21 July 1877
docBody.p:
The cutting from the Scotsman wh. you sent me was very welcome to myself first of all & next, to Froude, who carried it away with him and, from the first, comprehended what a fine symptom it was in his affair. I myself knew nothing about the Glasgow election at all & had forgotten that there was such a thing in the wind or that Froude had been the man proposed.Froude had been nominated as a candidate for Rector of Glasgow Univ. by the Univ. Independent Club, but declined the invitation and instead gave his support to Gladstone, who was nominated by the Univ. Liberal Club. It appears, the
MinistrySir Stafford Northcote (1818–87; ODNB), leader of the Conservative Party in the House of Commons, was nominated by the Univ. Conservative Club. are in great anxiety abt this exceeding small matter and are greatly eager that the bits of boys in red cloaksStudents at Glasgow Univ. used to wear red cloaks, which distinguished them from the general population. may honour them, the needy Ministry with their most sweet voices! wh. according to Froude there is not the slightest chance of their now doing.The Scotsman commented, 14 July: “Rectorial contests at Scottish Universities are not, as a rule, affairs in which the world generally is likely to take much interest, except in so far as they show that the principles upon which the Government of the country is based are recognised, though they can hardly be fully understood, by the youth who are found at the great educational institutions. Out of these ought to be coming many of the politicians and some at least of the statesmen of the future; and, therefore … the students may be none the worse … for the introduction of political considerations into the elections they are called upon to make. Mr. Froude, in the letter which he has addressed to the Committee who sought to promote his election … does not discuss this question, but he shows that he thinks the students may be able to give an effective utterance in the coming contest…. Nobody supposes that if the students were to throw over his advice, and to elect Sir Stafford Northcote, the fact would be any indication of the feeling of the country…. But whether the students should or should not follow the advice given to them by Mr Froude, that he should have given such advice is significant in more ways than one.” The Scotsman reported, 16 Nov: “The students of Glasgow University have returned Mr W. E. Gladstone as their Lord Rector by the largest majority recorded in the history of the venerable institution.” Surely this may be defined as the day of small things.Cf. Zech. 4:10. But rumours of every kind are floating about from hour to hour, & are really an insane kind of element to live in for the time being.

St. Swithan rained all SundaySt. Swithin (d. 863; ODNB), Anglo-Saxon saint; according to superstition, if it rains on his feast day, 15 July, it will continue to rain for the next 40 days. and continued raining, sometimes in great splashes and to a disagreeable extent for several days; but he has now ceased again & shews blue, lofty skies, as good weather as could be sent us at this crown of the year. London is fast thinning too & one sits with composure, reading here behind the house and wishing it would last and leave one quiet on those terms, though one knows too well it wont. I have finished Gibbon, with a great deduction from the high esteem I have had of him ever since old Kirkcaldy days when I first read the twelve volumes of poor Irving's copy in twelve successive days;See TC to JAC, 22 [23] June.—a man of endless reading & research, but of a most disagreeable style and of great want of the highest faculties which indeed are very rare, of what we could call a classical historian. Compared with HeroditusHerodotus, Greek historian; for TC's opinion of him, see TC to CEN, 2 Dec. 1875. for instance and his grand simplicity and perfect clearness in every part.
I am now working through a very fluffy and indeed worthless book by Mrs Oliphant, which she calls the Makers of Florence.Margaret Oliphant, The Makers of Florence: Dante, Giotto, Savonarola; and Their City (1877). I read with seven-leagued boots, skipping hugely; but find it sadly empty, do as I may. SavonarolaGirolamo Savonarola (1452–98), Italian Dominican friar, burnt to death in Florence for his espousal of clerical reform and republicanism. I did expect she might do something for but am mainly disappointed.

After an immense quantity of complex discussion Mary who really needs a six weeks holiday, will not consent to leave me here to my own shifts and can propose nobody to come and live beside me whom I can bear to think of. She decides therefore to stay till some solution turn up, of which I can trace in myself no feasibility unless August, with its bicking heats, force me to move off in some direction. Heigh ho!
