I have not yet read the Russian Pamphlet, which accompanied or followed next day the letter which is here enclosed;Friedrich Martens (1845–1909), Russian diplomat, jurist, and prof. of international law at the Univ. of St. Petersburg 1876–1905; he wrote, 5 July, announcing that he was sending TC his pamphlet, “Etude historique sur la politique russe dans la question d’Orient,” Revue de droit international et de législation comparée 9 (The Hague, Berlin, and Paris, 1877): 49–77. It was also pbd. in German, Die russiche Politik in der orientalischen Frage (St. Petersburg, 1877). He wrote that he wished to pay homage to TC for his heated defense of the cause of humanity and civilization on the Balkan peninsula, and to say that the Russian nation would never forget the courage with which he had defended it in its struggle with Turkey. but you shall have it early next week. The address was of amusing type, to “The Right Honorable Thomas Carlyle.” The man is a Professor in the University of St. Petersburg; but I do not promise you much from him— Many letters come daily; but not one in twenty of them is worth reading.

Just now your Letter of yesterday has come to hand. Thanks for your news: I regret much to hear you are out of sorts, but I hope and trust things will soon come round again. Poor Rob. Hanning,Their brother-in-law Robert Hanning in Canada; John A. Carlyle had written, 27 May, to say that he had heard that Hanning was very unwell; he wrote, 20 July, that he had had a letter from their niece Mary Holden: “Her mother, she says, was well, though anxiously nursing her father who is not expected to recover.” Robert Hanning d. 22 March 1878. he too one is sad and sore of heart to hear seems coming to the finis. Adieu, dear Brother. Accept this miserable blash is all I can do today. Give my blessing to Jean and to all the rest,—would it were good for anything.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 28 July. MS: NLS 1763.320. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Written on 5 Great Cheyne Row headed notepaper.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row, Chelsea. S.W.
28 July 1877.
docBody.p: I felt greatly pleased & was heartily obliged to you for the promptitude with which you offered to take a long railway journey & come up here to join me. Luckily by that time there was a settlement near at hand & clearly under way, rendering your kind offer and the gt bother it must have involved you in unnecessary at present. Mary is now engaged to go for a few weeks of yachting with Froude & his familyFroude had invited Mary Aitken to join him and two of his children, Ashley Anthony and May, on a yachting trip from Cowes, Isle of Wight, to Derreen, Co. Kerry, SW Ireland, where he regularly leased a house from Henry Petty-Fitzmaurice (1845–1927; ODNB), 5th marquess of Lansdowne; see 46:75TC to JAF, 14 Sept. 1869. who are very anxious to have her, having a vacant berth in a yacht all to themselves and furnished with every convenience wh. can render such an expedition promising. They go off Monday come a week, starting early in the morning for Cowes, where the yacht lies in perfect readiness. Mary for my behoof has engaged Miss CraikMary Craik (1827–1909); her family were old friends of the Carlyles; see 43:27043:biographical notes. She had stayed with TC and JWC in St. Leonards, helping care for JWC, May–July 1864; see 40:93TC to GEJ, 8 May 1864, and 129TC to HL, 9 July 1864. & will before then give her every instruction; so that I may settle myself here composedly till the weather become too hot for town of which there is no promise or threat (it being still damp & today itself rainy); in the interval till she return to me I consider myself as well situate as I could readily be anywhere else & if the heats of August do come I am not without resources for flying into some neighbouring part of the country (I think either with Miss Bromley on the Epsom DownsTC stayed with Caroline Davenport Bromley for several days from 10 Aug. at Walton Heath, Epsom. or with Henry Cowper in a big house where he is to be alone) in both of wh. places I should have full liberty to drive about or walk about and enjoy whatever good the country had to offer me.

Froude's lease of the yacht is for five weeks from the Monday after next & their intended course is about the Lands End & adjacent shores whence to Dereen on the S.Wn extremity of Ireland; but Mary does not lay her account with staying all that time; nor is it fixed that they shall hold by these localities & in fact Mary will have the amplest opportunity to quit where & when she
likes & towards any goal she likes;Froude leased the yacht 6 Aug.–9 Sept.; John A. Carlyle wrote, 9 Aug.: “From Mary … there came a postal-card this morning dated Yarmouth [Isle of Wight], & she speaks of being here in some ten days if all goes well on the voyage.” but it seems she has told her Mother all about that. I will only hope that everything may go well & that you may offer again by & by to let me have the pleasure of seeing you here again so soon as it shall be convenient to us both. Nothing in all these shifting consultations has grieved me more than to miss the opportunity of seeing Brother Jamie here again;—which I fear is a chance that is now quite past,—he himself seeming to have given up the visit to Birmingham,Jamie regularly visited his son-in-law William Scott and family in Birmingham; see TC to JAC, 28 April. though both he & John might be accomodated here readily enough in Mary's absence, when London itself & I quiet & solitary in it wd still be visible,—if they cd be tempted to resume their enterprise.TC was presumably unaware that John A. Carlyle had written to his nephew James Carlyle Jr., 8 July: “Today I have received the enclosed note from your cousin Mary, & as she is likely soon to leave Cheyne Row for a time it would be necessary for your father & John to put off that intended visit till she got back.” He writes that he intends to visit James and his father tomorrow “to talk about the visit to Chelsea among other things” (MS: NLS Acc. 9086). He then wrote to TC, 10 July: “[Jamie] & John have given up all idea of going to Birmingham just now. Both of them are bad travellers, & dislike long journeys, & John cannot well get away from home at this busy season when all his turnips need attention as well as every thing else.” Jamie's son John lived with him at Scotsbrig and managed the farm. The bookTC presumably refers to Fatal Days; Notes by an Amateur on France, Europe, and the Sixteenth of May (London and Brussels, 1877), purportedly by a French liberal politician named M. de la Franche-Comté, but probably written by John Edward Jenkins (1838–1910; ODNB), author, satirist, Liberal M.P. for Dundee 1874–80. Jenkins wrote several satirical works, often anonymously; see also 47:42TC to CDB, 11 July 1870. you got yesterday will I hope be entertaining to you. It amused me considerably & threw light upon the singular quandary or Macmahon coup d’etatPatrice de MacMahon (1808–93), French general and politician, president of France 1875–79, and a conservative Catholic, had, 16 May, dismissed the Republican prime minister, Jules Simon (1814–96), and replaced him with an “Ordre Moral” administration led by Albert (1821–1901), duc de Broglie. This precipitated a constitutional crisis, the dissolution of parliament, and new elections, 14 Oct., in which the Republicans won a majority of 120 seats, de Broglie was forced to resign, and MacMahon himself resigned in 1879. wh. is occupying people's attention here & is already generally attributed to the Jesuit party & hope of giving papistry a new standing ground in France & chance of keeping its head high for a little while there.In Fatal Days MacMahon is accused of being guided by the Jesuits: “They have cleverly contrived on their own part to merge Catholicism in Jesuitism,” and to have used “the extremes of the [Republican] extremists against moderate and opportunist Liberals” (Fatal Days 32). MacMahon's involvement with the French Catholic church, which wanted the French government to support Pope Pius IX's (1792–1878) campaign for restoration of papal government in the Papal States, was seen as an indicator that he favored restoration of the monarchy in France.
We are very much bothered with continual rumours most of them nonsensical & empty as the wind about the Russian-Turk War,Despite Disraelis's support for Turkey, Britain was continuing to hold a neutral position in the Russo-Turkish war; see TC to JAC, 28 April. Lord Derby, the foreign sec., noted in his diary, 28 July: “I left this cabinet with more uneasy and unpleasant sensations than I have yet experienced in these transactions: the war fever is clearly getting hold of my colleagues, and they have the excuse that it prevails strongly in the party generally, and in H. of C.— Even Salisbury [see TC to GEH, 24 Nov. 1876] seems in part gained over…. Austin Henry Layard (1817–94; ODNB), British ambassador at Constantinople] telegraphs as to the risk of disorder and massacre in Constantinople, which might be a reason, & certainly could be used as a pretext, for sending the fleet up. But Layard is eager for armed intervention by England: and I think that with this object he magnifies the danger” (Derby Diaries, 1869–1878, ed. John Vincent [1994]: 424). wh. everybody sees to be drawing rapidly towards total demolition of the Turk; but is still attended here with a faint but very dismal suspicion that Dizzy will in the end contrive to lead us into the abominable puddle,—though the wisest people I speak to regard that as an impossibility even for Dizzy at this stage.

An intrusive visitorPossibly Friedrich Althaus (1829–97), writer and historian, prof. of German at Univ. Coll., London; see 49:148TC to FAL, 5 Sept. 1874. D. A. Wilson notes: “One afternoon towards the end of July, Friedrich Althaus, who had not seen Carlyle for seven years … came calling again…. When Althaus had been with Carlyle an hour, Miss Aitken entered to remind her uncle of his walk, suggesting to the visitor: ‘Perhaps you might go with him?’ … In Regent Street, Althaus drew [TC's] attention to a full-length portrait of Lord Beaconsfield which was on exhibition,—‘“Our miraculous Premier” [see TC to EOT, 4 May]—I believe your phrase will stick to the noble Lord.’ Which drew from Carlyle a hearty laugh, and a word or two of scorn blended with pity. In Regent Circus they separated with a hearty handshake and good wishes on both sides, and saw each other no more” (Wilson, Carlyle 6:409–10). For their contact seven years previously, when Althaus was completing Joseph Neuberg's German translation of Frederick, see 46:10–12MAI to FAL, 12 Feb. 1869. is up stairs waiting for me & I have only before hastily ending to send my loving regards to one and all of you & to beg for another letter soon, wh. shall be quickly answered.

closer.salute: I remain ever / Your affecte Brother,

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, [11 Aug.]. MS: NLS 528.48. Hitherto unpbd. Probably written in Caroline Davenport Bromley's hand, with TC's signature. Written on Walton Heath printed notepaper. Dated by John A. Carlyle's reply, 13 Aug.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I got out hither safe yesterday evening & was received with the most perfect
welcome & I am lodged to perfection in one of the wholesomest airiest & quietest of scenes. I also managed to get 2 or 3 hours of solid sleep, though that is my greatest difficulty at present. I have two things to ask first, concerning the Czar of Russia's photograph which I hope you still have ready at handJohn A. Carlyle had written, 20 July, acknowledging receipt from Mary of “a nice photograph of the Emperor of Russia,” presumably Alexander II (see TC to GEH, 24 Nov. 1876); his letter concluded: “What am I to do with the photograph of the Russian Emperor?”— Please send that off directed hither to me, or get it back from whoever has it & dispatch quàm primùm [as soon as possible]. Secondly, but this is less pressing; if you have the French English book called “Fatal Days,” write my name inside of it, & send it off addressed

Mrs Anstruther / Ballykinrain / Killearn / StirlingshireJohn replied, 13 Aug.: “Your letter of the 11th has reached me this morning, & I at once send you the photograph of the Russian Emperor. I have also forwarded the ‘Fatal Days’ to Mrs Anstruther at Ballykinrain.”
This is all at present but I will write again soon / Ever yr affecte brother

div3.sourceNote: TC-HL [HPL], 1 Sept. MS: Keble Coll., Oxford; text from typed transcript. Hitherto unbpd. Henry Parry Liddon (1829–90; ODNB), theologian, canon of St. Paul's Cathedral 1870–90.
div3.head: TC TO HENRY PARRY LIDDON

docBody.p: I willingly accept this honour you propose to me, and thoroughly agree with what you intend and express in regard to that committee.The “Russian Sick and Wounded Fund Committee,” of which Liddon was an honorary sec.; he was a prominent critic of Disraeli's pro-Turkish policies. In a letter to the Times, 30 Aug., pbd. 31 Aug., he wrote: “May I be allowed to invite attention to a Committee which has been formed, under the title of the Russian Sick and Wounded Fund, for the purpose of aiding Russian sufferers in the present war? The names composing this Committee can be referred to no one of our political or religious parties…. The Turkish forces are within comparatively easy reach of the supplies so liberally furnished by English sympathisers, while the Russians are operating at a great distance from their base…. As your impartial Correspondents have noted, the Russians take as much care of the Turks who fall into their hands as of their own sick and wounded; and I trust that … some practical efforts of English sympathy in a quarter where they are greatly needed … would be warmly appreciated.” The Times, 6 Sept., listed the current committee members, including TC. Of course you understand that old age and its infirmities will forbid any practical exertion on my poor part; but my poor mite of due subscription, when it comes to that, and my loyal good will at all times will not be wanting.
With many thanks and respect I am always / Yours faithfully / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 15 Sept. MS: NLS 528.76. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
15 Sep. 1877.
docBody.p: Last Saturday I partly meant to write to you a word or two, but by several hindrances could not get it done, and, alas, today when I do come to fulfilling of my purpose, I find that there is really next to nothing to be said and that when I have told you of our continuing in our average state I have as good as nothing to say. My employments are nothing but reading (poor bad books for most part) and my adventures nothing but journeys in the omnibus and calls on people or from people, who are of next to no importance to me.

On Monday I went with Lady Ashburton and her daughter to the National Portrait Gallery, wh. at least screened us from rain and offered an extensive subject for such contemplation as one was capable of. The Lady herself for the better portion of the time was not there, and the Hon. Mary, who is one of the most modest and sincere of human creatures seemed to have a boundless interest in whatever was really interesting among the multitude of figures that came before us. Next day there came by appointment Mrs Greville the “Exuberant,”Sabine Matilda Greville, b. Thelluson (1823–82), widow (m. 1862) of Richard Greville (ca. 1788–1866); society hostess, living at 23 Wilton Cres., Knightsbridge; nickname unexplained. for the purpose of conducting me to Grosvenor HouseLondon home of Hugh Lupus Grosvenor (1825–99; ODNB), 1st duke of Westminster; the house contained a large gallery displaying his extensive art collection. there to see a certain Lord Ronald Gower, an enthusiast for Marie AntoinetteRonald Charles Sutherland Leveson-Gower (1845–1916; ODNB), 2d bart., author and sculptor. His marble statue Marie Antoinette Leaving the Conciergerie was exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1877. Marie Antionette (1755–93), queen of France 1774–92. & apparently for her alone in nature, to see a statue of her and give him the pleasure of &c &c, which on a windy, dim day was by no means a rapturous enjoyment.Gower noted in his diary, 12 Sept.: “Mrs. Greville drove the ‘sage of Chelsea’ to Grosvenor House to-day in a royal carriage! her sister, Lady Probyn, having the use of one of these regal conveyances. ‘I don’t think,’ Mrs. Greville wrote after this visit to Grosvenor House, ‘Carlyle had the least idea he was reclining in a royal carriage. I am afraid he believed it to be my natural property.’ Carlyle was in good spirits and talked much, but somewhat indistinctly. He appeared interested in the statue, and made allusion to the Queen's shoe, which she repaired herself when in prison, and generally of her heroic conduct during her infinite misfortunes” (Lord Ronald Gower, My Reminiscences [1883] 2:157–58). Mrs. Greville's sister was Letitia Maria, b. Thellusson (ca. 1836–1900), Lady Probyn, m., 1872, Sir Dighton Macnaghton Probyn (1833–1924; ODNB), army officer and courtier. We accordingly looked at all that, really more or less admired the statue and found the young Lord a quietly good and honest gentleman, not
without intelligence whom I had seen once before & quite forgotten.TC does not mention their previous meeting; Gower later wrote: “In London at the end of January (1876) I made the acquaintance of … Thomas Carlyle; this occurred in the rooms of Burlington House. I was introduced to Carlyle by his friend, Miss Davenport Bromley; he was genial and talked much … doubtless the talk concerned the pictures he had come to see. He looks wonderfully hale and hearty for fourscore; his cheeks as ruddy as those of a charity-school boy” (Gower, My Reminiscences 2:129–30). The house, Grosvenor House, which you may recollect with its many pillars on your left hand coming westward towards the Park is an uncommonly fine affair, immense suites of rooms full of pictures and quite palatial in type, all that I transiently looked at, well steadying myself on the slippery waxed floors, & felt thankful to get out of. But was informed that the young Lord must come down with me to Chelsea to look at the picture of “The Little Drummer,” which he accordingly did in a politely simple manner & then driving off with the Exuberant left me,Gower's diary entry of 12 Sept. continued: “We drove back together to Carlyle's house at Chelsea, where he showed us his portraits of Frederick the Great, also those of Martin Luther's parents. Of these he is very proud. Carlyle was full of cordiality and good-humour; his natural and inborn courtesy is marked, insisting, for instance, on escorting Mrs. Greville back to her carriage and seeing her drive from his house, standing with his good gray head uncovered in the street. It is impossible not to feel an attachment for him, combined with the veneration that all must have for that vast intellect” (Gower, My Reminiscences 2:158). For Antoine Pesne, The Little Drummer, see 41:88–89JWC to LLA, 2 Nov. 1864. TC acquired several portraits of Frederick the Great while working on Frederick; see for instance 30:147–49, 33:209–12, 35:31–32, 41:155–56. For Lucas Cranach's portraits of Hans and Margarette Luther, see 45:25–27TC to JMN, 5 Sept. 1867. promising or threatening to return &c. A quiet pipe “bacca” finished off this admirable scene and issued in a farther journey per omnibus and back, with a sad feeling of a blessed day issuing for me unwillingly in zero.

My last bit of reading has been a Life of Sir Sydney Smith, by Barrow Junr,John Barrow, The Life and Correspondence of Admiral Sir William Sidney Smith, G.C.B., 2 vols. (1848). John Barrow (1808–98), civil servant in the Admiralty, promoter of exploration, and author. probably the worst written book of its century (or let us say the worst but one car il y a presse [because there's a hurry])TC refers to a saying of Nicolas Chamfort (1741–94), French writer; see TC's note in Froude, LM 1:134 (CL 14:18). but giving a few real glimpses into the surprising faculties and exploits in early life of that remarkable man whom I recollect as a hero of my childhood, but who sank into absolute neglect after his 50th year,—the reason being, as one could dimly see, that he got into busy-bodyism to an enormous degree and became more or less a bore and a trouble to all kinds of official men.Sir (William) Sidney Smith (1764–1840; ODNB), naval officer; he made his name leading the defense of the Turkish garrison of Acre against Napoleon, 15 March 1799–20 May 1800. After 1814 he left active service and lived mostly in Paris, although continuing to try to involve himself in current affairs. I know not what you are reading,
nor whether this book would at all suit you,—perhaps it might now or someday? The pamphlet that comes today appears to be making a great sensation in Boston, which some publisher is wanting to infect his fellow creatures with here. I have read only scraps of it here and there and found it really rather logical, a hard headed kind of story, but not of any interest to me, who latterly avoid that kind of thing called Descent of Man &c &c.Rev. Joseph Cook (1838–1901) of Boston, Massachusetts, gave a series of “Monday Lectures” in which he attempted to reconcile religious and scientific thinking; this pamphlet was possibly a section of his Biology, with Preludes on Current Events (1877). John A. Carlyle replied, 17 Sept.: “I received … the little pamphlet from America, which you had only partially read. I have tried to read it all, but got little good of it, the theories of Darwin & his followers being rather uninteresting for me. But its author, the Revd Joseph Cook, is evidently well acquainted with the subject, & what he says may do good to many who take some interest in the matter.” Charles Darwin, The Descent of Man (1871). To you therefore I give the function of lighting your pipe with it or giving it away to some enquiring soul who might chance by singular accident to be likely to profit by it.

Dear Brother the day is getting on and this is mere wasting of it as you perceive. So why add any more? Do you know a book by Froude called “Short Stories on Great Subjects”John replied: “I read all the little Essays of Froude, of which you had all the published volumes, when I was with you last winter, & found many of them interesting; & I should be glad to see the new volume you speak of when you have done with it.” Froude, Short Studies on Great Subjects, first series (1867), second series (1871), third series (1877). of which there is a new volume just come out? If you have not read it, it is well worth your looking into. Froude has been in London since his yachting ended,See TC to JAC, 28 July. but I did not see him, nor shall yet for a day or two. I should like much to hear of your coming up to see me again, but all is yet lying undecided and indistinct on that matter. One thing is ever certain my love for you all and my heart's wish for all that is good for us. Amen.
docBody.closer: Ever your affecte, / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 29 Sept. MS: NLS 528.77. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:334. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row, Chelsea. S.W.
29 Sep. 1877.
docBody.p:
I am very penitent and very sorry for the mistake I made in reference to Froudes new Short Studies and the hope I raised in you of some good reading
being found there. I found there had never been two volumes or three volumes at all & that the volume I had got was merely a new edition in which were three papers, two of them well worth reading, if you had not seen them before (which Mary considered improbable);See TC to JAC, 15 Sept.; Froude's Short Studies third series contained nine articles, some previously printed in Fraser's Magazine. John A. Carlyle replied, 4 Oct.: “As for Froude's new essays they may wait till I get back to London, as the one on Euripides is all that I have not already read; so far as I can remember.” the first of these papers was what Froude had called a Sea-study namely a reading of Euripides, after long separation from him, branching out into an earnest investigation of Euripides's religious ideas, and of the singular forms of religion he had emplified in his dramas,—for example in Iphigenia, which he conjectured might be Jepthagenia and connected with the sacrifice of Jephtha's daughter &c; all which, on a serious reading of the piece, I considered to be well worth attention.“Sea Studies” concerned Euripides (ca. 480–ca. 406 BC), ancient Greek dramatist. In Greek mythology Iphigenia was a daughter of Agamemnon, whom he sacrificed to the gods at the start of the Trojan War. Jephthah was a judge in the Bible who sacrificed his daughter as thanks to God after a successful battle; see Judg. 11:30–36. In both cases, some versions of the story say the young women escaped but had to live out their lives in exile or seclusion. The second notable piece was Divus Caesar, and dealt earnestly and in a striking way with the singular ideas on religion entertained among the Romans.“Divus Caesar” concerned the Roman belief that their emperors became gods. This, too, I considered worthy of a serious reading, if you had not already seen & read it. The third paper was merely a hurried detail of his many travelling experiences in the Cape Territory“Leaves from a South African Journal”; Froude had twice been to South Africa on behalf of the British government to try to promote a confederation of South African states; he was there for several months each time: Aug. 1874–Jan. 1875 and June–Nov. 1875; see 49:116TC to JF, 3 July 1874, and 227TC to JAF, 6 Aug. 1875. and glimpses yielded there of the singular country and singular inhabitants black and white. If you have not seen these papers, dear Brother, and have any wish to see them please tell me at once & the volume shall be at once be sent to you.

I have myself been reading for the last ten days in Suetonius,Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (69–after 122), Roman historian. of which I got two translations an EnglishPossibly Suetonius, The Lives of the Twelve Caesars, trans. Alexander Thomson (1796), or the rev. edn., T. Forester (1855); see 25:289TC to LOA, 16 Nov. 1850. and a FrenchPossibly either Suétone: Traduction nouvelle, trans. Philippe de Golbéry, 3 vols. (Paris, 1830–33), or Suétone. Texte Latin avec la traduction en français, trans. Théophile Charles Étienne Baudement (Paris, 1845). both rather good and the latter of them furnished with the original Latin always in sight, but without any annotation for which I apply more or less successfully to the English one. I remember long ago finding among your books at Scotsbrig on a rainy day a
translation by L’EstrangeSir Roger L’Estrange (1616–1704; ODNB), author and press censor; he translated various works from Latin, Greek, and Spanish, but does not appear to have translated Suetonius. However, his name appears on the title page of The Lives of the Twelve Caesars, The First Emperors of Rome. Written in Latin by C. Suetonius Tranquillus. And now done into English by several Hands. With the Life of the Author, and Notes upon those Passages which relate to the Roman Customs. Licensed Feb. 14. 1686/7. Ro. L’Estrange (1689). L’Estrange had been an official press censor until 1679, when the Licensing of the Press Act lapsed, but apparently his name continued to appear on several publications after that. TC mentions reading John's copy of Suetonius at Scotsbrig in the rain, Aug. 1856; see 31:159TC to JWC, 8 Aug. 1856, and 195TC to JAC, 27 Aug. 1856. John replied: “I still have the old translation of the Twelve Caesars which you speak of, & find it has notes of yours on its margins. It is a very dull book, but I also have the original of Suetonius printed by Plantin, with notes by Lavinus Torrentius of 1578, which used to help me in reading the work.” Laevinus Torrentius (1525–95), bishop of Antwerp, L. Torrentii in Suetonii XII. Cæsares Commentarii (Antwerp, 1578); Christoph Plantin (1520–89), Flemish printer and publisher. which I read with great entertainment no doubt this is still among your books and I could almost wish you to seek it out again and try it. I have now got before me a French Translation of the Historiae AugustaeHistoriae Augustae Scriptores VI is a late Roman collection of biographies of the Roman emperors, 117–284, purportedly by six different authors and modeled on the work of Suetonius. TC's French trans. was possibly either Écrivains de L’Histoire Auguste, ed. C. L. F. Panckoucke, 3 vols. (Paris, 1844–47), or Écrivains de l’Histoire Auguste, trans. Guillaume de Moulines (Paris, 1806). of which I can get the original in the London LibraryThe two Latin versions in the London Library were Augustae Historiae Scriptores Sex, cum not. var. et Gruteri, 2 vols. (Amsterdam, 1678), and Historiæ Augustæ Scriptores VI, accur. Cornelio Schrevelio (Leiden, 1661) (Catalogue of the London Library [1865]: 40 and 354). and mean to attack next. I dont know if I ever told you that in the course of the late months I read Gibbon all over again with various reflections naturally, and especially with a considerable abatement of my admiration for Gibbon's talent in all particulars, except that of copious and faithful reading, which is certainly very great.— You never tell me what you are reading or how your time is occupied, which defect I would humbly pray you to amend in some measure.John A. Carlyle replied, 4 Oct., complaining: “At the libraries here I am not able to get any new books that are interesting to me. I have a Biographical Dictionary of the late Robert Chambers…. It is loosely written & incoherently, but it is fully better done than any thing I have seen of his…. I have many other old books in various languages & often get entertainment & refreshment from them.” Robert Chambers (1802–71; ODNB), writer and publisher, Biographical Dictionary of Eminent Scotsmen (Glasgow, 1833–35). From now on John's letters regularly contained details about what he was reading.

Multitudes of useless books & there are very few of them which seem worthy of being sent to you. Today I have just finished the Fortnightly Review, which in general is very stupid; but there is one paper consisting of dialogues
between the late Senior & Thiers,Nassau W. Senior, “Conversations with M. Thiers,” Fortnightly Review 22 (Oct. 1877): 539–61. Nassau William Senior (1790–1864; ODNB), political economist; Louis Adolphe Thiers (1797–1877), first president of French Third Republic 1871–73; see 47:163TC to JAC, 27 Feb. 1871. The conversations took place March–April 1852 in Senior's house in London when Thiers was visiting Britain; TC met him at this time; see 27:89TC to JN, 18 April 1852. For Senior, see 29:109TC to LA, 1 June 1854; TC had known him since the mid-1830s. The article was ed. by Senior's da. Mary Charlotte Mair Simpson, b. Senior (1825–1907). John replied: “I at once sent on the Fortnightly to Dr Russell after reading the article you suggested, for none of the other articles had any interest for me.” Thiers by far the more copious of the two collocutors, which with perhaps some glimpses at the others you might think worth threepence & look at before you send to Russell.— I am very idle, as you see and lead mostly a solitary life; my health is not to be complained of.
I usually get some sleep now and then a good sleep; but it seems to do me little good, my weakness especially in the stomachic regions being so great. However I go down to the bottom of the embankment nearly every morning and almost daily in the afternoon fly off with a Brompton Omnibus on the route we used to go last year. Froude is come definitely home and I had a rather pleasant walk with him two or three days ago no other company but what has rather been an interruption and annoyance to me than a help or comfort. The other day for instance on solemn petition and appointment for a long hour and half with a Mr Hone,Alfred Hone (1810–83), sculptor, only surviving son of William Hone (1780–1842; ODNB), radical satirist, writer, and publisher, a hoary deafish, very clean & rather inarticulate old man, who came to consult with pious earnestness as to what could be done about a life of his Father the late notable William Hone of the Athanasian parodies,William Hone was prosecuted for blasphemy for three parodies that he wrote in 1817, including “The Sinecurist's Creed,” a parody using the form of the Athanasian Creed, a statement of Christian Trinitarian doctrine, to attack three prominent Tory politicians. For TC's earlier contact with Hone, see 12:122TC to AC, 27 April 1840. whom probably you remember. I could help the poor man very little in spite of my wish to help him for I well remembered his Father, and considered him a signally genial, honest and worthy man, whose life grounded on the documents laid before me might, (if well done, but, alas, not otherwise) make a really good bookFamily papers were eventually collected by Hone's granddaughter Margarita Ellen Hone Soul (1857–1951), including material dictated by Hone to his da. Sarah (1801–83); these formed the basis of F. W. Hackwood, William Hone: His Life and Times (1912). and be symbolic of whatever was best in his time in the character of the Plebs of England. But, alas, I could remember no likely man to give it a chance of being well done and could only recommend him to go to Chapman and ask MorleyThe Fortnightly Review was pbd. by Chapman & Hall, and ed. by John Morley 1867–82; see TC to JAC, 8 April 1876. to take an earnest glance
at the affair. This poor man in spite of my wish to help him was painful to me, rather than pleasant.—

A great deal of building, barrowing and trimming is going on on the Northward side of the embankmentAt a meeting of the Metropolitan Board of Works, 13 April, it was proposed that “to prevent damage being done to the gardens on the Chelsea Embankment and the serious nuisances resulting from their unprotected condition, a wrought-iron fence fixed upon stone kerbing be erected upon the gardens at an estimated cost of £2,700” (Globe, 13 April); work began on the project in Sept. but for several weeks all operations about the injured part have ceased and one has a straggling and confused kind of walk before getting on the smooth flags, which are perfect walking so soon as one does get; the trees also are considerably grown & I often hope you will see them before long.

I have been seriously unfortunate about seeing of my friends this year Jamie & his Son John I at one time made sure of for a few days when my hopes suddenly collapsed,See TC to JAC, 28 July. Sister Jean, too, along with Maggie promised and I hope still promises me the satisfaction of seeing her once again,John A. Carlyle wrote, 4 Oct.: “Jean & Maggie think of going to see you before I go, but Annie has to get home before they can decide at what time you are to expect them. She will probably be here tomorrow.” not to speak of yourself. Between which two hopes there seems to be some difficulty in making a wise adjustment. I hope you will be able to settle it wisely among yourselves. All I can say for my own share is that my own desire & hope is and has all along been the wish to see once more the brothers and sisters whom I have left to me, that I do not expect from any of you assistance otherwise and will therefore leave it to yourselves. To you in particular I hope I need not say that these doors are always wide open & that if at any time you have the notion to come to us, you have only to come and find a brother's welcome. Pray see if you can settle it with Jean & Maggie in the wisest way possible.

Besides the Fortnightly Review, I have got one of the intrinsically silliest books but Mary sent it to you yesterday!— Let me at any rate recommend you to look through it or even perhaps read the whole of it, for it did amuse me, remembering the little gabbing Miss DorsaySarah Anne Dorsey, Panola: A Tale of Louisiana (Philadelphia, 1877). Sarah Anne Dorsey, b. Ellis (1829–79), novelist and historian; she visited Britain summer 1871. Lady Stanley wrote to her son Lyulph (who had become friendly with Sarah Dorsey on a trip to the U.S.), 2 July 1871: “The day after you went came that letter from Mrs Dorsey so I wrote to her & took her to Carlyle who discoursed to her for one hour & a half & she was most delighted” (John Rylands Library: Eng. MS. 1092 letter 104; courtesy of the University of Manchester). On her return to the U.S. Dorsey wrote to TC, 1 Nov. 1871, sending him two books, a copy of Anna Leonowens’ memoir of her life in Siam, and a book by Bret Harte, which TC sent on to John; see 48:31TC to JAC, 20 Jan. 1872. She had also given TC a copy of her Recollections of Henry W. Allen (1866; see Carlyle's House 77). John replied: “I also got the Louisiana book which Mary had sent off on Friday, found it rather interesting, though I had never heard of Mrs Dorsey before, & have now got through it. I have given it to sister Jean, but hardly think she will be able to read it.” who had done it and throwing
some glimmerings here and there upon Louisiana & life there. Here is Froude and at any rate my whole stock of clatter is done. I send my love and blessings to all

div3.sourceNote: MA-WSD, 6 Oct. MS: Rodger L. Tarr; text from typed transcript. Hitherto unpbd. William Scott Douglas (1815–83; ODNB), editor.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO WILLIAM SCOTT DOUGLAS

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle bids me acknowledge, with many cordial thanks, the second volume of your beautiful edition of Burns.The Works of Robert Burns, ed. William Scott Douglas, 3 vols. (Edinburgh, 1877); the work was dedicated to TC: “These volumes are dedicated to Thomas Carlyle, the countryman of Robert Burns, and the most luminous illustrator of his life and writings” (The Works of Robert Burns 1:v). Three further vols. were pbd. 1878–79. TC's copy is listed in Sotheby's catalogue: “Burns (R.) Works, 6 vol. Library Edition, presentation copy from the Publisher to Thomas Carlyle, to whom the work is dedicated, original cloth 8vo. Edinburgh, 1877–9. On a compliments slip in volume 4 is the following note by Mary Carlyle: ‘This is the last Book T. C. read (this vol) M C.’” (Sotheby's [1932] 16).

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 14 [13] Oct. MS: NLS 528.78. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Letter misdated; TC wrote on Saturday.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Last Saturday some trifling accident or other prevented me from writing you a word, and I must by no means neglect that duty today. For the rest what I have to say amounts to little or nothing beyond what I suppose you are already aware of, the assurance of my thoughts being with you; and that we are going on here in the usual way.

I get a gt many useless books, which I dare not think of sending you, nor among the Pamphlets selected today (most probably not for approbation, but
for rejection & for gradual cremation), is there any one, except the Essay by Unus de Multis, that is to say by AllinghamUnis de Multis, “Modern Prophets,” Fraser's Magazine 16 (Sept. 1877): 273–92. Allingham noted in his Diary for Oct.: “C. to-day praised highly ‘Modern Prophets’ in Fraser, said it would be a satisfaction to many minds. ‘You have left these Prophets “sitting on their seats of honour,” but you have been more good-natured to them that I could have been—though there is plenty of satirical pungency too’” (Allingham Diary 257). Allingham often wrote under a pseudonym. John A. Carlyle replied, 15 Oct., that they had all found Allingham's article very interesting: “It is quiet, temperate, modest, clever & effectual…. Give my kind remembrances to him & say that I like his article very much.” himself, an article that appeared in the last Fraser, but probably was turned over unread by you as by myself, until Allingham told me of it, and brought me a copy. Pray read it. I thought it very gently & very emphatically done, worthy of being read & considered before you return it hither. Poor Allingham has a good deal of natural faculty & worth; and has met with no due recognition hitherto. Poor soul, his deliverance has not yet come; nay I find his Magazine is to be suppressed; & his poor £400 a year to be thus cut away from him.Fraser's Magazine had been owned since 1863 by Thomas Longman (1804–79; ODNB) and his brother, William Longman (1813–77; ODNB), publishers; Allingham remained editor until June 1879; the title was changed to Longman's Magazine in Nov. 1882. It appears the Longman's have determined upon selling it to the Nineteenth Century,For the Nineteenth Century, see TC to JAC, 28 April. one of the beggarliest bags of wind now afloat. I hope however, he has other prospects opening to him that will be much more advantageous & of solid use to him. I might also send you a good number of distracted letters; but cui bono better that they go at once to the exterminating fire.

Froude is off on a new rustication, till about Monday next; with him, too, I have some bother about a certain injury he has done, or rather the apology about some misstatement of his respecting the late Lord Brownlow in the last edition of his Book lately offered to you;In his article, “On the Uses of a Landed Gentry,” Short Studies on Great Subjects (1877) 275–303, Froude had written criticizing the enclosure of common land by the 2d Lord Brownlow at his estate, Ashridge, in Hertfordshire, and praising the actions of Augustus John Smith (1804–72; ODNB), landowner and philanthropist, who believed enclosure of common land to be wrong. Froude wrote: “Instead of bringing an action against the noble lord [Brownlow], [Smith] brought a hundred and fifty navvies one dark night down from London. When morning came fifteen hundred yards of iron railings were lying flat upon the ground. They were never set up again, and Berkhampstead Common still belongs to you and to me, and to anyone who chooses to enjoy himself there” (Short Studies in Great Subjects [1877] 277–78). The Brownlow family, now headed by the 3d Earl Brownlow, were very upset by the reprinting of the article. Froude wrote to the editor of the Times, 25 Nov.: “In an address delivered by me last year … and since republished, I am informed that I did some injustice to the late Lord Brownlow. I was speaking of the attempted enclosure of Berkhamsted Common, which I regarded, and which I am obliged to say I still regard, as wrong and unjustifiable. / But although the enclosures were made in Lord Brownlow's name … I am assured by those whom I am bound to believe that he was a generous-minded, excellent man, incapable of doing or of sanctioning any act which he had not supposed to be right. / I shall be obliged … if you will give me an opportunity of expressing my regret for having spoken of Lord Brownlow in terms too harsh for the occasion, which have given pain to his family and friends” (Times, 27 Nov. 1877). TC was friendly with Lord Brownlow's mother, Lady Marian Alford; she wrote to him on her return from Paris, 29 Nov.: “I came home so far from well, that my brother delayed giving me the correspondence with Mr Froude—which he thought could have made me very cross as well as unhappy. I am more grateful … than I can express to you, and I am very sorry that the correspondence between my brother Northampton, and Mr Froude has come to such an untimely end. / I should like to go & see you tomorrow & talk it over—may I? … Your sympathy in my trouble emboldens me.” Her brother was Admiral William Compton (1818–97), 4th marquess of Northampton. Lady Alford wrote a pamphlet about the event, Berkhampstead Frith, or Common, and Ashridge in the Nineteenth Century (privately pbd., 1878), giving the family's side of the argument in great detail. but, deservedly perhaps, not sent.
We lately had a short letter from Ruskin, about his last distracted Fors,Ruskin's Fors Clavigera, letter 82, “Heavenly Choirs” (Sept. 1877); see Ruskin's Works 29:220–47. which letter I here enclose. He seems to grow more & more distracted, making some people guess that he will possibly turn to papistry at last & become a monk of Assisi. I hope better things, though I thus speak.Cf. Heb. 6:9.

There has come, I suppose by your impulse, a set of photographs of the whole Scotsbrig family & as head of it a very excellent one of Brother Jamie,John replied, 15 Oct: “I agree with you in thinking the Carlisle photograph of Jamie & his grandson one of the very best I ever saw. Last time I saw John [Jamie's son] he spoke of having bargained with the Carlisle artist to come to Scotsbrig & photograph the whole family there—a plan not so expensive as going in a body [to] Carlisle would have been.” for which I am greatly obliged, & mean to write thither about in a day or two. It seems they are all pretty well in that region.

We expect Sister Jean & Maggie shortly now & hope to get a great deal of good discourse during their stay here. I need not add any word more, time being absolutely done. I only beg for a letter at your first leisure; and I send my love and blessing to you and to all the household.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 27 Oct. MS: NLS 528.79. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:335–36 inc. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Very much pinned into a corner & very near missing my chance again altogether, I zealously send you a few insignificant lines. Merely to indicate that
we are essentially in the old way and would tell you interesting news, if there were any. I have been reading various books & going up generally every day in omnibus and on foot to Portland Place & perhaps a little of the Regent's Park,Allingham noted in his Diary, 27 Oct.: “To C. about 4. C. and I to King's Road. Chelsea omnibus to Charing Cross. We walk down the Embankment as far as Somerset House, ‘one of the most dignified buildings in London’” (Allingham Diary 257). thence returning to pass the evening as you used to see in sleeping and dining and at last after midnight always creeping into bed and lying invisible oftenest sleeping better or worse till morning come again. We are having latterly a good deal of rain, but on the worst day it scarcely hinders me to get down to the end of the embankment & back,—perhaps twice over, if the day is obstinately wet. The day before yesterday rain pouring all day Mary & I went honestly down and back between four & five oclock,—she in Ulster I in Mackintosh impervious to the steadily pouring rain. I have had various Roman books, as you have heard, but am for the present out of these & into the Lives of the Saints, the Hermits of the Thebaid (?) an old French book in three dumpy octavos, translated by Arnaud of the Port Royal (written in Greek sometimes in Latin other times, by St. Jerome, Athanasius &c &c),Les vies des Saints Pères des déserts, et de quelques Saintes, écrites par des Pères de l’Eglise, et autres anciens auteurs ecclésiastiques, Grecs et Latins, trans. [Robert] Arnauld d’ Andilly, 2 vols. (Paris, 1647–53). TC may have been reading the three-volume edn. (Paris, 1736). Robert Arnauld d’ Andilly (1589–1674), Jansenist, councilor of state, teacher at the Port Royal des Champs Abbey, SW of Paris. The Thebaid, desert area round Thebes in ancient Egypt, which became a place of retreat for Christian hermits. St. Jerome (ca. 342–420) and Athanasius (ca. 296–373), early Christian theologians and historians. which is occasionally very interesting but far oftener drearily wandering in clouds of superstitious credulity, of which one can take little hold. A very different book has been that just published by Victor Hugo on the late Napoleon's Coup d’Etat.Victor Hugo (1802–85), French author, Histoire d’un crime (Paris, 1877); it concerned the coup d’état, 2 Dec. 1851, by Louis Napoléon Bonaparte (1808–73), president of France 1848–52, who became emperor Napoleon III, 1852–70; see 26:248TC to JWC, 3 Dec. 1851. It is in pieces very clever, but such pieces (character of Louis, called Napoleon, of MornyCharles Auguste Louis Joseph de Morny (1811–65), 1st duc de Morny, French statesman, half brother and supporter of Napoleon III. & a few others) rise up like bright little islands in a dim sea of infinite details which to an outsider like myself are of little or no value. The Book is not mine, nor do I know if it is in the London Library. I by no means think it is worth your buying & indeed this is but the first volume of it,—foolish book by a most ingenious, clever man; to whom Democracy and French Revolution are the holy of holies. I see Froude about twice a week, to whom Fitz James Stephen will probably tomorrow be added. The latter is likely to be made a judge straightwaySir James Fitzjames Stephen; he had spent the previous decade attempting to codify criminal law, and was appointed to a High Court judgeship in Jan. 1879; see TC to JAC, 18 Jan. 1879. which will be a fine success, both to the Judicature and to
himself. LeckyWilliam Hartpole Lecky. lent me the Lives of the Saints &c and has many books especially translated into French. He is a capital Latinist, I think; but seems to have little more Greek than myself, a very friendly, polite man, but essentially a common place & on some sides a very prejudiced. The day before yesterday I finished Hanna's second volume on Erskine,Letters of Thomas Erskine of Linlathen, ed. William Hanna, 2 vols. (Edinburgh, 1877). TC had received the first vol. in April; see TC to JAC, 12 May. John A. Carlyle replied, 29 Oct.: “Hanna's edition of Erskine's Letters is the most interesting book I have had of late, & the few letters of yours are the best in the book. Hanna was very glad that he got permission to publish them.” William Hanna (1808–82; ODNB), Free Church minister and writer. which pleased & gratified me very much & filled me with mournful recognition of probably the truest Christian man that was left in the world. Eheu, eheu!

But I must certainly stop here, there being more still to write and the day falling down blacker & blacker in floods of rain. My love and blessing to all and sundry of you. Write soon, if you can and will.
docBody.closer: Ever your affectionate / T. CarlyleRobert Browning wrote to TC, 17 Oct.: “I beg your acceptance of the translation I ventured upon at your desire,” and sending a copy of his trans. of The Agamemnon of Aeschylus (1877). The book was dedicated to TC: “[I]t was commanded of me by my venerated friend Thomas Carlyle, and rewarded will it indeed become, if I am permitted to dignify it by the prefatory insertion of his dear and noble name” (The Agamemnon of Aeschylus xi). Allingham reported TC's reaction in his diary, 27 Oct.: “‘[Browning] called down some months ago to ask if he might dedicate it to me. I told him I should feel highly honoured. But—O bless me! … [F]or my souls’ salvation [I] couldn’t make out the meaning…. Browning says I ordered him to do this translation … and I did often enough tell him he might do a most excellent book … by translating the Greek dramatists—but O dear! he's a very foolish fellow…. He picks you out the English for the Greek word for word … then … snips up the sense and jingles it into rhyme!’” (Allingham Diary 257–58). TC's copy is listed in Sotheby's catalogue (Sotheby's [1932] 14).

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 3 Nov. MS: NLS 528.80. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Thanks for your prompt and kind long letter. I am greatly occupied at present and have only a few minutes to myself; but it is lucky there is nothing that is much worth writing & only a word to assure you of nothing being wrong here. I am very sorry to hear of poor Jean's illness.John A. Carlyle wrote, 29 Oct.: “You will have heard that our sister has been unwell, & sometimes confined to bed for a day or two. Her complaint seems to be some form of indigestion. Dr Borthwick has been attending her, & said he found her very much better today…. In general she has had very little pain.” Alexander Borthwick (1823–78), M.D., general practitioner in Dumfries. We have the general idea that she
cannot come to us, even with Maggie's help; but it still seems she has a wish in that direction which would give me great pleasure if it were to take effect. Tell her not to fret or regret whichever way it turns out. As to your own coming hither I confidently expect you; and the time when we leave you altogether to decide on the data that are not before us, but lie under the roof where you now are. I wish you to take it all into your own hands and do whatever seems feasablest and best to you. Pray decide it among yourselves, and the first notice we have that either of you is coming will be a piece of welcome news.

For the last week I have been mainly puddling in that dreary cesspool of Magazines which contains nothing but distress to me. I know not whether it will have been worth your while to look into the Nineteenth Century with the fash attached to it, but it is gone to BallikinrainAnnabella Anstruther's home in Stirlingshire. fairly out of your way. Let me know next time whether or not.

Mary has got up an actual speculation of our starting a Brougham here & we are to try it for a week, three days of which are still to come. I find it much more a fash than any true accommodation or alleviation; but we persist through the other three days & do not prophecy what is yet to become of it. Froude and I had rather a pleasant drive yesterday, intersected with a walk in the Regent's Park and thence home at dusk; glad at least to have got home again. This I think is all that I have got to say at present. As to the truss you speak of and the fash you have with it, I am convinced it does not differ from my own similar concernJohn wrote, 29 Oct.: “My rupture often troubles me, for I have not yet been able to get a[n] efficient truss, though I have had three or four in succession. At present I am expecting one from an Edinburgh artist recommended by Dr Borthwick & hope to get it in a day or two. I am able however at present to get exercise enough by taking due precautions.” See also TC to JAC, 22 [23] June. TC had had a hernia for many years, and had tried various different trusses; see 45:42TC to HL, 3 Oct. 1867, and 70–71TC to HL, 28 Nov. 1867. In July 1868 he had a hernia operation in Edinburgh; see 45:154TC to JCA, 30 June 1868, and 161TC to JF, 2 Aug. 1868; neither the hernia nor a truss have been mentioned since, until now. & that I could very soon instruct you in the way of dealing with it which for most part proves successful with myself.
I send my love and blessing to every one of you and am always, dear Brother,
docBody.closer: Affectionately yours, / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 10 Nov. MS: NLS 528.81. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
We received your letter yesterday, with great thankfulness for the details you give us especially for the good news you give of Sister Jean, wh. I hope
will hold good & come to fulfilment shortly. She knows how much I should wish to see her again.John A. Carlyle wrote, 8 Oct.: “Jean is now much better than she was last week, & she still speaks of going to see you in Chelsea as soon as she possibly can along with Maggie…. The change to Chelsea I think might do her good, but she will still have to wait some time before undertaking the journey.” The weather is not bad here rather it is latterly divided into alternate days of rain and bright sunshine. Thus I had this morning after a dreary drooket day of rain yesterday a very clean comfortable walk to the bottom of the embankment and back, I really do think one of the pleasantest morning walks for a weak old creature that the like of him would fall in with. I read during the mornings & after tea at night in that strange old book upon the Hermits of the Thebaid, which if well considered, has still manifold relations to the most sacred elements of our being; and is, by the aid latterly of considerable skipping a goodish kind of book for me. It is honestly translated, as perhaps I told you, by the venerable Arnaud Racine'sJean Racine (1639–99), French dramatist; he was enrolled in the Petites écoles de Port-Royal, where he was greatly influenced by Robert Arnauld d’Andilly; see TC to JAC, 27 Oct. Uncle and keeps one in the company of men in the highest degree well intending. I have a number of new books here but they are all weltering in the miserable puddle of Scepticism and Anti-scepticism which to me is mere weariness; and I forbore sending any of them to you. The embankment has been a terrible plunge of absurdity & seems to me a disgrace to the poor Bazelgates & architects of the work. They make excuse for themselves as if the City Guardians of the Thames had done it all by pulling up certain wooden piles from the wooden side of the embankment,Sir Joseph Bazalgette (1819–91; ODNB), civil engineer, chief engineer of the Metropolitan Board of Works 1856–89, and designer of the Thames Embankments. City Guardians were local administrative boards mainly dealing with the poor law, rates, and sanitary issues. Critics of the embankments (including TC) claimed they had increased the velocity of the water on the river and left gaps on the banks where excess water had gathered. “[Bazalgette] denied that the Thames Embankments had had the effect of raising the tides. They had increased the velocity of the stream, but had decreased the volume of water, and they had equalised each other.” He argued: “[A]ll that was wanted was a general power to compel frontagers to carry out the necessary works. There were small isolated spots on the river where the bank required to be raised” (Evening Standard, 10 May). For TC's earlier praise for Bazalgette and the Thames Embankments, see 49:106TC to JRU, 13 May 1874. by which the city gains about £50; but on looking and considering I found it all proceeded from their own profound & most blameable neglect of the laws of hydraulics & total oblivion to take any true charge of the oozing water which has come down upon them from Bayswater & the SerpentineUnusually high spring and autumn tides had caused serious flooding along the Thames. The Evening Standard reported, 9 Oct.: “The inhabitants of the southern banks of the Thames were visited yesterday afternoon by the overflow of a strong flood tide, driven up the Thames by a NNE wind, which prevailed during the whole of the day. The residents in the neighbourhood of Battersea, Vauxhall, Lambeth, and Bankside were wholly unprepared for the calamity, and although immediate steps were taken to prevent the entrance of the water into the low-lying courts and houses, the destruction to property and the inconveniences to the people were immense.” Bayswater is an area in NW London with natural springs; the Serpentine is a large artificial lake in Hyde Park, which at the time was fed from the Thames. & is like to cost, perhaps £200,000 before they now get it
set right. The Hydrostatic Paradox and omnipotence of oozing water is a thing they will never forget again.

I do not think I ever saw the Life of Paul JonesJohn wrote, 8 Nov.: “I … got from Dr Borthwick an old Life of Paul Jones, by some American I think, published by Oliver & Boyd long ago. It contains many letters of Benjamin Franklin to Jones, several of Washington &c, & gives one a much higher idea of Jones than usual.” John Paul Jones (1747–92; ODNB), born John Paul, in Arbigland, Kirkbean, Kirkcudbright; he added the Jones to his name in America, where he became a naval officer in the American Continental navy (1775–87) and later the Russian navy (1788–89). Benjamin Franklin (1706–90), polymath, a founding father of the U.S.; George Washington (1732–99), soldier and statesman, 1st president of the U.S., 1789–97. The book was probably Memoirs of Rear Admiral Paul Jones, 2 vols. (Edinburgh, 1830), the only book about Jones pbd. by Oliver & Boyd; the editor of the work is not named. TC had previously read this book in 1833; see 6:385TC to JAC, 17 May 1833. There were several accounts of Jones's life pbd. in America, including Life and correspondence of John Paul Jones … from original letters and manuscripts in the possession of Janette Taylor [Jones's sister], ed. Robert Charles Sands (New York, 1830), and Life of Rear Admiral John Paul Jones, compiled from his original journals and correspondence, ed. Benjamin Walker (Philadelphia, 1845). John continued: “Dr. Borthwicks father knew some of his aunts about Dumfries & liked them well.” Jones's parents were John Paul (1700–67), m., 1733, Jean, b. MacDuff (ca. 1710–ca. 1780s), so it is possible Dr. Borthwick's father, Capt. Alexander Borthwick (1770–1849), could have known Jones's aunts; but it is more likely that he would have known Jones's sisters, Janet (ca. 1739–1817), who m., 1770, William Taylor, watchmaker of Dumfries; and Mary Ann (b. ca. 1741), who m., 1st, Robert Young, and 2d, 1777, Mark Louden (1751–1837). Jones left all his property to these two sisters and their children. you speak of; sometime when you have all quite done with it, I may ask you for a short loan of it, which would be worth my while.— We are very sorry to hear the tragic account you give of poor Mary. I think you should go down thither some good day & investigate the matter yourself. Poor Mary I know is terrible off for teeth & it would no doubt be a gt relief to her were that rectified.Their sister Mary Austin; John wrote, 8 Nov.: “Mary herself is frail enough now, & is hardly ever able to take any breakfast at all, but keeps moving about the house as usual, & makes no complaints.” He replied, 20 Nov.: “When I saw her last we had some talk about her trying to get new teeth; but on examining the mouth I found that her gums & teeth are in a worse state than my own—much worse I should say—so that it would be useless for her, as it would for me, to employ any dentist. She is always able to take some tea & cream at least for breakfast.” I did employ Jean long since to assure her of my prompt desire to furnish the expence; but somehow, owing to the distance of the Carlisle dentist there cd never be anything done
in it; if there is anything actually practicable I pray you push it forward on my behalf towards speedy fulfilment.— — Lecky repeatedly asks me if you are not coming up; so does poor old Dr Blakiston, who has grown very weak, but always keeps up his heart and is always loyally seconded by Bessy,Dr. Peyton Blakiston and his wife, Bessy; see TC to JAC, 7 Sept. 1876. who is in truth his shield and staff, though herself often suffering. DarwinErasmus Darwin. I have not seen for several weeks but understand him to be not worse than usual, though seldom going out. He was out once a week ago when Mary & I called. The Brougham speculation is entirely finished. My clear decision being that I can have nothing to do with it; but Mary has by no means entirely renounced it, attracted by Chapman'sFrederic Chapman. intimation about an eligible horse. Her I will cautiously & sceptically attend on the matter & we shall see.William Allingham noted in his Diary in Nov.: “The Brougham—‘Oh, I shall give that up—I find instead of it being mine, I should be its. I cannot go whither I would—the man cannot find out the places. Mary, I believe, has some other plot: I must keep my eye on her!’” (Allingham Diary 258). I write no more at present & will expect hopefully a word from you very soon. My love & blessings to you all. I ever am
docBody.closer:
Affectionately yours, for T. Carlyle
M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 17 Nov. MS: NLS 528.82. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I have nothing to send you today except perhaps the Melbourne Newspaper from DuffySir Charles Gavan Duffy, speaker of the Legislative Assembly in Victoria 1877–80, had spoken at a reception at the Melbourne Chamber of Commerce, 8 June, to honor the Canadian trade representative, an advocate of free trade principles. The Melbourne Argus, 9 June, reported Duffy's speech: “He [Duffy] had started in this Colony with a strong conviction in favour of free trade. He was in London when … the tariff of this Colony [was altered] in a protectionist direction…. He saw plainly that the tendency of opinion in this Colony was in favour of protection of some sort. He then took the step of consulting three eminent gentlemen in England … John Bright, John Stuart Mill, and Thomas Carlyle. He said to John Bright—‘All my life will be spent in Australia. I am a free trader, as you know. They are going to have a protective policy there. Am I to retire, therefore, from public life? What would you do under the circumstances?’ John Bright, a practical man, said—‘If there are particular industries that can flourish in that country, and if it is the determination of the people to encourage them, I would grant bonuses on certain industries liberally, in order to promote them; or I would come to an agreement with the Protectionists to protect a certain number of articles for a certain number of years, and let them try their experiment.’ He afterwards consulted Mr. Mill, [who said] nearly the same as Mr. Bright…. He also spoke to Mr. Carlyle, and that gentleman replied … —‘No country under the sky has ever got manufactures except by spending the funds of the State to plant them, and unless Australia does that, it will get no manufactures’” (Melbourne Argus, 9 June, pbd. Report of the Canadian Commissioner at the Exhibition of Industry, held at Sydney, New South Wales, 1877 [Ottawa, 1878]: 94). & what will be much more comfortable to you, the assurance
that we are all in our usual state and that nothing sinister has happened to us or our affairs here. The Duffy business I have often heard has been often agitated in the antipodal region and a good while ago there was a letter by BrightA copy of Duffy's speech was sent to John Bright (1811–89; ODNB), radical politician; in a letter of 31 July, denying that he had ever delivered this opinion to Duffy, he concluded: “Victoria is young, and thinks she knows more and better than we know. But when she finds herself not at the head, but at the tail of the great Australian communities, as to her success and the growth of wealth, she may discover that industry has no greater enemy than a protective or restrictive tariff” (Daily Mail, 8 Aug.). TC met John Bright in 1847, when they disagreed profoundly; see 22:58JWC to TC, [11 Sept. 1847], and 68TC to JWC, [14] Sept. 1847. about it, defending the sacred Gospel of Free Trade but for my own share I have paid no more regard to it than it merited from me that is to say no regard at all. Perhaps it may amuse you for a few minutes to witness the agitation of Duffy and Co. I have also a few minutes ago received from Dickson of Cincinnati a pamphlet on the subject of “Money” which I design to glance over and will send to you in fee simpleWilliam Martin Dickson, Some Aspects of the Money Question (Cincinnati, 1877); for Dickson, see TC to JAC, 30 June. “Fee simple”: absolute possession, to dispose of at will. on Monday, if I live. Yesterday there went off to Sister Jean, without her name written on it by me a kind of history of Miss Wynne,Memorials of Charlotte Williams-Wynn, ed. Harriot Hester Lindesay (1877); Charlotte Williams-Wynn (1807–69; ODNB), diarist, friend of the Carlyles since 1845; see 19:102TC to JAC, 17 July 1845; she was to have been one of the guests at the tea party JWC was planning when she died; see 43:211–12JWC to TC, 21 April 1866. Harriot Hester Lindesay (d. 1878) was Wynn's sister. John A. Carlyle replied, 20 Nov.: “[Jean] likes the book you sent her about Miss Wynne very much & had got nearly through it.” who was once very familiar in this house & always held in great estimation as a person of real worth & intelligence. Jean will probably be able to read it with some interest and perhaps after her, you. I have been busy with Paul Jones, and have still the half of the last volume to read. It is certainly one of the worst written books ever sent forth as a biography; but I get from it for the first time some flickering authentic notion of who and what Paul Jones really was,—a man of the most self-conscious vain-glorious and generally unwise habit of mind, but of great courage, tenacity & skill in naval war,—not a hateful man either, but rather a pitiful and valuable. You shall have the book back soon, or rather we shall return it direct to Dr Borthwick.

I cannot make out the least to my satisfaction what is the condition of poor Jean's healthJohn replied: “[Jean] looks fully as well as usual, but there seems to be some derangement in the digestive organs.” He said that Dr Borthwick had been to see her, and felt “it would not be wise or safe for her to attempt such a long journey [to London] just now … so she has given up the idea of going till she gets better & stronger.” Jean wrote, [ca. 3 Dec.] that she had sent TC a Waterbeck ham: “I really could not think of any thing else to be got here which wd have the least chance of being of any real use. My best blessing be with you on Birthdays & all the days that [are] appointed to us here below.” The ham presumably came from Thomas and Robert Carlyle's grocer's shop in Waterbeck (see TC to JAC, 9 June), apparently known for their hams; see 25:94TC to MAC, 11 [Jun.] 1850. or when & by what course of events I may hope to see either her or you in this house. All I can say is, it would give me real satisfaction to see either the one or the other of you, in actual fact. We have still alternating days of bright sunshine in the middle part, or perhaps alternately of mud & continual damp or wet. There has not yet been once a November fog, but perhaps that is in store for us too. The top of the embankment, too, seems not advancing towards completion and the way on to it is always disagreeable, but after the walk itself for three quarters of a mile may vie with any in the world. Mary and I were down together yesterday and this morning to the bottom of it, and enjoyed the diligent movement of barges & traffic chick-chicking their watery way up towards Hammersmith.

Tom's Letter from CanadaTheir nephew Thomas Carlyle. was welcome to us. Pray take care of having some answer sent, with many regards of mine, as well. Our time is all done now and I can only add, blessings and farewell to one and all of you.
docBody.closer:
Ever, dear Brother, / Your
affectionate, / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 24 Nov. MS: NLS 528.83. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
5, Great Cheyne Row,
Chelsea. S.W.
24 Nov. 1877.
docBody.p:
I am heartily glad to hear that at last you are actually coming up to us. The conveyance by night in an empty first class carriage of the Midland railway was quiet, regular & other wise recommendable: the seat offered ample opportunity to stretch yourself out. I was never in the Pulman Car by night,
nor did I ever see the beds there that I have heard of.John A. Carlyle wrote, 20 Nov.: “I think I might perhaps venture to go [to London] next week, if convenient for Mary & you…. I should take passage right through at once to London, either by our forenoon or night train, which last professes to have comfortable beds. Didn’t you once try them?” Pullman cars were first-class coaches with a steward service, first used in Britain by the Midland Railway, 1874; they were designed in the U.S. by George Mortimer Pullman (1831–97). On the whole I should recommend the day train with plenty of wraps; but indeed you yourself are far more skilful & experienced in travelling than I am; and I need not attempt to give you any of my advice. Tell me what day we are to look for you and at what hour and you shall have a brother's welcome whenever you arrive.

I sent you yesterday [one] of the foolishest and most chaotic books in the world, which I began looking through in great disgust, but on proceeding I gradually found there was more authentic hints and details about the whole worldwide jumble of what they call the Eastern QuestionSir Tollemache Sinclair, A Defence of Russia and the Christians of Turkey … the Eastern Question, from 1686 until Aug. 1877 (1877); John replied, 26 Nov.: “I find Sir T. Sinclair's book interesting though badly arranged & repulsive at first. One gets more information from him than from any other book-maker about Turkey & Russia & the war now going on.” Sir John George Tollemache Sinclair (1825–1912), son of TC's old friend Sir George Sinclair (1790–1868; ODNB); see 36:28636:biographical notes; TC had sent an earlier work of his, The Franco-German War (1871), to Jean, Feb. 1871; see 47:162TC to JCA, 25 Feb. 1871. than in any other book; & that in a careless way it was well worth struggling through, aided by extensive skipping. Try it a little & fling it out without reluctance if it do not suit.

This week I got an ugly fit of nose cold & spent a very bad day in what the Scotch call snifters & in spite of Mary's feet bathing of me, &c &c, with her best skill, had a bad night, with little or no right sleep. The sniftering has gone & has left no sensible feeling of catarrh; but I am ill off ever since for sleep & gave up for three days the process of washing; but cannot hitherto manage to have an average of tolerable sleep, added to which the weather is very bad mostly consisting of bright blinks followed by miserable muggy rains. This morning I returned again to my bath aided by a little hot water & made out the journey to the end of the embankment, which is still unpleasantly encumbered at this end,For renovations to the Chelsea Embankment, see TC to JAC, 29 Sept. but when once you are upon it becomes first-rate walking, with seats interspersed; which in a Mackintosh you can freely sit down upon. I got in without damage; but am still in a queasy state & only hope to be in better order when you arrive. I have often thought of my last sight of you walking in the garden with a sternly sorrowful face;See TC to JAC, 28 April. & am cheered with the thought that I shall see you again in this world which latterly I have often doubted of
not doing.

There is nothing worthy of the least mention among our acquaintances here. The only other practicality I have to add is that there is a great desire to hear when you will come, as soon as you can fix.John replied, 26 Nov.: “I still purpose to start this week for Chelsea. I have several things to get … & should hardly be ready for starting before Saturday morning at soonest. I have resolved to go by the day, & not by the night train which starts after eleven o’clock, as I have never been accustomed to travel by night, & the time of starting is some hour & a half after the time when we go to bed here.”

div3.sourceNote: TC-CW, 29 Dec. MS: Yale; text from typed transcript. Hitherto unpbd. Camille Wright, b. de Moyen (ca. 1811–82), wife, m. 1835, of Thomas Wright (1810–77; ODNB), historian and antiquary.
div3.head: TC TO CAMILLE WRIGHT

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle presents his compliments to Mrs Wright and regrets that the state of his health did not permit him to be present at the Funeral today.Wright d., 23 Dec., at his home, 282 King's Road, Chelsea, and was buried in Brompton Cemetery, 29 Dec. He and TC had not apparently been friends, although he had provided some documents for Cromwell; see 20:114TC to EC, [28 Jan. 1846], and Carlyle, Works 9:274–78. TC had also borrowed his books Political Songs of England (1839) and Political Poems and Songs (1859–61); see 42:182TC to JWC, 10 Aug. 1865.

div3.sourceNote: MA-JR [MAI-JRU], 16 Jan. MS: BL. Pbd. Brent Kinser, “ Finding Cassandra: Alfred Lyttelton's Encounter with Carlyle, 21 July 1878,” CSA 30 (2014): 175; text from pbd. source.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO JOHN RUSKIN

docBody.p: I have only one moment before the post leaves, to give you my Uncle's best love and to say that he is delighted to think he is going to see you so soon. He will be most happy to see the young gentlemanAlfred Lyttelton (1857–1913; ODNB), sportsman and politician. whom you are going to bring.It took much longer than he had hoped as Ruskin was severely ill for several months between Feb. and June; he and Lyttelton finally visited 21 July, the day before TC and Mary left for Scotland. For an account of the visit, see CSA 30:172–74; Edith Lyttelton, Alfred Lyttelton: An Account of his Life (1917) 71–73; Wilson, Carlyle 6:423–24.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 27 April. MS: NLS 528.84. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: We received your kind and punctual letter and were very much obliged by it. There is nothing new among us here since you left.John A. Carlyle had been staying in Cheyne Row since early Dec. 1877; he returned home 18 April. I have been considerably bothered with want of sleep but seem to be doing a little better the last two nights & except weakness and weariness in the scene now so empty to me have nothing to complain of. We saw Blakiston & Mrs B. the day before yesterday, who spoke of you with great regard and were very kind, poor souls. John Stanley whom we otherwise called Colonel Stanley, who had long been an ardent follower of mine & was familiar to me from his boyhood suddenly died (at least to me suddenly) on Tuesday morning last,Col. John Constantine Stanley d. 23 April. Maude Stanley wrote from Wimpole St., 21 April: “[E]ver since I received your note I have been here nursing Johnny who is dangerously ill. He lies unconscious from poison in the blood from a kidney disease.” TC had stood godfather to his first child; see TC to JSTA, 2 July 1876.—a great shock to me when I heard it from Miss Bromley before going out that day. The same morning about five, as you already know poor Dilberoglue got his release.Stauros Dilberoglue d., 23 April, at his home, 13 Barnsbury Pk., Islington. I many a time wonder that I have any friends left, who can be taken away from me & added to the great multitude already gone.

I have been reading a good deal in Goethe & find him very clever as always, but difficult to understand completely & rather unsatisfactory for that reason. Latterly I read a book by Renan called Melanges,Joseph Ernest Renan (1823–92), French biblical scholar, religious historian, and philosopher, Mélanges d’histoire et de voyages (Paris, 1878). which I thought would have been much more instructive than it proved to be indeed I found Monsieur R. a decidedly light horseman & shall not be in haste to read any other book of his. Lecky brought this Renan to me. He since favoured me with Victor Hugo's second volume of Histoire d’un CrimeVictor Hugo, Histoire d’un crime. Déposition d’un témoin, 2 vols. (Paris, 1877–78); TC had recently read the 1st vol.; see TC to JAC, 27 Oct. 1877. which is much more intertaining and clever, though foolish.

Of you I have great miss & indeed see nobody or hardly anybody that gives me the least satisfaction. Patience, patience, that is the thing we all need. I am glad you have got your first operation successfully over.John wrote, 25 April, that he had waited to write “till Dr Borthwick had got his first operation done. Yesterday he & Dr Thomson … came and made their first operation
