successfully extracting rather more than two quarts of liquid—which gives me sensible relief for the time at least, but I have not been able to walk much.” John had had a troubling hernia for some time (see TC to JAC, 3 Nov. 1877) but this was probably for an abdominal tumor. Dr. Alexander Thomson (ca. 1833–1903), physician, and surgeon at the Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary. May it not be necessary
again for a good while. You will go over to Annandale so soon as you are fairly rested.

With kindest love to all and sundry, especially to my dear Sister Jean whom I daily think of and would gladly help if I could.Jean wrote, 4 Jan., in reply to a letter from TC, now untraced: “I received your most kind letter duly & I cannot tell you how refreshing it was to me! Yes my heart too continues firm & I can still remember your returns from Edinr in my earliest childhood as the highest spots in my young life. You wd sometimes set me on your foot keeping hold of one little arm & gaily swing the little to turn round the room till I was wild with delight. Then you would take me kindly by the hand & let me trot by your side & ask me about all my bits of troubles as no one else did. May God bless & comfort you for your life-long affection & kindness to us all. / I was much obliged to you for the very interesting Bks you sent me all thro the winter they were a great boon to me when there was nothing else that I could do…. Charlotte W. Wynn I enjoyed most of all. I have just been re-reading several chapters of her book today. She must have been a very clever, good kind of woman. / I am happy to tell I am a good deal better than I was … & feel much stronger.”
docBody.closer: Affectionately your / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 5 [4] May. MS: NLS 528.85. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature. Letter misdated; TC is writing on Saturday, 4 May.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
I write to you in the greatest haste a few lines to say that we are all in our usual state of health & nothing sinister has happened; thinking that even this will be welcome to you on the Sunday morning. I have heard no word from yourself during the week but Mary has given me from Dfs sources tolerable news of you, wh. I was very glad of. It seems you have gone out to drive twice which I much approve of and hope you will continue.John A. Carlyle replied, 5 May: “I always get more or less injury in my present from driving…. I am still unable to walk any distance, & since Friday I have confined myself to the garden here…. Dr Borthwick called & saw me yesterday, & thinks the tapping again may not be required for some considerable time…. I am glad that I started in time from Chelsea, for I could not now stand the long journey as I did in April. The opening under the skin, above the navel is larger than it was but not painful, & my pad is still effectual in keeping the lump outside nearly level.” We are puddling along here in the usual element of vague unpleasant rumour; & I am now just about
to get out into my usual driveAfter his initial reluctance, TC had agreed to keep using the brougham; see TC to JAC, 10 Nov. 1877. Jean wrote, 4 Jan.: “I am right glad to hear you have at last consented to have carriage exercise instead [of] walking so much.” accompanied this time by a German professorPossibly Karl Adolf Buchheim (1828–1900), prof. of German language and literature at King's Coll., London, 1863–1900; see 45:109–10TC to KAB, 24 March 1868; otherwise unidentified. a good enough fellow who speaks English & is busy writing what he has for twenty years been preparing to write a history of our bloody MaryMary I (1516–58; ODNB), queen of England and Ireland 1553–58, given the epithet “bloody” because of her fierce persecution of Protestants. in wh. I cannot say that I take almost any interest.

The Leckys are off for Italy. We have seen DarwinErasmus Darwin. who was in his usual spirits & health though not yet going out favourable as the weather is. I need not continue this; but let the whirl sink down. I send my love to one & all of you, especially to Sister Jean, whom if I had any fingers of my own I wd write to oftener than I do. Good be ever with you all. I miss you here very much.

closer.salute: I ever am your affectionate Brother,

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 25 May. MS: NLS 528.86. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Thanks for your good letter of this morning, which was very welcome to me & very satisfactory.John A. Carlyle wrote, 24 May, saying that he had generally been feeling better. I had last Monday an excellent letter from Sister Jean,Jean Aitken wrote, 19 May, saying that she had injured the forefinger of her right hand “so that I could not make any use of the hand for some weeks.”. which I will surely contrive to answer and for which I wish you in the meantime to give her my very kindest thanks. You seem to go on steadily & well at Dumfries, though under limited conditions. I think it a great misfortune that you cannot contrive a little vehiculation of some kind as I hope you will by & by. That little Arab pony, if you could get a proper carriage for it would be a most admirable increment to your resources.

For my own share, I am doing a little better in the way of sleep, though still not much & I still continue to think of Asses milk,Jean wrote: “I shall enquire about asses milk. I have no knowledge of the matter myself—only hearing old people speak of its wonderful qualities for elderly people and delicate youngsters.” though still only in a vague
way thinking of it. I am busy reading Goethe; have lately done Egmont, Torquato Tasso, Natürliche Tochter & indeed all the other big plays. I am inclined to be disappointed with them, but on the whole not much for there is endless ingenuity, grace of execution & other fine quality. On the whole I have got to the tenth volume of the WerkeGoethe's Werke, 54 vols. (Stuttgart, 1828–33); vols. 8–10 included Goethe's dramas and librettos, Götz von Berlichingen (1773), Egmont (1788), Iphigenie auf Tauris (1779), Torquato Tasso (1790), Die natürliche Tochter (1803), Elpenor (1781–83), Clavigo (1774), Stella (1776), Claudine von Villa Bella (1789), and Erwine und Elmire (1776). & mean to continue, though the print is uncomfortably small & the paper dusky coloured. I am greatly pleased to hear that the Friedrich pleases you.John wrote: “I have got a great deal of good in reading the Life of Frederick, & have nearly done with the ninth volume…. No book I have ever read gives so clear & lively account of its subject…. The labour you must have had in writing it one can see must have been immense.” It took TC twelve years to write Frederick. I have lost it considerably out of my thoughts & am resigned often enough to think it worth nothing but it did cost me a deal of trouble & was a full burden for all my strength during many years.

We have very wet weather here & sometimes stormy; but suppose it to be very healthy for the season & its growths & expect that in June the sun will come out in his strength. The Leckys, as you know, are away to Como &c & I cannot find their absence to be much of a loss to me in fact I become more & more short of interesting company here & have with only a couple of exceptions nobody that can give me a genial half hour. Good in these circumstances if one do have any serious company with oneself. To Tyndall I gave the FarbenlehreGoethe's Zur Farbenlehre, 2 vols. (Tübingen, 1810), which he sent to TC in a “Packet containing Books” mid-June 1830; see 5:151–52TC to G, 31 Aug. 1830, 154–55TC to G, 31 Aug. 1830. In an address to the Royal Institution, 19 March 1880, Tyndall spoke of TC's giving him the work in May 1878: “My reverence for the poet [Goethe] had been awakened by the writings of Mr. Carlyle…. There was, however, one of the poet's works, which … remained for a long time only imperfectly known to me…. I laid it aside … believing that Goethe in the ‘Farbenlehre’ was wrong in his intellectual, and perverse in his moral judgments…. [TC] presented to me, as a ‘farewell gift,’ the two octavo volumes of letterpress, and the single folio volume, consisting in great part of coloured diagrams, which are here before you. Exactly half a century ago these volumes were sent by Goethe to Mr. Carlyle. They embrace the ‘Farbenlehre,’—a title which may be translated, though not well translated, ‘Theory of Colours’—and they are accompanied by a long letter, or rather catalogue, from Goethe himself, dated June 14, 1830…. My illustrious friend wished me to examine the book, with a view of setting forth what it really contained. This year for the first time I have been able to comply with the desire of Mr. Carlyle” (John Tyndall, New Fragments [1892] 47–48). He wrote thanking TC for the book, 29 May: “We have just returned from our trip … and found your gift here awaiting us. / I attach to it an immense value. / Tomorrow at 2 we will run down to see you. I have got a little of the mildest and richest Irish whiskey now distilled, which I wish you to taste.” & understand him to have engaged to study it. To me he seemed to have a kind of dim anticipation like what my own is that Goethe's notion of the matter is after all the true one. Tyndall whom I am to see again by & by
is the only man living that could bring the matter to an equitable test for the great Goethe. Alas, dear Brother the time is quite up and I must abruptly stop. With truest regard, I ever am
docBody.closer: Yours affecte, / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 22 June. MS: NLS 528.87. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: I have hardly anything that is new to tell you, but in the imminence of intrusive interruptive people, I will hastily send you the usual Saturday's gazette, which will testify my good wishes at least. The enclosed letter from the Sunderland CorkcutterThomas Dixon; see TC to JAC, 4 Dec. 1875. Dixon wrote, 19 June: “I have found the owner of the plate of Holl's Engraving of the John Knox portrait, he is willing to supply you copies printed on any kind of paper you choose at a moderate price, so I thought you might prefer them for your essay to the Autotype ones.” will tell its own story & if I only add that the engraving of Knox, which is within it has been rejected by Mary & me as “improved” into unveracity in part and could not be recommended to Chapman to be concerned with at all.Chapman & Hall were printing Early Kings of Norway and The Portraits of John Knox as vol. 39 of the people's edn. of TC's Complete Works, 1878; see TC to JAC, 23 Sept. 1876. The portrait of Knox that TC believed to be a true likeness, the Somerville portrait, was engraved by Benjamin Holl; in the first printing of the Portraits of John Knox the picture was reproduced by the autotype process from Charles Knight's publication of George L. Craik and Charles MacFarlane, Pictorial History of England (1849) 2: opp. 548; see 48:131TC to JAC, 30 Dec. 1872. I mean it as you will otherwise see as a gift to Sister JeanJean Aitken had written to TC [22 March 1874] asking for a copy of the portrait; see 49:70TC to JAC, 21 March 1874. John A. Carlyle replied, [23 June]: “I will get the Knox Portrait framed for Jean, who accepts it gladly.” & wish you to get it put into a frame for her & tell me the cost. I have enclosed it to herself with a few hasty but sincere words & hope she may find it worth hanging up in her room.

Within the last three days there has been a change in the weather to blazing almost windless heat: considerable changing of costume in consequence & practice of sitting on the Japanese chairUnidentified. at the back of the house, as now with poor Mary writing on her knee. I feel very weak, but generally get some sleep at night and struggle on (henceforth in a straw hat) to a walk half way down the embankment which is nearly utterly deserted & if windless very hot. Yesterday the man of the broughams instead of sending a brougham at
the time for going out sent word that a marriage had taken place somewhere & that there was not a brougham possible within his utmost circle of research. I had to go with Froude, consequently, in the underground & above ground railway to Kew Gardens found a beautiful verdure & shade there for a little while & then home again tired to the very bone with the necessary walking thereto & not till today feel refreshed to my usual state again. Of public or private news I can say no word & will in fact here terminate, as there are at least two intrusives expected and nothing more that is worth pen & ink.

I wish you were here beside me, but, alas, know it to be impossible. Please to return the Corkcutter letter in case there should be any question (which I dont expect) about the “improved” Knox engraving. With my hearts love to all of you, I ever am your affecte Brother,

closer.note: TC apparently wrote to John, ca. 15 June (letter untraced), complaining of problems with his ears, and asking about the surgeon Joseph Lister (1827–1912; ODNB), as John replied, 16 June: “Mr Lister would not take any fees from me, and I don’t think he will take any from you, for he knows well what relation you had to his father-in-law Syme. But he would be glad to see you at any rate, & I think him a very good surgeon & a safe man to consult. My own idea is that you have only got some hardened wax in your ears, such as you have often had before, & Mary could easily get it out by a little oil & then syringing after getting it softened.” Jean also wrote to TC with the same advice. Lister was prof. of surgery at King's Coll., London, 1877–92. He had previously worked in Edinburgh, 1853–60, with James Syme (1799–1870; ODNB; see 45:23045:biographical notes), and m., 1856, Syme's eldest da., Agnes (1834–93). Syme had been friendly with John A. Carlyle (see 46:41–42TC to JAC, 28 April 1869, and 103TC to JAC, 1877-11-03), and had performed TC's hernia operation, July 1868; see TC to JAC, 3 Nov. 1877.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 21 Sept. Pbd: Copeland 251–53.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE
div3.docBody:
24 Cheyne Row, Chelsea,
21 Sep. 1878. My Dear Brother,—
We got your letter this morning, and were very glad to hear that things went so tolerably with you in your present sad imprisonment. We had not the bit of bad weather you speak of,John A. Carlyle wrote, 20 Sept.: “We have had some very stormy weather since you left us [13 Sept.], & I rather suffered from entire confinement to the house on some days…. But I am now as well again as when you started for London.” TC and Mary had spent 22 July–13 Sept. in Dumfriesshire; the Glasgow Herald reported, 25 July: “Mr Thomas Carlyle, with his niece, Miss Mary Aitken, who acts as his secretary, is at present occupying Park House, on the Troqueer side of the river. Mr Carlyle has hitherto in visiting his native district … sojourned with his sister and brother-in-law (Mr Aitken) at the The Hill. But Dr Carlyle, the philosopher's brother, is, and has for some time been, an invalid at The Hill; and in these circumstances another residence was sought, which would at once be retired, and, in respect of distance from The Hill, convenient.” They also spent a week or so with TC's brother Jamie at Scotsbrig, and met with Annabella Anstruther at Annan [10 Sept.], where they had lunch at the Buck Hotel (Wilson, Carlyle 6:428–29). Anstruther wrote, 13 Sept.: “Will you allow me to say a few words of thanks for your goodness to me last Tuesday at Annan—never shall I forget the kindness of your farewell to me…. This I hope will find you snug & well in your ain house at hame.” or had it only in
a milder type. We also get out daily in a drive of two hours which might be pleasanter were we in better circumstances to enjoy it, but it does us good and forms a variety in our rather stagnant ways. I also contrive to get some modicum of sleep every night and have now got rested from the great confusions of our journey hither, in which till Crewe we could get no place to ourselves. The scene on Carlisle platform was beyond all others I have seen the most chaotic and disturbing to me. The Town seems quite empty of people we have business with. We have seen only Blakiston and his Bessy Blakiston is as nonsensical as formerly. He spoke of writing to you, but I know not whether he has done it. His knowledge about your circumstances seems to me to amount to zero. Yesterday we called at Darwin's door, heard he was in his usual way of health, but as nephewsErasmus Darwin, who lived at 6 Queen Anne St.; he had at least five nephews, it is not known which are referred to here. of his had just driven up to his door, we did not venture in. Froude is still at SaltcombeThe Moult, Salcombe, Devonshire, house rented by Froude for the summer from William Courtenay (1807–88; ODNB), 11th earl of Devon, politician and philanthropist; see Dunn, Froude 2:456–57. for a month to come. Till then does not make his appearance here. I have nearly done my reperusal of Frederick and know not what book next to apply to. But something I will devise for that poor purpose. The Town is very empty, but begins in a slow way to repeople itself.
We are much concerned to hear by James of NewlandsTheir nephew James Carlyle. that poor AustinJames Austin, their sister Mary's husband, d. 20 Sept. John wrote, 27 Sept., that their brother Jamie and his two sons, James and John, had been at James Austin's funeral on 24 Sept.: “Our James [Aitken] was there too, & told us poor Mary had got thro’ it with perfect calmness & presence of mind. James calculated that there were some two hundred people attended it—some from great distances.” lies at the Gill in dangerous circumstances; jaundice is the last figure of his illness. Mary, it appears, is in her usual way. Here our weather is generally good and I often have a walk down to the bottom of the embankment, which is strange and I suppose salutary to me. A sad thought to me in this operation is that, alas, you cannot share it with me, or for the present enjoy anything like it. No word from Canada,While TC and Mary were staying at Park House they were joined by Alexander and Thomas Carlyle, sons of TC's brother Alick, who were visiting from Canada. Alexander later wrote: “[M]y brother and I stayed with Carlyle and his Niece Mary for I think a little over a week; and walked, drove and talked with them at all practical hours. I can safely say I never enjoyed a visit more! Carlyle seemed then in fair health and talked much every evening, sometimes for hours together. He was very charming, and with a variegated smoking cap on his head he looked like a revered king! … My brother and I were very sorry when we had to take our leave, I for a double reason: for Mary and I had been engaged for some years,—ever since our first meeting in 1871 [see 47:222TC to SWA, 9 Aug. 1871]. She was willing to go to Canada with me; but my Uncle could not spare her; so that nothing could be arranged at that time for our wedding” (A. Carlyle, Jottings 71). but certainly some must be coming. My kindest
love to Jean. Tell her if I had a hand, she should not long expect a letter from me! With kindest love to one and all of you, I ever am / Your affecte Brother, / T. Carlyle.
Will you kindly send Emerson back when everybody had done with it.John A. Carlyle wrote, 20 Sept.: “I got the little Emerson book & will send it back at any time you wish. It is a better thing than any other of Emerson's works that I have seen of late years. Jean is now reading it.”

div3.sourceNote: MA-EDC [ECO], 4 Oct. MS: Moncure Conway Papers, Columbia; text from typescript. Ellen Dana Conway, b. Davis-Dana (1833–97), abolitionist, feminist, and Unitarian, m., 1858, Moncure Daniel Conway (1832–1907), Virginian abolitionist and Unitarian, and minister at the South Place Chapel, N London, 1864–84; see MAI to ECO, 16 Sept. 1875.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO ELLEN DANA CONWAY

docBody.p: I hope you will excuse me for not replying to your kind note sooner. It is a disappointment to me that I was not able to accept your invitation for today. As to my Uncle, he never by any chance dines from home now. I read your letter over to him he bids me thank you for your kind feelings to him which he hopes you will continue to entertain, and offer you his kind regards. We are very glad that you are better again. I am hoping to pay you & Hamlet houseThe Conways lived at Hamlet House, Hammersmith, 1876–79. a Monday visit very soon.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 11 [12] Oct. MS: NLS 528.88. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC. Mary misdated; dated by JAC to TC, 11 Oct.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Thanks for your kind & minute letter which awaited me this morning at breakfast. You seem to have much worse weather than ours. It is this morning
sensibly colder with us, but as bright as possible & except one day this week we have had none rainy. In spite of your weather, thank heaven you seem still moderately well, have good sleep comparatively & seem to have hope that these lumps in the inside, though still very mysterious, seem to be slowly improving.John A. Carlyle was suffering from abdominal tumors; see TC to JAC, 27 April. He wrote, 11 Oct.: “This morning I had no trace of pain … after my good sleep. The two lumps in front near the navel are gradually though slowly diminishing in size, I think, & there is no pain in either of them. On the whole I am not worse than usual.” If you could but get out to drive, things would look really well. Could I but once get you up here again to be beside me what an immense improvement it would be and solacement to my feelings!
Madame Olga Novikov
Wikimedia Commons

We go out to drive regularly at three p.m. & study to get in generally before half past five, a wet day is no disadvantage to us, rather it makes one thankfuller for the clean impenetrable carriage, with the fresh air visiting us and the rain incapable of any unpleasant admission even by the side windows. Yesterday we were with Mrs Lecky at Richmond Park & found the rural aspects still very pleasant. Today we are thinking to take out Mme NovikoffOlga Novikov had been introduced to TC by John Tyndall, Dec. 1876; see TC to GEH, 24 Nov. 1876. She visited London again, 1878, and wrote to her friend William Thomas Stead (1849–1912; ODNB), liberal newspaper editor and spiritualist, from Symond's Hotel, Brooke St., Mayfair, 6 Oct.: “I spent a charming couple of hours with dear old Carlyle. We walked together, we drove in an omnibus. He then brought me to my hotel and begged me to come any day I liked ‘before three—then we’ll have another drive, but in a carriage, which is supposed to be a kind of promotion. You know I never thought last year I’ll see you again. So strange that I’m still alive,’ said he. The dear old man! He seemed really, actually, glad to see me, and repeatedly said so!” (W. T. Stead, The M. P. for Russia [1909] 2:6–7). a flourishing Russian lady who is here for a little while, much concerned with her Russian interests & her Czar's relation to the miraculous Dizzy & his Afghan difficulty.Novikov later wrote: “Carlyle and I had one great thing in common: our distrust of Disraeli and our sympathy with the oppressed Slavs. In 1878, when the jingoes were shouting their loudest over the Russian Mission to Afghanistan, which had precipitated the Afghan War, Carlyle referred to politics as ‘a sore subject nowadays with our damnable premier,’ as he called him. He was always generous with regard to the humble efforts of the ‘Rooshian Leddy’ as he called me” (Olga Novikoff, Russian Memories [1917] 81). Russia, although the victor of the Russo-Turkish war, 1877–78, was unhappy with the results of the Congress of Berlin, 1878. Influenced by Otto von Bismarck, the Congress thwarted Russia's plan to unify the Balkans under its leadership, by granting control of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Austria-Hungary and nominal autonomy to much of Bulgaria under the administration of the Ottoman Empire. For a map of Europe at this time, see 135. Afghanistan, situated at the crossroads between Russia and the British empire in India, was subject to pressure from both countries, who offered financial and military aid dependent upon their agents being given positions of influence. A Russian diplomatic mission arrived in Kabul, July 1878, and Disraeli's Indian viceroy, Edward Robert Bulwer-Lytton (see TC to JAC, 5 Feb. 1876), demanded that Sher Ali Khan (1825–79), amir of Afghanistan, 1863–66 and 1868–79, accept a similar British delegation. The amir refused, and on 21 Sept. the British were turned back at the frontier. It is not known whether there will be war there; & I confess
the Dizzy affair in sum has got so abominably ugly to me that I resign myself to neglect of it, looking only forward with confidence to the disappearance by and by of Dizzy & all his lying basenesses & nonsenses.
Map of Europe, 1878
Wikimedia Commons
Lecky the day before yesterday went with me in a drive towards Ruskin's place & back again, without attempt to find Ruskin whom we understand to be in Scotland & threatened with softening of the brain,Ruskin had suffered a breakdown earlier in the year. He wrote, 23 June: “I have not written to you, because my illness broke me all to pieces, and every little bit has a different thing to say,—which makes it difficult in the extreme to write to any one whom one wants to tell things to, just as they are, and who cares very truly whether they are right or wrong. It was utterly wonderful to me to find that I could go so heartily & headily mad; for you know I had been priding myself on my peculiar sanity! … I have regained great part of my strength, and am not in bad spirits,—on the condition, otherwise absolutely essential, that I think of nothing that would vex me.” He visited various friends later in the year, including William Graham (1817–85; ODNB), art collector and patron, at Dunira, Crieff, Perthshire. at lowest with much spiritualism, which to friends of his looks rather ominous of that. Lecky had been in Venice, then in Verona &c & finally at Geneva, where he found the whole town utterly deserted by the rational & respectable classes & in a roaring blaze for a whole week with its Centennary of Rousseau,Centenary celebrations for Jean Jacques Rousseau (1712–78), Swiss writer and philosopher; see 38:227–28JWC to MR, 30 Sept. 1862. the illuminations & processions in regard to which illustrious character filled all hearts & throats. Lecky among other things mentioned that while still in Italy he had carefully read your translation of Dante,John A. Carlyle, Dante's Divine Comedy, The Inferno (1849). esteemed it decidedly the best translation he had ever met with & regretted as I myself did & do that there is nothing of it except the Inferno realized. Froude I believe is expected in a week or two who will be useful twice a week in taking me intelligible roads which he alone of all my carriage friends can do. Irish GrahamWilliam Graham (1839–1911; ODNB), Irish philosopher and political economist, living in London since 1874, and from 1875 lecturer in mathematics at St. Bartholomew's Hospital. is here too, but is worth little to me, busy occupied getting ready some paper for the XIX Century,The Nineteenth Century; see TC to JAC, 28 April 1877. TC had written a note of introduction for Graham to the editor, James Knowles, who wrote, 21 July: “I am sure from what you say of him that he must be a man likely to be of much service to Editors of Reviews which aim at getting a character for being ‘solid and honest’—and I thank you very much for your recommendation of him to me.” so called, which I guess will not be accepted. There is in fact little comfortable company for me to be picked up; but one must learn to make his own suffice him both in carriages & elsewhere. I have been struggling vainly for I think three weeks to get a word of answer put together for the Crown Prince of Prussia in answer to a
beautiful book he sent meFrederick William (1831–88), crown prince of Prussia, whom TC had met July 1874; see 49:122TC to JAF, 13 July 1874, 127TC to JAF, 18 July 1874, and 201TC to JAC, 15 March 1875. Book unidentified. but cannot yet tell whether I shall get it done today or not. In fact I have a constant feeling of childhood & utter inability to do anything. Lecky brought me a book after the drive we had vehemently treating & scolding of the French Centennary of Voltaire.François–Marie Arouet, known as Voltaire (1694–1778), French writer and philosopher. It is not very long, but it is very spiteful & condemnatory & brings out in the DoupanloupFélix Doupanloup (1802–78), French liberal Catholic, bishop of Orléans 1849–78; his pamphlet, Premières Lettres à Messieurs les Membres du Conseil Municipal de Paris sur le Centenaire de Voltaire (Paris, 1878), was part of his campaign to prevent the French government from recognizing the centenaries of Voltaire and Rousseau. style everything that could disgust the French with their Voltaire & Rousseau, a beggarly heart is in the thing & the French have paid no more regard to him than if he had lain asleep instead of writing. Tom of Canada has sent us the photograph of poor Alick's tombstone which is well meant on his part, but of a disappointing nature to me who am unable to read any line of the inscription.Their nephew Thomas Carlyle; for Alick's tombstone, see MAI to TCA, 13 Dec. 1876. I send you a copy however. There are three more, but perhaps none of the Scotsbrig
people want to have it. Tell me how that is however. Jenny's Canada letter I return. I know nothing about the various personages she names, wish very heartily that her new son in law may prove a more eligible article than the former.Their sister Janet Hanning; her da. Catherine had recently m. George Franklin and moved to Toronto. It's not known to which of her two other sons-in-law TC refers. Send my love to her poor Jenny herself, whom I can remember since so long. Have you ever written to poor Mary of the Gill since her Husband's death. I feel as if I should have written to her, but what could I say. Poor fellow I can never forget the last sight I had of him & he is daily hanging about my thoughts ever since his departure from this world.Their sister Mary's husband d. 20 Sept.; see TC to JAC, 21 Sept. John replied, 18 Oct.: “I forwarded your latest letter with sister Jenny's enclosed to poor Mary; & she returned both with the enclosed little scrap.” Mary wrote to John, [15 Oct.]: “Many thanks for your letter, and the others also…. We think we will have a better crop of every thing this year. I feel ashamed to speak to you of money considering what you have already done for us—if it had not been for your kindness we had a great deal less than nothing off the Gill the last year” (MS: NLS 1775G.181). John explained: “I had asked her if she had any money to go on with, as last year was the worst of all since she first went to the Gill. In August last I sent her £50 to help in paying, & yesterday I sent her another £50 as she seemed to be without cash.” I beg all blessings if my prayers were worth anything on Sister Jean & all the rest of you; being as ever your affectionate Brother
docBody.closer: For T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 18 Oct. MS: NLS 528.89. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Thanks for your kind letter which came by the second mail today. With us as with you there has nothing peculiar happened especially nothing to be called bad. Our weather here has been exactly like yours, foggy and blustery without rain, but with considerable increase of cold. One day for a little while there was a darkness as of London fog,The Times reported, 18 Oct.: “A London fog, which extended itself down the valley of the Thames, made racing at Sandown rather disagreeable this afternoon. Very little was to be seen of the course…. The atmosphere got a little clearer as the afternoon drew on, but a good deal of the racing had to be left to the imagination.” two mornings I think there was a cessation of the steamers, till the fog cleared off. Most mornings I contrive to get down to the bottom of the embankment, though it becomes more difficult to me. I feel singularly free from any disease but my weakness seems to increase towards absolute babyism. My poor head is perfectly clear too; and I have for
most part a tolerable share of sleep in the course of the four and twenty hours. Oh how I wish I could confirm into certainty your feeling of hope that the extraneous thing within you is actually promising to diminish & to become harmless which would be the consummation of my constant wish about it! If you were once able to walk or ride in a carriage, it would be the best news I could hear in the world.

Except the Russian LadyOlga Novikov. there has nobody arrived here and she I must say, though a good & handsome figure, passionately desirous of peace between England & Russia, she is not of interest to me otherwise. She has been out twice driving with us, but I really think sitting by myself would be almost as good. Of my JewPaul Friedmann (1840–ca. 1900), wealthy philanthropist and author, b. in Königsberg to a Jewish family, he converted to Christianity. Alarmed at the persecution of Jews in Russia, he later tried to establish a Jewish colony on the Arabian peninsula. & my Lecky I can say little better but only a little. Dizzy & his pranks have long been utterly contemptible to me and are now as good as absolutely wearisome. Let him go to the devil in his own way.

I have been reading the Life of Sterling,Carlyle, The Life of John Sterling (1851); TC was introduced to John Sterling by John Stuart Mill, Feb. 1835; see Carlyle, Works 11:105. wh. has disappointed me in regard to the talent vested in it, but it has brought my first London friend & the times that then were solemnly home to me. I have now taken into Swift's Gulliver,Jonathan Swift, Gulliver's Travels (1726). which I consider a work of consummate talent, but naturally dont interest myself deeply in. I am on the whole apt to be ill off for reading, but am never quite beaten either.

I am sorry to hear of Jean's being weak again. I hope she may come back to you a little improved.John A. Carlyle wrote, 18 Oct.: “Jean & Maggie went off to Moffat on Monday last, & we have heard they were doing well there, & meant to go on to Edinr to get teeth repaired.” I am right glad to hear what you have done about poor Sister Mary.See TC to JAC, 11 Oct. I expect a note from her in answer to one I wrote; & judge she must be provided for as to the rent question for the present. We heard of Masson's journey to Dumfries. I am glad you saw him & his Son.John wrote: “On Monday Profr Masson & his eldest son called & sat with me half an hour. They had come to see Dumfries, & meant to go on to Ecclefechan in the evening.” David Masson had only one son, David Orme Masson. The question has risen in a faint way about Edinr Lockhart'sWilliam Ewart Lockhart RSA (1846–1900; ODNB), painter, b. Dumfriesshire, now living in Edinburgh. painting me. Say a word sometime of what you think of his capacity for that task, hitherto found so impossible. I have not seen Darwin for above 2 weeks neither has Blakiston come athwart me, though Mary did see them both one day.
Alas, alas, is not this enough of nothingness. With my liveliest regards to your self and all the household, I ever am, dear Brother
docBody.closer: Your affecte / T. Carlyle

postscript.p: Mary sends her best love to you.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 26 Oct. MS: NLS 528.90. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:336–37 inc. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: I received your kind letter the first thing this morning & was sorry to find that it must have been written under pain and obstruction in bad weather, in solitary imprisonment & other sorrows,John A. Carlyle wrote, 25 Oct.: “This has been rather a stormy week with us, & unusually cold too, so that I have only once got out of doors. I have now got a fire in the night-time in my bedroom…. Without something to read I should be rather ill off for I am often solitary the whole day…. I don’t yet feel worse than usual though I get rather less sleep. I must just do the best I can in the circumstances, & trust to providence for the rest.” which I daily think of with affectionate regret and am quite unable to help.

There has nothing new happened here. Our weather, too, is bad like yours and I get out daily for a driveAllingham noted in his diary, 26 Oct.: “To Carlyle's to-day about three, and find him looking well…. C., F. [Paul Friedmann], and I drive to Regent's Park, where I get out. We talk of Shere Ali [see TC to JAC, 11 [12] Oct.]; of Dizzy; ‘England is disgraced; never before has she had such a man at her head’” (Allingham Diary 266). which, alas, you cannot do. I never look into your room without a sad regret that you are not here; but, alas, alas, you absolutely cannot come & you would not be nearly so well lodged as where you now are. We must hope and be patient.

I was naturally struck with the announcement of poor Laing's death.David Laing; he d. 18 Oct. of kidney failure, at his home in Portobello. The Scotsman printed an extensive obituary, 19 Oct. A considerable light of knowledge is thus extinguished & a very harmless brother mortal is carried away into eternity before us. I seem somewhere to have learnt that his death was caused by a fall he got but can find no confirmation of it from Mary or otherwise.— — Froude came home the day before yesterday & yesterday shewed himself here, looking little the better we thought for his long rustication;Froude had spent the summer at Salcombe in Devon; see TC to JAC, 21 Sept. but ready to talk at great length, though about nothing that I had much interest in. We took him up in the carriage to a Mme Novikoff's a Russian lady & left him there at the hotel in Brooke St.Olga Novikov was staying at Symond's Hotel, Brooke St.; see TC to JAC, 11 Oct. It is likely
he may be back again on Tuesday. But, alas, I get extremely little good of any kind of company now left me in the world.— We had not heard of your having had a letter from Nephew Tom in Canada: if you chance to be writing again please tell him that the real name of his Farm is Bieldy knowesTheir nephew Thomas Carlyle had bought a farm, ca. 1864–65, near his parents’ farm, the Bield, which he named Bieldy Knowes; John had helped him with paying the instalments on the property; see 42:215TC to JN, 3 Sept. 1865; see also Marrs 745. Thomas and his brother Alexander had recently visited TC and Mary while they were staying at Park House, Dumfries; see TC to JAC, 21 Sept. not Bieldy knowe.— — My reading has been desultory, discontinuous & insignificant, mainly from Swifts Gulliver & certain of his Essays & Poems. Gulliver I reckoned & reckon extremely clever, generally entertaining too & pleasant all except the Horse & Yahoo department which I found extremely dirty & miserable.Swift, Gulliver's Travels part 4, “A Voyage to the Country of the Houyhnhnms.” Today I have been trying SterneLaurence Sterne (1713–68; ODNB), writer and clergyman; TC had read Sterne in his youth and enjoyed the humor of his writings. whom I have not looked at for many years & cannot be said to have liked or got profit from. SkeltonJohn Skelton (see TC to JAC, 15 Dec. 1875), probably Essays in Romance and Studies from Life (Edinburgh, 1878). of Edinr sent me his Book which no doubt you, too, have got. If not which is unlikely I will at once send you this copy not on loan but in gift.— We heard of Sister Jean having a mind to go to Edinr with Maggie as yesterday but know not whether she effected that small purposeJohn wrote, 25 Oct.: “Jean & Maggie are still in Edinburgh, but are expected home soon.” a more comfortable clause of the announcement was that she seemed to feel considerably livelier. I trust she will get whatever little business she may have in Edinr successfully completed & let my kindest wishes & regards be awaiting her at her return. I remain ever, my dear Brother
docBody.closer: Affectionately yours / T. Carlyle.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 2 Nov. MS: NLS 528.91. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, unsigned.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Thanks for your weekly letter, which it is good to be very punctual with. This one has set our imaginations at rest & assured us at least that nothing
strange or sinister has happened since we heard last. It was welcome news to us that Jean had come home successfully. There is a fair probability that the Jaunt will do her good for some time.John A. Carlyle wrote, 1 Nov.: “Jean & Maggie have just got back from Edinburgh & both, she particularly, are looking much better.” I regret to hear of your bad weather; in which we partake more or less here though in a milder form, being able always to get out, under cover or otherwise, while you, alas, are kept prisoner in the house. It grieves me much to think of you confined in that manner. It is one of my most ardent wishes that I heard any clear tidings of your getting towards a deliverance; but we must wait, we must wait. For the last two weeks you say nothing of your feelings or notions about that internal abscess.John replied, 8 Nov.: “The hole above the Navel, through which the dropsical water used to come, gradually closed itself & is now a small lump without pain of any sort.” Please tell me when you have anything the least definite to say. As to me, I have as usual nothing to report about and intrinsically do not feel to ail anything except unspeakable and I sometimes think increasing & sometimes not increasing weakness as of a very young child,—the arrival in fact of second childhood such as is to be expected when the date of departure is nigh. I am grateful to heaven for one thing that the state of my head continues unaltered and perfectly clear, surely a blessing beyond expression compared with what the contrary would be. Let us pray & be grateful to the great Giver of good & for patience under whatever his will may be. I, too, have been getting rather less sleep in the last week. I am trying slight remedies and still manage, day and night together, to realize what of sleep will do. Froude, the Leckys and all my so-called companions are come back, tho’, alas, their company yields me little enjoyment; but indeed is better than absolute nothing. Last week I have been occupied altogether with the new periodicals, which generally I can get little good of,—though that, too, is better than none at all. The Fortnightly Review is to go to you today. There is not much of worth in it, but you may read Mat. Arnold's articleMatthew Arnold, “Porro Unum est Necessarium,” Fortnightly Review 24 (Nov. 1878): 589–604. and half-read some others. Fraser had scattered over it some articles worth looking into; perhaps it may be worth your borrowing from the library & examining in one or two short places, Colorado one of them & The Eastern Hermit.“Colorado: The Home of the Farmer,” by “An English Farmer Now Settled Three Years in the State,” Fraser's Magazine 98 (Nov. 1878): 622–30; and “Ivy Leaves. From the Hermitage, Epping Forest,” by “Eastern Hermit” [pseudonym of William Allingham], Fraser's Magazine 98 (Nov. 1878): 662–66. I have, however no really interesting reading & have sometimes thought even of going into the Bible the significance of which is deep & wonderful almost as much as it ever used to be to me. There has broken out
a kind of sunshine, as sometimes happens & the time of our drive is close at hand. I send my love and blessing to Jean & all of you. I ever am, and remain

postscript.p: Will you kindly forward The Fortnightly to Mrs Anstruther, Lainshaw, Stewarton, AyrshireLainshaw Castle, Stewarton, Ayrshire, home of Capt. John William Herbert Cunninghame (d. 1915), and his wife, m. 1867, Emily, b. Graham (1837–87); presumably Annabella Anstruther was visiting them.

div3.sourceNote: MA-WP, 8 Nov. MS photocopy: Source unknown Hitherto unpbd. W. Payne not further identified.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN TO W. PAYNE

docBody.p: Mr Carlyle bids me return the Miniature,Miniature not further identified. with his thanks for your kindness in sending it to him. It is not at all like any of the Portraits that Mr Carlyle has ever seen of John Knox.
docBody.closer: I remain / Sir / Your faithful Servant / Mary Carlyle Aitken

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 9 Nov. MS: NLS 528.92. Quot: A. Carlyle, NL 2:337–38. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your welcome letter of tidings has just arrived for which we are very thankful. We have nothing here to report of sinister, much the contrary indeed if we consider the financial earthquakesThe City of Glasgow Bank went into liquidation, 1 Oct., partly as a result of fraud and mismanagement, but also due to the current industrial economic depression throughout the U.K; while Scottish banks were particularly hard hit, many English and Welsh provincial banks were also affected. Other banks hurried to support investors and ward off a financial collapse; the Scotsman reported, 9 Nov.: “The banks in most cases have made very liberal advances to all the City of Glasgow Bank depositors, where anything like good security could be advanced, so that many people have tided over the difficulty with less trouble than they anticipated.” See also Michael Collins, “The Banking Crisis of 1878,” The Economic History Review 42 (Nov. 1989): 504–27. that are going on all round us, from
certain of which we have in the last week about miraculously escaped, nor in regard to health have I anything that is truly bad to report. But the fact is, so far as I can read it my strength is nearly faded quite away & it begins to be more & more made evident to me that I shall not long have to struggle under this burden of life, but soon go to the refuge that is provided for us all. For a long time back, I have been accustomed to look upon the “ernsten Freund [risen Friend, i.e., Christ]” as the most merciful & indispensable refuge appointed by the great Creator for his wearied children whose work is done. I read always but can get no reading that is of the least use to me. Today I am reading Voltaire's ZaireVoltaire, Zaire (1832), a five-act tragedy in verse. TC owned Œuvres complètes de Voltaire, ed. Jean Clogenson et al., 97 vols. (Paris, 1825–34), which he purchased in 1856; see 31:62TC to JAC, 11 April 1856; see also David Sorensen and Brent E. Kinser, “‘A Signal Acquisition,’” CSA 32 (2017): 5–50, and Carlyle's House 98. and find it a tragedy almost contemptible to me & void of meaning or interest. Greater part of the week I was reading a German translation of the Russian PoushkinAlexander Pushkin (1799–1837), Russian poet, novelist, and playwright; there were various German translations of his works, including Alexander Puschkin's Dichtungen, trans. R. Lippert (Leipzig, 1840); Gedichte von Alexander Puschkin, trans. E. von Olberg (Berlin, 1840); Alexander Puschkin's Poetische Werke aus dem Russisichen, trans. Friedrich Bodenstedt, 3 vols. (Berlin, 1854–55); and Gedichte, trans. Heinrich Ludwig Schmitt (Wiesbaden, 1872). For TC's earlier, somewhat different opinion of Pushkin, see 15:239TC to KAVE, 19 Dec. 1842. who has been greatly celebrated to me,
but miserably disappoints me on trial & now almost think of giving him up altogether as a genius of no talent at all or of none that is the least useful to me.
I shall certainly find something else that will be better than Poushkin.

A day or two ago we saw Darwin looking very lean and pale, but unusually spirited and conversible,—talking of colour blindness and of Goethe's Farbenlehre,See TC to JAC, 25 May. which I begin to think may actually turn out the true account of vision, which also is Tyndall's dim prophecy of the matter. Though the weather here is much better than yours, Darwin never goes out more than you do; reads books &c lying on his back,—having unlike me a hand that will hold them. My carriage companions are highly uninteresting for most part, especially a Russian, Mme de Novikoff, who is much repandue [spread about] and writes in the Northern EchoThe Northern Echo, newspaper ed. by Novikov's friend William Thomas Stead (see TC to JAC, 11 [12] Oct.), who pbd. many of Novikov's articles on Russia; she wrote, 21 Oct.: “It is impossible for a Russian to pay a friendly visit even at London without being regarded as a Russian partisan or even as a Russian agent…. We do remember well all that has been said and written in London during these two last momentous years, owing to which national feelings attained a bitterness which can be modified only by energetic efforts of all who really care for a good understanding between the nations” (The Northern Echo, 21 Oct.). Novikov wrote to Stead, 23 Oct.: “I went to see Carlyle yesterday. No sooner did he see me than he exclaimed: ‘Ay, ay, I think your article very good and interesting. I am not going to pay you any compliment but it is perfectly true’” (W. T. Stead, MP for Russia 2:7). almost elegiacally lamenting the Jingo“Jingo” is a nickname, derived from the chorus of a popular music hall song, for those who praised Disraeli's anti-Russian policy, and hence one who generally advocates a bellicose policy in dealing with foreign powers. feelings of the English. She has also joined herself cunningly to Froude's daysFroude became friendly with Novikov in 1877, and they corresponded regularly; he also wrote a sympathetic preface to her pamphlet Is Russia Wrong? (1877). & spoils any good that is in him by clatter that I find to be without interest to me. Lecky comes on Mondays and is very tender and polite but in general of no interest to me. Mary seldom goes except when I am going to be left alone. The most interesting is a Jew named FriedmannPaul Friedman; see TC to JAC, 18 Oct. who has wandered much over the world & has many a curious anecdote to tell though in a voice like the sharpening of saws. Allingham whom you know comes usually on Saturdays, with plenty of public news and tolerates this good jew. Allingham's WifeHelen Allingham; William Allingham noted in his diary, 6 Nov.: “H. went again to-day about 12:30 to C.'s, and brought back two life-like sketches in colour. He was mild and genial to-day, and bade her come again. / C. said to me, ‘Your wife is the only person who has made a successful portrait of me, though many have tried’” (Allingham Diary 267). For Helen Allingham's portrait of TC reading in his chair, see opp. has for the last three days been sitting painting me while I read one hour each day &
has made two small water colour sketches which appear to me to have a great deal of likeness.
Thomas Carlyle reading in the Drawing Room, 1878, watercolor by Helen Allingham
Courtesy of the National Galleries of Scotland
Boehm is in treaty about a statue of Knox, which is actually going up as frontispiece to the Haddington School houseThe memorial stone of the Knox Memorial Institute, Haddington, to be built on the site of Knox's former grammar school, was laid 31 Aug. The Scotsman reported, 2 Sept.: “The Institute … is intended at once to perpetuate the memory of John Knox, in the place of his birth, and to provide such a high-class seminary as is required of the town by the Education Act…. When completed the buildings will have the form of a parallelogram, with the Institute standing out in front and the elementary class-rooms behind…. The principal features of the design … are a central tower, 14 feet square, and 80 feet high, having at the height of about 30 feet a canopied niche, in which a full-length figure of Knox will be placed.” TC hoped that the commission for the statue would be given to the sculptor Joseph Boehm, but it went instead to David Watson Stevenson (1842–1904; ODNB), Edinburgh sculptor, and was paid for by sisters Jane Trail (b. ca. 1801) and Anne Trail (b. ca. 1807), from Aberlady, East Lothian. The Knox Memorial Institute was formally opened on 31 Jan. 1880. & I hope may succeed with his project; at least if he do not, I can do nothing more. I have sent their architect (Starforth,The architect was John Starforth (1822–98); see 49:189–90TC to JB, 15 Feb. 1875; he designed many churches, including Greyfriars Church, Dumfries, built 1866–68. who built the Greyfriars Church at Dumfries) a complete Copy of the Essay on the Knox Portraits; Boehm will do that figure of Knox for the cheapest price; and the commonly received David Laing Knox or Torphichen KnoxFor TC and David Laing's disagreement over the Somerville and Torphichen portraits of Knox, see 49:74–75TC to DL, 26 March 1874. he will not for any money whatever attempt to carve. So we can do no more. I enclose a letter from Miss Bromley which you need not mind returning.

We are delighted to hear that Jean feels improved by her jaunt. Dont forget to send us word about that little lumpAlexander Carlyle later wrote on the MS: “A growth of something like a tumour (the exact nature of which was unknown to the Physicians, having never seen a similar case) on Dr. C's breast. It grew worse & worse & caused his death within a year. / A.C.” which for your sake is so important to me. God bless you all
docBody.closer: Ever your affectionate Brother, / T. Carlyle.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 15 Nov. MS: NLS 528.93. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:339–40 inc. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Thanks for your punctual letter, which lay waiting for me when I got in from my poor cripply walk half way down the embankment. I am not now
able to get to the bottom of the embankment but have to stop half way and rest a little and return. My limbs getting quite lame about the middle of the back part of the thighs reminding me daily of old Ziethen's description to Friedrich, Die Füsse wollen nicht fort.“The feet won’t go so well”; according to TC in Frederick, the remark was made in 1799, not by “old Ziethen,” Frederick's great cavalry general (Hans Joachim von Ziethen [1699-1786]), but by another elderly soldier, Captain von Rathenow, in response to Frederick's surprise that he was still alive; Frederick was in a carriage at the time with Ziethen's son Friedrich von Ziethen (1765–1854); see Carlyle, Works 19:307. I have been thinking even more constantly than ever of your imprisonment during these wild mornings while even with us the weather has been so bad and certainly, as I daily considered, it would be worse with you. I am not sure that you take the best plan in keeping your fire alight all night. Would it not be better to go to bed with a good warm fire and then to have it lighted again in the morning near rising time. There is an excellent recipe against cold in down quilts to cover the feet or even the whole body if necessary but probably as Mary says you already have one of these. The thick night socks are also very useful on the feet.John A. Carlyle had taken to having a fire in his bedroom all night as he suffered much from the cold. He wrote, 22 Nov.: “I now wear at night the soft, thick pair of socks Mary sent me, & get much good of them especially in the early mornings.” I have these & also a soft red flannel night shirt (on the top of my ordinary night shirt) & coming down to my heels, which Mary has provided for me and which I feel to be a great comfort. By one method & another I generally contrive to get a sleep till towards three or four in the morning, after which I awake and have to drink a tumbler of what I feel to be rather poorish milk, with a gulp of whisky swallowed in the middle of it, which sometimes leaves me, and sometimes does not, to fall asleep for an hour or so; but afterwards lets me awake again and struggle on in a confused way till some gleam of light appears & I can summon RoseCheyne Row servant; see TC to JAC, 15 Dec. 1875. to pull up the curtains of the windows & gradually procure me a drop of warm soup & some modicum of hot water to temper the bath. I generally try to smoke while she is down stairs on this errand, but I succeed badly in it and never in my life felt so weak as now. The truth is I habitually feel myself as if on the edge of deathAllingham noted in his diary, 14 Nov.: “To Carlyle's at 2.30, and found him stepping—slowly climbing—into the usual hired carriage. He said, ‘I feel I may die any time’” (Allingham Diary 267). and am grateful to the Giver of all Good for this gate of deliverance appointed for all the weary. What you say of your hands being too cold to hold a book reminds me of a kind of gloves made of soft Indian wool, wh. are very useful for screening the hands from cold. I have an old pair which do me good service of this kind & a new pair might be provided
for you.

Today is fair with something even of sunshine; the rest of the week we have had nothing but rainy winds & bluster & except for the carriage could not get out at all. Lecky comes to me on Monday very possibly Mrs Lecky on Wednesday, Froude is found duly on Tuesday and Friday. Mary goes with me but does not care about going when there is anybody else. Today will come Friedmann the Jew a man of considerable information, having travelled much, more entertaining than loveable. With my remaining fellow creatures, I study to have as little concern as possible. Their intercourse bringing to me nothing but trouble. My reading, which as in your own case is my sole resource gets on I think somewhat worse than yours. I have tried the Russian Poushkin, but as I mentioned already, without any real fruit. I have been reading a life of MagliabecchiAntonio di Marco Magliabechi (1633–1714), Florentine scholar, librarian, and bibliophile; book unidentified, possibly Rev. Joseph Spence, A Parallel In the manner of Plutarch: Between a most celebrated Man of Florence [Antonio Magliabechi]; and One, scarce ever heard of, in England [Robert Hill] (1758).—which contains a hirsute portrait of him one of the ruggedest & ugliest conceivable & a good many details that seemed to me incredible. I have even been thinking to try and read again either Shakespeare or the Bible but have for the present a new French book on Russian literaturePossibly Céleste Courrière, Histoire de la littérature contemporaine en Russe (Paris, 1875); otherwise unidentified. which I must first despatch or dismiss. These are all my poor adventures, dear Brother, not worth detailing except to yourself. God grant us patience is my constant prayer. The end surely is near & then all these troubles will have vanished. My kindest continual regards to Sister Jean. My blessing to all of you.
docBody.closer: I ever am / Your affectionate Brother, / T. Carlyle

postscript.p: Will you kindly return the Copy of the inscription on Brother Alick's Tomb which we sent to you.See TC to JAC, 11 [12] Oct. We cannot make out the last sentence from my copy of the photograph.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 30 Nov. MS: NLS 528.94. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your kind & punctual letter lay on the table this morning when I came down; after a variety of preliminaries and a bit of painful crippling walking I read it over on getting into the house again. You have fully as bad weather
as we though not worse, and of a different type. Ours is mostly wet, thick & dark and of a low temperature, shrouded in dark fog, though once a week or so we may have an exception & momentarily see the sun. Yesterday morning I saw films of ice not thicker than paper. The first real frost visible this year, and today it is all gone again, and we are replunged into the unkindly mist. Froude has been away from me doing a short visit at Lord CarnarvonsFor Lord Carnarvon, see TC to JAC, 23 Dec. 1875; his country estate was Highclere Castle in Hampshire, 5 mi. (8 km.) S of Newbury, Berkshire. & is again to be absent in some country house during most of this week. Carnarvon he describes as being thoroughly disgusted with what is called the conservative party and ready to join the so-called Liberal, whenever opportunity offers. That he describes as being also Lord Derby's humour; in short in both instances, a thorough detestation of Beaconsfield Dizzy and repentance that they had ever been concerned with him.Both Lord Carnarvon, the colonial sec., and Lord Derby, the foreign sec., had resigned from Disraeli's cabinet early 1878 in protest at the prime minister's decision to send British warships into the Sea of Marmara as a warning to the Russians not to advance on Constantinople. It is not expected that the short parliament now at hand will do more than batter at him with more or less vehemence, but totally unable to stop his jingoes and him. I very little concern myself with his procedures, nothing new in the infinite detestation I bear them nor to myself anything really profitable. I have had a good deal of hovering to and fro in my reading, which is for most part uncomfortable and uninstructive to me, but perhaps I may be able to devise something more satisfactory by degrees. Mary has had a project of getting you a pair of gloves like a pair I myself have, which are made of some kind of down and are eminently useful for keeping the cold out of ones hands while reading or the like. These it seems cannot be had on Saturday; but they shall be sent to you within a day or two.

I am very glad to hear of your getting down stairs to have some conversation with Sister Jean & the two lassies which naturally has some effect in cheering you & will be an agreeable element in your day. Patience, patience! we must all of us be patient. It is pretty much the only prayer we can offer up with the assurance of an answer for indeed the prayer itself is equivalent to an answer. We saw Darwin not long ago, very cheerful, though completely stationary within the house. I believe one of his nephews stays under his roof nightly. Did I tell you about the pecuniary disaster that has fallen on the Blakistons and one of his Sons and Baly?For Dr. Peyton and Bessy Blakiston, see TC to JAC, 7 Sept. 1876; they had been living in London since 1871, mostly with Charles Baly, dental surgeon, family friend, possibly related by marriage. Blakiston had three surviving sons: John Richard, Douglas Yeoman, and Matthew Folliott; it is not known which one is referred to here. Blakiston's and Baly's financial losses were possibly linked to the collapse of the City of Glasgow Bank, which had affected a number of other financial institutions; see TC to JAC, 9 Nov. one quarter of his income entirely
gone such is the financial gulf of deficit which everybody is silently expecting here. I need not continue these ugly details. I send my heart's love to Sister Jean and am truly glad to have your report of her and the lassies, that she is moderately off for sleep. I ever am, dear Brother,
docBody.closer:
Your affectionate
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 14 Dec. MS: NLS 528.95. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: On coming down stairs from a dim and painful night, I find your punctual letter hereLetter untraced. announcing that matters are no better with yourself probably in some respects even worse. We must be patient, dear Brother, and take piously if we can what days and nights are sent us. The night before last was unusually good with me, all the rest especially last night were worse than usual, and little or no sleep attainable by me. In fact I seem to perceive that there is only one hope that of being called away out of this unmanageable scene. One must not presume to form express desires about it, but for a long time back the above has been my clear conviction. About you, dear Brother, I think daily with a tender sorrow for your sake, and surely have to own with you that there is no good news to be expected from either side. God's will be done! The frost I expect will not abate yet & the darkness gives no sign of lessening either. Your case, dear Brother, I feel to be even worse than my own and I am often painfully thinking of you. Let us summon all the virtue that is in us, if there be any virtue at all, & quit us like men not like fools. Mary sends her kindest love. To me she is unwearied in her attention; rose last night for example as she ever does on my summons, but was not able last night for the first time to do me any real good. I send my love to Sister Jean and am always eager for news of her. Blessings be on you all. I ever am, dear Brother,
docBody.closer:
Affectionately yours
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 21 Dec. MS: NLS 528.96. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Thanks for your punctual and kind letter which again sets before us a dark & intricate scene of endurance & contrivance ending on your part with passably getting through the confusions of the week. You say nothing of the poor lumps laming you outwardly and inwardly nor of the eyeLetter untraced; John A. Carlyle had recently been suffering with his eyes; he wrote, 29 Nov.: “This week I have not been able to read so much as usual, for I seem to have caught cold in the right eyelid, & cannot see quite distinctly … it would be a great disadvantage to me not to be able to read freely.” He replied, 27 Dec.: “The large hole above the navel contracted itself gradually closed, & has since been painless. I cannot read much having only one eye that is free. The other has a bandage on it being sore outwardly when it gets the light in full.” which also I often think about.

We seem to have better weather here than you at least there is visibly less of frost in it, though perhaps a bigger share of fog add[ed] which in some cases becomes a day absolutely black & requiring candles within the house if you try to do any kind of work.

Good Dr Blakiston died on Tuesday lastDr. Peyton Blakiston d. suddenly of heart failure, 17 Dec. John replied: “I was not surprised to hear of Dr B's sudden death. Please tell me about Mrs Blakiston.” and is to be buried today. His death which was from heart disorder as he had always predicted carried him off in a moment. Bessie his Widow we have not seen but heard of as valiantly composed under this new stroke which she had long been watching against. I cannot say but that I reckon his deliverance merciful and good. Poor Mrs PauletElizabeth Paulet, b. Newton (1806–1879; see 13:189TC to JWC, [19 July 1841]); friend of JWC's from 1841, estranged 1849 (see 24:283–84JWC to JAC, [10 Nov. 1849]), they met again May 1865 (see 42:36JWC to TC, 24 May 1865). panting under asthma and unavailing arsenic I considered as desperate, but it seems there is within the last few days some faint symptoms of possible rally if that be welcome to the poor sufferer as no doubt it is.— I go out daily to drive & manage to endure two hours of sheltered locomotion of that kind & suffer less not more than you would expect. I have continually a miserable nausea in the stomach but by night, by swallowing my tumbler of milk with a good gulp of chartreuse,French liqueur made from alcohol and medicinal herbs. subdue it for the time. I have given up cold bathing & content myself with washing the face under easier circumstances. I have a fire kindled in the bedroom upstairs which helps me sensibly.— — I can get
no good reading. Last night after dinner & my sleep I read the Book of Job, I must say with wonder more than with satisfaction.
From Sister Jean last night Mary had a beautiful red dressing gown of which she is very proud. Give my poor blessing to sister Jean & all the rest. I ever am, dear Brother,
docBody.closer:
Affectionately yours
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 11 Jan. MS: NLS 528.97. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Your welcome letter was punctually here this morning and gave me a glad surprise to find that the week had been so gentle and favourable to you. We have had weather dark windy and very cold, though with nothing like so much frost as you and till this morning we have had no snow; in fact it is not from the cold that I have ever chiefly suffered but from the miserably feeble state of the stomachic department and from the sufferings following at night yet not very often issuing in total want of sleep. Let us endeavour to be content and patient and not to strive against the inevitable.

I am delighted to hear of the symptoms you seem to trace in your internal trouble. May your conjecture prove to be the fact.John A. Carlyle wrote, 10 Jan.: “I have an idea that something is rectifying itself gradually in right side of the abdomen where the water used to collect itself in such large quantities, but of course this is only a conjecture.” I am sorry to hear nothing of the eye improving and bearing to be open; but there, too, we must wait and hope. You did very well and generously to Jenny in Canada.Their sister Janet Hanning; John wrote to her, 9 Jan.: “I got your letter some ten days ago. I have been unwell & unable to write, but can send you a few words today. I enclose an order for £30 which is for your own use” (MS: Yale). Janet Hanning's da. Catherine had recently married and moved to Toronto; see TC to JAC, 11 [12] Oct. 1878. Her new Son-in-law seems to have got some employment in Toronto; so that she will now with her good new houseTC and John had both sent Jenny money to help with building herself a new house, April 1869; see 46:38–39TC to JAC, 15 April 1869. be able to manage through the winter. I had a letter the other day from poor Mary at the Gill acknowledging some £25 I had sent her,TC usually sent his sisters money at New Year; his checkbook recorded: “2 Jan. 1877 / Mrs Austin / (Gift) / £25..0..0” and “4 Jan. 1878 / Mrs Austin / The Gill / £30..0..0” (TC's checkbook; MS: NLS 20753); this gift is untraced. which till then she had not done. I enclose the letter which really
has been distressing and affecting to me. If you know anything about her situation in which I could be serviceable please let me know. She is evidently in a sore flutter and would be like some others of us glad to take flight if she but knew whither.

About a week ago we saw Mrs Blakiston (Bessy Barnet) who charged us to give you the very kindest message she could send. She is very far from being settled into composure,Bessy Blakiston's husband d. 17 Dec.; see TC to JAC, 21 Dec. 1878. but has irrevocably fixed never to cross her threshold again. She likes the dentist Baly very well and he her, but she can take no rest or composure and is wandering about many times through the night. We saw Darwin, too, one day, who is close prisoner to the house and looks very weak but makes no complaint and is able to read lying on his back on the sofa.
This is a poor bulletin on all sides. I can only send my poor affection to Sister Jean and the rest of you, and I remain
docBody.closer:
Ever yours affectionately
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

postscript.p: I send my best love to you, dear Uncle. / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 18 Jan. MS: NLS 528.98. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, with TC's signature.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
This morning yr kind & punctual letter lay waiting; & I was very glad to hear that the last week had not been worse than usual, but rather better & that there was even hope of your disordered eye getting round again,John A. Carlyle wrote, 17 Jan.: “I still cannot see with the right eye. It is not at all sore or discoloured in any way, but there is some moisture on the outside of it which clouds every thing I look at. One or two steadily warm & dry days I believe would cure it entirely.” which would be a great joy to me. Your pious foundation of the medical BursariesJohn wrote: “I enclose a copy of the Deed for the two Bursaries.” The Scotsman, 27 Jan., contained a report by the general committee of the Association for the Better Endowment of the University of Edinburgh: “Dr John Aitken Carlyle, The Hill, Dumfries, a Doctor of Medicine and of Laws of the University of Edinburgh, intimated his intention to place £1600 in the hands of the Association for the endowment of two medical bursaries in the University; stating at the same time his desire to leave the whole arrangements for the management of the foundation in the hands of the Association…. In carrying out the foundation of these bursaries, it appeared right to the Faculty of Medicine and the committee to give effect to a wish which Dr Carlyle had indicated that the subject of anatomy should be prominently recognised; and it was agreed that one of the bursaries should be open to students in the first year of their course of study in medicine, for proficiency in anatomy and chemistry, and the other to students of the second year, for proficiency in anatomy and physiology.” For a photograph of John A. Carlyle, see above.
is surely of a good complexion & calculated we may hope to endure for generations and do good to fellow creatures yet unborn.— — I myself have also to report rather a better week than usual, not above one night in it bothered by want of sleep. The state of my stomach on awakening is weak and painful nearly always and I have no pleasure in the attempted smoke of tobacco, which is my first operation. My reading is seldom very satisfactory to me. Voltaire's SiÃcle of Louis XIV & Louis XVVoltaire, Siècle de Louis XIV (1751) and Siècle de Louis XV (1768), vols. 27 and 28 of Œuvres complètes de Voltaire; see TC to JAC, 9 Nov. 1878. by no means interests me and I have latterly got into a Dows History of Hindostan,Alexander Dow, The History of Hindostan, Translated from the Persian of Mahummud Casim Ferishtah, 3 vols. (1768–72). Alexander Dow (ca. 1735–79; ODNB), Scottish army officer in the East India Company, and author. most confused book, but offering some of the strangest Brahmin religious speculations ever met with in human speech. There are rumours of Dizzy being privately in a dangerous state of health,The London Evening Standard, 10 Jan., cited a report in the Lancet: “The health of the Prime Minister has during the last few days given rise to considerable anxiety. We are glad to learn upon trustworthy authority that, although the noble Earl has been suffering from an attack of gout there is no reason to fear that it will assume a serious aspect.” the rest of the public news is in general wholly indifferent to
me. Sir James Stephen,Sir James Fitzjames Stephen (see TC to JAC, 27 Oct. 1877), in recognition of his contribution to law reform, was appointed to a High Court judgeship, 3 Jan. 1879. The position gave him financial security and enabled him to continue working on his extensive History of the Criminal Law (1883). He had been in India 1869–72; see 47:20TC to JFS, 3 June 1870. whose Indian letters you used to read has been writing and toiling at a great rate in late years and is now at last appointed judge, which relieves him from all his anxieties about finance and also leaves him with prospects of succeeding in his law improvements which are of great importance in his eyes. This is all, I think, that can be called news of the least interest to you.
John A. Carlyle
Thomas Carlyle Papers, Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Columbia University in
the City of New York
I send my kindest love to Sister Jean and thanks to MaggieTheir niece Maggie Aitken. for the news she sends on those subjects; and will detain my dear Brother no longer, but subscribe myself
docBody.closer: Ever his affectionate / T. Carlyle

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 25 Jan. MS: NLS 528.99. Pbd: A. Carlyle, NL 2:340–41 inc. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
We are very glad to hear what has somewhat surprized us that you have felt rather better than usual this week,John A. Carlyle wrote, 24 Jan.: “The last week has been a better one for me than any hitherto. I have had only one bad night, & during the daytime I have suffered less pain.” which has here been of so grim a complexion. We have had only a little fall of snow after loud tempests of windy bluster attended sometimes with whirlwinds of dust which however get but little hold of us in the inside of the carriage. We have evidently had but little frost compared with you; but the people have all got to skating diligently on the permitted placesThe Daily News reported, 24 Jan.: “The public were allowed yesterday to skate on the Round Pond in Kensington-gardens, which had as many as 3,000 on it during the day. On the Long Water about 7,000 were skating and sliding, and in St. James's-park some 14,000 were similarly engaged…. As many as 20,000 people were on the ice in the Regent's-park.”. & our water pipes are extensively burstingJohn wrote: “The frozen ground is very deep, & no thaw has reached any of the water pipes which should supply the houses with water. These pipes were stopped some ten weeks ago with very few exceptions of which our house is one.” and a frost is anticipated till end of February. I myself get along quite tolerably well; and
almost always secure both warmth and sleep. Mary the other day called with me on Bessy or rather while I sat waiting securely wrapped in a big Russian bear skin. She found Bessy very nervous and complaining of neuralgia, with which her face was swelled. She took hardly any notice of Mary's request to her to come down stairs and see me for a moment in fact it appears that Mary & Mme VenturiEmilie Venturi; she and Mary had become friends since Mary moved to London, and Mary had been taking art lessons from Venturi; see 49:153TC to JAC, 23 Oct. 1874. have determined between them, were the proper time come to get Bessy persuaded out of her foolish threep of never crossing her threshold again till all is done with her. They believe clearly that they can persuade her out of this sore aggravation to all her sorrows. She is for the present much to be pitied. We have not seen Darwin for a week or more; but believe him to be lying quiet on his back as usual and employing himself quietly in reading. On the Sundays we omit carriage driving & go usually in the Chelsea omnibus to St. Paul's CathedralAllingham had visited St. Paul's Cathedral with TC, 29 Dec. 1878, and later noted: “Our visit to St. Paul's pleased him so well that he went there on the five or six Sunday afternoons following with Mary, and was much impressed by the organ” (Allingham Diary 272–73). which is a beautiful serene place in itself and sometimes affords us in the Anthem and doxology a peal of exquisite music from the organ and vox humana. I am still reading various things, at present Plutarch's Morals in an excellent French translationOctave Gréard, De la morale de Plutarque (Paris, 1866). which is very pure and I might say equal to Christian in its sentiments; & does me if anything some good. There has been a little powdering of snow last night, which will at least lay the whirling storms of pounded brick which are laid over the streets for the sake of the horses. Mary and I go out together today without other companion. We are very glad to hear of Sister Jean & the rest being as well as usual; & send them our heartiest love.
docBody.closer:
Ever your affectionate Brother
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.
