div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 1 Feb. MS: NLS 528.100. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
The kind of weather you have seems to resemble our own; short of day light above all things and by no means excessively cold. Indeed we have had
extremely little cold compared with you, often hardly one degree below the freezing point and never above 5 or 6. I get along here in regard to health in all these outward respects tolerably well, nothing to complain of but the state of the stomach which is often qualmish and full of unpleasant nausea, in fact I often think with myself I am fairly too long here.

I am afraid your eye is still overshaded. I don’t know whether you can read much or not; but I send you today the Fortnightly Review, of which one [of] the first Articles is worth reading by JamesJames Aitken. if you cannot manage it, for it gives the clearest account that is possible of the Electric Light.John Tyndall, “The Electric Light,” Fortnightly Review 31 (1 Feb. 1879): 197–216. Fraser's Magazine is otherwise the best worth looking into but that I suppose you can get from Anderson at Dumfries.Wellwood Anderson (1829–1913), proprietor of John Anderson and Son, bookseller and stationer, High St., Dumfries. There are some Magazines or new books intended for Sister Jean that will come before long. Alas, I wish I had something that would serve you more in your solitude and confinement; but our resources are sadly limited. In Macmillan there is a strange thing, criticising one PaleyJohn Pentland Mahaffy, “The Age of Homer. Mr. Paley's Recent Criticism,”
Macmillan's Magazine 39 (Feb. 1879): 314–25. In the article Mahaffy (1839–1919; ODNB), classical scholar, prof. of ancient history at Trinity Coll. Dublin, refutes the theory of Frederick Apthorp Paley (1815–88; ODNB), classical scholar and writer, in Homeri Quæ Nunc Exstant: An Reliquis Cycli Carminibus Antiquiora Jure Habita Sint (1878), that the discrepant linguistic and mythical phenomena of the Iliad and the Odyssey could only be explained if they had been assembled from a variety of sources from different periods. who denies the antiquity of Homer & seems never to have heard of Wolff or Heine's Commentary upon him.Friedrich August Wolf (1759–1824), German classicist, and Christian Gottlob Heyne (1729–1812), his teacher at Göttingen Univ. Wolf had argued in Prolegomena ad Homerum (1795) that Homer's epics were a compilation of ballads or songs composed in an earlier, preliterate period. See Carlyle, Lectures on the History of Literature 1838, ed. J. Reay Greene (1892) 17–18, and Carlyle, “The Life of Heyne,” Works 26:319–54. See also 7:92TC to HI, 30 Jan. 1834, and 133TC to JSM, 18 April 1834. A man at Edinr “Marquis of Hartington”Spencer Compton Cavendish (1833–1908; ODNB), marquess of Hartington, politician, delivered his rectorial address at the Univ. of Edinburgh, 31 Jan. In his speech, reported by the Scotsman, 1 Feb., Hartington urged students to regard education as a means to political as well as professional advancement: “The education, or rather, the groundwork of the education which will fit you for eminence in a professional career, is that which will also enable you to discharge that political service to the State, which is your duty and your inheritance. Those studies which form and strengthen the judgment, which cultivate and discipline the imagination, which train the mind to think correctly and to concentrate its energy, which, in short, develop the moral and intellectual qualities according to a scientific or philosophical method … are equally adapted for proper exercise of the political influence, both direct and indirect, of good citizens.”
seems to have been making a most extraordinary Lord Rector's Speech eager to enlist the poor lads into politics as the one thing needful. But I will cease this empty clatter; and with my heart's love to you all leave you at peace.
docBody.closer:
Ever your affectionate Brother
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 8 Feb. MS: NLS 528.101. Pbd.: A. Carlyle, NL 2:341–42. Quot: Kaplan 549. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: It is sad to me to read what you say about your “improvement” this week. Alas the evil that remains to be improved is so great. It appears that you still cannot at all read even with one eye and are doomed all day to continue without employment.John A. Carlyle wrote, 7 Feb.: “I still cannot see with both eyes, for the right continues watering whenever I try to use it; but it is not painful, is quite clear; & I still hope it may get well rapidly whenever we get a few warm days. Of course I cannot read much with the sound eye, which soon clouds itself with matter too like the other apparently in sympathy with it.” I do hope the right eye will recover soon; and that by help of the left eye and it you will soon be able to read again. You seem to have had a great deal more of suffering from the cold than I have ever had here. Indeed there was no cold here at all comparable in intensity to your Scotch fit, but even at the worst, it was an insignificant part of my poor troubles; I was so quilted with clothes of all kinds too that it never got into me. I would have you to consider well whether you are not rather underclad generally; and if so to make good that error. All feeling of cold has disappeared here for several days and it almost seems as if spring itself had arrived at this premature season. I can read too when there are any worthy books procurable which is by no means always the case. You I expected would have got some good of a pair of Bismarck booksMoritz Busch, Bismarck in the Franco-German War 1870–1871, 2 vols. (1879), an “authorized translation” of Graf Bismarck und seine Leute während des Kriegs mit Frankreich, 2 vols. (Leipzig, 1878). Julius Hermann Moritz Busch (1821–99), travel writer, journalist, and press agent, known as “Bismarck's Boswell.” Allingham noted in his diary, Dec. 1878: “The book of conversations with B[ismarck]'s secretary, just published, was mentioned. I asked, ‘was it authentic?’ ‘Oh yes, it could not have been published without B.'s full consent. His object is to keep himself before the public’” (Allingham Diary 271). The other book was probably the trans. of Prince Bismarck's Letters to His Wife, His Sister, and Others, from 1844 to 1870 (2d edn., 1879), by Sir Henry Berkeley Fitzhardinge Maxse (1832–83; ODNB), colonial governor; TC's copy; see Carlyle's House 87. that have come to me but, alas, you cannot read them at present.

Poor Mrs Paulet is got out of all her troubles. I told you once that she was suffering from asthma & her utter weakness. She decided about a month ago to go down to Essex to a Brother she had a clergyman there; but the reverse of good attended her so far as the disorder went; and she died some ten days ago;See TC to JAC, 21 Dec. 1878; Paulet d., 30 Jan., at the home of her brother, Rev. Frank J. Newton, Shelley Rectory, Ongar, Essex, 9 mi. (14 km.) W of Chelmsford.—ending as we cannot but hope a great many miseries in exchange for peace. Alas, alas. The final mercy of God, it in late years always appears to me is that he delivers us from this life which has become a task too hard
for us.

Oh that I could hear of your getting out of doors, of being able to see & above all of being able to drive in a carriage. But we must not be impatient. The news from Annandale seems to be good. What I hear of Sister Jean is also favourable. Good be with you all. I send my poor blessing to you were it of any value.
docBody.closer:
Ever your affectionate Brother
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 15 Feb. MS: NLS 528.102. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your brief letter this morning distressed & surprized by your account of so much cold and of cold being such an enemy to you.John A. Carlyle had complained bitterly of the cold all winter; he wrote, 14 Feb., entirely about the weather: “This week we have had very changeable weather, sometimes warm from the South or West … sometimes very cold, as last night & today, from the North East, first with frost through the night, & in the day time strong North East wind which was very uncomfortable. On other days of the week we had pleasant weather, which made me a great deal better than usual.” We have had a very moderate temperature here in comparison with yours, no frost perceptible nor indeed has it been through cold I have suffered, but almost altogether thro’ weakness, great and steadily increasing. I believe or suspect always that I am far more warmly dressed than you but one thing is very certain the cold at Dumfries and everywhere else will infallibly abate and then heaven grant that your prophecies be fulfilled. Such imprisonment as you have suffered is
very grievous take it how one will, but your practical inability to read is a great affliction to me, you who were such an ardent and universal reader. Without reading I should be entirely at a loss to spend my time. Please tell me strictly how your eye is and whether you can do anything at all in the way of continuous reading. Also whether the obstructions in your inside & outside still render it impossible for you to make the least trial of carriage exercise. Dear Brother your sad imprisonment is daily present with me & it wd be my highest satisfaction if I cd in any way help you out of it.

I have heard nothing whatever from Ruskin whom I expected confidently at Dumfries,There is no record of Ruskin visiting Dumfries at this time; he wrote several letters from Brantwood during Feb., in some of which he complained of a horrible cold (Ruskin's Works 37:275). but the other night I received from him under the title of Proserpina No VRuskin, Proserpina. Study of Wayside Flowers Part V (1878), containing “Genealogy” and “Cora and Kronos”; see Ruskin's Works 25:338–371. one of the prettiest pieces of writing I have seen for many years, treating of the names & properties of certain early flowers, which greatly surprised and gratified me. I have understood that he is quite gone over to what they call SpiritualismFor Ruskin and spiritualism, see TC to JAC, 11 [12] Oct. 1878. & my conjecture is that he, who knows how much I detest & despise that horrible absurdity avoids writing to me on that account though he loves me as well as ever poor soul & can write upon other subjects so beautifully, as I say.— Dear Brother, I am as much whipt for time as need be & continually interrupted. I must abruptly cease, & subscribe myself, with heart's love to you & the rest.
docBody.closer:
Ever your affectionate Brother
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 22 Feb. MS: NLS 528.103. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your weather seems to be decidedly worse than ours; but happily your own health such as it was has not materially suffered by it. I do sincerely trust that your eyes will get well as the spring opens, and that you will have the benefit of reading, wh. is nearly all the recreation and use we can have of it now. We here had by far the heaviest fall of snow we have had this winter, about 6 inches of it, which fell in the night time without noise or disturbance and has lain perfectly quiescent slowly melting away ever since.The Times reported, 22 Feb.: “The metropolis and the suburbs yesterday were visited by one of the heaviest snowstorms of even this severe winter. The early morning was clear, with a slight frost. Towards 4 o’clock it became cloudy, and at a quarter-past 5 o’clock snow began to fall. Two hours afterwards the snow in some parts of London was said to be six or seven inches deep. The trees in the parks … presented a very singular and picturesque appearance, but the effects upon traffic were most disastrous…. The tramcars … could not travel for some very long time, and the omnibuses which took up the traffic charged double and treble fares.” The house water
here was never frozen up except for a few days when we noticed the main pipes frequented by people in the morning with cans in their hands but that is all past sometime ago the only obstruction we experienced was yesterday when we cd not get our drive owing to the heavy snow roads, which the people as their wont is had been very negligent to deal with. For my own part I have in general got little or no hindrance from the weather nor indeed have I been suffering except from the of course increasing weakness that acts chiefly through the stomach, yet oftenest get some modicum of sleep and have indeed great reason to be grateful for the deliverance, which I feel to be provided for me and which will come at God's good time, not sooner & not later.

You say nothing about your internal disorder, whether the malady there seems to be increasing or lessening but we judge at least from your letter today and the firmness with which it is written that things are not worsening but perhaps slowly bettering even there. My constant wish and prayer is that you were able to move about especially to move about in a carriage, but for that too we must wait & hope. I cannot be said to have much pleasure in my daily drive;Allingham noted in his diary, 22 Feb.: “Drove with Carlyle…. C.: ‘For [Charles] Darwin personally I have great respect; but all that of “Origin of Species,” etc., is of little interest to me. What we desire to know is, who is the Maker? and what is to come to us when we have shuffled off this mortal coil. Whoever looks into himself must be aware that at the centre of things is a mysterious Demiurgus—who is God, and who cannot in the least be adequately spoken of in any human words’” (Allingham Diary 274). but the thing generally seems to do me good & I commonly get a little hour or less of sleep after coming in from the strange jangle of all thoroughfares in city or in country. We have not seen Darwin this long time but sometimes hear of him & judge that he is lying on his back reading & keeping himself as quiet as anybody possibly could. There is plenty of idle news circulating up and down but except the newspaper placards, I myself read nothing of the newspapers. The state of the world, with Dizzy at the top if it, appears to me abundantly ominous but also abundantly contemptible & I say to myself always, what have I to do with it more. I need not detain poor Mary further who describes herself as “cutting with hunger,” her time of luncheon being come. I will send my kindest love to Sister Jean & my best blessing, if there were any good in that, to her and to all of you,
docBody.closer:
Ever your affecte Brother
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 1 March. MS: NLS 528.104. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p: Your account of last week's weather is very much a picture in stronger colours of our own: there seems to be something of real frost still in it, but with us that appears to be nearly altogether gone. I read with great interest of the change that has taken place in your internal obstructions especially of their filling with solid substanceJohn A. Carlyle wrote, 28 Feb.: “Two days ago the tumour above the navel, instead of remaining full of air was filled while I slept … with solid substance of some kind which still remains in it; & also a new round lump went beyond it & remains there. I believe the reason why I cannot stand driving is caused by the pain occasioned by the carriage motion.” which of course you cannot yet form much idea about. I beg of you to be very minute in telling me of whatever you have discovered on that head. I am myself tolerably well. The only change is I have got a little cold in the lungs which I never had before; but at the worst was quite insignificant & cost me almost no trouble at all. I still read and can get something more or less tolerable to read; but it is seldom that the thing read interests me almost at all.

I am very anxious to know what you make out about those internal lumps and what it is they are now suddenly filled with. You cannot drive, alas; and with me the two hours of driving are as it were the work of the day which ends about 5 oclock & yields me for most part a little hour of quiet sleep before dinner. I usually call nowhere but go driving oftenest on the streets wherever the road seems suitablest. Today I have got amongst other letters the one enclosed about the St. George's Guild, which if you are able to read it will more or less interest you, as a disclosure of Ruskin's latest intentions & hopes a Millenium to be produced by the St. George's Guild.The Guild of St. George, a charity for arts, crafts, and the rural economy, was founded by Ruskin in 1871, and formally constituted in a “Memorandum of Association” in 1878; see Ruskin's Works 30:3–12. The Athenaeum reported, 15 Feb.: “The first ordinary general meeting of Mr Ruskin's company of the Guild of St. George will be held at the Queen's Hotel, Birmingham, on Friday, February 21st, at two o’clock. This company, as is well known to readers of Fors Clavigera, was formed in the hope of maintaining some portion of our country in its primitive beauty, and with a wish to prove that the labour which is required for the life and progress of our race does not of necessity involve the disfigurement of the country or the partial degradation of the labourer. The company proposes to ‘buy land in England and thereon to train into the healthiest and most refined life possible as many Englishmen, Englishwomen, and English children as the land they possess can maintain in comfort.’ With this object schools are to be built, books, drawings, and pictures purchased, and museums formed, and, after having done as much manual work as will provide them with food, those willing to be taught are to be schooled in all branches of honourable knowledge and graceful art. The vital principle of the Guild is that whatever profit is made out of the management of the land is to be applied to the comfort and welfare of the workmen themselves; and it is also a rule that no machine is to be used where the hand will serve.” He is perfectly sane I think
in regard to all that, but I believe has other very distracted notions about Spiritualism so-called, a branch of matter which he keeps quite secret from me, knowing that I despise and even abhor it. He keeps quite hid from me. There was about ten days ago, a piece of really beautiful writing by him called Proserpina, Part V,See TC to JAC, 15 Feb. touching on the nomenclature and ways of certain kinds of flowers, which seemed to me full of real talent & even genius. The gomerill from Kirkmahoe called BurgessAndrew Hutton Burgess (b. 1835), journalist; M.A., Univ. of Edinburgh, 1862, formerly lodging at 36 Park Walk, Chelsea. TC previously helped him find work cataloging Lady Ashburton's library; see 46:148TC to LLA, 18 Jan. 1870. Kirkmahoe, parish in Dumfries and Galloway, 31/2 mi. (5.5 km.) N of Dumfries. whom probably you recollect as going off for Japan at a salary of £1000 a year is now returned hence apparently in a quite broken condition & I think is trying all he can to borrow or beg from me in which I do not calculate he will be successful.
Enough of these insignificant details. I send my love & blessing to Sister Jean & all the rest of you, and ever am
docBody.closer:
Your affectionate Brother
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 15 March. MS: NLS 528.105. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your kind & punctual letter lay waiting me this morning. I am very sorry to hear of your sufferings during the last week:John A. Carlyle wrote, 14 March, that their weather had been very changeable, including “sharpish frosts with snow which were not a little disagreeable to me…. [T]he wind is still from North or East, I have slept rather badly owing to these changes, especially last night.” with us here there has been no disturbance from weather indeed all through the winter our cold has been insignificant especially in comparison with yours. Yours too we can compute must be nearly ending now. My sorrow always is that you cannot get out or stand any locomotion. If you could endure the motion of a carriage! But, alas,
you cannot. I wish you would tell me how it is with those sad lumps internal and external; but you mention nothing of them.

I am myself quite tolerably well. Nothing to complain of but natural weakness; the weather perfectly tolerable to me. I generally get a fair proportion of sleep, and think with sorrow how much more favourable my position is than yours though six years older than you. Alas, alas. But you have still hope and are not wearied of life as I am. God be ever with you, dear Brother; and prepare us both for whatever lies ahead, especially for the unknown Eternity, which cannot be now far off.

A foolish YankeeUnidentified. is sitting waiting for me upstairs and poor Mary has had a bad cold and is hardly able to write so that I need not continue farther.— Tell me what it is you read when your eyes will allow.John wrote: “My eye is less sore than it was, & I can now read in the daytime when the weather is clear; & I hope the eye will soon be quite well again.” Give my love to Sister Jean and all the rest. Keep hoping, dear Brother! I ever am
docBody.closer:
Affectionately yours
for T. Carlyle / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: TC-JAC, 22 March. MS: NLS 528.106. Hitherto unpbd. Written in Mary Aitken's hand, and signed by her for TC.
div3.head: TC TO JOHN A. CARLYLE

docBody.p:
Your punctual and kind letter lay waiting for me this morning and we are not surprised that in the continuance of bad weather you do not feel much improved. In the last two days our weather too, which is generally much better than yours has greatly increased in wind and cold;—and indeed independent of all that I have had a rather painful bout of biliary revolution, which rendered two or three of my nights extremely uncomfortable; but happily all that now seems to be over, and we expect that March which did not come in like a lion may nevertheless go out like a lamb and summer at last come actually to hand. Meantime I regret continually that you have not had the benefit of London temperature which is greatly preferable to Scotch. We have had a tragedy going on quite beside us, in which Rose our excellent servantRose, servant at Cheyne Row; see MAI to MEW, 25 June 1877. Their other servant had apparently recently left, as John A. Carlyle wrote, 7 Feb.: “I hope [Mary] has got a better servant in place of her that left on Saturday last so foolishly.”
is deeply concerned,—the death namely of her young man, which has been more sudden than any case, consumptive or other, which I have ever been in sight of. He died last night, his pain and misery mostly sunk in delirious oblivion. Mary has put Rose to bed here to have her first complete sleep since the poor young man was got to be an out patient at the Consumption HospitalProbably the North London Consumptive Hospital, Hampstead, founded in 1860, primarily for those unable to pay for treatment. about a week ago; & has last night finished off his sad career. He was a peaceable diligent creature; and one can only be thankful that his sufferings were at least brief.

We had heard duly of the death at Bonerick. WillieTheir cousin William Wright (1796–1879), who d. 15 March. William was the eldest son of their maternal aunt Nicholas Aitken (b. ca. 1778; see 11:158TC to JAC, 28 July 1839) and Samuel Wright, of Bonerick, Irongray, Kirkcudbright, about 6 mi. (9.5 km) W of Dumfries; his brothers were John (b. ca. 1806–after 1881), Samuel (ca. 1811–80; see 44:156TC to JAC, 18 Feb. 1867), and Maxwell (the youngest, still alive in 1881). William's death was reported in the Galloway News and Kirkcudbrightshire Advertiser, 21 March. John wrote, 21 March, that their brother Jamie and his son James “had been attending the funeral of Wm, eldest of the brothers at Bonerick, & 82 years of age…. I knew Willie better than any other of the brothers & liked him better.” was the only one of these cousins whom I used to have some knowledge of. I did not know he was a year younger than myself. I always rather liked him. But my time is quite done dear Brother. I can only send my kindest love to Sister Jean & all the rest of you; and am
docBody.closer:
Ever your affectionate
for T. CarlyleThis is the last letter we have directly composed by TC. Allingham notes that in the spring of 1879 “Carlyle's health suddenly worsened: beginning it was thought from a chill, and the action of his heart. He became alarmingly weak. He ceased for a time to drive out: was very languid and slept much: he sometimes looked very sunken and low” (Allingham Diary 275). / M. C. A.

div3.sourceNote: MAC-MW [MEW], 31 [30 Nov.]. MS: NLS Acc. 9207. Hitherto unpbd. Mary Aitken married her cousin Alexander Carlyle, 21 Aug., and became known as Mary Aitken Carlyle.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN CARLYLE TO META WELLMER

docBody.dateline:
24 Cheyne Row, Chelsea
31Misdated, presumably 30 Nov. Nov. 1879
docBody.p:
How am I to thank you for your splendid present to me and above all how am I to apologize or in any way excuse myself for my long silence? If I were to try and express one half of the contrition I feel I should not leave myself an inch of space for anything else! So I shall only say that I do feel heartily
ashamed of myself and beg you to forgive me. The parcel arrived safe on Friday night and I shall not attempt to describe to you my varied feelings on looking at the contents; nor need I tell you that I felt my head as hot as if the beautiful Tischdecken [tablecloths], which your kind fingers had made for me were indeed coals of fire! I have never seen anything of the kind used in England as yet for the purpose you mention, but they are so pretty that I shall be very proud to lead the fashion the next time I have friends to tea. The designs and the colours are beautiful and I admire them and the workmanship very much indeed. Many cordial thanks to you, dear Miss Wellmer for your kind present and kind wishes. My Uncle at once took possession of the pretty little cushion for the back of his easy chair and has used it ever since it came. He too sends you many thanks for it and the kind letter you sent him.— — — Now I must begin to tell you news of our household here. First of all No 24 Cheyne Row is the very same old No 5 you remember only the numbers on the houses in this street were all altered some time ago and No 5 became No 24 “by order of the Board of Works.”See TC to JAC, 28 April 1877. Here my Uncle and I have been ever since you saw us here. Our household is the same as when you saw it, except that “Rose” is now head servant with a younger one under her and that my Husband has taken up his abode with us.Since their marriage Mary and Alick Carlyle lived with TC in Cheyne Row; for a photograph of them at this time, see 166. There is indeed another change which you will be very sorry to hear of for I remember my uncle Dr Carlyle was staying here then.Wellmer had visited TC and Mary in May 1876, while John A. Carlyle was staying with them; see MAI to MEW, 20 May 1876. About two years ago when he was up here, he suffered a good deal from what afterwards turned out to be an internal tumour; he consulted the best surgeons here, with the result that they advised him to leave London for Scotland (my Mother's house) where he would be better taken care of and also indicated to him that there was no hope of any cure. He went to Dumfries in April of last year,See TC to JAC, 27 April 1878. where after a great deal of suffering he died on the 15th of this last September, quietly & peacefully at the end. I expect it was his illness that was attributed to my Uncle Carlyle. It was reported several times that my Uncle Carlyle was dangerously ill and I had a great many enquiries on the subject. I am glad to tell you, however, that he is wonderfully well; only he is and has for long time been extremely weak. He is able to read, and enjoys a good book as much as ever; he has a drive of two hours every afternoon (his only exercise), and though it is grievous that his body should be so weak, it is an inexpressible comfort that his mind remains as clear as ever. He is in general very comfortable and contented and suffers from nothing but weakness, which indeed is a heavy enough ailment in itself, however.

This year he and I went to Scotland in June,TC and Mary left for Dumfries in the third week of June. we staid for a fortnight in my Mother's house at Dumfries where the poor “Dr” was and afterwards went for a month, or more to a furnished house about two miles off,TC and Mary stayed in Cassalands House, on the Dalbeattie Road on the W side of Dumfries. where one of my two sisters staid with us by turns all the time, & we saw our friends every day. On the 21st of August I was married to my Cousin Alexander Carlyle who came over from Canada a week or two before. We were married quite quietly in my Father's house no stranger being present except one Cousin who was Groomsman.Groomsman unidentified, but it was probably either James Carlyle Jr. or John Calvert Carlyle. We spent another three or four weeks at a little village about twenty miles from Dumfries,Moffat, town about 20 mi. (34 km.) N of Dumfries; Mary and Alick went there after the wedding, staying at the Buccleuch Arms Hotel, where TC later joined them. William Allingham visited Dumfries in Sept.; he called first at Cassalands House, 4 Sept., and was told that TC had gone to The Hill. He recorded: “To the Hill, pretty red-stone house, in shrubbery, with peep of the hills to eastward. / Portraits of Carlyle, Mary—Enter Mrs. Aitken. The Doctor very ill, poor fellow…. A doctor has been here, ‘but you know he [JAC] has no belief in medical skill.’ T.C. with Mary and Alick, at Moffat” (Allingham Diary 278). Allingham traveled the following day to Moffat and spent four days with them driving around the countryside, including visiting Ecclefechan to see the house where TC was born, while TC, Mary, and Alick went to Newlands to visit James and Catherine Carlyle. Presumably their cousin John Calvert Carlyle and his family had also come to Newlands from Scotsbrig, as Allingham says there were “fourteen small nephews and nieces” (Allingham Diary 281). my Uncle and my Mother being with us most of the time, and then returned to Chelsea (my Uncle, my Husband & myself) towards the end of September to settle down quietly for the winter.Mary and Alick had been engaged for several years, but Mary could not leave TC; see TC to JAC, 21 Sept. 1878. However, as Alick later wrote: “Carlyle himself solved the difficulty by inviting me to come over as soon as I could arrange matters and live with him in Cheyne Row with dear Mary as my wife…. I left Canada about the 1st of July 1879, and made straight for Dumfries where Carlyle and I drove over to the Hill, Mary's home, where the ceremony was done in his presence by the Parish Minister. Carlyle remained with Mrs. Aitken and her other two daughters…. After the wedding was over Mary and I, wishing to keep within call of our Uncle, took our ‘honeymoon’ only twenty miles off in the chief hotel of Moffat. We came down to see him frequently, and finding that he was not doing very well, we arranged for him to come to our hotel at Moffat, and stay with us after the first two weeks. Which he did, and continued there till the 16th of September. Dr. Carlyle who had long been ill died on the 15th of that month, and Mary accompanied Carlyle home to Chelsea the next day without letting him know the bad news. I joined them there after Dr. Carlyle's funeral” (A. Carlyle, Jottings 71). The journey to and from Dumfries is a very long one 8 hours, but there are no changes of trains and the carriages are comfortable so that it is not a difficult or complicated one— — My Husband is the son of my Uncle's and my
Mother's brother, who emigrated to Canada when my Husband was a baby, thirty-six years ago, and he remained there until three years ago when he died. My Husband was a teacher in Canada he was for some time a Professor of Natural Science at a College there. He is not doing any work here at present except helping to take care of our Uncle, in which he has proved himself very useful. If he and I live longer than my Uncle, his notion is that we should become farmers in Canada, where are his Mother & all his brothers & sisters. It is very kind of you and very generous to think of travelling so far to take care of my Uncle. He and I cordially thank you for this kind thought on your part. I was very busy and much tired and harrassed at the time I received the letter in which you first spoke of it, or I should have written in answer to it. He was very weak and ailing for a long time last spring and I was completely worn out with nursing him before we went to Scotland. But accept our thanks
now, though it is so late to offer them! He is well taken care of now, when my Husband brings with him plenty of new strength for the enterprise.
Mary and Alick Carlyle, 1879
Thomas Carlyle Papers, Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Columbia University in
the City of New York

The account of your summer excursions is very interesting. So you still read Schopenhauer and eat only vegetables! I read almost nothing, only keep a volume of a good book always by me & snatch half an hour or often enough only a quarter of an hour to read it. Even in this way one can do a little reading. My Uncle has read the whole of Shakespeare this winter, and nearly all Swift's works. Your little book-marker is at present doing duty in a volume of Swift. As to food for the body, I still eat a little butcher's meat, but not much. I could not keep my soul in my body without at least a little milk. The anti-
vivisection society here seem to be doing very well; but I dont hear much about them. My Uncle sees very few people here,William Allingham, among others, continued to call on TC; he noted in his diary, 4 Dec.: “Helen and I to Cheyne Row. Carlyle's eighty-fourth birthday. Mrs. Lecky there. Browning and Ruskin are gone. C. on his sofa by the window, warm and quiet, wearing a new purple and gold cap” (Allingham Diary 284). preferring to be quite quiet, and as I never go out to any entertainments & we have no entertainments here & I have no time for calling I see but few people and hear but
little news. But I think one is happier so. It is best when one can find one's work and try to do it.

Goodbye, dear Miss Wellmer. Excuse this much-interrupted, badly written and hasty scrawl, which has spread itself over so many pages. I promise you I shall not be so long in answering if you should be good enough to write again. With my Uncle's cordial and grateful regards and goodwishes to you and my own I am affectionately yours Mary CarlyleTC also continued to be generous to family and friends in need. Jean Aitken wrote to TC, 6 Nov.: “Ten thousand thanks for all your kindness to us—at all times. I sent in the cheque for £1000 today. I am ashamed to receive such a gift but it will be a great blessing to us all.” Although the Aitkens had built their house themselves, the land would have been subject to feu duty (see 37:76TC to JCA, 30 Dec. 1860), and it appeared that the landowner had the power to sell their house. She continued: “ He is to be paid off the last penny he can claim tomorrow so we shall be all delivered from him for ever & a day. [He] has been determined this 2 years to bring the House for sale—at a depressed time when it wd not have brought more than half its value…. [S]o we shall be delighted to see you all three at our clean comfortable fireside. And we intend to ‘ca’ cannie’ & be as thrifty as we can.” Mary noted in TC's checkbook: “4 Nov 1879 / Mrs J. C. Aitken / £1000.0.0” (TC's checkbook; MS: NLS 20753). Jean wrote again [23 Jan. 1880], hoping TC would come to visit them in the summer, as his visit the previous year did her no end of good: “I wish you saw how clean and comfortable the house is, it had not been possible to make any overturn that could possibly be avoided for a long time past & we all felt uncomfortable with the accumulation of disorder…. I need not try to disguise the fact that it was an ‘a-a-afu’ struggle’ for me while it lasted seeing I had no strength to help in any way.” TC also apparently sent money to Henry Larkin (1820–99; see 35:259–6035:biographical notes and 45:22645:biographical notes), friend of the Carlyles for many years, who had helped TC with maps and indexes for Frederick. Their last recorded contact was in 1872; see 48:105TC to JAC, 2 Nov. 1872. Larkin wrote to Mary Carlyle, 19 Oct.: “I am quite at a loss how to thank Mr Carlyle for his great kindness towards me, and for his very kind remembrance of my poor services of ‘auld lang syne.’ I can only ask you to
convey to him my very sincere gratitude, and to assure him that his generous gift will give me the comfortable consciousness of pecuniary independence for the next nine months or more” (MS: NLS 666.133). He then wrote to TC, 23 Dec.: “You will be pleased to know that your kind intercession has opened for me the gates of the Editorial Heaven! I have received a very kind letter from Dr Allon, accepting my article on ‘Planets, Moons and Meteorites,’ for the April number of the British Quarterly. … With many thanks for your many kindnesses.” Henry Allon (1818–92; ODNB), Congregational minister, writer, and editor. Henry Larkin, “Planets, Moons, and Meteorites,” British Quarterly Review (April 1880): 19–303.

div3.sourceNote: MAC-HGF, 25 Feb. Pbd: Daily News, 27 Feb. 1880. Herbert George Fordham (1854–1929; ODNB), writer on cartography.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN CARLYLE TO H. G. FORDHAM

docBody.p: I beg to inform you, with regard to the memorial to Dean Stanley,H. G. Fordham had presented to Arthur Penrhyn Stanley, dean of Westminster, a memorial with over 5,000 signatures objecting to the proposal to erect a monument in Westminster Abbey to Louis Napoléon (1856–79), French prince imperial, who was killed in the Anglo-Zulu War, 1 June 1879. One of the signatures purported to be that of TC; Stanley questioned the authenticity of TC's signature, believing, on the word of a friend of TC's, that it was a forgery. Fordham wrote to the Daily News, 26 Feb., enclosing Mary Carlyle's letter: “I have the honour to enclose for publication copy of a letter, which shows that the statement … made by the Dean of Westminster … has its only foundation in the belief of a third person” (Daily News, 27 Feb.). Stanley sent Fordham a letter of apology and explanation, 28 Feb.: “About three weeks ago I received a letter similar in substance to your memorial, signed ‘Thomas Carlyle, Chelsea.’ Wishing to ascertain from whom it came, I sent it through an intimate friend of Mr. Carlyle to the historian himself, who immediately disclaimed all knowledge of it. On receiving the printed signatures to your memorial, desirous to know whether the signature was genuine or not, I sent it with a similar inquiry to the same friend. His answer, as before, was an absolute negative, which I understood, as in the former case, to have been directly authorised by the historian. But it seems that Mr. Carlyle had repudiated with so much emphasis any complicity in the protest contained in the earlier letter that his friend had too hastily assumed the signature to be again apocryphal, and therefore had not thought it necessary to apply to Mr. Carlyle a second time. Hence the error into which I was led at the time of receiving the deputation” (Daily News, 2 March). The friend is unidentified. that I signed it for my uncle, Mr. Carlyle, at his request, and that the memorial undoubtedly expresses his mind on the subject.—

div3.sourceNote: AC [ACA]-HHF, 10 April. MS copy: Furness Memorial Lib., Univ. of Pennsylvania inc. Hitherto unpbd. Horace Howard Furness (1833–1912), American Shakespearean scholar.
div3.head: ALEXANDER CARLYLE TO H. H. FURNESS

docBody.p: Mr. Carlyle, desires me to say that he accepts with much pleasure and gratitude your volume on “King Lear.”Shakespeare, King Lear, ed. H. H. Furness (Philadelphia, 1880); TC's copy is listed in Sotheby's catalogue: “King Lear, 1880; Variorum Edition edited by H. H. Furness, presentation copy from the Editor, original cloth” (Sotheby's [1932] 121). He remarked to me also that yours is decidedly the best edition of ShakespeareFurness edited the Variorum Edition of Shakespeare, pbd. by J. B. Lippincott & Co. yet published.

closer.note: Jean Aitken wrote, [early spring]: “I am astonished at what Magt tells me of the amount of reading you are up to Shakespeare Gibbon &c &c it is truly surprising to me after all that you have come through! I hope the addition of Peggie to your household has not disturbed your regular quiet mode of life.” Her da. Margaret (Maggie / Peggie) was staying in Cheyne Row for a visit.

div3.sourceNote: MAC-JH [JCHA], 18 July. Pbd: Copeland 254–55.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN CARLYLE TO JANET HANNING

docBody.p: I received my Cousin Mrs. Baird'sMrs. Baird unidentified; Janet Hanning had four das., all married, but none of them to a Mr. Baird; nor were any of Mary's other Canadian cousins called Baird. Possibly Copeland mistranscribed the name. letter about ten days ago, asking for tidings of my Uncle. I am extremely sorry that you have been made anxious about him through my not writing; but indeed there have been many sufficient apologies for my want of punctuality in that way, which, however, I need not trouble you with here. It will suffice to say that I use the very first chance I have had to answer your enquiries.

It is not very easy to explain to you exactly how Uncle is. He is exceedingly weak, hardly able to walk fifty yards without help, and yet until about ten days ago, when he had a very severe attack of Diarrhoea which has left him much below par, he was what one might call for him very well. He generally spends his mornings till about half past two o’clock between lying on the sofa, reading in his easy chair, and smoking an occasional pipe; at half past two he goes out to driveAllingham noted in his diary, 10 March 1880: “I meet Carlyle's carriage in the street and get in. Mary alights, Alick stays. We drive through the Parks…. Carlyle, poor man, lies back crookedly in his corner, noticing nothing of the outside world. Yet he seems rather better than last time, a dim fire still in his eyes, a dusky red in his cheeks…. On politics he remarked, ‘This time will be memorable as the time when England was governed by a perfect Charlatan’” (Allingham Diary 285). for two or two and a half hours, sleeps on the sofa till dinner time
(half past six) then after dinner sleeps again, at nine has tea, reads or smokes or talks, or lies on the sofa till bed time, which is usually about midnight, and so ends the day. He looks very well in the face, has a fine, fresh ruddy complexion and an immense quantity of white hair, his voice is clear and strong, he sees and hears quite well; but for the rest, as I have said, he is not good at moving about. In general he is wonderfully good humored and contented; and on the whole carries his eighty-four years well. He desires me to send you his kind love, and his good wishes: as you know, he writes to nobody at all. I do not think he has written a single letter, even dictated one, for over a year.TC's last known letter was to John A. Carlyle, 22 March 1879.
We are very glad to hear that all is well with you and with all your family. I have not time for more just now, as I am interrupted. Good-bye, dear aunt.
docBody.closer: I am, Your affectionate Niece, Mary Carlyle.Mary does not mention that her first child, Thomas, had been born, 2 June. Emily Tennyson wrote to TC, 14 June: “I cannot hear of this happy event in your house without sending the word of affectionate congratulation which [Tennyson], no doubt, would have sent had he been at home. All blessing on the little Son and may he, like his Great Uncle, be a blessing to his own generation and generations to come and begin by making his Great Uncle scarcely less happy than his Parents, to whom I beg every kind message.”

div1.p:
MATERIAL RELATING TO TC'S FINAL MONTHS,
DEATH, AND FUNERAL

TC continued in this way of life for the next several months. Alick Carlyle later wrote: “After our first child was born [2 June 1880] Mary went with our son to her old home for a week or so [Sept.] and I was left in sole charge of Carlyle. We got on very well together, and I went out driving with him in the brougham every day” (A. Carlyle, Jottings 71–72). On their return home, Jean Aitken wrote to TC, [26 Sept.]: “I daresay you wd be glad to get your dear Mary and her fine blyth, bright boy back. We were all charmed with their short visit.”

Friends continued to visit; William Allingham noted in his diary, 4 Dec. 1880: “Helen and I call on Carlyle. His eighty-fifth birthday. C. seems better and easier; more himself” (Allingham Diary 306). He then noted, 17 Jan. 1881: “Helen visited Mary C. to-day. Carlyle keeps his bed yesterday and to-day. He lies now on a water-bed, which is placed in the drawing-room.…After taking finally to his bed the venerable man hardly spoke at all; there was no physical obstruction of the organs of speech, but almost total absence of will or wish to say anything” (Allingham Diary 308). William Lecky wrote to a friend, 17 Jan. 1881: “Carlyle has got very much weaker…both in body and mind, during the last few months. He has lately given up going out and almost wholly given up reading” (Elisabeth Lecky, A Memoir of the Right Hon. William Edward Hartpole Lecky [1909] 148).
Thomas Carlyle died 5 Feb. 1881.

Catharina Lecky wrote to her sister, 5 Feb. 1881: “Mr. Carlyle died this morning at 8.30, and though all life was nearly, or seemed nearly, gone out of him the last few days, still one feels very differently to-day that he is no longer there. We went at two, and only saw by the closed shutters that all was over. We went up to the room where he lay and looked at him for a moment. He is terribly thin, brandy-and-water and ether was all he had taken for days. He was hardly cold yet, and there was a little colour left in his cheeks. The end long expected was perfectly quiet: a sigh and nothing more” (Lecky, A Memoir 149).

div3.sourceNote: MAC-MC [MCON], 6 Feb. MS: Moncure Conway Papers, Columbia; text from typescript.
div3.head: MARY AITKEN CARLYLE TO MONCURE CONWAY

docBody.p: My Uncle's Funeral is to take place at Ecclefechan—the day not yet fixed. There will be no funeral procession in London; and this I trust will explain to you the absence of any further intimation on the subject.Mary wrote similar notes to many of TC's friends.
Many thanks for your kind note and to you and Mrs Conway for your sympathy.
docBody.closer: Ever yours truly / Mary Carlyle.

div3.sourceNote: AC-TC [ACA-TCA], 11 Feb. Addr: Bieldy Knowes / Brantford / Ontario / Canada. / Via Cork. MS: MUL. Pbd: Marrs 791–94. Text from MS transcript.
div3.head: ALEXANDER CARLYLE TO THOMAS CARLYLE

docBody.dateline:
THE HILL, DUMFRIES. N. B.Written on The Hill headed notepaper.
11th Feb. 1881.
docBody.p:
I snatch a few spare minutes—only a few—to send you a line, with a promise to write at greater length when I get back to poor old 24 Cheyne Row. My last two notes would prepare you for the sad news of our good old Uncle's departure; and you will doubtless have read Newspaper accounts of his death long before this can reach you. He died without a struggle or without any apparent pain at 8 ½ last Saturday Morning, the 5th of Feb. He had been growing gradually and rapidly weaker for some 3 weeks before the end came and so we were not unprepared; indeed for the last week, each night we thought would be the last. Between 5 & 6 in the morning seemed to be the most trying time: and he was often so low then that his breathing seemed to cease for more than a minute at a time & his pulse was scarcly [sic] perceptable [sic]. He was for the most part unconscious for several days before the end came. As is usual his mind reverted to very early times: he asked Mary once “has my Father gone to bed?” Once he called “Sandy” very distinctly. (He meant our dear old Father, for he never called me Sandy). Then he called “John”; and often he mistook Mary for his Mother, through [sic] his arms round her neck and cried “My dear Mother.” There was nothing whatever unpleasant in his imagination, and his countenance was that of one perfectly enraptured at meeting long lost & very dear friends. The last word I heard him utter was “Alick,” he called me to the bedside; but he was almost
instantly asleep or unconscious again; this was at 3 p m the Friday before he died. Mary & I both sat up with him every night (except one) for two weeks before he died. The last night (Friday night & Sat. Morning) I was not the least sleepy and sat reading before the fire while Mary slept for a few hours on the sofa in the Drawing room where we all were. I rose every few minutes and wet his lips with Brandy & water by means of a feather. The breathing was very light and rather peculiar; but after 6 he seemed to grow a little stronger & I went up to bed about 7. Mary (who had had some sleep) agreeing to remain near him. At half-past eight the breathing quietly ceased (as it had done often before); she ran to him and listened and the lungs moved once or twice again very gently and then stopped—forever. A slight tremor seemed to run through the body and a faint flutter or gurgling sound was heard in the inside and then all was still. And so passed away calmly & peacefully the noblest, greatest & best spirit that ever lived on earth!

Poor Mary who has been like a daughter to him (& he to her like the kindest of Fathers) for a dozen years, was & is much cut up at his loss. Indeed every one who knew him was unfeignedly sad at the sad news of his death. All the Newspapers had notices of his death and all were very appreciative and kind. The most tender and best notice of it that I have yet seen was in the Pall Mall Gazett [sic]The Pall Mall Gazette, 5 Feb., 2d edn. (a copy of which I will send you when I get back to Chelsea). But we had a terrible time of it during his illness with Newspaper men coming at all hours for news of his condition so that at present I almost hate the very name of Newspaper. We were also pestered with people coming to look at the body to all of whom we said No, except his most intimate friends. Dean Stanly [sic] came often and offered Burial in Westminster Abbey, but as this was against Uncle's wish we refused him. Then he wanted the remains to be taken to the Abbey and have the Funeral Service read over them, to which of course we did not consent. In accordance with his wishes the funeral was most simple and private. None were invited but the relations. Froude, Lecky & Tyndall came to Ecclefechan to be present at the funeral; & Mr & Mrs Allingham & Mrs Lecky & a Mr. GrahamWilliam Graham; see TC to JAC, 11 [12] Oct. 1878. followed the remains from Chelsea to the railway station in London, along with Mary & me. We left old Cheyne Row on Wed. at 7 ¼ p.m., and Euston station at 9 p.m. The hearse was run upon a truck and was in the same train that Mary & I came by. The hearse remained at Carlisle (in charge of the London Undertaker) & Mary & I came on to Lockerbie reaching that place at 6 a.m. We had intended to rest there till 10 or 11 when the Carriages ordered from Dumfries should pass on their way to Ecclefechan, one of which was to take us up. But all the inns were full and we had to sit in a cold room till a fire was made & a little breakfast got ready. At
10 Mary's Father and cousins John Aitken, Maggie Aitken & John GriersonJohn Grierson (1837–1926), solicitor, grandson of TC's maternal aunt Jean Aitken (1765–1810), m., 1793, John Grierson (1756–1828). arrived from Dfs. Hence Maggie Mary & I started at 11 and reached Ecclefechan Station at 12, the hour appointed for the funeral. After it was over we came on in the same carriage for Dfs. (Neither Mary nor Maggie left the carriage at Ecclefechan). I send you a ScotsmanThe Scotsman, 11 Feb. For photographs of TC's funeral, and his tombstone, see opp. by this Mail as it gives a pretty correct account of the funeral. The only error in it of importance is in saying that Lowell, the American MinisterJames Russell Lowell (1819–91), writer and diplomat, minister to the Court of St. James 1880–85, close friend of Charles Eliot Norton; see 46:165TC to JAC, 4 March 1870. was “invited.” He wanted to come we learned through Froude, but we did not invite him, for Uncle never liked him. You may read this note & Newspar [sic] account to any of the rest as I have not time to write. We go back to Chelsea on Monday to settle up affairs. But we have not decided where to go or what to do yet. Your loving Brother Alick.

Many thanks for the Photos—all here & at Chelsea think them most
excellent.

Mary send[s] you all her kindest love—& so do the rest here. (The Will has of course not yet been opened; but the Lawyer, Ouvry,Frederic Ouvry of Messrs. Farrer Ouvry and Company, 66 Lincoln's Inn Fields; for TC's will and codicil, see 48:151–58TC's Will. sent me an Epitome of it before I left. It is essentially like the Dr's).

figure.p:
Thomas Carlyle's Funeral
Courtesy of the National Trust

Thomas Carlyle's Tombstone
Courtesy of Ian Campbell

div1.p: Adamson, Samuel (1831–80), of British Linen Co. bank, Dumfries, where TC had an account; son of Robert Adamson (1787–1861; see 10:23TC to JA, 14 Feb. 1838, and 37:26137:biographical notes).

Aitken, Jean (“Craw”) Carlyle (1810–88), TC's sister; m., 1833, James Aitken (1809–87) from Troqueer, housepainter of English St., Dumfries; they moved from Assembly St., Dumfries, to their new house, The Hill, Lochmaben Rd., Dumfries, 1863. They had five sons: two d. in infancy (1834–36 and 1855–56), both named Alexander; James Jr. (1836–71), worked in mercantile houses in London, 1858–ca. 1864 and 1866–67, and Liverpool, 1864–66, and 1867–71, he died during a visit to London; Thomas (1841–69), was at an institute for the deaf in Glasgow from 1854 (see 29:186TC to JAC, 4 Nov. 1854), then lived at home ca. 1864–69; and John (see below). Their das. were Anne (1839–1919), Margaret (1845–1932), and Mary (see below).
Aitken, John (1843–1911), Jean and James's son, bank clerk at the Commercial Bank, Dumfries, then moved to London, Sept. 1871, working for Chapman & Hall. He left them, autumn 1876.

Aitken, Mary (1848–95), Jean and James's da.; she worked as a pupil-teacher in Peebles, March–Sept. 1867, then returned home. She accompanied TC to London, Sept. 1868, “for about three weeks,” but stayed more or less permanently. She worked as a teacher and secretary in London, Jan.–June/July 1873, and then returned to live with TC in Cheyne Row. She m., 21 Aug. 1879, her cousin Alexander Carlyle, they had two children, Thomas (2 June 1880–1903) and Oliver (Nov. 1881–1928).

Alford, Marianne Margaret Egerton, b. Compton (1817–88; ODNB), Viscountess Alford, known as Lady Marian Alford; art patron and writer on needlework; widow of John Hume Cust, later Egerton (1812–51), Viscount Alford; they had two sons, John William Spencer Brownlow Egerton-Cust (1842–67), 2d Earl Brownlow, and Adelbert Wellington Brownlow Cust (1844–1921), 3d Earl Brownlow, who m., 1868, Lady Adelaide, b. Chetwynd-Talbot (1844–1917). They lived at 11 Princes
Gate, Kensington, Ashridge House, Hertfordshire, and Belton House, Grantham, Lincolnshire.

Allingham, William (1824–89; ODNB), Irish poet and editor; he worked in the Customs Service 1846–70, and then became sub-editor of Fraser's Magazine, taking over as editor 1874–79. Friendly with TC since early 1850s. He lived at 131 Piccadilly. He m., 1874, Helen Mary Elizabeth, b. Paterson (1848–1926; ODNB), watercolorist; she painted portraits of TC, and also compiled the list of pictures for Carlyle's House Catalogue. The Allinghams had three children, Gerald Carlyle (b. 8 Nov. 1875), Eva Margaret (b. 21 Feb. 1877), and Henry William (b. 1882).

Anstruther, Annabella Agnes, b. Anderson (1839–85), m., 1866, as his second wife, James Anstruther (1803–67), W.S., of Treesbank, Ayr. She lived at Old Ballikinrain, Balfron, Stirlingshire, 16 mi. (29 km.) N of Glasgow. She was the da. of Thomas Anderson (1810–85), sheriff of Kilmarnock 1851–83, and Mary Ann, b. Caird. James Anstruther was the brother of Philip Anstruther (1802–63), who m., 1838, Mary Frances, b. Stewart-Mackenzie (1819–1913), sister of Lady Ashburton; see 38:273–7438:biographical notes.

Ashburton, Lady Louisa Caroline, b. Stewart-Mackenzie (1827–1903), m., 1858, William Bingham Baring (1799–1864; ODNB; see 11:40TC to MAC, 8 March 1839, and later vols.), 2d Baron, politician, and partner in Baring Bros., bankers. They had one da., Mary Florence (1860–1902). Lady Louisa was the da. of Mary Elizabeth Frederica, b. Mackenzie (1783–1862; ODNB), chief of Clan Mackenzie, and James Alexander Stewart (1784–1843); on their marriage (1817) the name Mackenzie was added to that of Stewart. Lady Ashburton had recently built Kent House for herself in London; she also owned Melchet Court (see 38:8JWC to LLA, 11 Nov. 1861), a country house 6 mi. (9.5 km.) W of Romsey, Hampshire, on the border between Hampshire and Wiltshire, a farm at Addiscombe, near Croydon, and Seaforth Lodge, Seaton, Devon. Lord Ashburton's first wife, m. 1823, was Harriet, b. Montagu (1805–57; ODNB; see 11:40TC to MAC, 8 March 1839, and 26:ix–xv26:introduction); they met the Carlyles in 1839 and became close friends. Where necessary for clarity, we refer in notes to Lord Ashburton's first and second wives as Lady Harriet Ashburton and Lady Louisa Ashburton respectively, although these are not the correct forms.

Austin, Mary Carlyle (1808–88), TC's sister, m., 1831, James Austin (1805–20 Sept. 1878), farmer of The Gill, 6 mi. (9.5 km.) SW of Ecclefechan. They had eight das.: Margaret (see Stewart); Grace (1833–1922), who m., 1856, William Yeoward (ca. 1824–1911), of Toronto, Ontario; Jessie (1836–
autumn 1876), who m., 1859, George Grierson (1835–1910), they emigrated to Ontario by 1860 and had nine children, after Jessie's death the family moved to Duluth, Minnesota, 1879; Jane (b. 1840); Mary Anne (b. 1842); Catherine (see James Carlyle Jr.); Isabella (b. ca. 1846), m., June 1877,
Robert Hoggan (b. ca. 1853); and Mary Carlyle (b. 1851); and one surviving son, James Jr. (b. 1848).
Baly; see Blakiston.
Baring; see Ashburton.
Bismarck, Otto von (1815–98), chancellor of the German Empire 1871–90.
Blackie, John Stuart (1809–95; ODNB), classical and Scottish Gaelic scholar, prof. of Greek at Edinburgh Univ. 1852–82; m., 1842, Eliza, b. Wyld (1819–1908).

Blakiston, Dr. Peyton (1801–17 Dec. 1878), and his second wife, m. 1862, Bessy, b. Barnet (ca. 1810–91), old friends of JWC and TC; see 43:26743:biographical notes; they had looked after JWC in St. Leonards, March–July 1864; see 40:25TC to ELS, 8 March 1864–83TC to JWC, 29 April 1864. They moved to London towards the end of 1871, and were living at 140 Harley St., Cavendish Sq., with Charles Baly (or Bally) (1846–1926), dental surgeon, family friend from St. Leonard's, presumably related to their widowed da.-in-law, Annie, b. Bally (1843–97), who had m., 1862, Peyton's son Peyton (1831–66; see 48:16TC to JF, 5 Dec. 1871). Blakiston had three surviving sons from his first marriage, John Richard (1829–1917), Douglas Yeoman (1832–1914), and Matthew Folliott (1835–1906).
Boehm, Joseph Edgar (1834–90; ODNB), sculptor. Originally from Vienna, he settled in London after his marriage, 1860, to Louisa Frances, b. Boteler (ca. 1835–90).

Braid, Betty, b. Pringle (1795–19 March 1875), Grace Welsh's Haddington servant, close to JWC (see 21:82JWC to JW, [30 Oct. 1846], and 24:221JWC to TC, [5 Sept. 1849]); b. in Prestonkirk, E. Lothian; m. Alexander (1792–1874), stonemason and shopkeeper. Three sons d. in infancy: Alexander (b. 1826), James (b. 1829), and James (b. 1831); George (1827–65) was the only child who survived into adulthood. They lived at Upper Stenhouse, Greenend, Liberton, S Edinburgh.

Bromley, Caroline Davenport (1820–91), da. of Rev. Walter Davenport Bromley (1787–1862), of Wootton Hall, Staffordshire, and his first wife, m., 1818, Caroline Barbara, b. Gooch (1791–1827). A friend of Lady Louisa Ashburton, she became a close friend of JWC's; she was now friendly with TC. Her London home was at 32 Grosvenor St., although she had apparently recently moved to 12 Montague Sq.; she rented a house in Barnes, Surrey, and had also recently bought a villa at Walton Heath, Epsom, near Banstead Downs, Surrey. She had two sisters, Louisa Cecilia Bromley Davenport (1827–1879), and Charlotte Bromley Davenport (ca. 1824–88), who m., 1855, Julius Talbot Airey (1816–95); and a brother, William Bromley Davenport (1821–84), m. Augusta Elizabeth (d. 1916); see 49:248TC to LLA, 7 Oct. 1875, and 26749:biographical notes; they lived at Capesthorne, Crewe, Cheshire. They had changed their surnames by royal licence in 1868.
Browning, Robert (1812–89; ODNB), poet; friend of the Carlyles since mid-1830s.
Brownlow; see Alford.

Carlyle, Alexander (Alick) (1797–30 March 1876), TC's brother; he m., 1830, Janet, b. Clow (1809–91), and immigrated with his family to Canada, 1843. They settled at the Bield, 4½ mi. (7 km.) W of Brantford, Ontario. They had nine surviving children. Jane Welsh (1831–84), m., 1852, Robert Sims (1825–80); they had four children, Alexander (1855–1922), Thomas (1856–1934), Jessie (b. ca. 1859), and John (b. ca. 1862). Thomas (1833–1921), m., 1867, Margaret, b. MacVicar (1847–1917); they had at least seven children, including Thomas Alexander (1869–70), and Hellen (b. ca. Dec. 1870). Janet (Jessie) (1836–1916), m., 1864, William Apps (1834–1911), miller from Ontario; they had at least five children, including Jessie (b. ca. 1867), Alfred (b. ca. 1870), and a da. (b. ca. Jan. 1872). John (1839–1924), moved to Brantford and became a carpenter, 1870, m., 1871, Helen, b. McVicar (1851–1927). Alexander (see below). James (1846–1924), farmed at Cedar Valley, Ontario, for some years, then moved to Toronto. Margaret (1847–1935), m., 1901, Edward Marrs (d. 1927), widower from Okmulgee, Oklahoma; see 1:166TC to AC, 23 Feb. 1819. William Graham (1849–1935). Robert (1851–1932). William and Robert lived with their mother until her death, then moved to Toronto, and later to Tucson, Arizona. An unidentified son (1832–33), Margaret (1835–36), James (b. 1840), and Euphemia (1853–54) all d. in infancy; see 32:4TC to AC, 3 Oct. 1856.

Carlyle, Alexander (Alick) (1843–1931; see 16:153TC to AC, 4 May 1843), Alexander and Janet's son, school headmaster; m., 21 Aug. 1879, his cousin Mary Aitken; lived with TC from 1879 and ed. various collections of the Carlyles’ letters and TC's writings. After Mary's death he m. Lillias, b. MacVicar (d. 1929), sister of the wives of his brothers Thomas and John.

Carlyle, James (Jamie) (1805–90), TC's brother, farmer at Scotsbrig; m., 1834, Isabella, b. Calvert (ca. 1813–59). Their children were James Jr. (see below), John Calvert (see below), Thomas (1839–41), and Janet (Jenny) (see Scott).

Carlyle, James Jr. (1835–88 [mistakenly given as 1871 in previous vols.]), James and Isabella's son, m., 1866, his cousin Catherine, b. Austin (1844–1908); see 44:64TC to JCA, 6 Oct. 1866. Their first child, James, d. at birth, 1867; they had nine further children: Isabella (1868–after 1901), Mary (b. 1871), James (1872–91), twin sons Thomas (1874–86) and John Aitken (1874–1931), Alexander (July 1876–1921), Phoebe Elizabeth (July 1878–1965), Hildred (Feb. 1880–1912), and William Austin (b. 1882). They lived at Newlands, near Eaglesfield, as well as sharing the tenancy of Craigenputtoch with James's father; see 44:196TC to JAC, 11 May 1867.

Carlyle, John (ca. 1792–1872), TC's half-brother; immigrated to the U.S. in 1837, then moved to Canada (see 12:228TC to AC, 15 Aug. 1840); he lived on a small farm at Mount Pleasant, nr. Brantford, Ontario. He m., 1817, Margaret (Peggy), b.
Benn (1798–1867); they had six children: Janet (1818–89), m., 1844, John Randall Ellis (1810–1911), postmaster and carpenter; Mary (1821–50); John (1825–26); John (1827–97), m., ca. 1852, Mary Catherine, b. Smith (1835–79); James (1830–1900), qualified as a doctor but worked for most of his life as a teacher, m. Wilhelmina Deborah, b. Patten (1847–1926); and William (1833–1911), teacher and later a school inspector, m., 1860, Emily b. Youmans (1835–1912), their da. Florence Emily Carlyle (1864–1923), became a prominent Canadian artist. William visited TC in London, Aug. 1864; see 40:182–83TC to JWC, 12 Aug. 1864.

Carlyle, John Aitken (Jack, “The Doctor”) (1801–15 Sept. 1879; ODNB), TC's brother, physician, and translator. He m., 1852, Phoebe Elizabeth Hough Watt, b. Fowler (1810–54), wealthy widow of Fitzjames Watt (1809–48), from Leek in Staffordshire, with four sons; she d. in childbirth, the child was stillborn. John A. Carlyle assumed responsibility for his stepsons; see Watt.

Carlyle, John Calvert (1836–1901), James and Isabella's son, m., 1868, Margaret Little, b. Murray (1848–92), of Blackwood Ridge, Middlebie; they lived at Scotsbrig with his father; they had 13 children, Isabella Calvert (1869–1915), Elisabeth Carruthers (1870–1947), James (1872–1931), Peter Murray (1873–1952), Janet (May 1875–after 1901), Thomas (April 1877–1955), John (Feb. 1879–84), Jane Welsh (June 1881–84), twins David (1883–84) and Alexander (1883–83), John David (1886–1970), Alexander (1888–88), and Helen (1889–1955).
Carlyle, Margaret, b. Aitken (1771–1853), TC's mother, m., 1795, James Carlyle (1758–1832), TC's father.
Carnarvon, Henry Howard Molyneux (1831–90; ODNB), 4th earl of Carnarvon, politician; colonial sec. 1866–67 and 1874–78. He lived at 43 Portman Sq., London, and Highclere Castle, Hampshire.

Chapman, Frederic (1823–95; ODNB), partner in Chapman & Hall, publishers, took over the management of the company 1864; he m., 1861, Clara, b. Woodin (1842–66), they had one surviving son, Frederic, and a baby who d. early 1866. He then m., 1870, Annie Marion, b. Harding (b. 1848), da. of Robert Palmer Harding (1821–93; ODNB), head of a London accounting firm.

Chitty, Joseph William (1828–99; ODNB), Q.C., friend of Forster's and one of the executors of his will; he m., 1858, Clara Jessie, b. Pollock (d. 1922). Chitty's father was Thomas Chitty (1802–78; ODNB), lawyer, legal writer, and teacher.

Cowper, Henry Frederick (1836–87), M.P. for Hertfordshire 1865–85, brother of Francis de Thomas de Grey (1834–1905), 7th Earl Cowper; their mother was Anne Florence, b. de Grey (1806–80), dowager Countess Cowper, who m., 1833, George Augustus Frederick Cowper (1806–56),
6th Earl Cowper. The family estate was at Brocket Hall, Panshanger, Hertfordshire, 22 mi. (35 km.) N of London.

Currie (Corrie), Alexander (Sandy) (b. ca. 1773), of Newfield farm, nr. Ecclefechan; his surviving sons were James (1815–96), sugar-planter in Mauritius, and John Irving (ca. 1810–79), and his das. were Mary (1812–76), Helen (ca. 1819–91), and George (ca. 1821–91); all old friends of the Carlyle family; see 42:156TC to JAC, 28 July 1865.

Darwin, Erasmus (1804–81), friendly with the Carlyles since 1835. His brother was Charles Darwin (1809–82; ODNB), naturalist and geologist, m., 1839, his cousin Emma, b. Wedgwood (1808–96); they had seven surviving children: William Erasmus Darwin (1839–1914; ODNB), banker; Henrietta Emma (1843–1927); George Howard (1845–1912; ODNB), mathematician and physicist; Elizabeth (1847–1926); Francis (1848–1925; ODNB), botanist; Leonard (1850–1943; ODNB), scientist; and Horace (1851–1928; ODNB), civil engineer.

Derby, Mary Catherine, b. Sackville-West (1824–1900; ODNB), countess of, political hostess; she m., first, 1847, (as his 2d wife) James Gascoyne-Cecil (1791–1868), 2d marquess of Salisbury; she m., second, 1870, Edward Henry Stanley (1826–93; ODNB), 15th earl of Derby, politician and diarist, foreign secretary 1874–78. They lived at 23 St. James's Sq., London.

Dickens, Charles (1812–70; ODNB), novelist; friend of the Carlyles since the early 1840s; m., 1836, Catherine Thomson, b. Hogarth (1816–79), separated from her in 1858; see 33:233TC to RWE, 2 June 1858.

Dilberoglue, Stavros (1818–23 April 1878; see 40:22740:biographical notes), Greek businessman, philanthropist, art collector, partner in the merchant shipping firm Cavafy & Co., and friend of the Carlyles since the 1860s.

Disraeli, Benjamin (1804–81; ODNB), politician and author; prime minister 1868 and 1874–80. He m., 1839, Mary Anne Lewis, b. Evans (1792–1872; ODNB). She was granted the title of Viscountess Beaconsfield, 1868; he was made earl of Beaconsfield, Aug. 1876.

Duffy, Charles Gavan (1816–1903; ODNB), Irish nationalist, lawyer, and politician, friend of TC's since 1845. He m., 1847, Susan, b. Hughes (1826–78); they immigrated to Australia 1855. Duffy returned to Europe in 1880.

Eichthal, Charles d’ (1813–80), baron, from a wealthy German Jewish banking family in Munich whom John A. Carlyle met in 1827; see 5:277TC to GE, 17 May 1831; Charles first visited the Carlyles in Dec. 1835; see 8:277TC to MAC, 24 Dec. 1835. His wife was Isabella, b. Khuen von Belasi (1826–88), and their only son was Karl (1845–1909).

Emerson, Ralph Waldo (1803–82; see 6:425TC to JAC, 27 Aug. 1833), philosopher, essayist, poet, and transcendentalist. He first met TC in Aug. 1833; in spite of their differences they had close ties; he introduced many Americans to TC and played a leading part in arranging the publication of TC's works in the U.S. Emerson m., 1835, as his second wife, Lydian, b. Jackson (1802–92);
their children were Waldo (1836–42), Ellen Tucker (1839–1909), Edith (see Forbes), and Edward Waldo (1844–1930), m., 1874, Annie Shephard Keyes (1847–1928).

Erskine, Thomas (1788–1870; ODNB; see 10:18TC to JAC, 1 Feb. 1838), theologian and retired advocate, living at Linlathen, Dundee; known to the Carlyles since the mid-1830s. He had two sisters: Christian Stirling (1789–1866), m., 1817, Charles Stirling (d. 1830); and David Paterson (1791–1867), m., 1821, Capt. James Paterson (1795–1856); their son, James Erskine Paterson (1826–97), m., 1852, Mary Jane, b., Macnab (b. 1826), and his family lived at 8 Newbattle Terr., Morningside.
FitzGerald, Edward (1809–83; ODNB), writer and translator, TC's friend since 1842; he lived in Woodbridge, Suffolk.

Forbes, Edith, b. Emerson (1841–1929), da. of Ralph Waldo Emerson, m., 1865, William Hathaway Forbes (1840–97), businessman; they were to have eight children, including Ralph Emerson (1866–1937), Edith (1867–1926), William Cameron (1870–1959), and John (1871–88).

Forster, John (“Fuz”) (1812–1 Feb. 1876; ODNB; see 6:118TC to GE, 15 Feb. 1832, and 11:7TC to JF, [25 Jan. 1839]), historian, journalist, and biographer; ed. of the Examiner 1847–55; sec., 1855–61, and commissioner, 1861–72, of the Lunacy Commission, friend of the Carlyles since the late 1830s and TC's literary adviser. He m., 1856, Eliza Ann, b. Crosbie (ca. 1819–94), widow of the publisher Henry Colburn (ca. 1784–1855; ODNB); from 1863 they lived at Palace Gate House, Kensington.
Frankau; see Neuberg.

Froude, James Anthony (1818–94; ODNB), journalist and historian, ed. of Fraser's Magazine 1860–74. He m., first, 1849, Charlotte Maria, b. Grenfell (1812–60); they had two das., Georgina Margaret (1850–1935), and Rose Mary (1852–ca. May 1875), and a son, Pascoe Grenfell (1854–79). He m., second, 1861, Henrietta Elizabeth, b. Warre (1824–74); they had a son, Ashley Anthony (1863–1949), and a da., Mary Caroline (“May”) (1867–1906). They lived at 5 Onslow Gdns., Fulham Rd.
Gladstone, William Ewart (1809–98; ODNB), politician; leader of the liberal party 1867–94, prime minister 1868–74, 1880–85, 1886, 1892–94. He m., 1839, Catherine, b. Glynne (1812–1900; ODNB).
Hamilton; see Tyndall.

Hanning, Janet Carlyle (1813–97), TC's sister; m., 1836, Robert Hanning (1796–22 March 1878), who immigrated to Canada in mysterious disgrace in 1841; she joined him in Hamilton, Ontario, Aug. 1851, with their two das.; Margaret (1838–97), m., 1876, John R. Leslie (ca. 1839–99), farmer; and Mary (b. 1840), m., 1864, Charles Coates Holden (b. 1836), they had at least two das., Jenny (d. Dec. 1870), and Jane. Janet and Robert had two more das. b. in Canada; Catherine (b. ca. 1852), school
teacher, m., 1878, George Franklin; and Jane (d. 1899), m. W. J. Laing of Toronto.
Herbert; see Carnarvon.

Howard, George James (1843–1911; ODNB), artist and politician, m., 1864, Rosalind Frances, b. Stanley (1845–1921; ODNB), women's rights and temperance activist; they lived at Naworth Castle, Cumberland.

Hunter, Jacob Dickson (ca. 1811–89), physician, living in Edinburgh; see 47:13TC to RWE, 31 May 1870. Friend of John A. Carlyle's, and cousin of, and physician to JWC's aunts Elizabeth, Ann, and Grace Welsh.
Huxley, Thomas Henry (1825–95; ODNB), biologist and educational theorist.
Irving, Edward (1792–1834; ODNB; see 1:92TC to RM, 12 Feb. 1817, later vols., and Carlyle, Reminiscences), the Carlyles’ great friend; religious leader and preacher.

Jewsbury, Geraldine Endsor (1812–80; ODNB; see 12:103–4TC to GEJ, 12 April 1840), novelist, reviewer, and misc. writer; friend of the Carlyles, particularly of JWC's, since 1841. She lived at 41 Markham Sq., Chelsea.

Laing, David (1793–18 Oct. 1878; ODNB), antiquary, librarian of the Signet Lib., Edinburgh, 1837–78. When TC became rector of Edinburgh University, 1866, he chose Laing as his assessor on the Senatus Academicus. Laing's youngest sister, Euphemia (1808–96), lived with him as his housekeeper; since 1845 they had lived in East Villa, 12 James St., Portobello (see 43:122TC to JRU, 14 Feb. 1866).

Lecky, William Edward Hartpole (1838–1903; ODNB; see 44:97TC to JAC, 28 Nov. 1866), historian, m., 1871, Catharina Elisabeth Boldewina, b. Baroness van Dedem (1842–1912), writer, historian, and suffragist.

Lytton, Edward Robert Bulwer (1831–91; ODNB), 2d Baron, 1st earl of Lytton (1880), diplomat and poet, m., 1864, Edith, b. Villiers (1841–1936; ODNB). His parents were Edward George Earle Lytton Bulwer Lytton (1803–73; ODNB), 1st Baron Lytton, writer and politician, m., 1827, Rosina Anne Doyle, b. Wheeler (1802–82; ODNB); both father and son were close friends of Forster. The family home was Knebworth House, Hertfordshire.

Masson, David (1822–1907; ODNB; see 16:312JWC to TC, [24 July 1843]), writer and editor, prof. of rhetoric and English lit., Edinburgh Univ., 1865–95. He m., 1853, Emily Rosaline, b. Orme (1835–1915); they had a son, David Orme (1858–1937; ODNB), and three das., Flora (1856–1937), Helen (b. 1864), and Rosaline (1867–1947); they lived at 10 Regent Terr., Edinburgh.

Maxwell, Sir William Stirling (1818–15 Jan. 1878; ODNB), art historian, book collector, and politician, M.P. for Perthshire 1852–68, 1874–78; known to TC since 1848. He m., first, 1865, Anna Maria, b. Leslie-Melville (ca. 1825–74), da. of David Leslie-Melville (1785–1860), 10th earl of Leven, and Elizabeth Anne, b. Campbell (1804–63). They had two sons, John (1866–1956), and Archibald (1867–1931). He m., second, 1 March 1877,
his long-time friend Caroline Elizabeth Sarah Norton, b. Sheridan (1808–15 June 1877; ODNB), author and law reformer; she was the widow, m. 1827, of George Chapple Norton (1800–1875). Stirling Maxwell lived at Keir, 3 mi. (5 km.) NW of Stirling.

Mill, John Stuart (1806–73; ODNB), utilitarian philosopher and economist; m., 1851, Harriet Taylor, b. Hardy (1807–58; ODNB), feminist and political radical, who strongly influenced his thinking. Mill met TC in Sept. 1831 (see 5:398TC to JWC, 4 Sept. 1831); they remained on friendly terms even after the MS of vol. 1 of The French Revolution was burned while in Mill's keeping (see 8:66–68TC to JFR, 7 March 1835), but later became estranged because of many differences in temperament and attitudes to social questions; Mill also believed that TC and other friends disapproved of his marriage. His sister was Harriet Isabella Mill (1812–97).

Millais, John Everett (1829–96; ODNB), painter. He m., 1855, Euphemia Ruskin, b. Gray (1828–97; see Ruskin, below). From early 1877 they lived in a house Millais had designed himself, at 2 Palace Gate, Kensington.

Motley, John Lothrop (1814–77), American historian and diplomat; see 44:129TC to JF, 24 Jan. 1867. He m., 1837, Mary Elizabeth, b. Benjamin (1813–74). He came to Britain as the U.S. minister, 1869–70, and returned to live in England, 1871.

Neuberg, Joseph (1806–67; see 11:231TC to JN, 21 Dec. 1839), German Jewish businessman, naturalized British 1845, and retired 1849; m., 1841, Marian (d. 1848; see 23:77JWC to JN, 22 July 1848). He was introduced to TC, whom he had long admired, by Emerson, 1848; helped TC as an unpaid sec., translated his work into German, and twice accompanied him on visits to Germany (1852 and 1858). His widowed sister, Rosetta (or Rosette) Frankau (ca. 1816–98), and her children lived at Roslyn Park, Hampstead; see 45:227–2845:biographical notes.

Norton, Charles Eliot (1827–1908), author, journalist, and Harvard Coll. prof. of Art 1875–98. He m., 1862, Susan Ridley, b. Sedgwick (1838–72), they had six children: Eliot (1863–1932), Sara (Sally) (1864–1922), Elizabeth Lily (b. 1866), Rupert (1867–1914), Margaret (1870–1947), and Richard (1872–1918). Norton's mother was Catherine, b. Eliot (1793–1879), and his sisters were Louisa (b. 1823), (married by 1872), Catherine Jane (1824–79), and Grace (1834–1926). He and his family spent 1868–73 in Europe, mostly in London, staying at 33 Cleveland Square, where he became friendly with TC.

Novikov (Novikoff), Olga, b. Kiréev (1840–1925: ODNB), Russian journalist; she m., 1860, Ivan Novikov (d. 1890), army officer. She visited Britain 1868, 1873, 1876, and 1878, becoming a prominent public figure supporting Russia and pan-Slavism, becoming known as “the M.P. for Russia.”

Oliphant, Margaret Oliphant, b. Wilson (1828–97; ODNB), prolific novelist, biographer, reviewer, and misc. writer; friend of JWC's since 1860;
see 37:62TC to JAC, 9 Dec. 1860; she lived at 6 Clarence Cres., Windsor. She had two surviving children, Cyril Francis (Tids) (1856–90), and Francis Romano (Cecco) (1859–94).

Ruskin, John (1819–1900; ODNB), author, artist, and social reformer; Slade Professor of Art at Oxford Univ. 1870–79. He m., 1848, Euphemia Chalmers, b. Gray (1828–97); marriage annulled 1854 (she then m. John Everett Millais, see above). Ruskin lived in the family home at 163 Denmark Hill, S London, with his mother, Margaret, b. Cock (1781–1871); after her death he moved to Brantwood, Coniston, Cumberland, 1872. His father, John James Ruskin (1785–1864), was a wine merchant.

Russell, Mary, b. Dobbie (1802–17 Dec. 1875; see 6:145TC to AC, 7 April 1832), close friend of JWC and her mother. She m., 1829, Dr. James Russell (ca. 1796–1878); they lived at Holmhill, nr. Thornhill.

Scott, Janet (Jenny), b. Carlyle (1843–74), youngest child of James and Isabella Carlyle; m., 1864, William Scott (b. ca. 1829), draper; they lived at 27 Bradford St., Birmingham; they had a son, John James Carlyle (b. 1865), and two das., Isabella (b. late 1860s), and Jessie Beattie (b. 1870).
